This is a digital copy of a book that was preserved for generations on library shelves before it was carefully scanned by Google as part of a project to make the world's books discoverable online.

It has survived long enough for the copyright to expire and the book to enter the public domain. A public domain book is one that was never subject to copyright or whose legal copyright term has expired. Whether a book is in the public domain may vary from country to country. Public domain books are our gateways to the past, representing a wealth of history, culture, and knowledge that is often difficult to discover.

Marks, notations, and other marginalia <note>original: "marginalia"; refers to notes written in the margins of a book by past readers or librarians</note> present in the original volume will appear in this file—a reminder of this book's long journey from the publisher to a library and finally to you.

## Usage guidelines

Google is proud to partner with libraries to digitize public domain materials and make them widely accessible. Public domain books belong to the public, and we are merely their custodians. Nevertheless, this work is expensive; therefore, in order to keep providing this resource, we have taken steps to prevent abuse by commercial parties, including placing technical restrictions on automated querying <note>original: "automated querying"; the use of software or "bots" to automatically search or download data</note>.

We also ask that you:

+ *Make non-commercial use of the files:* We designed Google Book Search for use by individuals, and we request that you use these files for personal, non-commercial purposes.

+ *Refrain from automated querying:* Do not send automated queries of any sort to Google's system. If you are conducting research on machine translation, optical character recognition <note>OCR: the process of converting images of typed or handwritten text into machine-encoded text</note>, or other areas where access to a large amount of text is helpful, please contact us. We encourage the use of public domain materials for these purposes and may be able to help.

+ *Maintain attribution:* The Google "watermark" you see on each file is essential for informing people about this project and helping them find additional materials through Google Book Search. Please do not remove it.

+ *Keep it legal:* Whatever your use, remember that you are responsible for ensuring that what you are doing is legal. Do not assume that just because we believe a book is in the public domain for users in the United States, that the work is also in the public domain for users in other countries. Whether a book is still under copyright varies from country to country, and we cannot offer guidance on whether any specific use of any specific book is allowed. Please do not assume that a book's appearance in Google Book Search means it can be used in any manner anywhere in the world. Copyright infringement liability can be quite severe.

## About Google Book Search

Google's mission is to organize the world's information and to make it universally accessible and useful. Google Book Search helps readers discover the world's books while helping authors and publishers reach new audiences. --- Page 8 ---
<meta>This preface establishes the author's critique of British economic theories, specifically those of Ricardo and Malthus, continuing from the legal front matter of the 1852 edition.</meta>

### PREFACE.
---

The entire British system of political economy tends to create conflict among people and nations. It is based on the doctrines of David Ricardo and Thomas Malthus <note>David Ricardo (1772–1823) and Thomas Robert Malthus (1766–1834) were influential British economists known for their pessimistic views on population growth and resource scarcity.</note> regarding rent and population. These doctrines teach that people everywhere begin the work of farming on the earth's most fertile soils, and that when the population is small, food is plentiful. However, they argue that as numbers increase, people are forced to turn to poorer soils, which yield steadily decreasing returns for their labor. As a necessary result of this increasing scarcity of fertile land, it is held that the landholder is able to take a larger share of the profits of labor. Thus, the landlord profits at the expense of the laborer, due to the same causes that lead to the worker's gradual submission to the will of his master. 

At the very foundation of this system, we find conflicting interests, and this discord is present in every following part of it. Over-population is held to be the result of a great law of nature, which suggests that humans increase in number faster than the food needed to nourish them can grow. The poverty, vice, and crime that exist everywhere are regarded as necessary consequences of this great law, supposedly coming from an all-wise, all-powerful, and all-merciful Being. War, famine, and pestilence are viewed as the means provided by that Being for keeping the population within the limits of the food supply. 

Charity is even regarded as almost a crime, because it tends to encourage the growth of the population. The landlord excuses himself for charging high rents on the grounds that it is a necessary consequence of the natural human tendency to multiply too rapidly. A stockholder of the East India Company <note>The East India Company was a massive British trading company that effectively ruled large parts of India; it was frequently criticized for its exploitative economic policies.</note>, who lives in luxury on the profits of his stock, regards it as a natural result of this law that he should receive such a large portion of the farm's earnings as rent. This leaves the poor farmer with only fifty cents a month to provide himself and his family with food, clothing <note>original: "raiment"</note>, and shelter. He eases his conscience by believing this is the unavoidable result of great natural laws. In this view, capital cannot become more productive except at the expense of labor, nor can wages rise except at the cost of capital.

Among the consequences of this "law of discord" publicized by Malthus and Ricardo is the idea that if people want to prosper, they must live far apart from one another. It is claimed that the rich lands of England are already occupied, and those who want to find fertile land must flee to America or to Australia. There, they are to produce food and raw materials to supply the British market. In this way, England seeks to establish a system of "commercial centralization." This is—as was so rightly stated seventy years ago by **Adam Smith** <note>Adam Smith (1723–1790) was a Scottish economist and philosopher, famous for writing "The Wealth of Nations."</note>—a clear violation of "the most sacred rights of mankind." That great man fully understood that if a farmer or planter is to flourish, he must bring the consumer to his side; and that if the craftsman <note>original: "artisan"</note> would...

<summary>The author critiques the British economic schools of Ricardo and Malthus, arguing that their theories justify poverty and exploitation as "natural laws." He asserts that these doctrines create social conflict and promote an unfair global trade system centered on England.</summary>
<keywords>Political economy, David Ricardo, Thomas Malthus, population theory, rent, labor vs capital, East India Company, Adam Smith, commercial centralization, economic justice</keywords>

--- Page 9 ---
<meta>This page continues the author's argument against the British economic system by contrasting it with the ideas of Adam Smith. It moves from a critique of Ricardo and Malthus to a defense of economic protectionism as a means of bringing manufacturing and agriculture together.</meta>

### PREFACE.

To flourish, a person must seek to settle in the place where raw materials are grown. There, he can aid the farmer by converting those materials into forms suitable for human use, which makes it easier to transport them to distant lands. Dr. Smith saw clearly that when people come together in this way, a general harmony of interests arises. Each person benefits their neighbor and profits from that neighbor’s success. In contrast, the tendency of commercial centralization <note>The practice of processing all raw materials in a single distant center (like London) rather than locally.</note> leads toward poverty and discord, both abroad and at home. 

The goal of protection <note>Economic protectionism, such as tariffs, designed to encourage local industry.</note> among ourselves is to aid farmers in their effort to bring consumers to their side. This carries out the system advocated by the great author of ***The Wealth of Nations*** <note>Adam Smith (1723–1790), whose work argued that the most natural progress of a nation is for its capital to be directed first to agriculture, then to manufacturing, and finally to foreign trade.</note>, while helping to destroy a system that has ruined Ireland, India, Portugal, Turkey, and all other countries subjected to it. 

The object of the following chapters is to show why protection is needed; how it operates in promoting prosperity and harmony among the various portions of society; and how certain it is that **THE TRUE, THE PROFITABLE, AND THE ONLY MEANS OF ATTAINING PERFECT FREEDOM OF TRADE** is to be found in that efficient protection which shall fully and completely carry out the doctrine of Dr. Smith. This is achieved by bringing the loom and the anvil <term>loom and the anvil: shorthand for the manufacturing and industrial sectors.</term> to take their natural places alongside the plow and the harrow <term>plow and the harrow: shorthand for the agricultural sector.</term>.

<summary>The author argues that economic protectionism actually fulfills Adam Smith’s ideals by bringing manufacturing closer to farming, thereby creating harmony and true free trade while avoiding the poverty caused by British commercial centralization.</summary>
<keywords>Adam Smith, The Wealth of Nations, protectionism, free trade, commercial centralization, manufacturing vs. agriculture, economic harmony, Ireland, India</keywords>

<meta>This page serves as the introduction to Henry Charles Carey's work, establishing the core inquiry into the relationship between agriculture and industry.</meta>

### THE
# HARMONY OF INTERESTS:
## AGRICULTURAL, MANUFACTURING, AND COMMERCIAL.
---

Why is protection <note>original: "protection"; referring to economic protectionism, the policy of taxing imported goods to protect domestic industries from foreign competition.</note> needed? Why can trade with foreign nations not be carried on without the intervention of customs officers? Why is it that this intervention should be needed to enable the loom and the anvil <note>The author uses "the loom and the anvil" as symbols for manufacturing and heavy industry.</note> to take their natural places alongside the plow and the harrow <note>The "plow and the harrow" represent the agricultural sector.</note>? These are the questions that have long occupied my mind, and to the consideration of which I now invite my readers.

Regarding the advantage of perfect freedom of trade, considered theoretically, there could be no doubt. The benefit derived from such freedom in the dealings between the several States <note>Referring to the internal free trade between the states of the U.S. Union.</note> was obvious to all. It would certainly seem that the same system, extended to include commerce with the various states and kingdoms of the world, could not fail to be attended with similar results. Nevertheless, every attempt at doing so had failed. 

The low duties on most articles of merchandise in the period between 1816 and 1827 had produced a state of affairs which led to the establishment of the first really protective tariff, that of 1828. The approach to almost perfect freedom of trade in 1840 produced a political revolution; and a similar but more moderate measure led to the revolution of last year <note>Likely referring to the U.S. presidential election of 1848 and the shift in economic policy.</note>. These were curious facts, and they deserve careful examination.

It may be assumed as a universal truth that every step made in the right direction will be attended with results so beneficial as to pave the way for further steps in the same direction. Conversely, every step made in the wrong direction will be attended with disadvantageous results, tending to produce a necessity for a backward movement. 

The Compromise Bill <note>The Compromise Tariff of 1833, which aimed to gradually reduce tariff rates.</note>, in its final stages, was a near approach to perfect freedom of trade, with the highest duty being only 20 percent. Believing it to be a step in the right direction, one of the enthusiastic advocates of perfect free trade proposed, soon after its passage, that starting in 1842, there should be a further reduction of one percent per year for twenty years. At the end of that time, all necessity for custom-houses would have disappeared. However, as the earlier stages of that bill gradually took effect, a state of depression so extraordinary was produced that it led to a political change before the bill even reached its final stages.

3

<summary>Henry Charles Carey introduces his investigation into why theoretical free trade fails in practice, arguing that historical shifts toward low tariffs in the United States have consistently led to economic depression and political upheaval.</summary>
<keywords>protectionism, free trade, tariffs, American School of Economics, industrialization, Tariff of 1828, Compromise Bill of 1833, economic history</keywords>

--- Page 17 ---
<meta>This page continues the author's critique of fluctuating American trade policies, specifically comparing the protective Tariff of 1842 with the "free-trade" Tariff of 1846.</meta>

# THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.

And the duties had scarcely reached the low point of 20 percent before they were raised to 30, 50, 60, or more, by the passage of the Tariff of 1842 <note>The Tariff of 1842 was a highly protective measure passed by the Whig party to reverse the effects of the Compromise Tariff of 1833.</note>. With the election of 1844, the supporters of free trade were restored to power, and two years later, the Tariff of 1846—the free-trade measure—was passed. In this act, the revenue duty <note>A tax on imports intended primarily to raise money for the government rather than protect domestic industry.</note> on protected articles was fixed at *thirty percent.* This was a step backward. Instead of moving downward from twenty percent, we went up to thirty. This served as an admission that such a close approach to free trade with foreign nations as was found in the 20 percent duties had not worked in practice. 

Since then, it has been admitted, even by the most determined advocates of free trade, that thirty percent was too low for certain commodities. Within six months of the passage of the 1846 act, its author <note>Robert J. Walker, the Secretary of the Treasury under President Polk.</note> proposed increasing the duties on various articles to thirty-five and forty percent.* This was another step backward. It is now admitted that there are other articles whose duties need to be raised, and daily experience proves that this must happen, or we must abandon some of our most important industries. 

The trend, therefore, is entirely backward. A thirty percent duty is now regarded as almost perfect "freedom of trade," and instead of proposing further annual reductions, each year brings a stronger desire for a significant increase. In all of this, it is impossible to avoid seeing that there is a great error somewhere. It is almost equally impossible not to want to understand why attempts to move toward free trade with foreign nations have so frequently failed, and why every tariff intended strictly for revenue ends up being higher than the one that came before it.

To satisfy myself on this matter, I have recently conducted the examination mentioned earlier regarding our commercial policy over the last twenty-eight years, starting with 1821—the earliest year for which detailed records have been published. Before I present the results, it may be helpful to say a few words about the merits claimed by both sides for their respective systems.

One party insists that protection is "a war upon labor and capital." They argue that by forcing both into industries that would otherwise be unproductive, the amount of necessities, comforts, and conveniences of life available to the worker is reduced. The other party insists that by protecting the worker from competition with the poorly fed and poorly clothed workmen of Europe, the rewards for labor will increase. Each side has its theory, and each is accustomed to providing facts to prove its truth. Both can do so by limiting themselves to short periods of time—choosing years with small harvests at one point and large ones at another—which is why someone searching for the truth becomes confused.† 

To my knowledge, no one has yet undertaken to examine all the facts over a long period of time to show what the worker's power to afford the necessities and comforts of life has actually been under these various systems. One of these systems must be true. The true system is the one under which labor is most highly rewarded—the one where the worker is able to consume the most food, fuel, clothing, and all those other good things for which people are willing to work. If we can determine the power of consumption <note>In this context, "consumption" refers to the ability of average citizens to buy and use goods.</note> at various times, and if the results show that it has always increased under one policy and always decreased under another, it will be as good as a mathematical demonstration of the truth.

---

* Treasury Report, Feb. 1, 1847.
† A person employed in preparing government statistics was once asked to prepare some tables. He inquired what policy he was supposed to prove. "Why," the other asked, "could you prove both sides?" "Equally well," he replied.

# THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.

...the truth of the one and the falsehood of the other. To accomplish this has been the object of the inquiry in which I have recently been engaged. It is necessary now to show the distinguishing features of the several systems that have been in operation during the period to be examined. They are as follows:

**First.** The Tariff of 1816 <note>Passed after the War of 1812 to protect infant industries, though it primarily benefited raw material producers.</note> was a measure favoring planters and farmers. Cotton and coarse cotton cloths were carefully protected. Raw iron itself was well protected, but almost all manufactures of iron—the goods for which pig or bar iron could be used—were admitted at a low 20 percent duty. Wool was taxed at 15 percent. Blankets, woolens, and <term>stuff goods</term> <note>Lightweight fabrics made of worsted wool without a nap.</note> paid 15 percent, and finer goods 25 percent until 1819, after which they paid only 20 percent. Spirits <note>Distilled alcohol, such as whiskey or rum.</note> paid a heavy <term>specific duty</term> <note>A fixed tax based on the quantity (e.g., per gallon) rather than a percentage of the value.</note> for the benefit of the farmers; but paper, hats, caps, leather products, printing types, and manufactured articles generally paid only 20 to 30 percent. Coal paid 5 cents per bushel, but the products made using that coal paid <term>ad valorem</term> <note>Latin: "according to value." A tax based on the percentage of the item's price.</note> duties. Protection was thus given to the coarse raw materials that least required it and was refused to the finished goods for which those raw materials were needed. As a matter of course, its protective features were totally ineffective.

**Second.** The Tariff of 1824, under which iron was, as before, well protected, but manufactures of iron and metals generally were admitted at 25 percent. The duty on wool was raised to 20 percent, intended to increase by successive stages until it reached 30 percent. Coarse woolens were fixed permanently at 25 percent. Finer ones were to rise gradually until they reached 33⅓ percent. Carpets paid from 20 to 50 cents per square yard. Hams paid 3 cents, and butter 5 cents per pound. Potatoes paid 10 cents, oats 10 cents, and wheat 25 cents per bushel; meanwhile, scythes, spades, shovels, and other tools required for raising wheat and potatoes paid 30 percent. Spirits were carefully protected. <term>Bolting cloths</term> <note>Fine fabric used in mills to sift flour.</note> paid 15 percent. <term>Sail-duck</term> <note>Heavy canvas used for making sails.</note>, <term>Osnaburgs</term> <note>A coarse, durable linen or cotton fabric often used for work clothes.</note>, etc., paid 15 percent. Cotton cloths paid 25 percent, with a <term>minimum</term> <note>A valuation system where all cloth was treated as if it cost at least 30 cents per yard for taxing purposes, effectively raising the price of cheap imports.</note> of 30 cents per yard. The general features of this law did not vary significantly from the Tariff of 1816, although protection was slightly increased.

**Third.** The first tariff that was thoroughly protective, and intended to be so, was that of 1828 <note>Known by its critics as the "Tariff of Abominations" due to its very high rates.</note>. It continued until 1832, when the first of two laws was passed that changed the entire policy of the country. This series constitutes the **fourth** stage.

**Fourth.** By the Act of July 14, 1832, railroad iron was admitted free of duty. Axes, spades, etc., remained at 30 percent. Bar and pig iron were carefully protected, but a large portion of the goods for which they were needed were admitted without duty or at the same rate as under our current free-trade tariff. Tea and coffee were free. Silks paid 10 percent. Wool was protected, but worsted stuff goods were admitted at 10 percent. Cotton goods paid 25 percent, with minimums of 30 cents for plain and 35 cents for prints. This remained in force until the following March, when the *Compromise Act* <note>The Compromise Tariff of 1833 was brokered by Henry Clay to end the Nullification Crisis; it scheduled a decade of gradual duty reductions.</note> was passed. Under this act, linens, stuff goods, silks, and other articles were admitted free of duty. Additionally, one-tenth of the tax amount exceeding 20 percent was to be reduced from all other goods, starting in December 1833. This reduction was to repeat every two years until 1841, when half of the remaining surplus would be cut, and the other half in 1842, at which point no duty would exceed 20 percent.

**Fifth.** The protective Tariff of 1842, which was followed by:

**Sixth.** The free-trade Tariff of 1846, which is currently in effect.

We have thus had six different systems. However, the first and second differ so little from each other that it is unnecessary to separate the years falling under them, whereas the early years of the *Compromise* differ so essentially...

from the two latter that it is practical to separate them. I shall, therefore, group the results as follows:

**First.** The tariffs of 1816 and 1824, ending with 1829.

**Second.** The tariff of 1828, beginning in October 1829 and ending when the Compromise Act <note>The Compromise Tariff of 1833 was designed to gradually reduce all tariff rates to a maximum of 20% by 1842 to ease political tensions between the North and South.</note> began to take effect in October 1834.

**Third.** The Compromise period, beginning in 1835 and ending in 1841.

**Fourth.** The years 1842 and 1843, the period immediately before and after the passage of the Act of 1842, which was defined by a strict revenue tariff of 20 percent.

**Fifth.** The tariff of 1842, beginning in June 1843 and ending in June 1847.

**Sixth.** The tariff of 1846, beginning in June 1847 and continuing to the present time.

You will notice that I have placed the year 1829 in the first period and 1834 in the second. It is not the passage of an act that produces change, but its practical operation; the first year of a new system's existence is merely the sequel to the one that is ending. When protection is given to cloth and iron manufacturers, mills and furnaces <note>Facilities for smelting iron ore.</note> are not built in a day, nor are they abandoned as soon as protection is withdrawn. If it had been possible, I would have used the exact same system for every period, but it was not. The Act of 1842 went into effect on September 1 of that year, and in the following year, the time for finalizing the Treasury <note>The government department responsible for managing national finances and accounting.</note> accounts was changed to June 30. Therefore, only the first ten months after it took effect could be included in the previous period. The Act of 1846 did not take effect until December 1, so only the first seven months following that could be included under the 1842 system. The law of 1842 was in effect for four and a quarter years, but I could only credit it with four years, which works significantly to its disadvantage and to the advantage of the 1846 system.

In some cases, even more than a year would be required to make an exact comparison of how different systems work. For instance, the immigration of one year is greatly influenced—perhaps even determined—by the state of the labor market from the previous year. A change in that market occurs at least a year after a law is passed. Thus, if the tariff of 1842 tended to raise a laborer's pay, its effects would not be obvious until 1843, and an increase in immigration would not occur until 1844 or even 1845. Wages were high in 1847–1848, and we saw a large amount of immigration in 1849. Wages are now falling, and immigration next year will likely be reduced.

The same logic applies to the supply of grain. A decrease in the demand for labor in mines and furnaces in 1842 encouraged people to move to the West. For the first year, 1843, those emigrants were only consumers. In the second year, 1844, they had grain to sell, and prices fell. In the current year, the demand for labor in mines and for building mills and furnaces has decreased, and migration to the West has increased. Yet the effect of this on the supply and price of food may not, and probably will not, become obvious until 1852.

Your predecessor <note>Likely referring to Robert J. Walker, the Secretary of the Treasury from 1845 to 1849, who authored the low-tariff Walker Tariff of 1846.</note> appears to have entirely overlooked the necessity of allowing time for new systems to develop and affect the movement of people. In his last report to Congress, he provided a comparison of <term>customs</term> <note>Taxes or duties paid on imported goods.</note> revenue from the last six months of the 1842 tariff and the first six months of the 1846 tariff. This was used to show that one was twice as productive as the other; yet, even a little reflection would have been enough to convince him that hardly any part of that difference...

<meta>This page continues Henry Charles Carey’s explanation of his methodology for analyzing American trade history. He argues that the immediate effects of a tariff are often misleading and proposes a more accurate way to calculate the true value of national imports and exports.</meta>

# THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.

The results had followed from the change in commercial policy brought about by the adoption of his tariff. The amount of goods that could be imported and paid for depended on the economic conditions that existed in the country during the previous year; therefore, the passage of the law had almost no immediate influence on those figures. In the same way, the customs revenue from September 1842 to November 1846 is often compared with the receipts of 1847 and 1848. However, it is well known that in 1842, under the Compromise Tariff <note>original: "Compromise"; the Compromise Tariff of 1833, which gradually reduced duties.</note>, imports had fallen so low that the government was forced to send representatives to Europe to try to secure a loan for its own support, even during a time of profound peace. If a cause has truth on its side, there is no need to present such misleading views. In the tables I am now offering for consideration, I have followed a consistent method as much as possible. I begin each period at the time when the system could fairly be considered fully operational—specifically, at the close of the fiscal year following the year the law was enacted. If an error exists at the start of a period, it will be balanced out at the end, ensuring justice is done to every system.

There remain two other points regarding these tables that I would like to bring to your attention.

**First.** In almost all tables of imports and exports, it is common to exclude specie <note>Gold and silver coins used as legal tender.</note> and bullion <note>Gold or silver in bulk, such as bars or ingots, rather than coins.</note>. This is a mistake that leads to errors and prevents a proper understanding of how the economic system is working. Gold and silver are commodities produced abroad that we consume in large quantities, occasionally exporting the surplus. There is no reason why they should not be treated exactly like coffee, wine, brandy, or any other foreign goods. When they are imported, they arrive in exchange for our own products; the total value of our exports is the combined sum of the merchandise and specie we receive. When they are exported, they are sent instead of our products and should be treated as foreign merchandise being re-exported. By subtracting them from the value of the merchandise imported, we can determine the true value of our domestic exports.

**Second.** It is common practice to assign arbitrary prices to exported goods to determine their monetary value. These prices are set at the ports where they are shipped and represent only what we *ask* for the goods we want to sell, not what we actually *get* for them. Furthermore, these prices represent the value *minus* the earnings of the machinery used for transportation, which then has to be guessed. Consequently, the tables published by the Treasury are completely worthless as guides for understanding the general course of trade. 

To gain a true understanding, the nation should manage its accounts like a merchant: recording not the price asked, but the price received, and then balancing its books by determining whether the year's business has increased or decreased its debts. The amount received for our exports constitutes their exact value. To find that amount, we should take the value of imported merchandise and either subtract any debt contracted or add any debt paid off during the year. For example, if imports are $100,000,000 and the debt contracted through the transfer of stocks <note>Public and private securities or bonds held by investors.</note> has been $10,000,000, the amount actually paid for by our exports is only $90,000,000. Conversely, if we have paid off that much debt, it should be added, giving us $110,000,000 as the true value of the exported goods. This method includes the cost of freight.

While it is impossible to apply this perfectly to the following tables, it can be done in part. It is generally understood that the amount of American stocks—both public and private—held in Europe in 1841 exceeded $200,000,000, and there is reason to believe they exceeded...

# THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.

By $170,000,000, this exceeds the amount held in November 1834, when the great wave of stock speculation began.* By subtracting this sum from the merchandise imported between the end of 1834 and the year 1841, we can determine the true value of the produce and goods we exported. A portion of this debt was settled <note>original: "absorbed"</note> in the years 1845, 1846, and 1847; on the other hand, new debts were created last year—and are still being created today—by sending securities <note>original: "evidences of debt"; financial documents like bonds or stock certificates representing money owed to foreign investors.</note> abroad. To calculate the actual trade balance, we should add the settled debt to the imports of the first three years mentioned and subtract the new debt from the imports of the last two years. This will give us the actual amount paid for by our exported produce, domestic goods, and the shipping industry used for transportation.

There are other, earlier years where corrections might be needed, but they are minor compared to those I have just mentioned. Small loans were made in those years, but it is likely that almost as much was paid off, except perhaps in 1825, when a considerable amount of European debt was created. However, the amount is so uncertain that I did not think it worthwhile to make a specific correction for it. Doing so would likely show a noticeable decrease in the value we received for our exports before 1829, which would make that period look even worse than I have already represented it.

With these remarks, I will now present the results of my research. In doing so, I will share every fact that I believe might shed light on this important question, concealing nothing. If those who have reached different conclusions than mine possess other facts, I encourage them to organize them as I have done here; in this way, we may gradually arrive at the truth. This is a vital question for the nation, and it is time it was examined as a purely scientific matter, rather than a partisan or regional one.

The following facts can be drawn from an examination of the accounts above:
**First.** That the amount received from foreign nations in exchange for our surplus products increased significantly while the Tariff of 1828 <note>A protective tariff designed to support American industry by taxing imports; it was highly controversial and often called the "Tariff of Abominations" in the South.</note> was in effect.
**Second.** That the amount received decreased greatly after the Compromise Bill <note>The Compromise Tariff of 1833, which was designed to gradually reduce tax rates over ten years to resolve the Nullification Crisis.</note> began to take effect.
**Third.** That the amount received from foreign nations was further and significantly diminished under the strictly revenue-focused clauses of that bill, and that the trend was downward when the system was changed.
**Fourth.** That the amount received increased rapidly under the Tariff of 1842 <note>A return to protectionist policies that raised taxes on imported goods to help the struggling U.S. economy.</note>, reaching nearly the same level that had been achieved under the Tariff of 1828; in both cases, the trend was still upward when the system was changed.
**Fifth.** That the amount received decreased in the year 1848.
**Seventh.** <note>The author skips "Sixth" in the original text.</note> That the amount of debt taken on in the last two years will likely lead to a further decrease in future years.

To establish a scale of value for our exports (including profits from the shipping industry), we should rank the periods in the following order:
First, and lowest: The years governed by the strictly revenue-focused clauses of the Compromise Act.

# CHAPTER THREE.
## A REVIEW OF THE COMMERCIAL POLICY OF THE LAST THIRTY YEARS.

I will now describe in detail the consumption of various goods <note>original: "commodities"</note>, both foreign and domestic. To ensure a correct understanding, I must occasionally make adjustments similar to those mentioned previously. My goal is to demonstrate how the ability to *consume* was driven by the ability to *produce* goods that could be traded for what was consumed.* While it would be ideal to do this for every case, it would make the analysis overly complicated and involve a great deal of labor.

In listing the imports from 1834 to 1841, I will always subtract one-fifth (- 1/5) to show the actual amount consumed and truly paid *for*. For the years 1845–46 and 1846–47, I will, in some important cases, add one-twentieth (+ 1/20) to account for goods that were imported in an earlier period but were *then paid for* by canceling certificates of debt. The figures for 1848 will be reduced by one-seventh (- 1/7) to show the amount paid for by the re-export of nine million dollars in foreign goods as physical gold or silver <note>original: "specie"</note>, and the export of eight million dollars in certificates of debt. The quantity paid for by our *exports* was thus almost doubled before the end of the second period in 1834. However, it diminished under the Compromise Act <note>The Compromise Tariff of 1833, which gradually reduced rates</note> and fell even further under the revenue system <note>The Tariff of 1846, designed to raise revenue rather than protect domestic industry</note>. As the Tariff of 1842 came into effect, we find a rapid increase in the power to purchase, until imports were checked by a massive increase in prices abroad and by the growth of manufacturing at home.

->## DOMESTIC PRODUCTION OF IRON.<-

*   **1810:** The total number of furnaces in the United States <note>original: "the Union"</note> was 153, yielding 54,000 tons of metal, equal to 16 pounds per person.
*   **1821:** The industry was in a state of ruin.
*   **1828:** Production had reached 130,000 tons, having little more than doubled in eighteen years.
*   **1829:** It was 142,000 tons. This was an increase of nearly 10 percent in one year.
*   **1830:** It was 165,000 tons. This was an increase of more than 25 percent in two years.
*   **1831:** It was 191,000 tons. This was an increase of about 50 percent in three years.
*   **1832:** It was 200,000 tons, giving an increase of over 60 percent in three years.
*   **1840:** The quantity reported by the census was 286,000 tons, but a committee of the Home League in New York <note>An advocacy group for American industry</note> calculated it at 347,700 tons. Taking the average of the two, it would be about 315,000 tons, which is an increase of 50 percent over eight years.
*   **1842:** A large portion of the furnaces were closed, and production had fallen to probably little more than 200,000 tons, and certainly less than 230,000 tons.
*   **1846:** It was estimated by the Secretary of the Treasury <note>Robert J. Walker</note> at 765,000 tons, having tripled in four years.
*   **1847:** It was supposed to have reached at least 800,000 tons.
*   **1848:** Production became stationary.
*   **1849:** Many furnaces are already closed, and production for the current year cannot be estimated above 650,000 tons. Due to the buildup of unsold inventory and the difficulty of selling it, it is obvious that the decline next year will be even greater.

From 1821 to 1829, the cost of iron, measured in the labor required to earn it, was high; this is shown by the fact that consumption was only twenty-five pounds per person. By 1832, it had risen to 47 pounds. However, when railroad iron was made duty-free <note>exempted from import taxes</note>, consumption fell over the next two years, indicating that it had become more difficult to obtain. From then until 1841, the average ability of the people to consume iron appears to have stayed almost completely stagnant, and in the two following years, we see it dropping rapidly. 

As the Tariff of 1842 <note>a protectionist tax on imports designed to help American industry</note> began to take effect, there was a rapid increase in the power to consume iron. This indicates that less labor was required for its purchase. By the year 1846–1847, consumption reached a point higher than ever before recorded, at almost 100 pounds per person. In 1847–1848, domestic production began to decline relative to the population, and imports increased. However, the total quantity in the market was only slightly higher than the previous year, and by the end of that year, unsold inventory had begun to pile up. In 1849, we see a rapid increase in imports and a decrease in domestic production; yet the total quantity brought to market is lower per person than in 1846–1847. Despite this, there is such a massive accumulation of unsold stock that seaports are overflowing with it. The inventory at the furnaces is so large that many producers will be forced to stop working, as many have already done.† It is obvious that the difficulty—

<meta>This page continues Henry Carey’s statistical argument that protective tariffs actually increase a nation's ability to consume goods. He transitions from discussing the total consumption of iron to the specific case of railroad iron and begins a new section on the coal trade.</meta>

-># THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.<-

...the cost of obtaining iron is increasing, and consumption is rapidly diminishing, with a tendency toward even further decline.

The important facts to be derived from this examination are—first, the small increase in imports that results, even temporarily, from the abolition of a duty. During the period from 1830 to 1832, railroad iron was subject to a duty, yet importation tripled in that time, and the final year saw the highest volume of the three. For the following nine years, it was totally free from duty; and although much of what was imported for railroads is said to have been used for other purposes, the increase averaged only seventy percent. By the Tariff of 1841 <note>This was a provisional tariff intended solely to increase government revenue and was limited to changes in only a few items.</note>, railroad iron was again made subject to a duty. Despite this, the import of rolled iron <note>original: "rolled iron"; iron that has been processed through rollers to create sheets or bars, commonly used for rails</note> in 1842 and 1843 was 46,000 tons, which was two-thirds more than what was imported duty-free in 1834.

Second: Under the protective Tariff of 1828, total consumption per person increased by fifty percent in four years. Under the system that prevailed from 1832 to 1843, consumption remained almost stationary and was likely lower per person than it had been at the start of that period. However, under the Tariff of 1842, average consumption increased in the first year from thirty-nine to fifty-seven pounds. By 1846 and 1847, it reached nearly one hundred pounds per person, exceeding the consumption of the "free trade" period of 1842–1843 by 150 percent.

If we look at the specific article of railroad iron, we find similar results. Up to 1842, not a single ton of it had ever been manufactured in this country. Yet the average consumption of all types of rolled iron in the ten years from 1832 to 1842—when it was duty-free—was only about 36,000 tons. Having only commenced in 1843, the domestic manufacture of railroad bars <note>The heavy iron rails used for train tracks.</note> had already reached about 50,000 tons by 1845. By 1847, it reached nearly 100,000 tons, and yet the average import of rolled iron for those four years was nearly as high as it had been before. Domestic production has now fallen almost to nothing, and yet imports have reached only 174,000 tons—of which, it is said, there is currently a two-year supply on hand to meet the present demand.

The questions to be settled are: Which system provides iron most cheaply? Which system allows those who wish to use iron to obtain it most easily? If "free trade" were the better system, then the power to import iron under it should grow more rapidly than the power to produce it domestically diminishes. However, we see here that the power to import actually diminishes as the power to produce falls. Conversely, the power to import grows alongside domestic production, reaching its peak under a system of protection.

In this case, it was necessary to separate the years 1842 and 1843 because the entirety of the latter year fell under the influence of the Tariff of 1842,* while the records for domestic production are calculated at the end of the year, rather than the middle, as is the case with imports.

The facts presented here deserve careful consideration. When we produced very little coal, we also imported very little, with total consumption being only six tons per thousand people. As domestic production grew, imports also grew; thus, in 1846 and 1847, when we produced *eighty* times as much as we did in the period from 1821 to 1829, we imported five times more.

From 1829 to 1834, and from then until 1837, the increase in consumption was rapid. From then until 1841, it decreased by ten percent. In 1842, it was barely higher than it had been five years earlier. In the five years that followed, it rose from 69 to 152 tons, showing a rapid decrease in the amount of labor <note>original: "labour"</note> required to be given in exchange for it. In 1848, under the influence of the Tariff of 1846 <note>The Tariff of 1846, or the Walker Tariff, significantly lowered the protective duties established four years earlier.</note>, production became almost stagnant. The decreased power of consumption is shown by the fact that although the quantity sent to market maintains the same ratio to the population, much of it is sold at a loss to the producer.

With every step in the growth of domestic coal production, the price has steadily decreased. In 1826, the price of a ton of anthracite in Philadelphia was six, eight, and sometimes ten dollars, yet the total import was only 970,000 bushels (about 30,000 tons). In 1846, the price of anthracite was about four dollars, yet the import was 156,000 tons. It appears from this that when a nation is capable of supplying its own needs, other nations wishing to sell must come to them and sell at the lowest price, and consumption is large. However, when a nation cannot supply itself, it must go abroad to seek supplies and pay the highest price, and then consumption is small. Applying this to iron, we find that when we had to look abroad for nearly all our supply, it sold at prices two or three times higher than those at which it is obtained today.

In 1846 and 1847, despite the vast increase in the coal supply, consumption was so great that we had to go abroad to make up the difference and pay the high prices that our own demand helped to produce—a situation that could not have happened if we had been prepared to supply the entire demand ourselves.

It remains to be seen whether the opposite of this proposition might also be true: namely, that when a nation creates a home market for nearly all its products, other nations must come and seek what they need and pay the highest price; and that when it does not create a home market, it must seek markets abroad and sell at the lowest prices. If both of these are true, it follows that the way to sell at the highest prices and buy at the lowest is to buy and sell at home.

---

\* It went into effect on August 30 of that year.

-># THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.<-

In estimating domestic consumption, I have consistently valued a bale at four hundred pounds, although I am aware that the weight of a bale has gradually increased. This change would be important to consider if my goal were to compare the year 1847 with the distant year 1831; however, it is unimportant when the goal is to compare years that are close together, as is currently the case.

The results in this instance correspond almost exactly with those obtained from the examination of iron and coal. The domestic consumption of the 1834–1835 crop per person was almost fifty percent higher than the average of previous years, while imports remained mostly unchanged. Under the Compromise <note>The Compromise Tariff of 1833, which mandated gradual reductions in import duties until 1842.</note>, consumption appears to have remained almost perfectly stagnant; the increase in domestic production was offset by a decrease in imports. In 1842–1843, consumption per person was hardly higher than it had been eight years earlier, at a time when it should have doubled. With the implementation of the Tariff of 1842 <note>A highly protectionist tariff passed by the Whig party to reverse the effects of the Compromise Tariff.</note>, we find that the consumption of domestic products was 75 percent higher, while imports also nearly doubled. It seems obvious that the ability to obtain clothing in exchange for labor increased during both protective periods and decreased as the country moved toward free trade. In 1848–1849, the demand for Northern manufactured goods decreased; and, as many mills are now closed that were operational only a few months ago,* there is reason to believe that the ability to obtain clothing in exchange for labor is in a state of gradual decline.

A portion of the cotton manufactured at home has been exported and was therefore not consumed domestically. Accounting for this would have made the table very complicated, and it did not appear necessary, as the proportions were well preserved. Exports were about one million dollars when domestic consumption was 100,000 bales, two million when it rose to 200,000, three million out of 300,000, and five million out of 500,000 bales.

-># THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.<-

Before the passage of the Tariff of 1824, the wool manufacturing industry was in a very depressed state. In 1825, the number of sheep was only fourteen million,* producing about thirty-five million pounds of wool. From that point on, the number increased, and the wool crops of 1829, 1830, and 1831 were estimated at fifty million pounds, produced by twenty million sheep. By the end of 1834, there had been a further increase,* though we do not know the exact amount; however, the value of wool manufacturing was estimated at 65 million dollars, compared to 40 million in 1831.

In 1840, the census records showed only 19,311,000 sheep; the population of sheep had decreased even as the human population grew significantly. The economic depression of 1841–1842 was accompanied by the slaughter <note>original: "sacrifice"</note> of sheep on a large scale. However, the recovery that followed was so rapid that by 1845, the number of sheep was estimated at twenty-five million,† and by 1848, it reached twenty-eight million. Ohio had only 2,065,000 sheep in 1846, but by 1848, the number had risen to 3,677,000. In New York, the number was 6,443,000 in 1845, and it has increased significantly since that date.

In 1840, wool deliveries at Pittsburgh and via the New York canals accounted for one-fifth of the total production recorded in the census. Since then, the figures are as follows:‡

domestic production <note>original: "the former"; referring to the domestic wool manufacturing mentioned on the previous page</note> grew, and imports were large. Since the passage of the Tariff of 1846, production has fallen to 500,000, and there is little demand even for this smaller supply.

We have seen so far that the investment of labor and capital into opening mines, building furnaces, mills, and factories, and operating those works was halted at the end of 1834. This investment did not start again until after the passage of the Tariff of 1842. We have also seen that it increased rapidly from 1843 to 1847, became stagnant in 1848, and is now declining. Both labor and capital seek employment; if they are denied work at home, they must seek it abroad. When employed at home, there is a tendency toward concentration and teamwork. When sent abroad, there is a tendency toward scattering, which reduces the power of working together. One of these paths tends to increase the wages <note>original: "reward"</note> of labor, while the other tends to decrease them. To determine the effects of these two systems, I provide:

First, The amount of IMMIGRATION, which shows how much the wages of labor attracted people from other nations to come and live among us; and,

Second, The amount of SHIPPING built, to show how the "importing" of people—the cargo that pays the highest shipping rates—helped increase the resources available for exporting goods:

Previously, I stated that immigration was not affected by changes in policy until more time had passed than was required for the other subjects we have considered. A change in policy tends to raise or lower the value of labor—to raise or lower the "price" of men—and after a rise has been achieved, people come to offer their labor for sale <note>Carey is arguing that people migrate to where wages are high, but it takes time for word of high wages to reach potential immigrants abroad.</note>. It will be seen that the number of immigrants in 1831 was lower than in 1830, and it was not until 1832 that it rose. With the exception of 1835, it continued to rise until 1836–37, when it reached 78,083, after which it fell. In 1843–44, it felt the effect of the disastrous year of 1842 <note>1842 was a year of severe economic depression in the United States, which Carey attributes to the low "revenue" tariffs of the previous years.</note>, and the number was only 74,000; it was not until 1844–45 that it began to grow rapidly. At the present moment immigration is large because of the great demand for labor in the years that have passed, but it is now feeling the effect of the current diminished demand and the resulting fall in wages.

The same is true for the shipping industry. The first effect of a rise in wages is to increase the ability of people to obtain the necessities of life. It is not until those needs are met that the power to consume foreign goods tends to increase materially. The increase in shipbuilding did not commence until 1832. It fell off in 1838. Thus far, the trend is precisely the same as that of immigration. It began again in 1844, somewhat ahead of immigration. It is currently sustained by immigration alone; and when immigration falls off, shipbuilding must fall as well. The close connection between the ability to secure valuable <term>return-freights</term> <note>original: "return-freights"; the cargo carried on a ship's journey back to its home port, which is essential for a voyage to be profitable.</note> and the ability to build ships is shown in the following table:

Whether the coming year is likely to offer incentives for increasing our <term>tonnage</term> <note>original: "tonnage"; the carrying capacity of a merchant ship</note> may be judged from the following comparative view of the arrivals at New York in the last four months of the two previous years, compared with the present one, as provided by the Commissioners of Immigration:

Instead of an increase of about forty percent, there is a decrease of over twenty percent. It is obvious that this decline must continue, as shown by the facts contained in the following paragraph, which I take from the *New York Herald*:

> "**EMIGRATION TO EUROPE.**—The fine and well-tested <term>packet-ship</term> <note>A ship that traveled a regular route carrying mail, passengers, and freight.</note>, *Ashburton*, sailed yesterday for Liverpool, carrying 104 passengers. Having taken a glimpse at 'the land of liberty' and not finding it the <term>El Dorado</term> <note>A legendary city of gold; here meaning a place of easy wealth.</note> they expected, they decided to return home. They were mostly natives of Ireland. The *Jamestown* and *Constellation* sail tomorrow with similar groups."

Every man who returns home in this way prevents the emigration of a hundred others who would have otherwise crossed the Atlantic.

| 1842 | 1,129,000 | 11 | | | |

At no period in our history has the process of depopulation proceeded with the intensity that is now being seen. Emigrants from Europe are now returning home disappointed, while the movement to the West is almost miraculous. The quantity of land sold does not, as I understand it, give a full picture of the land actually being occupied, because of the legal protections given to <term>squatters</term> <note>People who settled on public land without a legal title, hoping to gain ownership later.</note>.

It is estimated, we are told, that between thirty thousand and fifty thousand people have been added to the population of Iowa within *six weeks*. By the <term>close of navigation</term> <note>The time in winter when ice prevents ships from traveling on rivers and canals.</note>, it is expected the population will have increased by twenty-five percent since the 1st of September. This is the trend in all the new states in the West and Southwest. If we add the migration to California to this, it is doubtful if the population of the older states will be as large at the end of the year as it was at the beginning.

> ...the Atlantic ports, some of which have been anchored there for nearly four months, not one is advertised for a return trip home. This, of course, is easily explained. There is no cargo to bring back except passengers and gold dust, and as these mostly prefer the steamers, the ships have nothing to do but wait and see what happens. Meanwhile, the absence of so many vessels, and the unlikelihood of an early return, are strengthening the rates for local shipping. Rates must soon advance rapidly; if it were springtime now instead of fall, I think it would be difficult to secure shipping contracts at current prices.

A vast amount of capital has been tied up in idle ships, and others must now be built to take their place. If those ships were back again, shipbuilding would currently be entirely stopped.

† To this must be added the settlement of Texas and Oregon.
‡ To these must be added the settlement of California.

<summary>Henry Carey discusses a sharp decline in immigration to New York and an increase in people returning to Europe, while noting a massive internal migration toward the American West and California. He argues these shifts are disrupting the shipping industry and the population balance of the older states.</summary>

### PRODUCTION OF FOOD.

The ability to supply food to those who live in towns or near markets, and also to export it in exchange for other goods, can be seen as evidence of how productive labor is when applied to farming. This table shows that despite the rapid growth of manufacturing between 1830 and 1834, food exports were not only maintained but actually increased. The trend toward depopulation had slowed, and the ability to obtain iron to help with cultivation had increased. After that, as the trend toward depopulation grew—and as immigration, manufacturing, and the ability to obtain iron leveled off—food production dropped so much that prices rose high enough to make it profitable to import it. One might even doubt whether the total quantity produced between 1835 and 1840 was any greater than in the previous five years, despite the increase in the population. Starting in 1845, we see production gradually increasing again, despite the massive amount of labor dedicated to producing coal, iron, cotton and woolen goods, ships, and steamboats. How great this increase was can be seen by comparing the 1840 census returns with the Patent Office estimates for 1847:

| Year | Wheat | Barley | Oats | Rye | Buckwheat | Ind. Corn <note>Indian Corn, known today as Maize.</note> | Totals |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1840, | 84,823,272 | 4,161,504 | 123,071,341 | 18,645,567 | 7,291,743 | 377,531,875 | 615,525,302 |
| 1847, | 114,245,500 | 5,649,950 | 167,867,000 | 29,222,700 | 11,673,500 | 539,615,000 | 868,273,650 |
| | | | | | | | |
| Increase, | 29,422,228 | 1,488,446 | 44,795,659 | 10,577,133 | 4,381,757 | 162,113,125 | 252,748,348 |

Here we see an increase of no less than 40 percent in just seven years, while the population only grew by 23 percent. If divided equally among the population, there would have been 36 bushels per person in the first case and 42 in the second. Thus, we see that making it easier to obtain the machinery of cultivation <note>Carey uses this term to describe iron tools and farm implements.</note> leads to an increase in agricultural products. Furthermore, an increase in the capacity to produce cotton and woolen cloth allows the farmer to receive a larger amount of clothing for every bushel he produces than he could before.

The net export of food per person is as follows:

| | | |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1821 to 1829, . . . 0.89 bushels | 1834, . . . . . . . . . 0.29 bushels | 1845, . . . . . . . . . 0.38 bushels |
| 1830, . . . . . . . . . 0.47 bushels | 1835 to 1841, . . . 0.25 bushels | 1846, . . . . . . . . . 0.65 bushels |
| 1831, . . . . . . . . . 0.71 bushels | 1842–43, . . . . . . 0.81 bushels | 1847, . . . . . . . . . 1.28 bushels |
| 1832, . . . . . . . . . 0.82 bushels | 1844, . . . . . . . . . 0.41 bushels | 1848, . . . . . . . . . 0.60 bushels |
| 1833, . . . . . . . . . 0.85 bushels | | 1849, . . . . . . . . . 0.45 bushels |

We see, then, that with the exception of the year of the famine in Ireland <note>The Great Famine (1845–1852), which created an enormous temporary demand for American food exports.</note>, the export has never reached one bushel per person. Furthermore, it has invariably been largest during periods of **protection** <term>The policy of placing tariffs on imports to encourage domestic manufacturing.</term>—those periods in which the largest and most valuable domestic shipping freights could be obtained. As we have moved toward **free trade**, the power to maintain trade has diminished; as we have moved away from it and toward protection, trade has increased along with the growth of immigration.

The effect of this is seen in the constantly increasing quantity of Canadian produce that passes through New York on its way to England. It is stated that while in 1848 only 50,000 barrels of Canadian flour passed through New York, the quantity in 1849 that came through by the single route of Oswego <note>A major port city in New York on Lake Ontario.</note> was 200,000 barrels, in addition to 623,000 bushels of wheat. This, being produced in a foreign country, must of course be subtracted from our total amount of exports. However, if the "import of MEN" <note>original: "import of MEN"; Carey refers to immigrants as a form of imported "capital" or labor power.</note> (immigration) should diminish, the cost of outward shipping must rise, and the trend of sending Canadian flour or wheat to market through the ports of the Union will disappear.

It is not possible to determine exactly what the production of grain was before the census of 1840, but we know that in the period from 1830 to 1834, prices were moderate and consumption was high. It is unlikely that production per person was as high as that recorded in the 1840 census, because the improved transportation in the later period allowed farmers to dedicate more of their labor to cultivation. If we estimate it at thirty bushels per person, it will probably be close to the truth. In the following period, production was so low that prices rose to a point that allowed imports from Europe; this price increase so far exceeded wage increases that it caused almost universal conflict between employers and workmen. It is doubtful if production then exceeded twenty-five bushels per person. 

Gradually, the tendency toward depopulation <note>The movement of the established population away from settled areas to the Western frontier.</note> diminished, and in 1840, we find production at thirty-six bushels, rising to forty-two in 1847. The same causes that reduced production in 1836 are now at work again. Immense numbers of people are moving and changing their places of labor; those who have gone to California, New Mexico, the Salt Lake region, etc., can hardly be estimated at fewer than one hundred thousand. These men are no longer producers. Thus, while we have added 280,000 people from abroad this year who require feeding, we have exported great numbers of our own people who have not only stopped producing but have also taken vast quantities of food with them. One might reasonably doubt if the product of this year exceeds thirty-eight to forty bushels per person; this is partly why prices have been maintained so far. Nevertheless, there is a gradual trend toward falling prices, showing that the power to consume is diminishing faster than the power to produce.

Anyone who remembers the events of the period between 1835 and 1839 will recall that the ability to obtain food in exchange for labor decreased significantly. This country has never experienced so much anxiety regarding the harvest as it felt in 1838. From that time on, the tendency toward dispersion <note>The scattering of the population toward the frontier.</note> diminished; in 1839 and 1840, labor commanded good supplies of food, which is obvious from the fact that immigration rose, reaching a peak of 101,000 in 1841–42. By that time, however, the value of labor and food had greatly fallen, and—

<summary>Carey argues that protectionist policies and high immigration levels correlate with higher domestic food production and exports. In 1842, immigration fell to a lower point than had been seen for twenty years; the consequence was a great decrease in immigration during the two succeeding years. From then until 1847, the increase was very rapid; however, in the following year, it became stationary and is now falling rapidly.

We see here a rapid increase in consumption from 1829 to 1834. Consumption then decreased in its actual amount until 1844, while the average of 1846–7 and 1847–8 was only slightly less than double that of 1842–3. The ability to consume foreign sugar has kept steady pace with the increase in the domestic supply. This resulted in a total consumption for the year 1847–8 that exceeded the period from 1821 to 1829 by more than 150 percent, and was almost double that of 1842 and 1843.

The power of producing food thus kept pace with the power to apply labor and capital to the conversion of food and other raw materials into iron, cloth, and other commodities required by man. In this way, both kept pace with the tendency toward the concentration of population. With every increase in the power of production, consumption grew, and the laborer received larger returns for his work, which encouraged immigration. Conversely, with every decrease in the power of production, the ability to pay for foreign commodities diminished. This is why the early years of the transition toward **free trade** <term>The policy of reducing tariffs and trade barriers.</term> were marked by the creation of a massive debt, the interest on which must now be paid.

### INTERNAL COMMERCE

We may now examine how much the power to maintain internal trade increased or decreased alongside the power of production. For this purpose, I provide the **TOLLS** <term>Fees paid for the use of transportation infrastructure like roads or canals.</term> on the three principal routes between the East and West, and the **TONNAGE** <term>The weight of cargo or the capacity of ships passing through a specific point.</term> that passed through the Louisville and Portland Canal <note>A vital bypass for the Falls of the Ohio River, crucial for Midwestern trade.</note>. 

In examining these figures, it is important to remember that the income from European immigrants in the last two years has been immense. Despite this, there has been a large decrease in the two routes for which I have been able to obtain complete records. It follows, naturally, that the income from merchandise has greatly diminished in proportion to the population. Should immigration continue to decline, the deficiency in the receipts from these public works will become a serious concern for the treasuries of both New York and Pennsylvania.

*   In 1841, it had risen to only 56,252 tons.
*   In 1846, it was 106,836 tons.
*   In 1847, it was 139,399 tons.
*   In 1848, it was 166,400 tons.

We can see that while it increased by only 28,000 tons in the first seven-year period, it gained 110,000 tons in the last period, with nearly all of this growth occurring since 1843. At the present time, there is no upward trend. The primary driver of this trade is the transportation of immigrants, and any decrease in immigration must be followed by a decrease in shipping capacity <note>original: "tonnage"</note>.

In 1842, the STEAMBOAT TONNAGE on the western rivers was only 126,278, and the trend was downward because business was very slow. This can be seen from the number of trips made by certain boats:

| Year | Boats | Trips | Year | Boats | Trips |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| 1839 | 85 | 141 | 1841 | 82 | 162 |
| 1840 | 28 | 147 | 1842 | 29 | 88 |

By 1846, only four years later, the figure had almost doubled to 249,055. In the two succeeding years, it increased rapidly, as may be seen by the following record of boats built at Cincinnati:

**1845–6: 5,657 tons. | 1846–7: 8,268 tons. | 1847–8: 10,232 tons.**

In the last year, the trend has been downward; the boats built totaled only 7,281 tons, and the number of arrivals was only 3,239, compared to 4,007 in the previous year.

We find the same results everywhere. From 1835 to 1843, there was scarcely any increase; but from that date, everything came to life and grew with rapidity. By 1848 and 1849, everything tended downward, despite the great increase in population.

## NEW YORK

Since New York is assumed to be the place that benefits most from complete free trade, we can gain insight by examining the effects of various economic systems as shown by the number of houses built in that city. This is compared to the total population of the country, for which New York serves as the commercial capital. The earliest record I have been able to obtain is from 1834:

| Year | Houses built | Per million of population | Year | Houses built | Per million of population |

Brooklyn has expanded rapidly since 1842. If it had been possible to obtain a similar record for that city—which is essentially a suburb of New York—the difference would have been much more striking. However, the data we have is enough to show that the number of houses in New York grew alongside the growth of factories and furnaces, and decreased—as they are decreasing now—when those operations ceased.

## PHILADELPHIA

It is also useful to track the progress of Philadelphia, as it distributes a large portion of the nation's coal and iron and serves as a center for trade between the East and the West. However, it is impossible to determine the exact number of houses built there because several districts did not keep such records until recently. To show population growth over different periods, it is necessary to use the returns from the State censuses, which are taken every seven years <note>original: "septennial"</note>, and those from the federal government, which are taken every ten years <note>original: "decennial"</note>.

The state returns only list the number of "taxables" <note>individuals subject to taxation, used here as a proxy for the general population</note>. By multiplying that number by five, the total population was almost always accurately estimated, and I have done so throughout. However, some say the number of non-taxable residents has increased so much in recent years that it is now necessary to multiply by five and a half. The census of next year will determine if that is the case.

It is clear that the nation's productive capacity declined from 1835 to 1841, and even more rapidly in the two years that followed. Because of this, the ability to pay for foreign goods decreased so much that consumption could only be sustained by buying goods on credit. These goods were to be paid for in the future, with interest accumulating until the debt was settled. The following table shows the **VALUE OF EXPORTS** <note>In this context, the author is measuring the value of foreign goods the country was able to "buy" using its own exports and shipping services.</note>, representing the amount of merchandise received from abroad in exchange for American goods and shipping fees.

|:---|:---|:---|:---|

| 1830 | $4.32 | | |
| 1831 | $6.10 | | |
| 1832 | $5.51 | | |

| 1834 | $7.08 | | |

| 1844 | $5.03 | | Interest paid |
| 1845 | $5.16 | | |
| 1846 | $5.75 | | $5,000,000 |
| 1847 | $7 | | $5,000,000 |
| 1848 | $5.88 | $8,000,000 | |
| 1849 | $5.19 | $22,000,000 | |

As the power to produce goods declines, the power to purchase goods also declines; this creates the necessity of buying on credit. This is exactly what happened from 1835 to 1841, and the result was nearly universal bankruptcy. We are moving toward that same goal today. The amount now required to pay annual interest is about $14,000,000—which is $2,000,000 more than was required just two years ago.

The following table compares two types of goods. One of these, flax (linen), was largely exempted from taxes by the <term>Compromise Tariff</term> <note>The Compromise Tariff of 1833 gradually reduced taxes on imported goods over ten years.</note> and remained so until September 1841. The other, China and earthenware (pottery), was subject to the same tax rules as other manufactured goods. The table shows very little difference in their trends, which proves that the amount of goods a country imports depends on its *ability* to afford them, rather than the specific tax or duty placed upon them.

The fundamental question to be resolved is: "Under which system is the worker able to obtain the largest quantity of food, fuel, clothing, and the tools for production and transportation—<term>protection</term> <note>The policy of protecting domestic industries by taxing imported goods.</note> or free trade?" 

The former is criticized as a "war upon labor and capital," yet it seems clear that the power to consume all those things for which people are willing to work—and in which others are willing to invest capital—was greater under the two protective tariffs than at any other period. It also seems clear that this power is now gradually, but certainly, diminishing. Wages are falling, and the result is a reduction in immigration and an increasing trend toward emigration. Both of these are accompanied by a decrease in productive power, which will be followed by a further decline in wages and a further increase in emigration. 

The shipping industry grew alongside immigration, and freight costs fell. However, with the decline in immigration, freight costs must rise. Many of the commodities that we have recently exported will have to remain at home; thus, there will be a diminished power to import goods, accompanied by a decrease in the <term>public revenue</term> <note>The government's income from taxes and duties.</note>. Improving this revenue was one of the goals proposed when the policy of 1846 <note>The Walker Tariff of 1846, which moved the U.S. toward a "revenue only" tariff system and lowered rates.</note> was adopted. How the different systems have operated on the receipts from import duties so far can be seen by examining the following table.

We can see here that the importation of taxable goods increased so much under the <term>tariff of 1828</term> <note>A highly protective tax on imports designed to shield Northern industries from foreign competition.</note> that the revenue per person was greater than in the previous period. This occurred even though the taxes on railroad iron, tea, and coffee were abolished in 1832. The case would, however, appear much stronger if we accounted for the movement of <term>specie</term> <note>Money in the form of gold or silver coins.</note>. The period from 1821 to 1829 was a time of great economic exhaustion, and the exports of gold and silver exceeded imports by an average of almost one million dollars a year. In contrast, the imports of the following period exceeded exports by an average of five million dollars a year. 

The total difference is therefore six million dollars a year. If this amount had been imported in the form of taxable goods—as it was in the previous period—and if the taxes on tea and coffee had been kept, the revenue would have exceeded two dollars per person.

In the next period, we see a great decrease in revenue. This indicates a diminished power to pay for foreign goods, resulting from less productive labor at home.

In 1842–1843, there is a small increase resulting from the <term>tariff of 1842</term> <note>A protective tariff that reversed the downward trend of earlier "free trade" policies.</note>, which was in effect during the last nine months of this short period.

From June 1843 to June 1846, the amount rises to an average of $1.40 and stays there during the first three years of the period. The passage of the act of August 1846, combined with the <term>warehousing system</term> <note>A system where imported goods are stored in government-supervised warehouses until the duties are paid.</note>, tended to reduce the amount received by the treasury in the final year of this period.

In 1848, we find the average was maintained, though without the increase that might naturally have been expected due to the great demand for <term>breadstuffs</term> <note>Grains or flour, such as wheat or corn.</note> following the failure of the potato crop in Ireland.

In the last year (1848–1849), which was the second year the <term>tariff of 1846</term> <note>Also known as the Walker Tariff, which moved the U.S. toward lower duties and "free trade."</note> was in effect, the amount of revenue derived from merchandise *paid for by our exports* has declined significantly.

When comparing the receipts under the tariff of 1842 with those of 1828, it is necessary to remember that in the latter period, before any goods could be purchased, a sum of ten million dollars had to be set aside to pay interest on the debt incurred during the free-trade period. At a thirty percent tax rate, that would have generated three million dollars, or about fifteen cents per person.

The total amount of interest now to be paid is about fourteen million dollars. This debt must be settled by our exports before we can purchase foreign goods. The consequence of this will be a great deficiency in future revenue.

With these facts before us, we may now examine the different revenue systems that have been proposed. The <term>English school</term> <note>Classical economists like Adam Smith and David Ricardo, who argued that free trade naturally leads to the most efficient use of resources.</note> of economics holds that because cultivation begins on the richest soils, agricultural labor is highly paid at first. Therefore, diverting any part of the population to manufacturing is seen as a loss. 

However, observation shows that the first farmers invariably start on the poorer soils. The rich lands of river bottoms and the underlying beds of marl and limestone are only brought into cultivation at a later period. The English school holds that manufacturing labor must be more expensive in a new country than in an old one because of the abundance of fertile land and the profitable nature of farming. They argue that domestic industry can only survive through laws that restrict imports. They believe a double loss results from such restrictions: labor is taken away from profitable agriculture and given to the comparatively unprofitable task of processing agricultural products into goods.

The author also begins a critique of classical "English" economic theories regarding land use and labor.</summary>
