<header>THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.</header>

various goods needed for human use. They also argue that these people, who are thus unproductively employed, are supported by taxes imposed upon the consumers of their goods. Furthermore, they claim that every dollar paid to the government for the import of items that are partially manufactured at home is accompanied by a payment of five, ten, fifteen, or twenty dollars to a specific class of producers. These producers are essentially living off the taxes imposed on their neighbors for their support. This idea can be found fully developed in a report by the late <term>Secretary of the Treasury</term> <note>Robert J. Walker, who served under President Polk and was a major advocate for the lower tariffs of 1846.</note> from 1846. In that report, it is argued that all the coal consumed in the Union costs the consumer $1.60 *more* than it would under a system of free trade, even though the average price of all the coal sold at <term>Pittsburgh, Wilkes-Barre, Mauch Chunk, and Pottsville</term> <note>Major coal-mining and industrial hubs in Pennsylvania during the 19th century.</note> did not, at that time, exceed $1.50.

To relieve the consumer from this perceived double taxation, the **English school** <note>Also known as the Classical school of economics, which favored free trade and minimal government interference in markets.</note> holds that all taxes intended for revenue should be placed on goods that cannot be produced within the country—such as tea, coffee, etc.—and that all goods that *can* be produced domestically should be allowed to enter the country duty-free. This is the theory that shaped the <term>Tariff of 1846</term> and the subsequent efforts to amend it by taxing tea and coffee.

The other school of thought holds that goods which can be produced at home should be protected by taxes, while those which cannot be produced domestically should be admitted free of all duties. This was the view that led to the abolition of all taxes on tea and coffee by the Act of 1832.

The value of these two systems must be judged by their results. In the first eighteen months of the Tariff of 1832, tea and coffee were admitted duty-free. This resulted in a loss to the government revenue of nearly three and a half million dollars per year, plus a significant loss from duties on silks, which were also made free. However, the protection of domestic manufacturing was generally maintained, and the consumption of taxable foreign merchandise remained so high that the national revenue increased faster than the population. 

In the following period, protection was gradually reduced, leading toward its total disappearance as the <term>Compromise Bill</term> <note>The Tariff of 1833, which was designed to gradually lower all tariff rates over a decade to appease Southern states.</note> came into full effect. Consequently, the productivity of labor decreased so much that the money paid into the Treasury from duties on foreign goods fell to an average of less than half of what it had been from 1829 to 1834.

Under the <term>Tariff of 1842</term>, the revenue rose gradually with a steady upward trend. However, as the <term>Tariff of 1846</term> came into operation, the trend moved in exactly the opposite direction.

### PUBLIC EXPENDITURE.

When people live in close connection with one another, they are able to protect themselves and have little need for fleets or armies. In such cases, a few officials can perform the duties necessary to maintain the government. The people then exercise a high degree of **self-government**.

In contrast, when people are widely separated from each other, they are unable to protect themselves as easily and require fleets and armies for their protection. Many more officials are then needed to run the government, and the power of self-government is reduced.

As the number of fleets, armies, and government officials increases, the cost of government also increases.

As we have seen, the policies of 1828 and 1842 tended to concentrate the population and encourage people to work together, thereby increasing the power of self-government. However, the policy of 1833 and the current policy of 1846 tend to disperse the population and diminish the power of cooperation. Consequently, they lead to a reduction in the power of self-

government. I now intend to show the effect these two systems have had on public spending. The real "war on labor and capital" is any policy that increases the cost of government. This reduces the ability to build up capital that could otherwise support workers. Every step toward reducing government spending helps raise wages. Conversely, every increase in spending reduces the ability of both workers and business owners <note>original: "capitalist"</note> to afford the necessities, comforts, or luxuries of life.

As debt decreases, credit grows; as debt increases, credit declines.

# THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.

Our ability to pay for foreign goods <note>original: "commodities"</note> was high, and government income was large. As a result, the public debt was completely paid off <note>original: "extinction of the public debt"</note> by the end of 1834. Consequently, the country’s credit was very strong.

However, the policy of 1832–33 reduced domestic production and lowered wages. Even though our credit remained high, we began obtaining cloth and iron in exchange for debt certificates <note>IOUs or bonds issued to foreign creditors</note>. The result was that by the end of 1841, our foreign debt reached two hundred million dollars, and we were unable to pay much of the interest on it.

Under the Revenue Tariff of 1841–42, both public and private income almost vanished, and bankruptcy and the refusal to pay debts <note>original: "repudiation"</note> were the inevitable results.

Under the Tariff of 1842 <note>A protective tariff that increased duties on imports to encourage American industry</note>, production increased and wages rose. The ability to pay for foreign goods grew, public and private revenue increased, and we began to reduce our debt. This resulted in the complete restoration of the nation's credit.

Under the current Tariff of 1846, production is diminishing and wages have fallen. Our power to pay for foreign goods is shrinking, and we are once again buying cloth and iron by trading debt certificates for them. The amount of debt sent to Europe in the two years ending June 30, 1849, is estimated at thirty million dollars. We have already eaten, drunk, and used these goods, but we have yet to pay for them.

To show the results of this study of Union policy at a glance, I have provided the following diagrams, which clearly illustrate the trends under the various systems.

**No. I** covers the nine years from 1821 to 1829, before the Tariff of 1828 took effect.

**No. II** covers the years of the protective Tariff of 1828, from 1829 to 1834.

**No. III** covers the years of the Compromise Tariff <note>The Tariff of 1833, which gradually lowered rates over ten years</note>, from 1834 to 1841. In this data, I have consistently subtracted one-fifth from the consumption of imported goods, as that portion was obtained only by increasing our debt.

**No. IV** represents the period under the strictly revenue-focused clauses of the Compromise Tariff. This period includes one or two years, depending on the data set. Returns for coal and transportation tolls follow the calendar year, while commercial data follows the fiscal year ending June 30. Using a single year for this period places half of it into Period III (the Compromise) and the other half into Period V (the Tariff of 1842).

**No. V** represents the Tariff of 1842.

**No. VI** represents the Tariff of 1846.

In the diagrams showing the movement of iron, coal, cottons, and woollens, consumption is shown with two lines: one for domestic products consumed and the other for the total quantity. Examining these will show that the level of consumption depends on domestic production. Any drop in domestic production is never made up for by an increase in imports—even though the theory behind the Tariff of 1846 suggests it should be.

### CHAPTER FOUR.
#### HOW PROTECTION TENDS TO INCREASE PRODUCTION AND CONSUMPTION.

Two systems are currently debated throughout the world: on the one hand, the system called protection, and on the other, the system called free trade. Each claims to be the one under which the worker receives the largest reward for his efforts. It is for the purpose of testing the validity of those claims that I provided the numerous tables in the last chapter; by using them, I now propose to examine how this question affects various parts of society. This is the most vital issue for the Union <note>The United States</note>, because *within it, all other issues are included*. The discord currently existing between the North and the South stems from the decreasing value of the profits from slave labor. If it can be shown that a single system can promote the interests of both the North and the South—and both the free person and the enslaved—then harmony may replace conflict. The disagreements regarding internal improvements <note>original: "internal improvements by aid of the general government"; this refers to government-funded infrastructure like roads, bridges, and canals</note> funded by the federal government stem from a perceived necessity to scatter our population prematurely across vast areas. If it can be shown that a single system can enrich the North, the South, the East, and the West—enabling them all to build their own roads—harmony may be restored. I believe the frequent conflicts between employers and employees, capitalists and workers, and bankers and their customers can all be traced to this same cause. If that cause can be removed, harmony and good feelings can be restored and maintained. Every question affecting the peace and tranquility of the Union, or its people, will be settled once we have determined for ourselves the answer to the one great question: "Which is the system under which the worker obtains the largest reward for his labor?" When that is done, it will be seen that there is a perfect harmony of interests throughout the Union and among all its people.

Before proceeding further, I urge the reader to carefully examine those tables, always bearing in mind the precise point of the question being discussed. Everyone *admits* that protection <term>protection</term> <note>Protectionism: the economic policy of restraining trade between nations through methods such as tariffs on imported goods to foster domestic industry.</note> tends to increase the domestic production of the protected goods. Therefore, that does not need to be proven. However, it is *asserted* that protection tends to raise the price of the protected article and decrease the ability of people to consume it, *whereas* the removal of protection supposedly reduces its cost and increases the power of consumption. That claim is denied, and *that is exactly what* needs to be proven. If this assertion were true, then the power of consumption would have to decrease as protection increases. However, we see that the consumption of iron, coal, cotton, and wool increased with great rapidity in the years between 1830 and 1834, and again from 1843 to 1847 <note>Periods when the U.S. had higher protective tariffs</note>. If the claim were true, the amount of people and goods passing on the roads and canals, and the number of trades performed in our cities, should decrease under protection.

<summary>Henry Carey argues that the economic debate between protectionism and free trade is the key to resolving all American social and regional conflicts. He asserts that, contrary to free-trade theory, protectionist policies historically increased the consumption of essential goods like iron and coal.</summary>
<keywords>protectionism, free trade, labor rewards, North-South conflict, internal improvements, economic harmony, consumption, tariffs</keywords>

--- Page 55 ---
<meta>This page continues the author's argument from Chapter 4, providing historical evidence that protective tariffs—rather than hindering trade—actually increase a nation's ability to consume both domestic and foreign goods.</meta>

->THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.<-

On the contrary, they increased with great rapidity in both of the above-named periods. If it were true <note>The author is refuting the free-trade argument that protectionism hurts the economy.</note>, then it would have to reduce the wages of labor and thus diminish the reasons for foreigners to come among us and occupy our vacant lands; yet immigration increased with great rapidity under both protective tariffs. If it were true, then it must diminish our power to trade with foreign nations and the incentives to build ships; yet shipping grew with great rapidity in both those periods.

<margin>/</margin>
If we now examine the period between 1834 and 1843, it is impossible to avoid being struck by the fact that the power to consume foreign products did not increase as domestic production diminished with the move toward free trade. In fact, consumption was actually lower in quantity than it had been under the system of protection. The building of foundries and rolling mills <term>rolling mills: factories where semi-finished metal is passed through rollers to create sheets or bars</term> was stopped, yet we consumed less foreign iron than before. So it was with cotton goods: the import of these fell from over *fifty* million yards down to *eight* million. We slaughtered our sheep, but the importation of foreign cloth decreased. We prevented an increase in the domestic consumption of cotton, but shipping did not grow despite the increased necessity of depending on foreign markets. We adopted a course that we were assured would raise the wages of labor, but immigration ceased to grow. So it is now. The building of cotton mills has stopped, but our entire import from last year—in which we incurred a debt of twenty-two million—only slightly exceeded one pound of goods per person. We have closed foundries and rolling mills, but we consume far less iron than before. We have abolished the system that was regarded as "a war upon labor and capital," yet immigration is diminishing and there is no demand for capital. Steam engines are idle, and there is no demand for new ones, except for a few steamships. Railroad tolls are diminishing, and steamboats on the Western waters are idle. Iron is low in price, but it is not wanted. The same is true for coal, cottons, and woolens—and almost every type of merchandise. The power of consumption is diminishing because the demand for labor and capital has largely diminished.

<margin>/</margin>
The power of the people to pay taxes for the support of government depends on their power to consume commodities that are taxed. If protection diminished wages, it would naturally diminish revenue. However, when we examine the facts, it is shown that—despite a great increase in the free list <note>free list: a list of imported goods that are not subject to any customs duties or taxes</note>—the revenue increased under the Tariff of 1828. It then fell off so much afterward that the government was forced almost to beg for loans in the markets of Europe. With the Tariff of 1842, revenue grew rapidly, but with the Tariff of 1846, it is diminishing in actual amount per person, despite the purchase of more than twenty million dollars' worth of goods on credit in a single year. If that debt were called for now, the revenue of the current year would not exceed that of 1842.

The question to be settled is: "Does the power to import grow as the power to produce shrinks following the withdrawal of protection?" If it does, the facts must prove it. There is no question that the power to produce iron and cloth grows with protection. As I have already said, that is admitted by all. If it were not, the facts prove it. The burden of proof lies, then, with the opponents of protection. To establish their system, they must show that the power of production and consumption grows now as it grew three years ago, and that it grew from 1835 to 1843 as it grew from 1830 to 1834.

The first thing that must strike everyone who examines the tables in the last chapter is the universally tiny amount of foreign products received in exchange for the vast bulk of cotton, grain, and provisions sent to foreign countries. For example, in 1842–43, the import of cotton cloth was much less than one yard per person of the population, and likely less than one-fourth of a...

<summary>The author argues that historical data from the 1830s and 1840s proves that protective tariffs actually increase domestic consumption, immigration, and government revenue, while moves toward free trade lead to economic stagnation and debt.</summary>
<keywords>protectionism, free trade, tariffs, Tariff of 1828, Tariff of 1842, Tariff of 1846, immigration, government revenue, iron industry, cotton manufacturing</keywords>

--- Page 56 ---
<meta>This page continues Henry Charles Carey’s argument that protective tariffs actually empower a nation to consume more, both domestically and internationally. He compares historical periods of protection with periods of free trade and begins highlighting the positive social and economic impact of local manufacturing, specifically in the American South.</meta>

-># THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.<-

...pound of cotton. In other years, we see that it has varied from two to four yards, but in no single year has our consumption of cotton that has been woven on foreign looms significantly exceeded one pound per person.

The total imports received from Europe in exchange for all our products can be summarized roughly as follows: fifty cents' worth of iron, half a pound of wool, about the same amount of flax, one or two ounces of silk, and enough china and earthenware to make a decent cup and saucer. To this, we can add the *twisting and weaving* of a pound and a half of cotton per person. To obtain all of this, we give up a large portion of the land and labor of the cotton-growing states, as well as those workers employed in raising tobacco and rice. We also give up as much food as would feed the men, women, and children who could spin and weave five times as much cotton, wool, silk, and flax as we currently import. Furthermore, we use more capital in horses, wagons, railroads, engines, cars, steamboats, canal boats, ships, wharves, and warehouses than would be needed for the machinery to convert all our cotton into cloth and produce more iron than has ever been made in Britain. We use almost as much labor as would do that work—and despite all this, **we are left in debt.** This is certainly a case of using great resources to achieve **small results.**

Every part of the data tends to prove that while the amount of foreign goods received in payment for our exports increased between 1829 and 1834, it decreased between 1835 and 1841. It decreased even further in the years **1842** and **1843**, then rose rapidly from 1844 to 1847, and has declined since then. These facts seem to support the conclusion that the ability of both laborers and capitalists to consume foreign products increased under the two protective tariffs <note>The Tariffs of 1828 and 1842</note> and declined whenever the country moved toward free trade. If we now want to understand why this is the case, it may be helpful to look at individuals. We find that the person who produces the most essential goods is always the one who can most freely enjoy the luxuries of life. Conversely <note>original: "vice versa"</note>, the farmer who gets the least food from his land is the one who can least afford clothing, coffee, tea, or books.

It is also worth noting that any significant increase in the consumption of foreign products following a move toward free trade seems to lead to exhaustion and bankruptcy. In contrast, every increase in domestic production resulting from protection has merely been the foundation for a new and larger increase—one so great at times that it caused fears it was unnatural and could not be maintained. We have never discovered exactly how far this could go, because the only two periods of full protection were each limited to four years. To understand the cause of this, a researcher should examine the visible facts wherever a factory <note>original: "manufactory"</note> or furnace has recently begun operating. Those found at Graniteville, South Carolina, are described this way by a highly intelligent correspondent for "The New York Herald":

> "The effect of building this factory in the neighborhood is almost magical. Hundreds of poor white residents, who were previously almost destitute, have found employment. Methodist and Baptist churches have been built. A free school has opened, and about 70 students attend. There is a large and convenient hotel, where I am writing this letter. The town is laid out in streets, and over 80 very neat and comfortable houses with attached gardens have already been built; these rent for $16 to $25 per year. Some of the girls in the factory are very pretty and well-dressed; from what I can gather, the change in their appearance is extraordinary. The superintendent, Mr. George Kelly, who came here to set the factory in motion, walked with me through the factory and the town. He told me that he only brought four or five experienced people with him from the—"

The labor used to build these mills was pure profit. The men and their families were already there, and they had to be supported by someone whether they worked or not. All the labor used to run the mills is profit. These people have begun to produce. From 'unproductive consumers,' they have become 'productive consumers.' In their former condition, they could consume almost no clothing, no tools requiring iron, no furniture, books, or newspapers—hardly anything, in fact, but food. Having become productive, their *entire surplus* can go toward purchasing things other than food, and this creates a market for cloth, iron, and other goods that did not exist before. *Every producer is a consumer to the full extent of his production, and by enabling these poor people to produce more, the planter*

-># THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.<-

This following system creates a market on the land for the products of the land, equal to the entire excess of production. The more that is produced, the more *must* be consumed.

This assertion may at first appear to be of doubtful truth, yet a little examination will, I think, be enough to establish its perfect correctness. A man who earns six dollars a week might save one of them and put it into a savings fund. The fund then lends that dollar, along with others, to someone who wants to build a house. That person pays it out to workmen who purchase food and clothing with it, and thus that surplus dollar is consumed. The capitalist, using his savings, builds houses, ships, or factories, and the workmen he employs purchase food, clothing, and housing with his money. The average consumption of a year always *is* and *must* be equal to the average production; if we desire to know the extent of one, we only need to determine the extent of the other.

In 1839, we imported forty-three million yards of cotton cloths of various kinds. The consumers of these cloths were customers to the planter only to the extent of eleven million pounds of cotton—less than 28,000 bales. This is only as much as would be processed by twenty-eight mills of moderate size, or fourteen larger ones. To build those mills in any single cotton-growing State would require no extraordinary effort whatsoever. Once built, it would be found that they would be pure profit, for their operation would not cause the slightest decrease in agricultural production. 

The laborers are already there, and a large portion of their time is absolutely wasted. The horses and wagons are there, but are largely unemployed. The timber is there, cluttering the best lands of the plantation. The men and the horses must be fed anyway, and the wagons must be kept in order. If you create a market for this wasted labor, the laborers will consume more food, but the primary increase in spending will be on clothing (thus making a market for cotton), on houses (making a market for stone and lumber), on furniture (requiring lumber), and on books and newspapers (making a market for rags <note>original: "rags" — at this time, paper was manufactured from recycled cotton and linen rags rather than wood pulp</note>). Consequently, the cloth-makers, carpenters, masons, cabinet-makers, paper-makers, and printers will all want cloth, shoes, and houses, creating a further market for cotton, leather, lumber, and stone. By exchanging goods locally, every single man becomes a producer. In contrast, when exchanges are made over great distances, the transporters and middlemen <note>original: "exchangers"</note> are more numerous than the producers. Since consumption *must* match the level of production and *can* go no further, we may now see why consumption tends to increase so rapidly when men work in combination with each other.

In four years, we built mills that processed 300,000 bales of cotton—eleven times as much as was contained in all the cloth imported in 1839. To have created triple that number would have required no effort, nor would it have resulted in any loss of agricultural products, for that labor was being wasted in every county of the South and West. To run them now would cause no decrease in the production of food or cotton, for triple the labor required for a factory is currently being wasted in almost every county of the Union, and in *every single one* south of New England. 

To the labor-power of men, horses, women, and children now absolutely unemployed, let us add the amount of effort wasted on the road, and the manure <note>Carey highlights "manure" because local farming allowed animal waste to fertilize nearby fields, whereas long-distance transport "wasted" this natural fertilizer on the roads.</note> now wasted on the road. Then we may form an estimate—though even then a very insufficient one—of the increased production that would have resulted from the creation of those mills. Let us then reflect that all these people are already being fed, and that their surplus earnings would be used to purchase things other than food. We may then see the massive size of the market that would be made on the land for the products of the land.

-># THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.<-

A major error exists in the common perspective regarding the national division of labor. This error originated with the English school of political economists, whose system is entirely based on the idea of making England the "workshop of the world." <note>Carey is critiquing the "British System" of free trade, which he believed forced other nations to remain purely agricultural while England monopolized manufacturing.</note> Nothing could be less natural than this. That school teaches that some nations are naturally suited for manufacturing while others are suited for the labors of agriculture. It argues that agricultural nations benefit by being forced to focus on that single pursuit and making all their trades at a great distance. In this way, they contribute their share to maintaining a system of "ships, colonies, and commerce."

The entire basis of their system is <term>conversion and exchange</term> <note>Original: "conversion and exchange." Conversion refers to manufacturing raw materials into goods; exchange refers to the trading of those goods.</note>, rather than production. Yet neither processing nor trading adds anything to the actual amount of goods available to be exchanged. The great boast of their system is that the people who trade goods are numerous while the producers are few.\* They believe that the faster the number of traders grows compared to the number of producers, the faster the nation advances toward perfect prosperity. 

However, those who process and trade goods must live, and they must live off the labor of others. If three, five, or ten people are supported by the product of a single laborer, it follows that everyone will receive only a small portion of the necessities or comforts of life. We see this in practice: a farm laborer in England often receives only seven shillings a week—the price of a mere bushel and a half of wheat.

If someone claimed that some nations were suited to be growers of wheat and others were suited to be the grinders of it, or that some were suited for cutting down trees and others for sawing them into lumber, it would be considered completely absurd. Yet that is no more absurd than the claims made every day regarding the <term>conversion</term> <note>manufacturing</note> of cotton into cloth—claims believed by tens of thousands of our own countrymen. 

The loom is just as appropriate and necessary an aid to the planter as the grist-mill is to the farmer. A furnace is as necessary to both the planter and the farmer as a saw-mill. Those who are forced to live far away from iron producers work at as great a disadvantage as those who cannot access a saw-mill or a flour miller. The loom and the anvil, like the plow and the harrow, are simply small machines. They are naturally attracted to the "great machine"—the earth. When they are drawn together, everyone works in harmony, and people become rich, prosperous, and happy. On the contrary, when some disruptive cause pulls them apart—forcing the products of the "great machine" to travel to the small machines far away—the land invariably becomes poor. Consequently, the people become poor and miserable, as is the case in Ireland.

To those who doubt the extent of the loss caused by this unnatural division of labor, I recommend visiting any farm located thirty or forty miles from a furnace or a factory. There, you can see the truth for yourself on the ground. You will see days constantly wasted because there is no local work available. You will see other days wasted on the road carrying small amounts of produce to distant markets. You will see a general listlessness caused by a lack of motivation to be active. Meanwhile, children remain totally unemployed, and the schoolmaster stays away because there is no money to pay him to stay at home. As a general rule,

***

\* In 1831, out of 3,400,000 families in Great Britain, only 960,000 were engaged in agriculture (the work of production). The town population—those who live by processing and trading—is steadily increasing compared to the producing population. As a necessary consequence, there is a steady increase in poverty, vice, and crime.

-># THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.<-

Our farmers attach scarcely any value to their time. They choose to go to a distant market instead of selling at a nearer one, even when the difference in the price they might receive for their few pounds of butter or baskets of vegetables is utterly insignificant compared to the loss of time and labor. They do this because, to a great extent, their labor is totally valueless <note>In an agricultural economy without local industry, labor that is not actively planting or harvesting often has no "market value" because there are no other jobs available.</note>. Let the inquirer look at these things for themselves, and then consider the enormous proportion of labor that is misemployed in poorly cultivating large areas of land instead of small ones—in maintaining fences and roads that are entirely out of proportion to the actual product of the land. Finally, let them add the waste of intellect resulting from the lack of proper instruction and frequent communication with their fellow men—and then let them determine if the loss is not *five times as great* as what would be required to pay for all the cloth and iron (including raw materials) consumed on the farm. 

Place a mill there, and all of this is saved. The farmer, his horses, and his wagon are employed in hauling stone and timber for the mill and for houses. His children find employment in the mill, or in producing things that can be used by those who work in the mill. All their extra earnings may go toward buying cloth and iron, for they already had enough *food*. I say "all," because with the mill come improved roads and the ability to send many things to market for which a local market could not previously be created.

The mill, the furnace, and the coal mine are <term>saving-funds</term> <note>Original: "saving-funds." Carey refers to what we now call savings banks, which allow small amounts of capital to accumulate over time.</note> in which the people of the neighborhood deposit the labor and the materials that would otherwise be wasted. Where these depositories exist, farmers and planters become rich. Where they do not, they remain poor. To those who desire to understand the wonderful effect of the daily deposit of small quantities of labor, I would recommend an examination of the savings bank systems of Europe and this country. There, you will see how much can be accumulated from small savings when a safe place of deposit is offered, and from that, you can form a judgment of how much is likely to be wasted for want of such institutions. 

The people of New England have saving-funds in which they deposit what would otherwise be the wasted labor of themselves, their horses and wagons, and their sons and daughters. They also save much of the produce that would otherwise be wasted, creating by that very act a market on the land for the products of the land. Thus, they are enabled to save the manure <note>In 19th-century agriculture, "saving manure" was a critical practice for maintaining soil fertility and preventing the exhaustion of the land.</note>, and they grow rich because of these economies. The people of other states waste labor, water-power, and various kinds of produce. They destroy their timber for want of a market for it, and they waste their manure; thus, they remain poor because of this extravagance. One cent per day for each person in the nation is almost eighty million dollars in a year. Is there not wasted, for want of a demand for it, enough labor to <term>quintuple</term> <note>Original: "quintuple." To increase fivefold.</note> that sum per head? If so, the amount is four hundred million dollars, or forty times the price (including raw materials) of all the cotton cloths we can afford to buy from abroad.

Were all this saved, it would create a market for four hundred million dollars worth of cotton and wool garments, linens, iron, hardware, agricultural implements, coal, and all the thousand other things required for the comfort and enjoyment of life. I say four hundred million worth of those things, for they already had food; since they are all consumers to the full extent of their production, they must expend almost the entire extra production on things other than food. To the extent of these four hundred millions, they would be customers to the land and its owner, for the earth is the sole producer.

Doing so, he would find there all the labor and all the machine-power requisite for the production at market of 60,000 tons of coal per week,

It reduces the demand for labor, and consequently the reward of the laborer and the mechanic. It reduces the power of railroad owners to construct new roads, and thus again reduces the demand for labor and the power to pay for cloth or food. Thus may it be traced, step by step, throughout the whole nation, every interest taking its share of the loss.

Let the inquirer next visit a factory of any kind, and he will see that the whole value of the labor employed there is a creation that owes its existence to the fact that the mill has been built to be a savings fund. In this fund, each family may deposit the labor—physical and mental—that would otherwise be wasted, receiving in exchange the cloth, hats, coats, shoes, stockings, books, and newspapers that could not otherwise have been obtained. Let him then trace these savings, and he will find them producing an increased demand for food—and better food—and a demand for cotton, wool, iron, fuel, and all other products of the earth, to the benefit of every owner or cultivator of land, whether farmer or planter.

The people of New England save labor, and by doing so they grow rich and are enabled to make roads by which they travel rapidly to market. They save the refuse <note>Refuse here refers to organic waste and manure, which New England farmers used as fertilizer to maintain soil fertility, whereas frontier farmers often exhausted the soil and moved on.</note> of their products, which goes back into the land, and that also grows rich. The people of the South and West, for want of such labor-saving funds, waste more time than would pay ***many times*** over for all the cloth and iron they can consume. Then they are unable to make roads, the consequence of which is that transportation to market is costly. They have to travel a great distance for every exchange, however small. Their needs for making roads are great, but their power to make roads is small. They waste all the refuse of their land, which is exhausted, and then they run away to other lands, ***increasing their necessities and diminishing their power.***

But, it is asked: cannot too much coal, iron, cotton, wheat, and other good things of the world be produced—more than can be consumed? Those who ask this question do not recollect that every man is a consumer to the whole extent of his production. The more coal and iron are produced, the more wheat and cotton are consumed. The more wheat and cotton are produced, the more coal and iron are consumed. Consumption and production go hand in hand, and when there is a surplus <note>original: "glut"</note> of anything, it is the result of an error in the system that requires correction.

Coal is now superabundant. The market is overloaded with a quantity smaller than that which was readily consumed two years ago, and less by one-third than would be required now, had the power of consumption increased at the same rate as during the period from 1843 to 1847 <note>This refers to the period under the Tariff of 1842, a protectionist measure that Carey argued promoted domestic growth before it was repealed by the Walker Tariff of 1846.</note>. -># THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.<-

Some say that the cause of reduced production cannot be found there. They are right, but by saying this, they condemn the system. The tax <note>original: "duty"</note> on coal was reduced so that workers might obtain fuel more easily, but it has actually become so much harder to get that consumption has already noticeably decreased, with every prospect of it dropping further. The total amount of imported iron and cotton cloth is nothing compared to the growth of production between 1843 and 1847. Thus, we see that the supply is shrinking rather than increasing relative to the population under a system that was supposed to help the worker, the farmer, and the planter obtain cloth and iron more easily.

It is not simply that coal needs protection for its own sake—or that iron or cotton need it for theirs—but that each needs it for the other. The coal producer suffers when the iron furnace is closed; the iron producer suffers when factories are no longer being built; and the cloth maker suffers because labor is being wasted everywhere, and the people's power to buy cloth is diminished. The "harmony of interests" between agriculture and manufacturing is as perfect as the internal movements of a watch; no one can suffer without causing injury to everyone around them. The cotton grower suffers when the workers in cotton factories, mines, and furnaces are unemployed, and those workers suffer when bad circumstances reduce the profits of the farmer and planter.

There is more labor and product wasted in the states south of the Mason-Dixon Line than would be required to turn all the cotton they produce into cloth *ten times over*. Likewise, more is wasted in the states north of that line than would be required to produce all the iron made in Great Britain *ten times over*. This may seem like an exaggerated statement, yet it is less than the truth, as a close examination will show. If you want evidence of this, look at the fact that the manufacturing of cotton and wool doubled in five years—and that iron production, which was under 250,000 tons in 1843, reached nearly 800,000 tons in 1847. Did this decrease agricultural production? On the contrary, was the supply of food not greater than had ever been known before? We added at least two hundred million dollars in manufacturing, not only without losing production elsewhere, but with a larger increase than had ever occurred. It was precisely when home consumption had become so massive that people began claiming we had a surplus of three hundred million bushels of food that needed an export market. All this labor was "saved labor," and many of the resources used would otherwise have been wasted.

Next, look at another fact: it was *precisely when the growth of manufacturing was stopped*, from 1835 to 1839, that the food supply became so short. Despite people eating less because of high prices, we were forced to import more than four million dollars worth of wheat in a single year. Looking at the experiences of these two periods—1835–1841 and 1844–1847—proves conclusively that the closer the factory <note>original: "the loom and the anvil"</note> is brought to the farm <note>original: "the plough"</note>, the larger the profit is for the farmer. How could it be otherwise? The closer the place of exchange, the less labor and fertilizer <note>original: "manure"</note> are wasted on the road, and labor can be applied more steadily to a "machine" (the land) that is constantly increasing in power. For example, a demand for lumber allows a farmer to sell his trees; with that profit, he drains his land and is thus able to cultivate more and better soil. The farther away the factory is, the more labor and fertilizer are wasted in transport. Consequently, less of both can be given back to the land, and the best lands necessarily remain clogged with trees that have no value, because the labor required to clear them is worth more than the land itself once it is cleared.

This is obvious from the fact that immigration increases. People move from areas of low wages to seek higher ones. From 1829 to 1834, immigration grew. From then until 1843, it remained almost stationary. From that point to the present time, it has increased with vast rapidity. From now on, if the existing system is maintained, immigration must diminish, because the power to obtain food, clothing, fuel, and housing—in other words, wages—has declined.

It is obvious that the productivity of labor increases based on the rapid growth of canal and railroad tolls. These tolls remain stagnant whenever we adopt policies that tend to separate the loom and the anvil <note>original: "loom and the anvil" — a metaphor for manufacturing</note> from the plow and the harrow <note>original: "plough and the harrow" — a metaphor for agriculture</note>. The same is true for the growth of steamboats and shipping in general. The more that is produced, the more can be consumed, and the more goods will be brought to market.

In my view, there is no single perspective from which we can regard the facts currently before us that does not confirm these views. If all the machinery now used in Lowell and Providence <note>Lowell, Massachusetts, and Providence, Rhode Island, were the primary centers of the American textile industry in the mid-19th century.</note> for the manufacture of coarse cloths <note>basic, heavy fabrics used for workwear or industrial purposes</note> were removed and replaced by machinery suited for making fine cloths, muslins, and silks, the output would be ten times as much as we currently import, with very little increase in the amount of labor employed. If all that coarse machinery were then distributed throughout the South, it would enable the people of the Southern States to convert three hundred thousand additional bales of cotton into cloth. This would happen not only without a decrease in agricultural exports, but actually with an increase, because labor would then be applied more effectively. To accomplish all of this—by building mills and making machinery—would require an amount of labor equal to *only a very small portion of what is currently wasted in a single year, and not as much as is wasted this year in Pennsylvania alone.*

The people of the North would then utilize a higher level of intellect than is currently required; wages would rise, and the consumption of woolen and cotton cloth, silks, sugar, tea, and coffee would grow rapidly. The people of the South would experience the same effects. Their own consumption of cotton would increase fivefold, and they would consume more and better food than they do now. They would require better houses, and the demand for timber and stone would lead to the clearing of their land. Increased wealth and population would provide them with better roads; the men who came to build those roads would eat food and wear coarse cottons, and thus the planters themselves would be able to become major customers for the fine fabrics produced in the North.

By consuming more tea and coffee, the producers of those items would be able to purchase more cotton, and thus the planters' market would grow in every direction. The demand for machinery, furniture, and thousands of other items would lead to new improvements in manufacturing. The producers of tea, coffee, sugar, and cotton would be able to consume more of these goods, while the makers of machinery and furniture would need more iron, lumber, and cotton.

***

* I take the following from the *Cincinnati Gazette* as evidence of the vast amount of smaller items, composed of materials that would otherwise be wasted and prepared largely by labor that would be wasted if not for the proximity of a market:

> "It is well understood what our larger manufactures for the South are, especially by those familiar with the machinery of sugar plantations. Our small manufactures—consisting of bagging, buckets, tubs, plows, etc.—are less known. The exports of some of these for four seasons will serve to show both the requirements of the South in this regard and our ability to supply them."

-># THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.<-

On the other hand, let us imagine that the cotton mills were closed and the supply of cloth decreased by the amount produced from 600,000 bales of cotton—that the furnaces were closed and the supply of iron decreased by 800,000 tons—and that the coal mines were closed and the supply of fuel decreased by three million tons. Could we afford to import and pay for the shortfall? Would the total cotton crop then earn more than we currently get for only three-quarters of it? It would not. Our ability to import foreign cloth, iron, and fuel would not increase; instead, *it would decrease*, and we would consume only one pound of cotton per person instead of ten or twelve. The ability to pay for all the cotton and iron produced at home results from the saving of labor; with the loss of the ability to save that labor, the ability to consume its products would also vanish. Therefore, a partnership between the producer and the consumer here at home seems more profitable than a partnership with people abroad that causes division among those at home.

## CHAPTER FIVE.

### WHY IS IT THAT PROTECTION IS REQUIRED?

If all the labor used to turn food and cotton into cloth, and food, ore, and fuel into iron, is truly "saved labor"—if the entire result is actually profit—why do people need protection <note>original: "protection" — the use of government policies, such as tariffs, to encourage domestic industry by making imports more expensive</note> to enable them to produce cloth and iron? The question is a natural one and should be fully answered.

Protection is necessary precisely because it is "saved labor," and because the loom and the anvil <note>metaphors for manufacturing</note> are merely secondary to the plow and the harrow <note>metaphors for agriculture</note>. A person’s first and greatest goal is to obtain food and clothing materials for themselves and their family. Neither of these is ready for use in the state the earth—that great machine of production—provides them. Grain requires grinding, and wool requires spinning and weaving. The man pounds the grain and his wife tries to turn the wool into some kind of cloth, however crude. They work with poor machinery and lose a lot of time; however, this loss is still less than if they had to carry the grain to a distant flour mill or the wool to an even more distant textile mill. Gradually, the population grows, and the blacksmith arrives to exchange horseshoes for food. The carpenter arrives to exchange labor for food. The saw-miller arrives to exchange his and his family's labor...

...machines for food. In all these cases we see the cooperation of efforts <note>original: "combination of action"</note>, and with its growth, men obtain horseshoes and houses more easily than before. Next, the small gristmill arrives, and the miller provides the labor of grinding in exchange for food to eat. Again, the small woolen mill arrives, and the miller gives his labor to the carpenter and sawmill owner in exchange for labor and lumber, to the blacksmith for his ironwork, and to the farmer for food and wool. Next, the small furnace arrives, and the furnace operator, in the same way, exchanges with his neighbors. With the progress of this cooperation, men obtain food, fuel, clothing, iron, furniture, and houses with increasing ease at every step. The first and greatest desire of man is to associate with his fellow man; this is so because he feels that the improvement of his physical, moral, mental, and political condition always accompanies such association.

Throughout this country, there is a lack of cooperation. Men are perpetually fleeing from each other, scattering themselves over large areas and wasting the labor that, if saved, would make them rich. This inability to combine their efforts is the result of artificial causes. The adoption of the protective system <note>The use of tariffs to support domestic industry.</note> was produced by an instinctive effort to obtain, through its aid, that which would have come naturally and without effort if those causes had not existed.

If we now look to the early history of these provinces, we shall see the gradual tendency toward the establishment of furnaces, woolen mills, etc., for the purpose of enabling men to combine their efforts to obtain iron, cloth, and other necessities of life with the least loss of labor spent on transportation. By doing so, they could save their own labor to be used for production, while their sons and daughters earned wages by converting wool into cloth or ore into iron.

The goal of the colonial system was to "raise up a nation of customers," a project "fit only," says Adam Smith, "for a nation of shopkeepers." He was, however, inclined to think that even for them it was unfit, although "extremely fit for a nation whose government was influenced by shopkeepers." <note>Adam Smith (1723–1790) was a Scottish economist; Carey is quoting from *The Wealth of Nations* to criticize British mercantilism.</note> As early as the period immediately following the Revolution of 1688, we find the "shopkeeping" influence exerted for the "discouragement" of the woolen manufacture of Ireland. While the people of that unfortunate country were thus prevented from converting their own wool into cloth, they were prevented by other laws from making any exchanges with their fellow subjects in other colonies, except through the medium of English ports and English "shopkeepers."

Such being the case, it was unlikely that any efforts at cooperation among distant colonists—to make labor more productive of the comforts of life—would escape the jealous eyes of men whose mercantile instincts had prompted them to adopt such measures toward their closer neighbors. The first attempt at manufacturing any kind of cloth in the American provinces was followed by interference from the British legislature. In 1710, the House of Commons declared "that the erecting of manufactories in the colonies had a tendency to lessen their dependence upon Great Britain." Soon afterward, complaints were made to Parliament that the colonists were setting up manufactories for themselves, and the House of Commons ordered the Board of Trade to report on the subject, which was done at great length. In 1732, the exportation of hats from one province to another was prohibited, and the number of apprentices allowed for hatters was limited. In 1750, the erection of any mill or other machine for splitting or rolling iron was prohibited; however, pig iron was allowed to be imported into England duty-free...

...free, so that it might then be manufactured and sent back again. At a later period, Lord Chatham declared that he would not allow the colonists to make even a hob-nail <note>A short nail with a thick head used for the soles of boots; Chatham’s quote illustrates the extreme level of British control over colonial manufacturing.</note> for themselves. This is a clear example of the system regarding these colonies. We shall now examine the system as it related to the rest of the world.

By the Act of 5 George III (1765), the exportation of artisans <note>original: "artisans"; skilled manual workers or craftsmen.</note> was prohibited under a heavy penalty.

By the Act of 21 George III (1781), the exportation of equipment required for the manufacture of woolens or silk was likewise prohibited.

By the Act of 22 George III (1782), the prohibition was extended to skilled workers in printing calicoes, cottons, muslins, or linens, and to the making of blocks and tools used in their manufacture.

By the Act of 25 George III (1785), it was extended to tools used in the iron and steel industries and to the workmen employed in them.

By the Act of 39 George III (1799), it was extended to coal miners <note>original: "colliers".</note>.

These laws continued in full force until the year 1824. At that time, the prohibition on the export of artisans was abolished. The laws relating to the export of machinery were relaxed so that "permission may now be obtained for the exportation of all the more common types of machinery." Discretion was given to the Board of Trade, which decides upon each application "according to the merits of the case." It is said that merchants now experience little difficulty, as they generally know which machines will be granted "the indulgence" <note>original: "the indulgence"; here meaning special permission or an exemption from a general rule.</note> and which will be denied, almost as certainly as if it had been settled by an Act of Parliament. Yet, it is considered advantageous to leave this to the Board's discretion so they may have "the power of regulating the matter according to the changing interests of commerce."\* Under this system, the total amount of machinery exported in the eleven years from 1824 to 1835 averaged only two hundred thousand pounds per year <note>original: "per annum".</note>.†

We see, therefore, that the entire legislation of Great Britain on this subject has been directed toward one great object: preventing the people of her colonies and those of independent nations from obtaining the machinery necessary to combine their efforts to produce cloth or iron. This system *compelled* them to bring their raw materials to Britain so she could convert them into finished goods. Britain would then return a portion of those goods to the producers, burdened with the high cost of transportation and heavy charges for the work of manufacturing. We see, too, that despite the repeal of part of this system, it remains at the discretion of the Board of Trade whether or not they will permit the export of machinery of any kind.

If there were not a natural tendency for the producer of iron, cloth, and hats to take his place alongside the producer of food and wool, there would never have been any need for the laws passed regarding Ireland and the colonies. If that tendency did not exist, the laws prohibiting the export of machinery would never have been required. That tendency did exist, and it exists everywhere. These laws were passed for the purpose of preventing the gradual development of a natural state of things and forcing an unnatural one, whereby Great Britain might be made "the workshop of the world." The object of protection has been, and is, to restore the natural state.

The effect of these laws has been to create an unnatural division of the British population. In that country, the loom and the anvil have become more important than the plow, rather than supporting it. This has resulted in a great deterioration in...

<meta>This page continues Henry Charles Carey’s critique of the British industrial system. He argues that England’s monopoly on manufacturing and land consolidation enriched a few while impoverishing the masses, and explains how other nations eventually resisted through protective tariffs.</meta>

...the condition of both the laborer and the capitalist. For a long period, the few people engaged in manufacturing made vast fortunes. Meanwhile, the owners of land were able to collect enormous rents <note>In this context, Carey refers to the increasing cost of land use driven by population growth and the lack of available new land.</note>, because the consumers of food increased more rapidly than the producers of food. Land ownership gradually consolidated into fewer hands, and the small occupant of a few acres gradually gave way to the large-scale farmer, who cultivated hundreds of acres with the help of hired labor. The few became richer, and the many were forced into the poor-house. The value of labor, measured in food, decreased, and the value of capital also decreased. This happened because both labor and capital were—as they still are—shut out from employment on the land. Agriculture is the only employment in which both can be used to an unlimited extent with a constant increase in the return for labor.

Gradually, however, machinery was smuggled out of England, and skilled workers <note>original: "artisans"</note> escaped from the country. At length, it became necessary to legalize the export of both, and from that time, manufacturing in mainland Europe has made great progress. The people there, however, have suffered under great disadvantages, just as we have. England had monopolized machinery for so long that she had acquired skills that could not easily be matched. Furthermore, by this improper distribution of her population, she kept the price of labor and capital at a lower point—relative to the advantage with which they might have been applied—than her neighbors did. Her industrial establishments were gigantic and always ready to crush any competitors who might try to start up. Meanwhile, the constant changes in her financial systems—the inevitable results of the colonial system—were enough on their own to spread ruin among all the nations connected with her. Our own experience has been the same as the rest of the world’s.

The inevitable result of this state of affairs was resistance from the various independent nations of the world in the form of protective tariffs <note>Taxes on imported goods designed to protect domestic industries from foreign competition.</note>. One of the first results of this resistance was a change in the law that had prohibited the export of machinery. From that period to the present, England has been engaged in an effort to undercut <note>original: "under-work"</note> other nations despite their efforts to shut her out. With each stage of her progress, the condition of her factory workers <note>original: "operatives"</note>, as well as that of her farm laborers, has grown worse. Women have been substituted for men, and children of the youngest possible ages for women. The hours of labor have been extended so far that government regulation <note>original: "Parliamentary interference"</note> became absolutely necessary. That regulation was opposed on the grounds that all the profit from the machinery came from running it for one additional hour. In the mining sector of her trade, the system is the same. It is impossible to read the government reports on the condition of manufacturing and mining laborers without being horrified by the terrible consequences of this effort to tax the world by monopolizing machinery. The moral effects are as bad as the physical ones. Frauds of every kind have become almost universal. Flour is substituted for cotton in the making of cotton cloths to such an extent that, fifteen years ago, the amount used for this purpose was estimated at forty-two million pounds.* The quality of iron, and of all other goods, is consistently reduced to the lowest point necessary to prevent other nations from producing such goods for themselves.

According to the census of 1831, the number of families in England and Wales was 3,303,504. Of these, 1,170,000 were families of agricultural occupants, or of agricultural and mining laborers—the producers of things to be...

...converted or exchanged; leaving **2,133,000** for the converters <term>those who process raw materials into finished goods, like factory owners and workers</term> and exchangers <term>merchants, wholesalers, and retailers</term>, and for the money-spending classes—paupers on one hand, and state annuitants <term>people who live off government pensions or interest from government bonds</term>, noblemen, and gentlemen, on the other. Thus, the products of one laborer had to be divided among three.

By the census of 1841, it was shown that, despite an increase of **630,000** adult males over the previous ten years, there had been an actual decrease of **19,000** in the number of people employed in agriculture. Thus, we have almost **four** persons to consume the products of **one**.

Since that date, the trend has continued in the same direction. The transporters, converters, and exchangers have been steadily and rapidly increasing in proportion to the producers.

With each step in her progress, Great Britain thus becomes less of a producer and more of a mere exchanger, dependent upon the profits of converting and exchanging the products of other nations. This steadily increasing imbalance between producers and exchangers led to the state of things that required the repeal of the Corn Laws <term>tariffs and other trade restrictions on imported food and grain enforced between 1815 and 1846</term>. Since that repeal, there is an evident increase in the tendency to become a mere exchanger of the work of other men's hands. The volume of her trade does not grow at the rate required by this change. A farmer may live and maintain his family on a crop of five hundred bushels, or even less. However, a shopkeeper, to live just as well, must have five thousand bushels pass through his hands; and what is true of the individual shopkeeper is equally true of a "nation of shopkeepers," as I will now show.

The man who raises his own food and sells **$100** worth of it has that entire sum to spend on clothing and other comforts of life. He is selling the product of his own labor.

The man who buys food for **$100** and then sells his finished products for **$200** has only **$100** left to spend on things other than food. To the extent of **one-half**, he is selling the product of other people's labor.

The man who buys food and leather, each for **$100**, must sell **$300** worth of shoes to have **$100** left to spend on things other than food. To the extent of **two-thirds**, he is selling the labor of others.

It is the same with nations. When they sell their own products, their power to purchase from others is equal to the total amount sold. When they sell the products of others—whether in the same or a modified form—their purchasing power is only the difference between the price they paid and the price they received. A bale of cotton exported as yarn is simply the bale that was imported as raw wool; to the extent of the wool's cost, it represents no part of the power to purchase goods for consumption. A barrel of American flour exported in the form of cloth or iron is simply the imported barrel of flour, and represents no part of the power to purchase coffee, tea, or sugar.

The actual or declared value of the exports of the produce and manufactures of Great Britain and Ireland was:

| Period | Type of Average | Value |

| From 1827 to 1834 | annual average | **38,000,000** |
| From 1845 to 1848 | annual average | **50,500,000** |

From these sums, the cost of the raw materials required to produce the exported commodities must be deducted in all cases.

The quantity of cotton manufactured in the first period amounted to **100,000,000** pounds per year, and the average price was **19 pence** per pound. <note>original: "McCulloch’s Com. Dict., art. As a result, the people of England—who are busy providing cheap clothing for the entire world—are not only poorly fed but also extremely poorly clothed. The cost of clothing, when measured in labor, is so high that it is beyond their reach,* and the total amount available to be spent for that purpose tends to decrease. Whenever a bountiful crop brings a large amount of cotton to market, the price drops to whatever level is necessary to allow domestic buyers to buy up the extra supply that cannot be exported. When the crop is small, consumption is restricted to the quantity that can be purchased by the small amount of money available. The total sum currently available for this purpose does not seem to vary much from 2 shillings per person—enough to buy three pounds of cotton at 8 pence per pound, or six pounds at 4 pence per pound. We see, therefore, that England clothes her people at the expense of the <term>cotton planter</term> <note>the farmers, often in the American South, who grew the raw cotton</note>. She has a fixed amount of labor that she can trade for cotton, and the price of the entire import is regulated by that limit. If the crop is large, she receives a great deal of cotton for her money; if it is small, she receives very little. Consequently, the producer not only fails to benefit from large harvests, but is actually harmed by them. It is more profitable for the planter to have a harvest of 2,000,000 bales than one of 2,700,000. Had this year's crop reached three million bales, the planter would have been ruined, because <term>freights</term> <note>the cost of shipping goods</note> would have been high while international prices would have fallen to the lowest point ever recorded.

Instead of applying her labor to farming her own soil, England pursues a strategy intended to force all the world's farmers and planters to conduct their trades in her markets, where she sets the price for the entire world. Her power to use the earnings of labor to buy goods beyond <term>prime necessity</term> <note>basic survival needs like food</note> is small and is steadily shrinking. Whenever the hard work of the producer is rewarded with a bountiful harvest, he is nearly ruined because the market price falls below the actual cost of production.

The system is so extraordinary that, in the future, people will find it almost impossible to believe it was ever tolerated. England possesses a fixed capacity for transportation and <term>conversion</term> <note>the process of turning raw materials into finished goods</note>. Being so equipped, she demands that all the cotton and sheep's wool in the world be brought to her so that it may be spun and woven, and so that she may take a "toll" for performing that work. The more material that is brought to her, the less of it she returns to the producer. Furthermore, the low price she pays the producer sets the price he receives from the rest of the world. The following statement shows how this system works:

| | 1815 to 1819 | 1827–1834 | 1845–1846 |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| Cotton consumed, lbs. | 100,000,000 | 275,000,000 | 596,000,000 |
| Value | £8,000,000 | £9,000,000 | £11,400,000 |

England pays for this cotton in cotton cloth and iron. The prices for these items during those periods were as follows:

In the last period, the *additional* costs for domestic and foreign freight, charges, and commissions (calculated at three cents per pound on 496,000,000 pounds) amounted to roughly $15,000,000. In exchange for this, the planter would have received 470,000 *additional* tons of iron in Liverpool. The value of that iron in Liverpool today would be about $11,000,000. Thus, the planter not only gave his cotton away for free but also effectively paid for a large portion of the shipping costs himself. The total return he received for 600,000,000 pounds of cotton was not as great as what he had previously received for only 100,000,000 pounds.

...obtain *three and a half times* the cloth that he could have had in the first case—and *six times* the quantity <note>Carey implies six times the labor or effort</note> to obtain a *smaller quantity* of iron. A more effective <note>original: "admirable." Carey is using the word sarcastically to mean "cleverly designed"</note> mode of taxing the world was certainly never devised.

The result of the system is that the productivity of agricultural labor is declining in every portion of the world that does not protect itself against this "war upon labor and capital," as I will now show.

Consumption is measured by production. Every person is a consumer to the full extent of their production. They will go to that point, and beyond it they cannot go. The first of their needs is food; next comes clothing; after this follow the conveniences and luxuries of life. If their productive power increases, their ability to obtain clothing increases rapidly, because the entire surplus is applicable to things other than food. If it diminishes, their ability to obtain clothing diminishes with great rapidity, for they must have food. I believe it will be evident from the following facts that this power has diminished and is now diminishing rapidly:

Sixty years ago, the price paid by the consumers of cotton to the producers of it was estimated at $40,000,000.

From 1827 to 1834, inclusive, the crops of the United States averaged 945,000 bales, and the home consumption was about 145,000, leaving 800,000 for export. The average price was about $40 per bale, and the total value <note>original: "product"</note> was $32,000,000.

In this period, India continued to produce large amounts of cotton and to manufacture cotton goods. The Chinese market was not opened to the <term>free traders</term> <note>merchants who advocated for the removal of trade barriers, specifically the end of the East India Company's monopoly</note> until 1831, and it required some time to substitute the cotton cloth of England for the cotton and cloth of India. With every day that has since passed, the production of cotton has declined as the manufacturing industry has been driven toward annihilation. At that time, cotton was extensively raised in the West Indies, Brazil, Egypt, Africa, Mexico, and elsewhere; the total product, exclusive of the United States, was estimated at 450,000,000 pounds, or about one-fifth more than that of the <term>Union</term> <note>the United States</note>. Averaging the whole at the same price, we would then see an annual expenditure for <term>cotton wool</term> <note>raw cotton fiber</note>, excluding our own, of $78,000,000.

From 1842 to 1848, inclusive, the crop averaged 2,060,000 bales, and home consumption was about 400,000, leaving 1,660,000 for export. Two hundred thousand of these may be attributed to the <term>Zollverein</term> <note>the German Customs Union</note> and other European countries that have protected themselves against the British system. This is not the increased quantity actually bought because of low prices, but rather the amount that would have been purchased even at high prices, leaving 1,460,000 bales as the quantity influenced by the system. The average price during that period was seven and a half cents per pound, or $34 per bale, and the average value of the portion of the crop thus exported was $50,000,000.

Since then, the cultivators of this most important commodity throughout the world have been ruined. It is highly doubtful if the total production outside of the United States is now more than half of what it was thirty years ago; at the most, it cannot exceed 270,000,000 pounds. If we now assume that quantity and, as before, set the whole at the same price, we shall obtain the following as the amount paid for cotton by almost the entire population of the world outside of the United States:

| For the crop of the rest of the world | $20,000,000 |

<meta>This page continues Henry Charles Carey’s argument regarding the economic exploitation of agricultural producers by the British industrial system. # THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.

This results in a decrease in the amount paid to the producers. Regarding the cotton of India, nearly its entire value is now consumed by transportation costs <note>original: "swallowed up in freights"</note>. While the cost to the consumer remains high, the return to the producer is scarcely more than two cents per pound. A more thorough examination of the subject would, I believe, show that cotton producers as a whole do not receive much more for their crops today than they did sixty years ago. Even though cotton has largely replaced wool, flax, and other materials throughout the world, the total return to producers outside the United States has increased by barely twenty million dollars in that time.

A similar examination of the trends regarding sugar, coffee, wool, and other articles would yield the same results, for the depletion <note>original: "exhaustion"</note> of resources is the same everywhere. The overall effect of this system is to reduce the farmer and the planter—the producers of the world's basic goods—to a state of humble dependence upon the owners of small-scale machinery used to convert wool into cloth. These producers could purchase such machinery themselves for less labor than they currently waste every year for lack of it.

Let us now look at the results as they appear in the territories directly dependent on England.

With this vast increase in the importation of foreign food has come the ruin of the people of Ireland. Deprived of their own manufacturing and commerce, the Irish people were forced to live by agriculture alone. Ireland was able to drag on a miserable existence only as long as her neighbor, England, was willing to compensate her for the loss of industrial labor by paying higher prices for Irish products than could be found elsewhere. With the repeal of the Corn Laws <note>The Corn Laws (1815–1846) were tariffs on imported grain designed to protect British landowners; their repeal shifted Britain toward a "free trade" policy that favored cheap food imports over local production</note>, that resource failed. The result is a state of poverty, misery, and famine that has forced the government to establish a system requiring landowners to support the people whether they work or not. Thus, one of the conditions of slavery has been re-established in that unhappy country. Once a great exporter of food, Ireland has now become a large importer. The primary market for Indian corn <note>Maize</note> is now Ireland—a country where producing food is almost the sole occupation of the people. Consequently, the value of labor (measured in food) is rapidly decreasing across a population of eight million people.

From an inquiry instituted by Lord Clarendon <note>George Villiers, 4th Earl of Clarendon, who served as Lord Lieutenant of Ireland during the Great Famine</note> in 1847, conducted with the utmost care, it was determined that out of the 20,800,000 acres in the kingdom, only 5,200,000 were under cultivation. The yield of cereal grains, chiefly oats, averaged 10 bushels (at 70 pounds each) per person, while the potato yield was 561 pounds per person. The livestock consisted of 2,591,000 cattle (less than one for every three people), 622,000 hogs (one for every thirteen people), and 2,186,177 sheep (one for every four people). Such are the products of an exclusively agricultural nation whose population was about half that of the United States <note>original: "the Union"</note> at our last census.

If it were possible today to determine the quantity of food produced per person in Great Britain and Ireland, it would likely be found to be lower than it was five years ago. Furthermore, the total quantity of food—both foreign and domestic—is probably not significantly greater than it was then. If this is true, it follows that all the labor spent on buying and processing foreign cotton to exchange for food is wasted labor. The average amount of food and other goods obtainable throughout the United Kingdom in exchange for any given amount of work is trending downward rather than upward. There is reason to believe this is indeed the case. As evidence, we can look at the spending for the support of paupers: in 1837 it was £4,207,000, but for the years 1844, 1845, and 1846, it averaged £5,890,000.
