This represents an increase of forty percent in eight years. By 1848, this expenditure had reached the enormous sum of £7,800,000. If we were to add the money spent for the same purpose in Ireland, we would find the growth to be absolutely terrifying.

In response to this, English economists would point to the increased consumption of certain goods; however, as we have seen, that increase is maintained by the oppression and ruin of farmers everywhere. The entire system is designed to increase the number of middlemen who stand between the producer and the consumer—people who live off the land and labor of others, weakening the power of the producer while increasing the number of non-productive workers. This is why Ireland is forced to waste more labor every year than would be required to produce all the iron and manufacture all the cotton and wool cloth made in England three times over. The poverty of producers is directly proportional to how much they are forced to trade in the British market, giving up the advantages they would gain if they could freely exercise the power of associating and combining their efforts to make their labor more effective.

The manufacturers of India have been ruined, and that great country is steadily and certainly deteriorating and losing its population. This surprises those in England who are familiar with India's vast resources but do not understand the destructive nature of their own system. The *London Economist* states:

> "Looking at our Indian empire, we cannot help but be struck by the remarkable advantages in climate, soil, and population that it offers to British commerce. At first glance, it seems to provide everything imaginable to encourage nearly unlimited trade. There is experimental hardly one important tropical product consumed in this country—whether as raw material for our factories or as an article of daily use—for which India is not as well or better suited to produce than any other country. Meanwhile, its dense and industrious population would seem to offer an unlimited demand for our manufactured goods. Nor are there any tax-related <note>original: "fiscal"</note> restrictions to block these beneficial results. Indian products have long been sold in our home markets on the most favorable terms, while British goods face only a very moderate duty when entering India. Yet, despite all these advantages, it is a well-known fact—proven by the declining supply of some of the most important Indian products and the stagnant or even falling export of our manufactures to those markets—that serious obstacles exist. Perhaps even more telling is the extremely unprofitable and unsatisfactory results of both the export and import trade with India recently. There are clearly great and serious barriers to achieving the fair expectations we had for our Indian trade."

Another writer <note>The London correspondent of the *National Intelligencer*.</note> describes India as a country whose exports are shrinking rapidly. He notes that sugar production is not increasing, indigo is decreasing, and cotton has been reduced by a third to a half. Government revenue is insufficient. Gujarat <note>original: "Gazerat"</note> and Kutch <note>original: "Cutch"</note>, which once supplied cotton to half the world, have almost stopped producing it. The growing and manufacturing of cotton have vanished from Bengal, which once provided the world with Dacca muslins—the finest fabrics in existence. Cotton fields everywhere have returned to a wild state <note>original: "relapsed into jungle"</note>.

Year after year, we are told of efforts being made to increase the production and improve the quality of Indian cotton. Yet, year after year, the prospect of improvement becomes more remote. This is inevitable, because agricultural improvement is impossible under the current impoverishing system—

<meta>This page continues Henry Charles Carey’s argument that the British economic system impoverishes its colonies. # THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.

This has become as difficult as possible. For a short period, subsidies <note>original: "premiums"</note> were granted for what is called "free sugar"—that is, sugar raised by the impoverished Indian peasant <note>original: "wretched Hindoo"</note> who dies of starvation as a result of the system. While that policy was maintained, its cultivation made some progress; however, since the removal of restrictions on sugar produced by slave labor, everything has been in decline.*

Ireland and India are thus in the same condition. The West Indies are ruined, and Canada, Nova Scotia, and New Brunswick now seek to be annexed by the United States <note>original: "seek annexation"</note> so that they may have protection from a system that is currently ruining them. Landowners everywhere know that the value of their land would double if this change occurred, and the laborer moves south of the border so that he may find employment and good wages, which cannot be found to the north of it. Those who remain north of the border now anxiously seek permission to sell their grain in the U.S. because American protectionism maintains a market that they currently cannot access.

In the current state of things, they have to compete with the low-priced labor of Russia and Poland, and they are ruined by it. They desire, therefore, that their competition should instead be with the protected farmers and laborers of the United States <note>original: "the Union"</note>.

Lord Sydenham, in a letter to Lord John Russell that accompanied his Report on Emigration to Upper Canada, observed:

> "Give me independent farmers <term>yeomen: small-scale farmers who own and cultivate their own land</term>, each with a few hundred pounds, who will buy cleared farms rather than venturing into the wilderness <note>original: "the bush"</note>. I will guarantee them comfort and independence at the end of a couple of years—pigs, pork, flour, potatoes, horses to ride, and cows to milk. *However, you must eat everything you produce, for there isn't a single buyer <note>original: "devil a purchaser"</note> to be found.* Still, the man's needs and those of his family are supplied; he has no rent or taxes to pay, and he ought to be satisfied."

Here is the cause of the desire for annexation that now exists throughout Canada. There are no consumers nearby, and the farmer cannot exchange his corn for cloth or iron. The consequence is that labor and land are almost valueless. It is the same everywhere. Every colony, therefore, desires to separate itself from England, and all would gladly unite with these United States for no other reason than to benefit from protectionist policies.

It must be obvious to anyone who takes the trouble to learn about the condition of the people in the British colonies—who have been forced to endure this system—that the colonial system is rapidly approaching its end. From this, one can see that the independent nations of the world must continue to increase and strengthen their measures of resistance until the system is ended, so that from then on, there may be perfect freedom of trade.

It is "a war upon the labor and capital of the world." Its goal is to prevent the spinner and the weaver from combining their efforts with those of the farmer.

<meta>This page continues Henry Charles Carey’s argument that the British economic system exploits both domestic and foreign labor. ...of the farmer and the planter. This system forces the planter to work in isolation, and therefore inefficiently. He must then give up two-thirds of his crop to maintain the horses, wagons, ships, men, brokers, and merchants whose services would be unnecessary if this system were abolished. Its effects everywhere have been to leave men depressed and poor. Desiring to free themselves from it, our ancestors fought the American Revolution. Now, the Canadians have formed a league for the same purpose, inspired by observing the wonderful economic results that have been achieved here in the United States.

So far, the system has been maintained in England by the power to tax the rest of the world for its support. India contributes three million pounds <note>original: "three millions sterling"</note> every year,* but its ability to pay is gradually diminishing. Canada and the West Indies have paid their share, but the connection with Canada is likely to end soon, and the West Indies are already ruined. The United States is the main support of the system, but that support is gradually being withdrawn. When it is completely gone, the destructive effects of the system upon England herself will become fully obvious. It will then be seen that the wealth of that country is really—to use the words of Thomas Carlyle—nothing but a magnificent "sham." A few people are rich, but the majority are poor, and the total amount of wealth is not actually that great.

The total amount of capital invested in buildings, machinery, and other assets for cotton manufacturing in 1834 was estimated at twenty million pounds <note>original: "twenty millions of pounds sterling"</note>† or less than one hundred million dollars. This is only double what has been spent in the effort to open the anthracite coal mines of Pennsylvania. England also has machinery to produce a large amount of coal and iron, but the same quantity could be produced in this country in a few years without much effort. England has built a considerable number of railroads, but she collapsed <note>Carey likely refers to the "Railway Mania" financial crash of the late 1840s</note> under the effort. Furthermore, railroads are built in England at a much lower cost than here, yet we now have more miles of track in operation.

The "on paper" <note>original: "nominal"</note> cost of her roads is high because the prices paid for land are high, and large sums are paid to lawyers and property transfer agents <term>conveyancers: specialists in the legal transfer of property</term>. However, these are merely transfers of existing property, not true investments. The real investment is only the labor employed in grading the road, building the bridges, and producing the iron; the cost of these per mile is less than for any well-made road in the United States. England's power to make investments of labor is less than half of what the American capacity was from 1844 to 1847. It is less than one-third of what our capacity would be today if the production of coal, iron, and cotton goods had been allowed to increase at the rate it was growing then. Her system tends to enrich only the few, and the result is a show of wealth far, far beyond the reality.

The impoverishing effects of the system were obvious early on. The British sought to explain why it was becoming harder to obtain food, even though the entire focus of their laws was to increase the number of people consuming food and decrease the number of people producing it. This led to the invention of the Malthusian theory of population <note>The theory by Thomas Malthus that population growth will naturally outpace food supply, leading to poverty</note>, which is now half a century old. That was followed by the Ricardo doctrine of Rent <note>David Ricardo’s theory that as population grows, humans are forced to farm lower-quality land, making food more expensive and increasing the wealth of landlords</note>. This doctrine explained the scarcity of food by asserting, as a fact, that men always begin farming on the richest soils first. It claimed that as population increased, they were forced to resort to poorer soils, which gave a constantly diminishing return for their labor. This supposedly produced a constant necessity for people to separate from each other, if they would...

# THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.

...get enough food. Upon this theory is based the whole English political-economic system. First, population is assumed to be too large, even though there is hardly any part of the earth where the labor of the same number of people who now live in England could get even half the same results. Next, it is assumed that men who leave England always move to cultivate rich soils; therefore, every effort is made to force the population to emigrate. Lastly, it is held that their best policy when abroad is to devote all their labor to farming those rich soils and sending the produce to England so it can be turned into cloth and iron. They are warned that any interference with this "perfect freedom of trade" is "a war upon labor and capital."

Colonization is urged by everyone, and all join in the effort to force emigration in the direction needed to create "colonies of customers." It is impossible to read any work on this subject without being struck by how much this "shopkeeping" idea <note>The "shopkeeping idea" refers to the derogatory description of Britain as a "nation of shopkeepers," suggesting its foreign policy was driven purely by commercial interests.</note> dominates. It is seen everywhere. For instance, Hungary was supported in its efforts for independence because it was willing to have free trade, thereby creating a market for British manufactured goods. The tendency of the Ricardo-Malthusian system <term>Ricardo-Malthusian system</term><note>The economic theories of David Ricardo and Thomas Malthus, which suggested that population growth would eventually outpace food production and that land naturally loses productivity over time.</note> to produce extreme selfishness was never more clearly shown than on that occasion.

Unfortunately, this system has no foundation, because the facts are the exact opposite of what Mr. Ricardo stated. Throughout the world and at all times, men have begun farming on the poorer soils. They leave the clearing of fertile river valleys and the draining of swamps to those who come after them. It is actually the increase of population that has allowed men everywhere to bring rich soils under cultivation.* Therefore, food tends to grow faster than the population when there are no outside disruptions. For a population to increase, it is essential that the consumer (the manufacturer) settle near the producer (the farmer). When that does not happen, the inevitable result is a great waste of labor. Constantly farming the land without returning any waste <note>original: "refuse"; here meaning natural fertilizers like manure</note> to it exhausts both the land and its owner. This forces the owner to flee to other poor soils, which increases transportation costs and further reduces the amount of cloth and iron they receive in exchange for their labor.

Thus, we have two things here: first, a system that is unsound and unnatural; and second, a theory invented to explain the poverty and misery that are its necessary results. The miseries of Ireland are blamed on "over-population," even though millions of acres of the richest soil in the kingdom are waiting to be drained so they can become some of the most productive land in the world. Furthermore, the people of Ireland are forced to waste more labor than would be required to pay many times over for all the cloth and iron they consume.† The wretchedness of Scotland is also blamed on over-population...

To *maintain* this system, the price of labor in England must be kept steadily at a point so low that it allows her to underwork the Indian, the German, and the American, despite the added costs of shipping and taxes. To *terminate* it, the price of labor in England must be raised to a level that will stop that competition and force her to grow her own food, leaving other nations to consume their own. This would be the natural result of adopting a protective system, even if it were done by the United States alone.

The cause of the difficulty England now finds herself in is the unnatural imbalance between consumers and producers. Men are "cheap" and therefore undervalued. Create a market for these men, and their value will rise; this effect would be felt in every part of Europe. We have seen that immigration into this country increased from twelve thousand to sixty-seven thousand between 1830 and 1834; that it remained almost stationary from then until 1843; and that in the last four years, it has more than tripled. This would have produced a great demand for labor in various manufacturing branches, road building, land clearing, and house construction. By the year 1839, the number of immigrants would have reached 300,000, and five years later it would have exceeded a million. This growth would have become more rapid every year, because the demand for labor would have increased faster than the supply.

Before this time, the exodus from Great Britain and Ireland alone would have far exceeded half a million people per year. The effect of such a situation can be understood by reading the following article, which I have taken from the London *Times*:

> The flight of a quarter of a million inhabitants from these islands to distant parts of the world in 1847 was one of the most extraordinary events in the history of human migration. The United States gains what we lose.

If applied effectively, the correction will be swift, and from then on, trade can be free everywhere. If free trade is right, then custom-houses <note>A custom-house is a government office where duties or taxes are collected on imported goods.</note> should be abolished. Halfway measures are always wrong.

The direct effect of maintaining the current system—the Tariff of 1846 <note>The Walker Tariff of 1846 reduced tax rates on imports, moving the U.S. closer to free trade.</note>—is to encourage England to continue its efforts to monopolize the American market. In contrast, a return to the Tariff of 1842 <note>The Tariff of 1842 was a highly protective tax on imports that favored domestic manufacturing.</note>, if supported by the entire Union, would lead to results that would force a change in global policy. The direct effect of a total change in our system would be to teach the people of England a vital lesson: that if they "expect to be prosperous and happy, they must seek those blessings through a British policy—by cultivating domestic resources, protecting domestic interests, and strengthening the bonds of harmony through mutual dependence among themselves. They must abandon the vague and deceptive hope of finding compensation in foreign commerce for the destruction of their own domestic consumption."

The harmony of all real interests among nations is perfect. The English system is rotten and unsound; it is harmful to England itself and to the rest of the world. It is the root cause of poverty and misery both at home and abroad. Therefore, the more effective the measures we take to force England to abandon this system, the better it will be for them and for us. The road to absolute freedom of trade lies through perfect protection.

### CHAPTER SIX.

#### HOW PROTECTION AFFECTS COMMERCE.

COMMERCE IS the exchange of equal values. The more goods that are produced, the greater the number of exchanges will be, provided all other factors remain the same. Therefore, commerce tends to grow as production increases.

The "machine" of production is the earth itself. The instrument that makes it produce is man. To encourage a man to work, he must feel confident that he will receive something of equal value in return; the larger that return, the stronger his motivation to work. The more effectively his labor is applied, the larger his production will be, and the larger the reward he will receive for a specific amount of work.

For example, one man grows grain and another produces sugar. Each wants to exchange with the other, trading labor for labor.

* The current price of flour in England is about $5. What the price of pork is likely to be soon can be judged by the following excerpt from today’s newspapers:

A London letter, dated October 12, from a merchant house heavily involved in the trade, says: "We are pleased to provide you with our attached price list, where you will see the comparative imports for the last three years. The current year shows an increase of 25,000 more packages of American bacon than the last. We generally expect that prices must be very low this coming season because of the increase of hogs in Ireland and Germany, and the unusually high production of hogs and all kinds of meat in this country. We are inclined to think that if the same quantity and quality of American meat comes to this market next season as did this past season, half of it will have to be sold for soap-making purposes <note>This implies the meat would be so cheap and the market so oversupplied that it would be sold as industrial fat rather than as food.</note>. You will have heard that our government contract for pork was accepted at 10 shillings per hundredweight <note>original: "10/ per cwt." <meta>This page continues Henry Charles Carey’s argument for economic harmony, illustrating how the unproductive use of labor—such as for military purposes or excessive bureaucracy—diminishes the wealth and commerce of all nations.</meta>

->THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.<-

The quantity of grain that must be given for sugar depends upon the quantity of both that is produced. If the season is favorable for the first, the crop will be large. If it is unfavorable for the second, the crop will be small. In that case, much grain will be given for very little sugar; conversely <note>original: *vice versa*</note>, if the season is favorable for sugar and unfavorable for grain, much sugar will be given for very little grain. In either case, both parties suffer and commerce is diminished. Each person is, therefore, directly interested in doing whatever may be in his power to increase the returns on his neighbor’s labor, thereby increasing the total extent of commerce.

To increase production is, then, to increase commerce. By identifying the circumstances that tend to limit production, we will identify those that tend to limit commerce. To do so, we need only to call upon a few simple laws that may be found in any treatise of natural philosophy <note>In the 19th century, "natural philosophy" referred to the physical sciences, such as physics and logic.</note>. They are as follows:

First: The greater the power—all other circumstances being equal—the greater the effect will be.

The producer of food labors every day and all day. The producer of sugar labors only three days in the week. The quantity of food produced is large, while that of sugar is small. The food-producer gives much food for little sugar—effectively trading much labor for very little labor.

What is true of individuals is equally true of communities. If the community of food-producers works every day, and that of sugar-producers works only three days in the week, the whole of the first group will be taxed because of the indolence <gloss>laziness or inactivity</gloss> of the second, and commerce will be diminished. If the entire community of food-producers works every day, but one half of the iron-producers do not work—or if they apply their labor to tasks other than production—the quantity of iron produced will be small, and much food will be given for very little iron. If the food-producing community could induce the iron-workers to labor every day and all day, there would be more iron to trade for food, commerce would increase, and everyone would profit from it.

By what means could this be accomplished? To find out, we must inquire into the causes of why they work so little. In doing so, we might find that a large proportion of them were perfectly able to work productively but were unwilling to do so. We might find that some of them employed themselves in carrying muskets, casting cannons, building forts and palaces, or constructing and sailing warships; and that others did nothing except devise ways to support themselves and the military classes out of the labor of others. We might find that hosts of others were employed in carrying the products of other people's lands back and forth and keeping accounts of what they did. Thus, one half of the community produced nothing while consuming much.

The other half we might find to consist of men who were sometimes willing to work but unable because they had no work to do; and at other times they were able but unwilling because of the small payment they received. This low pay resulted from the necessity of contributing so large a portion of their earnings to support those who carried muskets, built ships, and kept the accounts. The result might be that we find that although the food-producers gave much, the iron-producers received very little, as the principal part was swallowed up by the intermediate men <note>These "intermediate men" refer to middlemen, such as transporters, retailers, and government bureaucrats, who Carey argues add cost without adding production.</note>, who consumed much while producing nothing. It is obvious that if everyone worked, three times as much iron would be produced, commerce would increase, and the producer of food would obtain far more iron in exchange for far less food. The food-producing community is, therefore, contributing largely toward the support of those in the iron-producing community who are able to work but are not willing to do so; their condition would be improved if they could induce those who are able...

# THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.

and willing to work to come out from among those who are neither able nor willing, leaving the latter class to produce food and iron for themselves. The amount of power applied will increase, and the total product will be greater, while there will be fewer people among whom to divide it. The return on labor will be larger, and the ability to accumulate wealth will be increased.

**Second.** The more directly power is applied, the greater its effect.

The producers of food and iron are far apart, and the labor required to carry out their exchanges is immense. The farmer obtains his iron through the indirect process of growing food for people far away. The ironworker obtains his food by making iron for people far away; many horses, wagons, ships, and men stand between them. The friction <note>In this context, Carey uses "friction" as a metaphor for the waste of energy and resources caused by distance and middle-men.</note> is great and production is small. The goods available to be exchanged <note>original: "equivalents"</note> are few in number, and commerce is limited. The value of a day's labor in either food or iron is small. If the iron producer could move closer to the food producer, the number of horses, wagons, ships, and men standing between them would be reduced, and the number of actual producers would increase. The goods to be exchanged would increase in number, commerce would grow, and the value of a day’s labor would be greater.

**Third.** The more steadily power is applied, the greater its effect. At one moment the wind blows a gale, while at another there is a calm. The steam engine works every day and all day; although the total amount of power applied may be less, the voyage is completed in a shorter time. To ensure the steady application of power, an air-chamber <note>original: "air-chamber" — a pressure-regulating tank used in 19th-century machinery to ensure a smooth, constant flow of energy</note> is provided. Through its aid, the force produced by the piston rod is distributed over the entire period between strokes.

The producer of food is often idle. At other times, he is only moderately employed. During harvest, he is rushed and loses part of his crop for want of help. If he could have the equivalent of an "air-chamber"—allowing his efforts to be spread evenly over the year—the return on his labor would be greatly increased.

The iron producer may work in all seasons, but a large portion of his work—the mining of coal and ore—can be done in advance. When he has a stock on hand, he can pause his operations for a time. If the food producer could persuade the ironworker to live and work nearby, the ironworker could help him gather his crops during the harvest. In return, the farmer could help mine or transport ore and fuel during other parts of the year. The farmer could then cultivate more land; the value of labor in both food and iron would increase, and commerce would expand as more goods become available for exchange.

**Fourth.** The more perfect the machinery, the smaller the quantity required, the less the friction, and the greater the effect. The iron wheels of an engine encounter little friction on an iron rail; the force of a man's hand can move tons there, whereas if that same force were applied to a wooden cartwheel, it could not move a hundred pounds.

The food producer currently obtains small supplies of iron from a distant ironworker in exchange for large quantities of food. He is therefore forced to use wood where he would prefer to use iron. The friction is great, and labor is unproductive. The value of a day's labor is small. If he could persuade the ironworker to move near him, the value of labor would be greatly increased, and he could use iron instead of wood.

**Fifth.** The more durable the machinery, the less labor is required to replace it, and the more labor can be dedicated to producing even more machinery. A wooden post rots and must be replaced, but an iron one lasts almost forever.

The producer of food, living far from the producer of iron, builds ships and...

<meta>This page continues Henry Charles Carey’s argument for economic efficiency through proximity. It explores how distance between producers and the presence of "non-producers" (like soldiers or the idle wealthy) act as a tax on those who actually work, specifically focusing on the relationship between food and iron production.</meta>

# THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.

A farmer fences his land with wooden posts. He spends much of his time repairing and renewing them. If he could convince the producer of iron to live near him, he would help in building furnaces and could then use iron posts. Consequently, the labor that would otherwise be spent renewing old wooden posts could instead be given to creating new machinery of other kinds to aid in production. In this way, the value produced by a day’s labor <note>original: "equivalent of a day’s labour"</note> would be increased.

We see, therefore, that the larger the quantity of labor, the more directly and steadily it is applied, and the more perfect and durable the machinery that assists it, the larger the return on that labor will be, and the greater the number of goods available to be exchanged <note>original: "equivalents to be exchanged"</note>.

Let us now suppose, first, that one community has the power to monopolize the production of iron. Suppose also that many of its members spend all their time in idleness, while others are only occasionally employed—that many spend their time serving in the military <note>original: "carrying muskets on their shoulders"</note>, while many others are dissolute and drunken—and that the result is that the quantity of iron produced is only one-half or one-third of what it would otherwise be. Commerce is merely an exchange of equal values <note>original: "equivalents"</note>, so the quantity of food that must be given for a ton of iron becomes double what it should be. It is obvious that the food-producing community is being taxed to support the idle and worthless members of the iron-producing community.

Second, suppose that, in addition to all this, the iron-producing community is able to force the food-producing community to remain idle when their labor is not needed on the farm, or to lose their crops for want of help during the harvest. It is obvious that this is a second tax imposed for the support of the non-workers among the producers of iron.

Third, suppose that the scarcity of iron forces the food-producing community to use wagons and common dirt roads when they might have had railroads, forcing them to spend ten days of labor on transportation instead of one. Here, again, we have a tax imposed to support the non-workers among the producers of iron. The food producers are forced to transport their products over great distances and are deprived of the power to build the roads that would make it easier.

Fourth, suppose that the producers of food are forced to employ more labor in building ships, wagons, and other perishable machinery than would have been required to build the furnaces and rolling mills—the durable machinery—needed to provide all the iron they consumed. Here we have a fourth tax imposed for the support of the non-workers among the producers of iron.

Each one of these operations tends to diminish the number of goods <note>original: "equivalents"</note> that may be exchanged, the number of trades actually made, and the value of a day’s labor in terms of food, iron, or other comforts and conveniences of life. The result is that the total product of labor is barely one-fifth of what it would be if everyone were productively employed.

With these points established, we may now examine the working of the colonial system <note>The "colonial system" refers to the economic policy where a mother country restricts its colonies to producing raw materials while monopolizing the manufacturing of finished goods.</note>.

Colonists are people who work. Of those who remain behind in the home country, a large portion do not work. Some live in poorhouses, and others live in palaces. Some spend their time in leisure <note>original: "dance and sing"</note>, and others serve in the army <note>original: "carry muskets"</note>. Some build warships, and others sail in them. The actual producers are few. The non-producers are many; yet they must eat, drink, wear clothing, and have houses, and these things must be provided for them by those who work. If everyone worked, the quantity of iron produced would be large, and those who produced food <note>OCR Note: This section was partially obscured by an ink blot.</note> would get much iron in exchange. As few people desire to work, and yet all must eat, the colonial system was invented for the purpose of forcing colonists to give a large amount of food and wool in exchange for a small amount of iron. The consequence has been the same everywhere.

<summary>Carey argues that economic distance and the maintenance of a large class of non-producers (like soldiers and the idle rich) act as a heavy tax on laborers. He identifies the "colonial system" as a mechanism designed to exploit working colonists by forcing them to trade large amounts of raw materials for small amounts of manufactured goods.</summary>

# THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.

While being taxed to support the classes who only spend money, colonists everywhere have been forced to waste a great deal of labor, to work with inefficient machinery, and to trade more of their products for the use of temporary equipment (like ships and wagons) than it would have cost to create tools that would last almost forever. As a result, production is low. The goods available for trade <note>original: "equivalents to be exchanged"</note> are decreasing in number. Commerce is dying.

The Irishman is forced to waste much of his labor.* He works with poor machinery. He gives up half of what he produces just to pay for the use of wagons and ships to transport it. He survives on his potato crop and lives in rags. He has nothing left to trade.† He flees to America, and because of this, the number of trades made within and from Ireland is diminished.

The Indian <note>original: "Hindoo"</note> flees from the valleys and plains to the hills to escape this system. Once in the hills, he finds no demand for his labor except in cultivating his small plot of land. He works with poor tools, and his meager harvest of fifty pounds of cotton per acre is transported to Manchester <note>the center of the English textile industry</note>. It is then sent back to him as cloth, but he only receives one pound of cloth for every ten pounds of cotton he sent. Thus, he gives away nine-tenths of his labor to pay for ships and wagons—temporary machinery—when one-fifth of that labor would have done the work at home if he had been able to have permanent machinery <note>such as local factories</note>. He flees again, or he dies of famine and disease, or he sells himself into slavery to go to Demerara <note>a colony in modern-day Guyana</note>; in this way, the number of trades within and from India is also diminished.

Everywhere, people are fleeing from British commerce, which pursues them wherever they go. Having exhausted the people of the lowlands of India, it follows them as they retreat toward the strongholds of the Himalayas. Afghanistan is invaded <note>referring to the First Anglo-Afghan War</note>, while Sindh and the Punjab are conquered. Provinces in Siam <note>modern-day Thailand</note> are added to this "free trade" empire, and war and devastation are brought to China <note>referring to the Opium Wars</note> so that the Chinese can be forced to pay for the use of British ships instead of building their own looms. The Irishman flees to Canada, but the system follows him there; he does not feel safe until he is within the United States <note>original: "this Union"</note>. The Englishman and the Scotsman try Southern Africa, and from there they flee to the even more distant Australia <note>original: "New Holland"</note>, Tasmania <note>original: "Van Diemen's Land"</note>, or New Zealand. The further they fly, the more they must rely on ships and other temporary machinery, the less consistently they can apply their efforts, the lower their productivity becomes, and the fewer goods they have to trade. And yet, we are told to look at the growth of the shipping industry—caused by these very desperate circumstances—as evidence of a prosperous commerce!

The British system is built upon cheap labor, by which is meant low

<meta>This page continues the argument that protectionism increases the value of labor and encourages local production, contrasting it with the British "free-trade" system that centralizes manufacturing and impoverishes distant producers in Ireland and India.</meta>

# THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.

This system results in low-priced and worthless labor.* Its effect is to cause labor to become more low-priced and worthless from day to day, thereby destroying the production upon which commerce must be based. The object of protection <note>economic policies, such as tariffs, designed to encourage domestic industry</note> is to produce "dear labor"—that is, high-priced and valuable labor. Its effect is to cause labor to increase in value from day to day and to increase the goods available for trade <note>original: "equivalents to be exchanged"</note>, leading to a great increase in commerce.

The goal of what is now called "free-trade" is to secure for the people of England the continued existence of their *monopoly* on machinery. By using this monopoly, Ireland and India have been ruined and their commerce paralyzed. Protection seeks to *break down this monopoly* and to cause the loom and the anvil <note>symbols of manufacturing and industry</note> to take their natural places beside the food and the cotton <note>symbols of agriculture</note>, so that production may be increased and commerce may revive. We may now examine how far it has tended to produce that effect here.

Before the passage of the Tariff of 1828, our trade in iron amounted to only **25** pounds per person. By **1832**, it had increased to **46** pounds per person. Commerce had thus grown. From **1834** to **1841**, it averaged **45** pounds per person. Commerce was stagnant. In **1841** and **1842**, it fell to **38** pounds. Commerce had declined under what was called free-trade. From **1844** to **1847**, the goods available for trade in iron had increased to **97** pounds per person. Commerce had grown under protection. Today, it is **73** pounds per person. Commerce has fallen with the reduction of protection. If we turn now to coal, cotton, woolens, ships, or railroads, we find similar facts everywhere. The number of exchanges grows under a system that looks toward the elevation of the laborer. It diminishes under a system that looks for growth through the depression of the laborer. The interests of commerce are therefore in perfect harmony with those of manufacturing and agriculture.

The one system repels population. The other attracts it, and hence it—

* <note>The poor silk weaver described in the following paragraph, which I take from the London *Spectator*, is typical of this system. What he needs is to move his labor from what is here called "production"—which is really only the processing of others' products—to the only thing that can truly be called production: increasing the *quantity* of goods to be consumed. He merely changes their form from raw silk to silk cloth. If his labor were employed on any of the many millions of acres of rich but uncultivated land within the kingdom, he would obtain more and better food at a lower cost of labor. He could then eat better and have more to offer in exchange. Commerce would then grow.</note>

# THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.

...is that we see the entire population of Europe eager to reach our shores. If we abolish protection <note>economic policies like tariffs that favor domestic industry</note>, immigration will cease and commerce will decline because there will be less cloth and iron to be traded for labor. If we make protection complete and permanent, immigration will increase rapidly because there will be more cloth and iron to be traded for labor.

If Ireland were free today, she would establish protectionist policies and thus stop mass emigration. Food, cloth, and iron would become more abundant, and commerce would grow. If Canada were independent, she would establish protection, and she would then retain the immigrants coming from Ireland or England. If India were independent, she too would establish protection, and the cultivation of cotton would be resumed on the rich lands of Bengal. In all these cases, production would increase, and the power to maintain commerce would grow. The people of the United States are the best customers for the people of England because they are, to some degree, protected against the exhaustion caused by the British system. Ireland cannot buy; she is reduced to begging. If she were independent, she would manufacture iron, and then she could buy fine cloths, silks, books, and pictures. The properly understood interests of all nations are in perfect harmony with each other.

The proclaimed goal of free trade is to increase commerce, yet commerce withers under it. Ireland now consumes only one pound of cotton per person. If you move an Irishman here to America, he will consume twelve pounds. Thus, 700,000 Irish people here would create more trade between cotton producers and consumers than is currently maintained with all eight million people in Ireland. If Ireland were free, she would adopt protection and trade would grow, for she would then need six pounds of cotton per person. The commerce of the *Zollverein* <note>The German Customs Union, which created a free-trade zone among German states while protected by a common external tariff</note> has grown under protection. The people of Germany now consume two pounds of cotton for every one they consumed before. Conversely, the commerce of India diminishes with every step toward what is called "free trade." The cotton producers on the lowlands of Bengal could once obtain four times the iron for a day's labor compared to what they get now, since the cultivators have been driven to seek out high and poor-quality lands.

The so-called free trader says to the farmer: "You can get English iron in New York for thirty bushels of wheat, but you must hand over ten bushels to the Treasury for permission to make the exchange. If you take a ton of American iron, you must give the producer forty bushels; therefore, you are being taxed ten bushels to support the iron manufacturer." 

However, if we abolish protection, we will have more food to sell abroad and more iron to buy abroad, which will require more wagons and ships. It will then take sixty bushels of wheat—perhaps even a hundred—to pay for a single ton of iron. The amount exchanged would then fall to 20 pounds per person, and commerce would be diminished.

The farmer has a choice: he can give *thirty* bushels to support people who "dance and sing and live in palaces" <note>likely referring to the British aristocracy</note> and those who carry muskets <note>the British military</note>, or he can give *ten* for the maintenance of the government under which he lives. The more he gives to the former, the more (and for longer) he must continue to give; the poorer he must become, and the less power he will have to maintain commerce. That this is the case will be obvious from examining the facts given in the last chapter. In the years from 1827 to 1834, 275 million pounds of cotton would have purchased 1,250,000 tons of iron. In 1845–46, it required 600 million pounds to pay for only 1,200,000 tons. What happened to the difference? Were the English miners better clothed? It was made known to the world that men and women worked together in the mines completely naked. Was the condition of the people any better? On the contrary, Ireland was rapidly becoming a massive poorhouse <note>a government-run institution where the destitute were required to live and work</note>, and the poor-rates <note>local taxes collected to provide relief for the poor</note> of England were fast advancing to the level they have now reached: £8,000,000 per year. 

Where, then, did the difference go? The question may be answered by pointing to the vast increase of public spending over the last fifteen years, during which the number of men who carry muskets and build warships has been so greatly increased. It can be seen in the innumerable and expensive commissions established to investigate the causes of distress and poverty; in the great fortunes of bankers and successful speculators; and in men like George Hudson, the "railroad king" <note>George Hudson (1800–1871) was an English financier who became immensely wealthy through unscrupulous railroad speculation before his eventual downfall</note>. It is visible in the large number of people who realized immense fortunes during the recent railroad craze as engineers, solicitors, counselors, and parliamentary agents, and in the many others who grow wealthy at the people's expense. The capacity for production is diminishing, and the few become richer as the many become poorer. With every step in this process, the ability to maintain commerce decreases, for as the people become poorer, their power to produce goods to be given in exchange becomes more and more limited.

Whatever event tends to diminish production—whether it be wars, revolutions, the increase of standing armies and fleets without actual war, or the growth of inequality where the few become richer and the many poorer—the effect is to impose a tax upon the consumers of the goods whose production is being restricted. Under a system of true free trade, the majority of this "tax" would be paid by the participants themselves, because the immediate effect of such events would be to stimulate other nations to work harder to fill the void that had been created. However, under the current system, which gives one nation <note>referring to Great Britain</note> a monopoly on the machinery for processing the products of other nations, a large portion of this burden can be, and is, thrown onto those other nations. In this way, they are forced to contribute heavily toward the maintenance of that entire class of people, both poor and rich, who prefer to live by the labor of others.

We have seen that the quantity of cotton consumed in 1845 and 1846 averaged 596,000,000 pounds, that the price of gray cloth <note>original: "gray cloth"—unfinished, unbleached fabric straight from the loom</note> was 6 shillings 7 pence, and that 34,700,000 pieces delivered in Liverpool would have been required to pay for the raw cotton also delivered in Liverpool—leaving all shipping costs, charges, etc., for the plantation owner to pay.

In England, we may estimate it at 3,000 pounds per worker, which would require 200,000 workers to process the whole quantity. The result is that cotton, which yields the planter only five cents per pound on his plantation and is sold in Liverpool at four and a half pence per pound, is eventually sold by the mill owner at a shilling per pound.* Yet, the payment for the labor used to convert that cotton into cloth is not even two pence, and probably little more than a single penny per pound. It is so clearly in the interest of mill owners to take large shares for the use of their machinery that there is no doubt they will continue this course. They will make every effort necessary to keep control of the cotton market for themselves. 

That control depends on maintaining a monopoly on machinery. The moment that monopoly is broken—and machinery becomes so common elsewhere that the planter no longer feels the necessity of *seeking* a market—the power of this "taxation" will vanish. Cloth will become cheap, consumption will triple, and the producer will grow rich.

about £5,000,000

At that rate, 450,000 tons would amount to £4,950,000. If the account were calculated more accurately, the total would probably not even reach 400,000 tons.

To add that quantity of iron in a single year to the production of this country would not require the slightest extra effort. And yet, we see here that in return for it, small as it was, England obtained in 1847 more than one-fourth of the products of the labor of all the sugar-producing countries on the globe! A very brief examination of this statement shows how the people of the world are taxed to support iron manufacturers, railroad speculators, and the host of middlemen who are so numerous in England. We have seen that iron was much more expensive in 1845–46 than it was from 1827 to 1834. In opposition to this unquestionable fact, the late Secretary of the Treasury <note>This likely refers to Robert J. Walker, who served as US Secretary of the Treasury from 1845 to 1849 and was a noted advocate for free trade.</note> asserted that "experience proves that from improved machinery, new inventions, and reduced cost of production, foreign articles are constantly diminishing in price."* In contrast to his claim, we have the fact that iron was not only more expensive, but cotton was cheaper. A person who traded two pounds of cotton in 1845–46 for less iron than he could have obtained for just one pound in 1833–34 realized that the price of iron was actually increasing, not decreasing. He found it much harder than in the earlier period to obtain what he needed to build machinery. His "wages," when measured in iron, were thus reduced, and his ability to accumulate capital was diminished. However, if he had traded directly on the spot with a local producer of iron, both would have prospered. 

Nevertheless, we are told by the same government authority that the necessary consequence of the protective system <term>The "protective system" refers to using tariffs on imported goods to encourage domestic manufacturing.</term> is that "wages throughout the country became lower than before, because the total profits of the nation's capital, engaged in all its industry, is diminished."† These theorists believe it is most profitable to trade with nations where labor is cheap; they argue that the lower the cost of labor there, "the greater is our gain in the exchange." In reality, the labor of Great Britain is cheaper than it was fifteen years ago because it is less productive. The less their people produce, the less they have to give us in exchange for our products. Consequently, we end up giving more cotton for less iron. 

If all the people of England were fully employed, they would produce far more cloth and iron. Wages there would then rise, and the amount of iron we receive for a bale of cotton would double. The more productively the people of the world are employed, the greater the value of their labor will be, and the larger the quantity of good things we shall receive in exchange for our own labor. Conversely, the larger their armies, the more destructive their wars, the more frequent their revolutions, and the more their non-producing classes—such as those in extreme poverty <note>original: "paupers"</note> and the nobility—abound, the lower the value of labor will be abroad. This weakens their power to maintain trade and reduces the advantage for those who trade with them. The less silk or iron they produce, the more food or cotton we must give them to get the same amount in return.

The document I referred to above belongs to the "school of discords." This is the school of thought that teaches one to buy in the cheapest market and sell in the dearest, regardless of the consequences. It sees a great advantage in reducing the price of cotton grown by the poor Indian <note>original: "Hindoo"</note> to a penny a pound, indifferent to the fact that famine and plague follow such a system. The policy that creates a *necessity* for depending on trade with people poorer than ourselves tends to reduce our own wages to their level and diminishes commerce. 

On the other hand, a policy that gives us the *power* to trade with nations that might be richer than ourselves would tend to raise our wages to their level. By bringing the Irishman here to America and enabling him to trade with us directly, we raise him to our level as a producer. By exporting our people to Ireland and forcing them to trade there, we would sink their wages to the level of that country. The policy that brings people here and raises them in the scale of civilization is the one that promotes commerce. The policy that causes them to return home—thereby stopping the tide of immigration and preventing progress—is the one that diminishes commerce.

† Ibid. <note>short for ibidem, meaning "in the same place" as the previous citation.</note>

# CHAPTER SEVENTH.

### HOW PROTECTION AFFECTS THE QUANTITY AND QUALITY OF THE MACHINERY OF PRODUCTION.

The object we seek to accomplish is the improvement of the human condition. The way to achieve this is by increasing a person's productive power. The more food a man can raise, the more and better food he can consume. This leaves a larger surplus that can be dedicated to purchasing clothing, educating his family, expanding his house, or improving his machinery. Additionally, it provides him with more leisure time to devote to improving his ways of thinking.

The better his machinery is, and the more easily it can be obtained, the greater his production will be. Machinery consists mainly of iron. Therefore, the more easily iron can be obtained, the more rapidly production will increase, leading to the improvement of the physical, moral, intellectual, and political capacities of humanity. Iron is the great instrument of civilization.

The more durable a person's work is, the faster his capital will increase. Where iron is abundant, it is used instead of wood in building houses—making them safe from fire—and in constructing ships and roads, which improves transportation. With every such step, his powers of production are increased.

To obtain iron easily, a person must have access to fuel at a moderate cost of labor—in other words, cheaply. Things are "cheap" or "expensive" not based on their money-price, but on the amount of labor required to obtain them. For example, the money-price of grain in Ireland is less than in England, yet the cost in labor is so high that the poor farmer must eat even lower-quality potatoes. The money-price of coal may be less than it was two years ago, yet consumption has decreased because the labor-price has risen. The money-price of cotton in parts of India where it is grown is about two cents per pound, yet the man who grows it covers his loins with a rag and does without clothing for the rest of his body because the labor-price of cloth is so high. Where production is small, the labor-price of goods is high, and consumption is very small; conversely, where production is large, the labor-price of goods is low, and consumption is great.

Large-scale production requires good and cheap machinery, and to obtain such machinery, we must have good and cheap fuel. An abundance of fuel and iron is the foundation upon which civilization must rest. Therefore, whatever policy best facilitates the acquisition of these materials is the one that will most rapidly increase the productive power of man and his capacity for improvement.

Iron ore and fuel exist throughout this country in a profusion unknown elsewhere. Nowhere else in the world can they be so easily obtained or so easily brought together for production. The anthracite <term>Anthracite is a hard, compact variety of coal that has a high luster and burns with a clean flame, making it highly efficient for industrial processing.</term> of Pennsylvania is the best fuel in the world, and it can be mined as cheaply as any other. It is layered <note>original: "interstratified"</note> with iron ore in great abundance. Limestone also abounds near the great Schuylkill <note>The Schuylkill region in Pennsylvania was a primary center for the American coal and iron industries during the mid-1800s.</note> region and can be obtained with as little labor as anywhere in the world. The ores and fuel of Ohio and the West are described this way:

> "The beds of ore are easy to access and are found alongside the materials necessary for their reduction <note>In metallurgy, "reduction" refers to the process of smelting ore to extract the pure metal.</note>; they cannot fail to be immense sources of wealth. Most of the workable beds of ore are located above the first workable bed of coal. The amount of workable ore in Muskingum County is estimated at 153,600,000 cubic yards, which, when smelted, will yield about..."

...half that many tons in pig iron <note>original: "pigs"; crude iron castings produced by smelting ore in a blast furnace</note>. We do not need to discuss specific locations now. Mr. Briggs concludes his report on iron ore as follows: — "A very conservative estimate of the amount of high-quality iron ore in the region explored this season is equivalent to a solid, continuous layer <note>original: "stratum"</note> sixty miles long, sixty miles wide, and three feet thick. One square mile of this layer—roughly three million cubic yards—will yield the same number of tons of pig iron when melted. This number, multiplied by the number of square miles in the layer, equals 1,080,000,000 tons. From just three counties, this would yield 400,000 tons of iron annually for 2,700 years—surpassing the greatest amount produced in England before the year 1829." — *Ohio Paper.*

"The country bordering on Carp River (Lake Superior) is perhaps the richest on Earth for iron ore. The 'Jackson Iron Company,' which we had the pleasure of visiting, is located about twelve miles from the Lake Shore and about three miles from the iron mountains. One of these mountains belongs to the aforementioned company, and the other to the 'Cleveland Iron Company.' These two mountains, we were informed, are by far the richest and most valuable iron deposits ever discovered—though it is said that iron ore is found spread across some seventeen or eighteen townships between Lake Superior and Green Bay. This ore contains 75 to 90 percent pure iron. The metal made from it by the Jackson Company has been subjected to the most rigorous tests and proves to be the highest quality iron made anywhere in the world, having been drawn down to the thickness of No. 36 wire. The Jackson Iron Company (under the superintendence of P. M. Everett, Esq., who we understand is now leaving and being succeeded by Czar Jones, Esq., of Jackson) has been producing iron for about twelve to eighteen months." — *Lake Superior News.*

Given these facts, one might assume that the consumption of fuel and iron would be high, but that has not been the case.

In 1810, domestic manufacturing amounted to only 50,000 tons. By 1828, it had reached 100,000 tons. In 1818, 1819, and 1820, it may have reached 70,000 tons, though even that is very doubtful. The total importation of bar and pig iron in those years was 40,000 tons, or 13,333 tons per year. The import of manufactured iron goods may have been half as much again. This would result in a total consumption of 90,000 tons (or 200,000,000 pounds) for a population of 9,400,000 people. This is just over 20 pounds per person. Therefore, the average consumption in the Union for all purposes—house-building, ship-building, agricultural tools, and machinery—was equal to little more than twice the weight of an axe per person per year. Yet there existed then, as there exists now, the capacity to produce iron at a lower labor cost than anywhere else in the world.

If we wish to understand the cause of this, it can be found in the fact that until the American Revolution, the manufacturing of iron—even as simple as horseshoe nails—was prohibited by British law. There was no incentive to build works for smelting ore when the pig iron could not be used. Consequently, the industry did not grow naturally, while England's industry was forced forward. When the day of nominal independence arrived, real economic independence was still far off. Under the various tariffs from 1789 to 1812, the duties <note>taxes on imported goods</note> were ad valorem <note>original: "ad-valorem"; a tax based on the value of the goods</note>, starting at 7.5 percent and gradually rising until they reached 17.5 percent before the War of 1812. 

The production of iron had made no progress, and the entire supply had to be sought from abroad; as a result, iron was scarce and expensive. The Embargo, the Non-Intercourse acts <note>economic sanctions during the Napoleonic Wars</note>, and the War of 1812 raised the price so high that many furnaces were built. However, with the return of peace, the duties on manufactured iron were reduced to 20 percent. The demand for domestic pig iron consequently dropped. The price in Pittsburgh, which had been $60, fell in 1820 and 1821 to $20, resulting in the ruin of nearly everyone involved in its production. This, however, was not a direct result of the duty reduction itself. At that very time, the duty on pig iron was $10 and on bar iron $30 per ton; thus, the selling price in Pittsburgh was *far less than the cost of shipping and the duty on imported iron.* Iron was nominally cheap, but...

...truly expensive—so expensive that consumption was crippled. Wages were at $6 per month, and wheat sold for 25 cents a bushel. This produced such a total inability to afford this most necessary of all commodities that, although the iron furnaces were closed, the total import of pig iron <note>original: "pig and rolled iron"; crude iron and iron that has been processed through rollers into sheets or bars</note> in 1821 was only 4,000 tons—or one ton for every 2,500 people. It is doubtful if the consumption that year exceeded six pounds per person. We see, therefore, that the power to import disappeared along with the power to produce, as has been shown to be the case on other occasions.

Who, then, were the losers by the greatly increased difficulty of obtaining this great instrument of civilization? To answer this question, we must first ask: who are the primary consumers of iron? Farmers and planters constitute three-quarters of the nation's population. If the loss were distributed equally, that portion of the loss would fall on them; but we shall find upon investigation that the entire burden must fall upon them, the producers of everything we consume.

The farmer needs iron for his spades and plows, his shovels and his pitchforks, his <term>trace-chains</term> <note>chains used to attach a draft animal to a wagon or plow</note> and horseshoes, and his wagon wheels; he needs it for his house, his barn, and his stable. He also needs it for his timber. If iron is abundant, saws are easily obtained, and a sawmill is established nearby. He can then have his timber converted into planks at a lower labor cost than was previously required just to haul the logs to a distant sawmill. He gains access to affordable mill-saws. 

If iron is abundant, a <term>grist-mill</term> <note>a mill used to grind grain into flour</note> comes to his neighborhood. Now he can have his grain turned into flour while giving up less grain as payment than was previously consumed by the horses and men used to carry it to a distant mill. If iron is abundant, spades and picks are easily obtained, the roads are repaired, and he travels more easily to distant markets. If iron becomes even more plentiful, the railroad enables him to transport himself, his turnips, and his potatoes with increased ease to markets from which he was previously excluded by the cost of transportation—except for small, high-value items like wheat and cotton. 

If iron is abundant, the woolen mill arrives, and his wool is processed <note>original: "converted"</note> on the spot by men who consume his cabbages, his veal, and his milk right there. These workers perform the manufacturing in exchange for services and goods that would have gone to waste if they had not been consumed in this way. At every step, he obtains the use of iron more cheaply—that is, at a lower cost of labor. If iron is abundant, the cotton mill now arrives; the iron railroad brings the cotton, and the farmer's sons and daughters gain the use of iron spindles and iron looms. These machines allow them to clothe themselves at one-twentieth of the labor cost required only twenty years earlier. Instead of receiving one yard of cotton in exchange for two bushels of corn, one bushel of corn now pays for six yards of cloth—and it is in this way that the farmer grows wealthy.

A careful examination of society will satisfy any inquirer that everyone engaged in transportation, <term>conversion</term> <note>the process of manufacturing raw materials into finished goods</note>, and exchange is merely an agent of the producers and lives off the commodities the producers create. The producers grow wealthy or remain poor based exactly on whether they are required to employ more or fewer people to facilitate their exchanges. The farmer who is forced to use a distant mill must employ many people, horses, and wagons to turn his grain into flour, and consequently, his land is of little value. Bring the mill close to him, and a single horse and cart, used occasionally, will do the work. The farmer who employs the people of England to produce his iron is forced to use the services of numerous people, ships, wagons, and horses to assist in the work. Bring the furnace to his side so his neighbor can produce his iron, and he and his sons can do much of the work themselves, providing...

...timber, ore, and the use of horses, wagons, etc., when they are not needed on the farm.

A farmer in Tennessee sends 300 bushels of corn to market, for which he receives in return one ton of iron. While the money-cost of this iron is $60, the actual labor-cost to the farmer is the cultivation of ten acres of land. If he could follow his corn, he would find that the men who mine and process his iron receive only 30 or 40 bushels of it. The remaining 260 or 270 bushels are swallowed up by the numerous transporters and middlemen <note>original: "exchangers"</note> who stand between himself and the men he thus employs. 

If, however, he could bring those men to his side—giving them double wages, say sixty bushels of corn—he would be a gainer to the extent of 240 bushels. While he has to give 300 bushels, his iron is expensive, and he can use very little. When he obtains it for 60 bushels, it is cheap, and he uses much. His production increases, and his ability to use iron increases along with it. Consequently, the demand for ironworkers increases, and all obtain food more readily; the result is that they have more to spare for clothing and for other comforts or luxuries of life.

Whenever there is a surplus of any commodity in the market, the price of the entire supply tends to fall to the level of the lowest price required to find purchasers. As long as we continue to have a surplus of food for export, the price of the whole must continue to be regulated by the price obtained for the trivial quantity sent to Liverpool. <note>Liverpool was the primary hub for American agricultural exports to Great Britain at the time.</note>

Whenever it is necessary to resort to distant places to procure even a small part of the supply of any commodity, the price of the whole is regulated by the cost of obtaining this last small portion. In 1847, we produced 800,000 tons of iron, yet the demand was so far ahead of the supply that we were obliged to import a small quantity. The price at which that import was obtained fixed the price for the entire 800,000 tons. The farmer is thus always selling in the cheapest market and buying in the most expensive one. The labor and capital required to produce a ton of iron are not as great as those needed for the production of forty bushels of corn, and yet he gives three hundred bushels for it because of the quantity of labor wasted in transporting the corn to the man who produces the iron.

The prices of labor and iron are both higher here than in Europe, and therefore we import both. The price of food is lower than in Europe, and therefore we export it. Whenever the import of labor <note>Meaning the immigration of workers</note> is sufficient to do away with the necessity for exporting food as a raw commodity, food prices will be high, and we shall cease to export it. Whenever the import of men is sufficient to do away with the necessity for importing iron, the price of iron will be low, and we shall essentially export food in the form of iron. Through this same operation, the farmer will be enabled to obtain high prices for his grain and to buy his iron cheaply. He will then buy in the cheapest market and sell in the dearest, and the value of his labor will be increased.

We have seen that in the period between 1821 and 1829—which includes the six years following the passage of the Act of 1824—the consumption of iron rose to about 25 pounds per person. In the three following years, under the Tariff of 1828, it rose to 47 pounds. By the Compromise Act <note>The Compromise Tariff of 1833, which sought to gradually reduce tariff rates</note>, the duty on railroad iron was abolished, and the consequence was that the power of consumption diminished, remaining at an average of only 46 pounds for the next nine years. Under the strictly revenue-focused clauses of the tariff, it fell to 38 pounds, which was less than the consumption level of eleven years prior. By 1846, it had risen to 94 pounds, and in the following year, it rose to 98. Who were the people who benefited by this change? Let us see. The abundance of iron facilitated the opening of coal mines by means of steam engines and other machinery, and the making of roads, by means of which coal and food...

...and timber could be transported to market, which greatly reduced the number of intermediaries <note>original: "persons intermediate"</note> between the producer and the consumer. The abundance of fuel and iron made it easier to build steamboats, significantly lowering the cost of shipping goods to and from market. It also facilitated the construction of mills and furnaces, where farmers and planters could conduct their own trades <note>original: "exchanges"</note> directly. Meanwhile, the increased ease of obtaining plows and harrows, spades and axes, helped increase the productivity of labor, leading to a large increase in the quantity of goods to be traded. In this way, the entire benefit of being able to obtain iron more easily went to the land’s cultivators—the farmers and planters.

But why should protection have been necessary to produce this result? In addition to the general reasons already mentioned, we must consider those specifically related to iron. In a table now before me,* the English prices of "merchant-bar" iron <note>Standard iron bars sold for further manufacturing.</note> are recorded as follows:

Here we see prices ranging from £4 10s (equivalent to $21.60) to £15 ($72), and every price in between. Why should these enormous variations occur? It costs no more labor to produce iron at one time than at another. A worker who mined a ton of ore or coal in 1832, when the price was £5 10s, could mine more than a ton in 1846 because machinery had been greatly improved; and yet the price was £9 then.

A bad season may hinder the growth of grain or cotton, and the "rot" <note>This refers to the potato blight (Phytophthora infestans) which caused the Great Famine in the 1840s.</note> may destroy the potato crop, thereby reducing the supply and causing a great increase in price. However, neither food nor cotton is subject to the extreme and sudden changes we see in iron, which ought to be perfectly stable. These changes are caused by the unsound nature of the British economic system and the perpetual fluctuations that result from it. The consequence is a recurring cycle of ruin for everyone in other countries engaged in iron manufacturing. In 1816, prices were high, and furnaces were built. In 1821, they were low, and iron-masters were ruined everywhere. In 1825, they were high, and furnaces were put back into operation. In 1831, furnace owners were ruined again. In 1836, prices were high, and in 1842, they were low, with the same cycle repeating on both occasions. So again in 1846, furnaces were built, and now, in 1849, they are being closed.

The result of this is that iron manufacturing throughout the country is in a primitive <note>original: "barbarous"</note> condition. Small, inefficient furnaces are common, where a great deal of labor produces very little iron. Every time England is forced to pause its efforts to maintain a monopoly on the production of this vital commodity, we can see the industry moving toward the land where alone it can be produced at a low labor cost—the land where ore, coal, and limestone are found layered together <note>original: "interstratified"</note>. The industry would have arrived there long ago if not for our frequent changes in national policy.

# THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.

It takes very little investigation to satisfy any inquirer that iron consumption in the United States was at its lowest precisely when prices in England were lowest, in 1822 and 1843. Today, consumption is again diminishing rapidly as our furnaces are being closed and their owners ruined. *The power to consume declines daily.* In another year or two, the price abroad will be high again, but by then it will take significant time to get the old furnaces back into operation, and even longer to build new ones. Iron-making is like buying lottery tickets: the losses <note>original: "blanks"</note> are far more numerous than the prizes. Once that time arrives, pig iron may again reach $40 and bar iron $80 per ton.

As long as a nation depends on England for any portion of its supply, prices will continue to be this unstable. Consequently, the consumption of this vital material and the facilities for producing it will remain limited. This entire deficiency falls on the producers of food, wool, or cotton, for it is the producer who pays the costs of transportation, processing <note>original: "conversion"</note>, and trade. Consumption for the current year will likely not exceed 700,000 tons, because domestic production has greatly diminished, and the stock on hand has increased to nearly the same amount as our imports from abroad. 

There is strong reason to believe that production will be even further diminished next year. In contrast, there can be no doubt that if the system of 1842 <note>The Tariff of 1842 was a protectionist measure that significantly raised duties on imported goods to favor domestic industry.</note> had remained unchanged, domestic production would have reached 1,300,000 tons (or 3,000,000,000 pounds), which is 125 pounds per person. Indeed, the increase in 1846 alone was almost equal to the total consumption per person in 1842–43. From that point forward, the price would have been regulated by the cost of production here at home, rather than by the fluctuating policies of foreign nations. Prices would have decreased daily as the machinery of production improved. 

The goal of the "colonial system" is to increase the number of transporters, processors, and traders <note>original: "exchangers"</note>, all of whom must be supported by the labor of farmers and planters. The goal of the protective system is to diminish that number. The question now to be settled is whether the laborers—the men who produce everything we consume—or the traders shall be the masters. Were the traders to succeed, we would have "freedom of trade" only in the sense that we would be compelled to forgo the cooperation <note>original: "association"</note> of men with their fellow-men for the improvement of their condition. The result would be the shutdown of every furnace in the Union. Everyone currently engaged in mining coal and ore would be forced to resort to farming <note>original: "raising of food"</note>. Food prices would then drop because of the surplus of farmers, while iron would become much more expensive. The cost of iron in terms of labor would increase so much that consumption would fall back to the levels seen in 1821. 

In contrast, perfect protection would soon quadruple our production. Vast numbers of people would mine iron and coal instead of raising food, which would make food prices higher and more profitable for the farmer. The labor-cost of iron would be reduced, and its consumption would increase. It is through the use of iron that production is increased, trade is made easier, manufacturing is improved, land value increases, and farmers and planters are made wealthy.

---

From 1829 to 1832, domestic production increased by about fifty percent. During that entire period, however, the Union was agitated by threats of nullification <note>The Nullification Crisis occurred when South Carolina declared federal tariffs unconstitutional and void.</note> and secession <note>original: "disunion"</note>. Consequently, there was no motivation to invest the large amounts of capital required for the cheap production of this important commodity in furnaces or rolling mills. From 1842 to 1847, production tripled, and perhaps even quadrupled. During the period in between, it remained almost stationary.

I propose to inquire what the result would have been if production had continued to increase at a rate of only 15 percent per year, and then to examine what the effect would have been on the working men, the planters, and...
