It will be seen that the highest increase of any year in this table is scarcely more than the growth that actually took place between 1843 and 1847, when everything had to be recommenced after a state of almost utter ruin. What amount of investment would have been required to produce this quantity of <term>pig metal</term> <note>original: "pig-metal"; crude iron cast into blocks called "pigs" for further processing.</note>? A furnace capable of producing 5,000 tons per year <note>The original text says "per week," but the author's subsequent math (requiring 240 furnaces to produce an additional 1.2 million tons) indicates he meant 5,000 tons per year.</note> may cost $30,000. We currently produce 800,000 tons. To have reached 2,000,000 tons would have required building 240 more furnaces than we actually built. Their construction would have cost $8,000,000. This is far less than the amount spent during that same period *in building packet ships* <note>original: "packet ships"; fast ships that sailed on a regular schedule carrying mail, passengers, and freight.</note> to run between New York, London, and Liverpool—setting aside all other expenditures on shipping, whether for building or operating them. Those ships have disappeared or will disappear, leaving nothing behind. The furnaces, however, would still exist. 

At one establishment in Pennsylvania, there are six furnaces capable of producing 800 tons of metal per week, or 41,600 tons per year. The cost of these may have been $200,000. To build ships capable of transporting that same quantity of iron would require an investment of at least $750,000. At the end of a few years, all of that shipping capital would be lost to wear and tear, while the furnaces might last for centuries. The tendency of the <term>colonial system</term> <note>A system where a nation exports raw materials and imports finished goods, which Carey argues forces a country to waste money on transportation rather than permanent production.</note> is thus to force capital into temporary machinery like ships, whereas the object of **protection** is to enable the owner of capital to invest it in something permanent.

It will be asked: what would we have done with all this iron? In answer, I say that every person is a consumer to the full extent of their own production. The man who made the iron would have needed food, fuel, and clothing. The man who mined the fuel would have needed iron, food, and clothing. The man who raised the food would have needed iron, fuel, and clothing. The man who made the clothing would have needed iron, food, and fuel. The man who raised the wool and the cotton would have needed food, fuel, iron, and clothing. Production would have largely increased, and there would have been a massive increase in the ability to consume all the goods necessary for human convenience and comfort. In other words, there would have been a great increase in the profits of capital and the wages of labor.

Had production grown at the rate I have suggested, we would have produced 15,000,000 tons between 1834 and the present, instead of only 5,000,000. These 10,000,000 extra tons would have filled the country with machinery, allowing farmers and planters to have consumers (factory workers) right by their sides. Additionally, it would have provided the iron for roads, allowing them to reach markets at half the current cost. Their need to travel to distant markets would have decreased, while their ability to do so would have increased. With every step of this progress, they would have become wealthier.

A nearby cotton or wool mill would have provided clothing in exchange for food and labor, reducing the need to look to distant markets while actually increasing the power to reach them. The higher demand for labor and its increased rewards would have significantly encouraged immigration; every new arrival would have been another person to feed and clothe, benefiting both the farmer and the planter. Farms and plantations would have been divided, and more food and cotton would be produced from small plots than are currently obtained from large ones. The land would have increased in value, and the farmers and planters would have grown wealthy because of increased production and lower costs of exchange. A portion of this surplus wealth would have been used to purchase books, newspapers, musical instruments, and pictures. In this way, intellectual progress would have kept pace with moral and physical improvement. Instead of this, the period from 1835 to 1843 was one of shrinking production and increasing poverty and crime, ending in bankruptcy and <term>repudiation</term> <note>original: "repudiation"; the refusal of several U.S. states to pay back their sovereign debts during the financial crisis of the 1840s.</note>.

What has been said regarding iron is equally true for coal, though it is unnecessary to go into every detail. If the Tariff of 1828 had been adopted as the permanent policy of the nation, the consumption of <term>anthracite</term> <note>original: "anthracite"; a hard, clean-burning coal found in abundance in Pennsylvania.</note> would by now have reached 10,000,000 tons. The vast coal fields of the West would also be producing millions of tons. In this way, the "food" of the farm would have been condensed into fuel and iron—making it easier to transport and providing the very means of transportation itself. Instead, we have seen a series of policy changes that have ruined almost everyone who worked to provide the nation with the extraordinary infrastructure connecting Philadelphia and New York with the great coal regions of Pennsylvania. State bankruptcy and debt defaults have been followed by the failure of companies that have done more for the real benefit of the United States than any others in our history. All of this was caused by a policy that reduced iron consumption to below 40 pounds per person, when it might have long ago reached 300 pounds.

If the production of iron and coal had been allowed to increase and the manufacturing of cotton had grown, we would now be using 1.5 million bales of cotton. If the wool manufacturing industry had been allowed to grow, we would now have a hundred million sheep, and all their wool would be needed for our own domestic use—because those who produce a lot, consume a lot.

The perfect harmony of interests is nowhere more clearly shown than in an examination of how we have handled both coal and iron. Both were heavily protected from 1816 to 1824, but neither industry grew because the iron, cotton, and wool manufactures did not grow. # THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.

A man who would protect himself at the cost of his neighbor makes a sad mistake. It is useless to produce iron without a market, and that market is to be found in the rolling mill, the foundry, the machine shop, the cutler's shop, and that of the axe-maker; they, in turn, must find a market among the producers of food, wool, and cotton. The shipbuilder uses a large amount of iron, and for him to do so, there must be a large market for sugar, tea, coffee, and other luxuries and comforts of life. The larger the market, the larger the consumption of iron will be; and the larger the latter, the more rapidly the former will grow. In a wise political economy <note>original: "political economy"; the 19th-century term for the study of production, trade, and their relations with law, custom, and government—what we now call "economics."</note>, there will be found no discords.

### CHAPTER EIGHTH.

#### HOW PROTECTION AFFECTS POPULATION.

Combination of action is indispensable to increasing the value of labor. The first cultivator can neither roll nor raise a log with which to build himself a house. Instead, he makes himself a hole in the ground, which serves in place of one. He cultivates the poor soil of the hills to obtain a little corn to supplement the supply of food derived from snaring the game in his neighborhood. His winter's supply is stored in another hole, liable to damage from the water that filters through the light soil—the only kind he is able to penetrate. He is in hourly danger of starvation. 

At length, however, his sons grow up. They combine their exertions with his, and now obtain something like an axe and a spade. They can dig deeper into the soil; they can cut logs and build something like a house. They obtain more corn and more game, and they can preserve it better. The danger of starvation is diminished. Being no longer forced to depend for fuel upon the decayed wood—the only kind their father could use—they are in less danger of perishing from cold in the elevated ground which they occupy out of necessity. With the growth of the family, new soils are cultivated, each in succession yielding a larger return for labor. They obtain a constantly increasing supply of the necessaries of life from a land surface that is shrinking in proportion to the number of people to be fed; and thus, with every increase in the return to their labor, the power to combine their efforts is increased.

If we look now to the solitary settler of the West, even when provided with both an axe and a spade, we see him obtaining the commonest log hut only with extreme difficulty. Then a neighbor arrives, and their combined efforts produce a new house with less than half the labor required for the first. That neighbor brings a horse, and he makes something like a cart. The product of their labor is now ten times greater than was that of the first man working by himself. More neighbors come, and new houses are wanted. A "bee" <note>original: "bee"; a community social gathering where neighbors join together to complete a specific task, such as a "husking bee" or a "barn-raising bee."</note> is organized, and by the combined effort of the neighborhood, the third house is completed in a day, whereas the first cost months and the second weeks of far more severe exertion. 

These new neighbors have brought plows and horses, and now better soils are cultivated. The product of labor is increased again, as is the power to preserve the surplus for winter use. The path becomes a road. Exchanges begin. The store makes its appearance. Labor is rewarded by larger returns because it is aided by better machinery applied to better soils. The town grows up. Each successive addition to the population brings a consumer and a producer. The shoemaker wants leather and corn in exchange for his shoes. The blacksmith requires fuel and food, and the farmer wants shoes for his horses; and with the increasing facility of exchange, more labor is applied to production. The reward of labor rises, producing new wants and requiring more and larger exchanges. The road becomes

The tendency toward unity and the collaboration of effort <note>original: "combination of exertion"</note> thus grows as wealth increases. In a state of extreme poverty, this cooperation cannot develop. A small, struggling tribe that starves on the resources of the topsoil across hundreds of thousands of acres looks with jealousy at every newcomer. They know that every new mouth to feed makes it harder to survive. In contrast, the farmer rejoices when a blacksmith and a shoemaker arrive. They come to eat the corn right there—the same corn he previously had to carry ten, twenty, or thirty miles to market to trade for shoes for himself and his horses. 

With every new consumer of his products who arrives, the farmer is able to focus more of his actions and thoughts on his home. Each new arrival actually increases his *ability to buy goods* brought from a distance, because he no longer feels the need to travel far away to find a market for his crops. Give that poor tribe some spades and the knowledge of how to use them, and the power of association <note>Carey uses "association" to mean the social and economic bonds formed when people live and work near one another.</note> will begin. As the food supply becomes more abundant, they welcome the stranger who brings them knives and clothing to trade for skins and corn. Wealth grows, and the habit of association—the first step toward civilization—arises.

It is not good for man to live alone, yet throughout this country, we find tens of thousands of men fleeing to the West. They go there to begin the work of farming far away from their fellow men, even while millions of acres of rich land in the older states remain untouched. If we look at the events of the last thirty years, we see that the urge to migrate increased rapidly between 1834 and 1842, when the building of mills and furnaces stopped. During that period, we settled Texas and Oregon. In the years that followed, the urge to emigrate decreased, only to break out again under the influence of the trade policy of 1846 <note>The Walker Tariff of 1846, which Carey opposed because it lowered protective duties on imported manufactured goods.</note>. The last twelve months have seen the departure of many thousands to California, Santa Fe, and elsewhere, while the migration to Iowa, Wisconsin, and other parts of the expansive West is entirely without precedent.

"It is estimated," says the editor of one of the Iowa papers:

> "That between 1,400 and 1,500 wagons have crossed the Mississippi at this place within the last five weeks, bringing immigrants from Ohio, Indiana, and Illinois, all of them seeking homes in Iowa. They have," he says, "generally gone to the new counties on and west of the Des Moines River, where we know they will find lands and other agricultural advantages equal to any in the world. Allowing five persons per wagon, between 7,000 and 8,000 persons have crossed at this place alone. We are told that the same extraordinary influx of immigrants has taken place at all the other crossings along the river from Dubuque down to Keokuk. It is, therefore, reasonable to suppose that 30,000 to 50,000 persons have been added to our population within the last month and a half, and the tide is still pressing toward us."*

If we want to find the reason for this current extraordinary trend of seeking the West, it can be found in the declining value of labor in the older states. The production of iron, coal, and cotton and woolen cloths—and of goods in general—has diminished. There is not only no demand for labor to build new mills and furnaces or to open new coal mines, but the number of people actually employed has decreased. The natural increase of our population is almost 600,000, and immigration this year is about 300,000; thus, 900,000...

# THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.

New people are added, while the number of those who can find work in the older states is lower than it was two years ago. All these people must eat; if they cannot trade their labor—working in coal mines or manufacturing cloth and iron—for food, they must grow it themselves. This is why the population of the newer states is currently growing so quickly.

Here is a case of apparent conflict. The people in the newer states need neighbors to help them build roads and construct churches and schoolhouses. It seems as though the economic situation that hurts the farmers of Pennsylvania, New York, and Virginia actually benefits those who are already in Wisconsin and Iowa. It appears they profit from free trade and would be harmed by protection <note>Protection, or protectionism, refers to government policies like tariffs that limit imports to encourage domestic industry.</note>. However, as strange as it may seem, the exact opposite is the case. The harmony of interests is perfect, and the conflict is only on the surface. The new states would grow faster under protection than they do now under free trade. If protection had not been abolished in 1832–1833, Iowa and Wisconsin would already be populous states, as I will now demonstrate. 

From 1821 to 1825, there was no incentive for Europeans to move to this country. Wages here were low, and finding work was very difficult. The average number of immigrants was only 7,138, and the final year of that period was barely above that average. By 1829, it reached 24,000. Five years later (1834), it was 65,000. The average for the next nine years was only 72,000, and in the last of those years, it was only 75,179. Like everything else, immigration was stagnant. In the four following years, it tripled. This year it may reach 230,000, though it has already begun to decline.

It is clear that the demand for labor grows as the variety of jobs increases. With every step in that direction, the reward for labor increases, allowing the worker to earn higher wages—that is to say, more food, fuel, clothing, books, and newspapers, and better schooling for his children—in return for the same amount of work. We see that the power to obtain these benefits increased rapidly from 1830 to 1834, and the result was a massive increase in immigration. With every such increase, there must necessarily be a greater ability for people to work together <note>Carey refers to this as the "power of combination."</note>, making it easier to obtain the things they work for. This offers new attractions for the laborer and produces a further trend in the same direction. 

In a former chapter, I suggested that immigration might have reached 1,000,000 people per year by now if it had doubled just once every four years. A doubling every three years would have brought it to 2,000,000 by this time <note>A large ink blot follows this number</note>. However, even using the lower figure, we would have brought in nearly 6,000,000 people during the intermediate period instead of fewer than 2,000,000. If we now add the natural population growth of all these people, we would currently have at least 5,000,000 more people than we actually do. While vast numbers of these would have been employed in increasing the value of land in the older states by opening mines and building furnaces, millions would have moved West. Access to the West would have been made easier every day by the increased availability of iron needed to build steamboats and railroads.

Many people attribute the high immigration rates of the last few years to political unrest in Europe, but the effect of those troubles has been small. All goods tend to seek the best market, and labor is no exception. Europeans are eager to move here because humans are a more valuable "commodity" here than in Europe. A worker here can get more food, fuel, and clothing, and better housing for the same amount of work than he can at home. As more people learn this fact, more people want to reach our shores. Had

If the demand for labor had continued to increase as it did from 1844 to 1847, immigration this year would likely have exceeded even half a million people. Instead, there is every reason to believe that there will be a great decrease.

### CHAPTER NINE.

### HOW PROTECTION AFFECTS THE MEANS OF TRANSPORTATION—INTERNAL AND EXTERNAL.

The more widely people are separated, the more difficult it is to build roads. This results in a greater amount of labor being wasted by the farmer in the work of transportation, and he remains poorer. Conversely, the more people are enabled to combine their efforts, the easier it is to build roads. When less labor is lost to transportation, more can be dedicated to production, and the farmer will grow richer.

Between 1835 and 1840, the trend was toward separation, and there was a great need for roads. The widely scattered settlers of Illinois, Indiana, Michigan, and Mississippi could not build roads by themselves, and no one would trust them individually with the resources necessary for construction. To solve this difficulty, they united to borrow the food, clothing, and iron required for the purpose, pledging the "faith of the State" <note>This refers to states issuing bonds or taking on public debt based on their creditworthiness.</note> to pay the costs. The result was universal economic ruin. People were scattering, and labor was becoming less productive. The consequence was that immigration stopped growing; *it was precisely when population growth from that source was halted that we were expanding the area of settlement, which diminished the power of working together to increase the rewards of labor.*

We are now doing the exact same thing. People are scattering themselves widely, and there is a great demand for roads. Every day, the newspapers inform us of new roads being built in the West using iron obtained in exchange for "certificates of debt" <note>Promissory notes or bonds that represent a debt to be paid back with interest.</note> that carry interest. The men who should be manufacturing iron are instead moving to the West and borrowing the iron they should be making themselves. If this system continues for long, the result must be the same disaster we witnessed in 1842–1843.

It is this unnatural expansion of a small population over a massive area that has caused the debate over "internal improvements" <note>Public works projects like roads, canals, and harbors funded by the government.</note> by the federal government—one of the most dangerous questions remaining to be settled. If the settlement and cultivation of new lands and the formation of new states proceeded naturally, the population would become wealthy enough to build their own roads and improve their own harbors. However, because that is impossible under the current system, they look to the government for aid. 

At this moment, it is proposed that a vast amount of land should be given away or sold at a very low price to help build a road to California. If this work is pursued vigorously, it will be finished fifty years before it could ever pay back the interest on its cost. This is because it would only encourage the further scattering of the population and the further decrease in the productivity of labor. We need concentration <note>Carey uses "concentration" to mean a higher density of people and industry working near each other, which he argues creates more wealth than "dispersion."</note> to make labor more productive and to promote immigration. If we achieve that, the natural and profitable settlement of the country beyond the Mississippi River will move so quickly that it will ensure a connection with the Pacific that benefits everyone in a reasonable amount of time. 

There is hardly a single instance on record of a road being successful when it was built just to attract a population, or one that relied entirely on *through* travel and trade—as this California road must do for a long time. To make roads productive, they must pass through regions where people consume a large portion of the land's products right where they are grown, allowing them to grow rich, and not through...

# THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.

In those areas where there is no local population to consume goods, everything produced on the land is shipped away, and the landowners remain poor. If a road is built under these conditions, it will result in a great financial loss somewhere, and wherever that loss falls, it will be a loss to the entire community.

The reason such roads are unprofitable is that transportation on them is almost entirely limited to bulky items that must be carried at low freight rates. The most valuable of all "commodities" is man, and on such roads, travel is minimal because the people are poor and must stay at home. Their agricultural products pay very little to the road's upkeep; furthermore, the small amount of profit left to them allows them to buy very little silk, cloth, or other manufactured goods upon which high tolls could be charged. Conversely, where there is a large consuming population along the route, local travel is high. The goods sent to market pay good freight rates, and the profits from those sales pay for a large amount of merchandise to be shipped back.

Applying these views to our trade with foreign nations, we can now see why the shipping industry grows alongside economic protection <note>Carey uses "protection" to refer to government policies like tariffs that encourage domestic industry.</note>.

The merchandise we send to Europe is bulky, while the goods we receive in return are compact. As a consequence, the outward-bound cargo has generally had to bear almost all the costs of the entire voyage.

From 1830 to 1834, however, the wages for labor were high enough to encourage a major increase in immigration. This provided a valuable "return cargo" of people. The income from these passengers tended to greatly diminish the freight charges on exported goods. Thus, the planter and farmer were able to consume more European merchandise—which pays high freight rates—and more tea and coffee. Meanwhile, the demand for raw materials used in domestic manufacturing also allowed ships to bring those materials back as part of their return cargoes, making it easier and cheaper to send our own products and merchandise to other parts of the world.

From 1835 to 1844, immigration was almost stationary, and so was the shipping industry. From 1845 to the present time, immigration has grown rapidly, and so has shipping. We now import 300,000 people annually. Given the usual allowance of two persons for every five tons of ship capacity, it follows that 250,000 tons of shipping, making three trips per year, are employed for this purpose alone. Freight rates to Europe are low because the return cargo (the immigrants) is large and profitable. First-class ships are now built specifically for the importation of people, and they will continue to be built as long as the number of passengers increases. If that number decreases, ship-building will decline and freight rates to Europe will rise, because a valuable return cargo can no longer be guaranteed. A rise in freight costs will naturally reduce the number of items that are profitable to export and the quantity of merchandise that can be imported from Europe. Furthermore, a decrease in the number of people requiring tea, coffee, and similar goods will further reduce the incentive to build ships.

If we were now importing a million people, the shipping required for that purpose alone would be 830,000 tons. Freight rates to Europe would be almost insignificant, as many ships would go there entirely in ballast <note>original: "ballast" - heavy material like rocks or sand placed in the hold of a ship to provide stability when it is not carrying a full load of cargo.</note>. Whatever increases the volume of imported goods also decreases the cost of transportation and increases the export of the products of the farmer and planter. If we imported raw silk, we would also import the French workers to manufacture it and the coffee for them to drink. The ships that imported the silk, the people, and the coffee would then be able to cheaply transport our cotton or cotton cloth back across the ocean. If we import raw gutta-percha <note>original: "gutta percha" - a natural, rubber-like latex from Southeast Asian trees, used in the 19th century for everything from underwater telegraph cables to golf balls.</note>, we obtain it from someone who wants to buy cloth, and that cloth can then be sent to them cheaply. However, if we only import finished gutta-percha goods, we obtain them from people who already have cloth to sell, and to whom our cotton cannot be cheaply sent. Therefore, if we desire to increase...

To achieve the goals of our commerce and navigation, we must adopt measures that will bring manufacturing <note>original: "the loom"</note> to take its place alongside agriculture <note>original: "the plough"</note>. In this way, the interests of farming, manufacturing, and shipping would be perfectly harmonized.

With such a high level of immigration, there would be an annual addition of 1,000,000 people with whom we would have *perfect* freedom of trade—unhindered by customs officers, sailors, or ships. At the end of ten years, this would add twelve or thirteen million people to our population, who would consume twice as much cotton as the entire population of Great Britain and Ireland consumes today. Thus, the goals of free-traders and protectionists would be almost perfectly aligned. The more this subject is examined, the more obvious it becomes that the *only* road to perfect freedom of trade is through perfect protection <note>Carey argues that protective tariffs actually lead to a self-sufficient economy that eventually requires less regulation.</note>.

## CHAPTER 10.

### HOW PROTECTION AFFECTS THE FARMER.

Among the world's large exporters of food are Ireland, Canada, Russia, and the United States.

The first, Ireland, exports both food and its people. Because the vast majority of her trade consists of exports, the food must bear the entire cost of the ship's round-trip voyage. Consequently, the profit to the producer is small and shrinking rapidly, leading to famine, disease, and a declining population.

The second, Canada, exports food and lumber. It imports some people for its own population and many others who eventually migrate to the United States. However, the excess of exports is still large enough that the producer must pay for nearly the entire cost of the round-trip shipping voyage.

Neither of these countries has any protection against the "colonial system" <note>A system where colonies provide raw materials to a mother country and buy back finished goods, often to the colony's economic disadvantage.</note>. The food they export returns to them as cloth and iron, free of import duties and almost free of freight costs, because the majority of the shipping traffic is moving away from them.

Russia also exports food, but she protects her domestic manufacturing and thus creates a home market for much of her produce. One authority states her capacity to supply grain is 17,000,000 quarters, while another says 28,000,000 quarters <term>a "quarter" is an old British unit of weight or volume for grain, roughly equal to 8 bushels or 480 pounds</term> (153 to 252 million bushels). We are told that:

> "In years when there is no foreign demand for this surplus, a portion of it is used, with little regard for efficiency, to fatten cattle for butchers and for their tallow. Much is absolutely wasted, and the rest, left unthreshed, is eaten by birds and mice." Also, "if a foreign market could be found for it, Russia could easily export 50,000,000 quarters of grain annually (equal to 450,000,000 bushels)."*

Russia's system is generally hostile to the growth of wealth and intelligence. Heavy taxes support large armies and a massive bureaucracy at the expense of the producing classes. Furthermore, the existence of serfdom <note>A condition of debt bondage or modified slavery where laborers are bound to the land.</note> and the requirement for the healthiest young men to serve in the military prevents any hope of social improvement; without hope, there is little motivation to work. Nevertheless, as we see, the Russian has food to waste, while Irish people perish by the tens of thousands from starvation.

In the United States, a system of protection exists. It is currently limited to thirty...

By its aid, there has been a diversification of industries <note>original: "pursuits"</note> that enables people to save much time and many resources that would otherwise be wasted. Meanwhile, women and children find employment at wages that allow them to be large consumers of both food and clothing. Wages are high, and this is why there is such a large import of that most valuable of commodities—human beings <note>original: "man"</note>.

Last year, we imported about **300,000** people. Estimating their food consumption at twenty cents per day each, this created a domestic market for the products of the land worth *twenty million dollars.* Their transportation required the constant employment of **250,000** tons of shipping. These ships carried freight to Europe at very low rates because they were certain of obtaining valuable return cargoes. The farmer thus gained a large home market and the ability to export cheaply to foreign ones. It is due to the combined operation of these two causes that the prices for wheat and flour have remained so high.

We may now, I think, understand many curious facts happening before our eyes. Food is so abundant in Russia that it is wasted, yet this country is among the largest exporters of food to Great Britain, where it sells at a price almost as high as in Liverpool—and now even higher. Russian produce must bear all the shipping charges for the entire round trip. Consequently, the producer remains poor and builds no roads; thus, the cost of transportation, both internal and external, continues and must remain high. The farmer in the United States sends his produce to market cheaply because the return cargo—being chiefly people—is valuable and occupies great space. He therefore grows rich, builds roads and canals, and constructs steamboats. Thus, the cost of transportation, both internal and external, is diminished so much that the difference in the price of a barrel of flour in Pittsburgh versus Liverpool is, considering the distance, almost inconceivably small.

The bulk of Canada’s trade is outward-bound. As a result, outward freight rates are high. Conversely, our imports of people and other valuable commodities keep our rates low. Therefore, the cost of transporting wheat and flour from our side of the border is so much lower than from the other that both now pass through New York on their way to Liverpool. The protective system <note>A policy of using tariffs to protect domestic industries from foreign competition.</note> thus not only has the effect of bringing consumers to take their places by the side of the producer—making it easier to consume the products of the land on the land itself and facilitating the exportation of the surplus to foreign markets by diminishing outward freight costs—but it has the further effect of producing among our neighbors a strong desire for the establishment of the same perfect freedom of trade that now exists among the several States, by becoming themselves a part of the Union. Protection, therefore, tends to the increase of commerce and the establishment of free trade, while the British system tends everywhere to the destruction of commerce and to the creation of a necessity for trade restrictions.

We see, therefore, that if we desire to secure command of what is falsely called "the great grain market of the world," it is to be achieved by adopting measures that will secure valuable return freights. The most costly and valuable of all "commodities" are human beings <note>original: "men"</note>. The least valuable are pig-iron <term>pig-iron: crude iron cast into blocks, requiring further processing</term> and coal. The more of the latter we import, the larger our surplus of food will be, the higher the outward freight costs (both internal and external) will become, the greater the waste will be, and the poorer the farmer will become. The more people we import, the smaller our surplus of food will be <note>Because the immigrants eat the food here.</note>, the lower the outward freight costs will be, and the more numerous will be the commodities that can be sent to Europe to be exchanged for luxuries that we cannot currently afford.

Were we now importing a million people annually, the downward freight rates on our canals and railroads would be greatly diminished. Meanwhile, the outward freight across the ocean would cost little more than the price of loading and unloading it. Yet, we would still be building ships, steamboats, and railroads at a rate we cannot currently imagine.

With the help of these people, coal and iron would be produced by the millions of tons. The increased ease of obtaining food and iron would provide new opportunities for building cotton and woolen mills, type-foundries, and printing offices. All the people employed in them would be large consumers of food, and thus the farmer would gain in every respect.

In Ireland, a laborer obtains 6d. or 8d. <note>6 or 8 pence; roughly a few cents in 19th-century terms.</note> for a day's labor when employed, but the yearly average is even less than the former sum. He is our great customer for Indian corn <note>maize</note>, the cost of which, by the time it reaches him, is about 4s. <note>4 shillings</note>, or five times what it yielded to the American farmer on his farm. Eight days of labor are thus required for the purchase of a single bushel. If you transfer that man to the coal fields of Ohio or Indiana, he may purchase far more with the work of a single day. He immediately becomes a much better customer for food and is able to consume large amounts of sugar and coffee (to the benefit of the merchant), wool (to the benefit of the sheep farmer), lumber (to the benefit of the man clearing land), and cotton and indigo (to the benefit of the Southern planter). In this way, every interest in the country profits by the transfer of poor cultivators from Ireland and Germany to the coal fields and iron-ore beds of the Union.

Place him in Alabama, and he will earn the current price of twenty bushels; he will then eat more and better food, and consume ten pounds of cotton where he now consumes only one.

The hand-loom weavers, of whom England has 800,000 (with no work for a third of that number),† consume very little food or cotton. Transfer them here, and they will become large consumers of both.

The agricultural laborer of England receives 8s. or 9s. a week, which is little more than the price of a bushel and a half of wheat. Transfer him here, and his services as a miner or laborer will enable him to earn the price of five or six bushels. He will then consume more and better food, and a large amount of cotton.

The poor Highlander, driven from his native hills to make room for sheep, starves in the miserable lodging-houses of Glasgow.‡ If he could be transferred here, he would become a large consumer of food and clothing.

Our current policy is the exact opposite of this. We are exporting people by the tens of thousands to California, and by the hundreds of thousands to the West. This diminishes the power of "combination of action" <note>economic synergy or the ability of people to work together in a concentrated area</note> and increases the necessity for using ships and wagons to carry their produce to market. So far, immigration from Europe has been maintained, and freight costs to Europe are consequently low; however, as the laborer's wages diminish, immigration must decline. When that happens, freight costs must rise. Thus, the same measures that diminish home consumption must also increase the cost of sending goods to distant markets. The cost of the voyage out and back *must* be paid by someone. If there is no return freight <note>goods being shipped back on the return leg of a journey</note>, the farmer or planter must pay the entire cost of the trip. If there is a large and valuable return freight, the farmer needs to pay almost no portion of the cost. Regarding California, we must pay the entire outward freight because there is no cargo to be returned. Therefore, bulky items—the produce of the farm—cannot be shipped there. The consequence is that every emigrant to that country is a customer lost to the farmer, and a customer only to a limited extent for the planter.

The most costly and most valuable of commodities, as I have already stated, is Man. The more valuable the commodities that can be imported into any country without going into debt for them, the richer that country will grow. This is equally true of every State, county, township, and town. No one can doubt this, and yet every portion of the Union is currently engaged in exporting this most valuable of all commodities to the West, to Texas, Oregon, and California, receiving—

# THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.

...nothing in return. We now import hundreds of thousands of people, yet the established Eastern States keep almost none of them. Everyone must move West because the operation of mills and furnaces has stopped, and the construction of new mills has ended until we see a change in national policy. 

Such is the effect of the "colonial system" <note>An economic policy where a powerful nation prevents others from developing their own manufacturing, forcing them to remain providers of raw materials.</note>, which was established to prevent people from different nations from working together effectively. This system is maintained by policies that are equally destructive to the interests of the people of England and the world at large. "Many of our manufacturers," says a Manchester broker, "have exported goods at a loss. If they have done so to keep foreign competition at bay and stop the growth of industrial plants abroad, it is an unenviable success." He adds, "Still, as this country is doomed to be a manufacturing state, nothing remains but to beat or be beaten."*

These losses happen constantly. They are a natural result of the "war upon the labor and capital of the world" in which England feels it must "beat or be beaten." Someone must pay for these losses. They are paid for by the laborers of England, who are forced to work for lower wages. However, they are paid for to an even greater extent by the laborers of the rest of the world. These workers are forced to remain idle and earn nothing to pay farmers and planters for food and clothing, even though they would gladly work to earn enough to feed and clothe themselves and their children.

Under these circumstances, it is obvious how low the power to consume food actually is. Even though three-quarters of the people in England are consumers of food rather than producers, their grain imports over the last two years of free trade amount to only two bushels per person. The amount England takes from us is insignificant; the following statement shows how trivial the total is when distributed among the population of the United States, even during the last two years of relatively large exports:

| | Flour (Barrels) | Wheat (Bushels) | Corn (Bushels) | Corn-meal (Barrels) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Year ending June 30, 1848 | 958,744 | 1,531,000 | 5,062,000 | 226,000 |
| Year ending Aug. 31, 1849 | 1,114,016 | 4,684,000 | 12,721,000 | 88,000 |

These last and largest amounts total, in round numbers, 10,000,000 bushels of wheat and 13,000,000 bushels of corn. After subtracting the cost of transportation, the total value produced on the farm is likely no more than $10,000,000—or less than fifty cents per person for the people of the Union. The likelihood that even this amount will continue to be exported can be judged by two facts: first, only extremely low shipping rates have sustained exports so far; and second, because food prices are so low in Europe, some are now calculating that grain may actually be exported *to* the United States.

> "The reports reaching us from your side regarding the wheat crop have led to the idea here that the United States might become a grain-importing country, as happened once about ten or twelve years ago. We consider this highly improbable ourselves, although the *Sturges* <note>A prominent family of English grain merchants</note> mention it in their commercial circular today. It is said that *Mark Lane governs the world's grain prices* <note>original: "Mark Lane"; the location of the London Corn Exchange, which was the global center for grain trading</note>; and if so, European prices will certainly be very low. Prices here have fallen by 5 to 6 shillings per quarter <note>A 'quarter' is a British unit of grain measurement equal to 8 bushels</note>—one-sixth of the total value—within the last month. Oats are down to 16 shillings per quarter." — *London Correspondent of the National Intelligencer.*

Despite the large increase in the farming population, the quantity of wheat and flour received at the coast <note>original: "tide-water"</note> on the Hudson River shows a decrease. The only increase is roughly 2,000,000 bushels of corn, which found a market abroad only because shipping costs <note>original: "freights"</note> were very low.

The arrival of immigrants <note>original: "import of men"</note> has created a market for $20,000,000 worth of food. Once these people are here, they remain consumers of food and customers for the farmer, unless they are forced to become farmers themselves and thus become rivals to the current farmers.

The "great grain market of the world" <note>This likely refers to Great Britain, which had recently repealed the Corn Laws to allow more food imports.</note> has absorbed half as much because of low shipping costs; however, as shipping costs rise, this market is diminishing and must continue to shrink as those costs increase. "Since the beginning of the California Gold Rush <note>original: "excitement"</note>, nearly seven hundred vessels," we are told,* "have left for the Pacific, many of which will never return to us." These ships will not be replaced unless shipping rates are high enough to pay their owners. If immigration continues, they will be replaced soon, and the cost of doing so will be paid by immigrants who come to be customers for the farmer and planter. If immigration does not continue, the ships will not be replaced, and the high shipping costs of the remaining ones must be paid by the farmers and planters seeking customers in Europe.

It must be obvious to all who study the tables given in the third chapter that immigration will be stopped. The difficulty of obtaining food, fuel, and clothing—which constitute real wages—in return for labor is increasing. The value of human labor <note>original: "man"</note> is falling, and the incentives for immigration are passing away. Should immigration diminish next year by 100,000 people, there will be a loss of market to the extent of $7,000,000. The California Gold Rush, which carried off so many thousands of the farmer's customers, along with the food to feed them on the road,† will no longer exist. Here is another hundred thousand customers lost to the farmer, and with them a demand for another $7,000,000 worth of food. The European market is being closed. Nothing that reduces production can maintain prices.

If we converted all the food that has been exported this year into iron and delivered it back to the farm tax-free <note>original: "free of duty," referring to the absence of import tariffs</note>, we would find that it would produce 250,000 tons of iron. This equals twenty-five pounds of iron for every person in the population. Let us now look at the neighborhood of an iron furnace and see how much lighter the cost of iron is when it is produced locally. In that case, it is paid for with goods that the earth produces in bulk—such as potatoes or hay—or with straw that would otherwise be wasted, or with labor not currently needed on the farm. Then, estimate how many tons of iron these grain producers might have obtained if they had created a market on their own land for the products of that land.

Let us now suppose that instead of shutting down old furnaces, we had built fifty new ones, each capable of producing 5,000 tons, along with rolling mills to convert that iron into bars. Suppose we had thus employed the labor of some of those immigrants and were now producing 250,000 more tons of iron than we did last year. Would that alone not have created a permanent local market for as much of the farmer’s produce as we have exported to England? Would that not have reduced the cost of iron? Would it not have raised the price of labor? Would it not have encouraged more immigration? Would it not have encouraged shipbuilding and reduced the cost of shipping <note>original: "freights"</note>? Would the farmer not then have more control over the English market than he can under a system that discourages immigration and shipbuilding? Does his *power* to trade abroad not increase as his *necessity* to seek a foreign market decreases? 

If we were importing large amounts of raw silk and laborers from Italy, could we not send cotton yarn to Italy more cheaply than it currently goes through England? And if we were importing silk weavers from France, could we not send food to France in return—in the form of coal and iron—at a lower shipping cost than what they now pay for English coal and iron, which must cover the cost of the voyage both ways? The greater the value of our import trade—and people are the most valuable "commodity" we can import—the greater the variety of goods we will be able to export.

Some argue that the farmer's condition is improved by having two markets (home and abroad) that he *must* use, and that if he only had the home market, prices would be lower. In other words, they claim that if he could sell everything he produces at home, he would make less than he does now by going abroad. In reality, the exact opposite is true when men are *forced* to seek a distant market.

The first questions to ask regarding this are: Why is the farmer obliged to go away from home to sell? Why does the supply of food grow faster than the demand? There are two reasons for this. First: we do not import enough consumers <note>meaning immigrants who would eat the food grown by American farmers</note>; and second: of those whom we do import, too many are forced to become producers of food themselves because of the difficulty of finding work in other industries where they would instead be consumers. A man who works in a coal mine earns $300 a year, and perhaps more. Much of this income goes toward buying food.

# THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.

and all of that income is used to pay for products of the earth, for every person consumes to the full extent of what they produce. Ten thousand miners and laborers provide a market for those products to the value of $3,000,000. Forty thousand mechanics, miners, and laborers provide a market for the farmer and planter to the value of $12,000,000, which is far more than we can expect to export in the coming years. We now receive more than 250,000 immigrants annually, and there are half a million of our own native-born population reaching adulthood every year. By moving 20,000 working men away from agriculture, we reduce the number of producers; by employing these 20,000 in other professions, we increase the number of consumers enough to prevent the "surplus" that we currently complain about. Judging from the past, however, adopting protectionism <note>original: "protection," referring to the policy of using tariffs to encourage domestic industry</note> as a permanent system would result in a massive increase in immigration. A large portion of these people would gladly remain consumers of food, whereas under the current free-trade system, they are forced to become producers of food <note>Carey argues that without industrial jobs, immigrants must become farmers, thereby increasing the supply of food and lowering prices for everyone.</note>.

When farmers have a demand at home for everything they grow, they receive a higher price than when they have to sell abroad. In the first case, they earn nearly as much *more than* the price in distant markets as the cost of shipping *from those markets* would be. Conversely, when they must sell abroad, they earn as much *less than* the price in those markets as the cost of shipping *to those markets—and the price of the entire crop is determined by whatever can be earned for that small remaining surplus.* For several years, grain and flour have been more expensive in the coal regions of Pennsylvania than in Philadelphia because the demand there has always exceeded the supply. If you close the mines, the farmers will be forced to send their products to Philadelphia, receiving city prices *minus* the cost of transportation. At the present time, the price of grain across the Union is sustained entirely by the domestic market, for flour currently sells in Liverpool <note>At this time, Liverpool was the primary international hub for American agricultural exports.</note> for less than the price in New York. If we close the mines and factories and turn miners and mechanics into farmers, the price at home must drop to the Liverpool price—which will then be *lower* than it is now—*minus* the cost of transportation, which will then be *higher* than it is now.

Even if we admit that we will always have a surplus of grain to export, the next question is: what strategy will guarantee the farmer the highest price in foreign markets? The answer must surely be the strategy that most effectively reduces the total amount of grain sent to those markets from this or other countries. If, then, the current system of global commerce tends to increase the supply of food, it must be harmful to the interests of the farmer. I believe it can easily be shown that this is the case.

We know that the more miners and mechanics we have, the more food we consume; and the more farmers we have, the more food we produce. This must also be true for other countries. We know that under a protective system, the number of miners and mechanics increases, and that under a free-trade system, the number of food producers increases. This must also be true for other countries. Therefore, it is clearly in our interest for Russia and Germany to consume more food and export less; if they and we both did so, the price of food would rise. Russia, Germany, and the United States have all established protective systems, and the result has been an increase in consumers and a decrease in producers. If the rest of the world followed our example, the supply of food now flooding "the great grain market of the world" would be reduced so much that prices would rise. This, however, is

# THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.

This is but one of the effects that would result from a general determination to dismantle the colonial system <note>The "colonial system" refers to the economic policy where a mother country (like Britain) prevents its colonies from manufacturing their own goods, forcing them to export raw materials and buy back finished products.</note>.

We have seen that the consumption of cotton in other countries is small, while here in the United States, it is large. The price of cotton has already fallen so low that planters are resorting to growing wheat instead. This is a move that must ultimately harm the traditional grain farmer by increasing competition. Now, if we were consuming 50% more cotton than we do at present, this problem would not exist. The price the planter could get would be high enough to prevent them from having to abandon cotton cultivation.

Let us now suppose that Canada, Russia, Germany, and Ireland could create a market for their currently wasted labor. By doing so, they would enable themselves to consume two or three pounds of cotton for every one pound they consume now, and they would be able to afford more food. Is it not obvious that the prices of both food and cotton would rise? It seems perfectly certain that such a result would follow the abolition of the colonial system in those countries. If this is true, then maintaining and extending the protective system <note>The "protective system" refers to using tariffs on imports to encourage the growth of domestic factories and industries.</note>—with the specific goal of ending the unnatural system Great Britain has established—is clearly in the interest of the farmers, the planters of the Union, and the entire world.

Let us next examine how this system works in Canada. Because there are almost literally no manufacturing industries of any kind there, there is no local market for the products of the land.

In Canada, "freedom of trade" is perfect. That is to say, the people of Great Britain enjoy a *complete monopoly* over the machinery. Only by using British machinery can the lumber and food produced by the people of Canada be converted into cloth and iron. The consequence is that the labor-cost of manufactured goods is so high that people can only afford to consume a small amount of them. The total export of cotton cloth from Great Britain to her North American colonies between 1840 and 1846 averaged only twenty million yards, including both fine and coarse fabric. Even if every yard were consumed there, it would only amount to ten yards per person—or about two and a half pounds of cotton for each individual. In contrast, consumption in the United States Union averages thirteen pounds per person, and it is even higher in the states closest to the Canadian border. 

If we want to know why consumption is so much lower on the Canadian side of the border than on the American side, the reason is found in this fact: the Canadian must give much more labor to obtain his cloth and iron than the American does. Even the price of Canadian wheat is lower; if that is the case, how much worse must it be for bulky goods that are too expensive to transport? As Sir Francis Head <note>Sir Francis Bond Head (1793–1875) was a British colonial administrator and Lieutenant-Governor of Upper Canada.</note> described it, the Canadian must "eat all he raises," because he has not created—and cannot create—a local market for his crops.

To the Canadians, it is perfectly obvious that food prices in the United States are maintained by our own domestic demand. This is why there is such a universal desire in Canada to abolish all restrictions on importing their goods into the Union. They currently have "perfect freedom of trade" with England—the supposed "great grain market of the world"—and they are being ruined by it. They desire trade with the great grain-producers of the world (the U.S. states), and to get it, they would gladly give up their trade with England. They would rather have local production than "free trade" and would even prefer to become members of the Union.

If Canada were part of the Union, her cotton consumption would rise to our levels. She would immediately begin to manufacture iron and cloth at home, creating a demand for the labor that is currently being wasted. Instead of buying only two and a half pounds of cotton per person from the planter, every Canadian would take twelve pounds. This would add fifteen million pounds of cotton to total consumption, which would be an immense advantage to the planter. Under those conditions, even a farmer in Illinois could safely allow free trade with Canada.

...his Canadian neighbors, because with increased domestic consumption, they would feel less necessity to go abroad to find a market for their products—a market that the colonial system <note>The "colonial system" refers to the British policy of preventing colonies from manufacturing their own goods, forcing them to export raw materials and buy back finished products from England.</note> currently denies to them at home. The farmer who believes in the advantage of free trade with England should vote for the free admission of Canadian wheat, which is grown by men who consume cloth and iron made by workers who eat the wheat of Poland and Russia. On the other hand, the farmer who sees that the price of wheat is sustained by domestic demand will be cautious about admitting foreign wheat duty-free. He will wait until, through annexation <note>In the mid-19th century, there was significant political debate regarding the potential economic or political "annexation" of Canada into the United States.</note>, the Canadian farmer can obtain the same protection that he himself enjoys, thereby enabling a local market to be created on the land for the products of the land.

Having thus examined the effects of protection, let us now look at what would happen if the world adopted the "perfect freedom of trade" urged by England. The result would inevitably be *the riveting upon the world of the existing monopoly on machinery for converting farm and plantation products into cloth and iron*. This would close the factories and furnaces of Russia, Germany, and the United States, compelling the people who work in them to seek other types of employment; their only resource would be to try to grow food. There would then be more food to sell, but who would buy it? 

We have already seen that Great Britain's total exports—after paying for the grain she currently imports—amount to only $4.32 per person. Small as that sum is, it tends to diminish. With that, she has to pay for her sugar, tea, coffee, cotton, wool, lumber, and all other foreign articles required for her own consumption, leaving her no power to pay for more grain. Nevertheless, grain would be poured into her markets, and the consequence would be that she would receive three bushels where she now receives only one, exactly as we have seen happen with cotton. "Mark Lane <note>Mark Lane was the location of the London Corn Exchange, the primary market that dictated global grain prices in the 19th century.</note> governs the world’s grain prices," and as the price obtainable for the surplus determines the price of the entire crop, the result would be that farmers everywhere would be ruined. This would bring no benefit to the manufacturers of England, for her own farmers would likewise be ruined, and her agricultural laborers would be laid off. This is currently the case in Ireland, where the population, deprived of employment at home, swarms to England and destroys the power of the English laborer to afford food, even at today's low prices—and the lower prices fall, the less demand there is for labor, and the less power workers have to obtain wages.

The proverb says, "do not put too many eggs in one basket." The object of the British system is, and has always been, to compel the world to put all its eggs in the same basket. The natural result is the occurrence of perpetual economic convulsions, producing devastation and ruin throughout the world whenever England's artificial system becomes disrupted. A review of her operations over the past thirty years shows that every four to six years, she offers the world strong inducements to send her all the sugar, coffee, cotton, and agricultural produce they can spare. About the close of the second year of this cycle, when the machinery for importation has reached full operation, a change is seen to have "come over the face of the dream." The entire energy of the country is then directed toward crashing prices to force exportation. 

The farmers and planters whom she so recently courted are now ruined. Their agents are selected as the first victims, and if the result is bankruptcy—whether public or private—it is followed by the foulest insults. Thus, insult is added to injury. The people of Pennsylvania and Maryland, Indiana and Illinois, Michigan and Mississippi, have had to endure all this as a result of the working of the Compromise Tariff of 1833 <note>The Compromise Tariff of 1833 gradually reduced American import duties, which Carey argues left the U.S. economy vulnerable to British market fluctuations and crashes.</note>. In 1846, the whole world was again urged to send food at any price.

# THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS

In 1847, the primary goal of the British market was to drive down prices. Rice was sold for nothing more than the cost of its freight and handling. Large shipments of corn actually left the shippers in debt just to pay those expenses. Once the "fever and the chill" <note>The author uses "fever and chill" as a metaphor for the volatile cycles of economic booms and crashes.</note> of that year passed, it was followed by a period of sluggishness, then by a period of moderate activity like the one we are seeing now. Next will come speculation, excitement, and large imports, which will inevitably be followed by the ruin of everyone involved as England tries to save herself. At this moment, England accepts certificates of debt as payment for iron—just as she did ten years ago—but the day is not far distant when these certificates will have to be paid back in gold.

If it were proposed to the people of the United States to make New York or Pennsylvania the only warehouse for all the products in the Union that needed to be traded or processed, everyone would see how ridiculous that idea is. A Michigan wheat farmer would be completely at a loss to understand why he should trade with a neighboring wool farmer by way of New York. Similarly, a South Carolina cotton planter would fail to see the benefit of a system that forced him to trade with a Virginia wheat farmer through Philadelphia or Pittsburgh. Yet, this is exactly the goal of the colonial system <note>The "colonial system" refers to the British economic policy of discouraging manufacturing in other countries so that they must remain suppliers of raw materials and buyers of British finished goods.</note>. 

The wheat of Michigan travels to Liverpool alongside Michigan wool, and the trade between the wheat grower and the wool grower is conducted in the markets of Leeds; as a result, three-fourths of the value of both the wool and the wheat is lost to transportation costs along the way. South Carolina rice goes to Manchester in the company of South Carolina cotton, and the corn and cotton of Tennessee cross the ocean together. This long journey is undertaken based on the idea that a planter can get more cloth for his rice, or a farmer more iron for his corn, through this indirect mode of exchange than he would if the trade happened locally. Many people doubt this is true, yet all English writers on political economy assure us it is a fact. Every measure now adopted by the British government is aimed at maintaining this *monopoly of machinery* <term>monopoly of machinery: the concentration of industrial manufacturing power in a single nation (England), forcing the rest of the world to use their factories</term>, through which the people of the world are forced to conduct their trades in British factories.

If such a system would be absurd under any circumstances, it is even more so in this case, where the British public’s ability to buy goods is so small and grows so slowly. Everything sent to England must be consumed there, unless it can be forced out to other markets by lowering the price. For everything she consumes—be it much or little—England only has about $4.32 per person to distribute, in the form of cloth and iron, among the world's farmers and planters. It is a "Procrustean bed" <note>original: "Procrustean bed" — A Greek mythological reference to a bed where the giant Procrustes would stretch or amputate his guests to make them fit; Carey uses it here to describe a rigid economic system that forces producers to suffer regardless of their actual needs.</note>, and the misfortune of poor farmers and planters is that whatever England cuts from the price of the portion sent to her, she effectively cuts from the price of the entire crop.

The world's producers have been, and are currently being, sacrificed for the benefit of the world’s "exchangers" <term>exchangers: the middlemen, merchants, and shippers who profit from the movement of goods rather than the creation of them</term>. This is why agriculture makes so little progress, and why the cultivators of the earth—the producers of everything we consume—are so universally poor and generally uninformed about their own true interests. However, the day cannot be far off when our farmers and planters will realize that their interests are not helped by a system that separates consumers from producers and makes cloth and iron so expensive that the average person can barely afford to use them.

The goal of protection <note>The "protection" Carey advocates for is the use of tariffs to encourage local manufacturing, which brings the factory (the consumer) closer to the farm (the producer).</note> is to reduce the distance and the waste between the producer and the consumer. This enables the producer to grow wealthy and become a significant consumer of cloth and iron. It is obvious that protection had this effect, given the massive increase in the consumption of both between 1843 and 1847. The ease of obtaining...

That iron enabled the farmer to improve his methods of production and obtain large harvests is obvious from the fact that the food supply increased so rapidly. That the free-trade system produces the opposite effect is obvious from the great reduction in iron consumption during the years 1842 and 1843, and from the reduction happening now. Total consumption this year does not even equal that of 1847, despite the vast increase in population.

The producers of food throughout the world have one common interest, which is to be promoted by the abolition of the existing *monopoly system* <note>Carey uses "monopoly system" to describe the British economic policy of centralizing all manufacturing in England, forcing the rest of the world to remain providers of cheap raw materials.</note>, which tends to destroy both the producers and their customers.

The farmer is also a *producer of wool*, and therefore I will briefly address that interest.

If we want evidence of the truth of what has been said regarding food, it can be found in the condition of the wool market for several years past. Our production is less than our ordinary consumption, and the consequence is that the price is *higher* here than in any other country in the world, by the total cost of transportation. Close the American woolen mills, and the price must fall to the level of European markets, *minus* the cost of exporting it there. The increased supply on the global market would, as a matter of course, produce a fall in prices, and then the sheep farmer would be ruined.

The changes in policy over the last twenty years have several times ruined the woolen manufacturers, and the sheep farmers have just as often slaughtered their flocks. The result is that we have fewer than 30,000,000 sheep today. If the policy adopted in 1828 <note>The Tariff of 1828 was a high protective tariff intended to protect Northern industries and Western agriculture from foreign competition.</note> had been maintained, we would now have 100,000,000 sheep and a market for all their products at higher prices than we see now. Prosperous laborers, miners, mechanics, cotton-growers, and food-growers would then consume six pounds of wool where they now consume only three, and our population would be 7,000,000 people larger than it is today. The discord that currently exists is the result of the "war upon the labor and capital of the world" maintained by England. When peace is restored by the abolition of this monopoly, it will be found that there is perfect harmony between the interests of the sheep farmer, the food producer, the miner, and the mechanic.

### CHAPTER ELEVENTH.

#### HOW PROTECTION AFFECTS THE PLANTER.

Having thus shown how the English (or colonial) system operates upon the farmers of England and the world at large, I propose now to examine how it operates upon the planters <note>In the mid-19th century, "planters" specifically referred to large-scale farmers in the American South, typically those growing cotton, tobacco, or sugar using enslaved labor.</note>.

Of all the products of the earth, cotton is the one best suited for clothing. It would be used universally if it were accessible to those who wanted it, but it is not. There are few commodities that can be more easily raised, and none that can be converted into clothing at a lower cost of labor. Yet, the arrangements for its distribution are so defective that by the time it reaches the consumer, it has become so expensive that consumption is almost non-existent.

The total quantity of cotton grown is probably 1,500,000,000 pounds, which is about one and a half pounds for every person in the world. Yet, despite how incredibly small this quantity is, the power of consumption throughout the world is so low that the...

# THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.

Cotton producers are currently competing with one another for control of the markets. This competition is so intense that whenever the crop in this country reaches one billion <note>Original: 1000,000,000</note> pounds, it is sold at a price lower than the actual cost of producing it. Some countries that used to export a significant amount of cotton now grow little more than what is needed for their own small internal use. Even here in the United States, there has been anxious discussion about limiting the quantity produced as the only way to avoid financial ruin. Throughout the South, planters are turning their attention to growing food, even though the market for every type of food is already oversupplied—and will remain so—unless we change our economic policy.

There is a constant complaint of "over-production." People even rejoice when a short growing season or some other accident reduces the crop by 200,000 or 300,000 bales, because the remaining portion sells for more on the global market than the entire crop would have otherwise. There is no better evidence that something is wrong with how goods are distributed.

Over-production cannot truly exist, but "under-consumption" can and does exist. The more that is produced, the more there is available to be consumed. Since every person’s ability to consume is exactly equal to their own production, the more a person can produce, the better it is for both them and their neighbor. This remains true unless there is some disturbing cause <note>Carey’s term for the British "colonial system" of trade, which he argues prevents direct exchange between farmers and manufacturers.</note> that prevents people who want to consume from producing the goods they need to trade with the cotton planter for the things they require for their comfort.

In examining the movements of the global cotton trade, I may occasionally refer to facts I have already mentioned. If I choose to restate them, it is because I believe it is best to collect all the necessary facts under one heading to ensure a proper understanding of this very important subject.

The two greatest cotton producers in the world are India and the United States. For a long time, India has exported food, cotton, indigo, and saltpeter to distant markets. These are bulky items, and the cost of freight and shipping absorbs nearly the entire value of the product. As a necessary consequence, the condition of the Indian people has steadily worsened. The difficulty of obtaining food has increased as their local manufacturing has declined. Repeated famines and diseases have killed millions, which has diminished their "power of combination" <note>In Carey’s economic theory, "combination" is the ability of people to live near each other and diversify their labor (e.g., having a blacksmith, a weaver, and a farmer in the same village).</note>. Consequently, India now exports *people* to take the jobs recently held by slaves in Jamaica, Guiana, Demerara, and other West Indian colonies. With every such step, cotton farming moves away from the rich, low-lying lands toward higher, poorer soil. The condition of the farmer gets worse because a larger portion of his crop is swallowed up by the cost of transportation.

In the early 1800s, Indian manufacturers supplied cotton goods to much of the world. However, England had invented machinery for production by then. To ensure she had exclusive use of this technology, England prohibited the export of machinery and the emigration of skilled artisans. In this way, she forced the cotton to come to the British loom, rather than permitting the loom to go to the cotton. Gradually, England cut off the Indian manufacturer’s foreign markets. However, the Indian manufacturer still had his home market as long as the East India Company <note>Original: "the Company"</note> maintained exclusive control of the trade. In 1821, the last year of that monopoly, England exported only 5 million yards of cloth and 4 million pounds of yarn to India. By 1832, that figure had reached 60 million. In the first half of last year, it reached 110 million yards of cloth and 10 million pounds of yarn. Though these figures seem large, it only takes about 100,000 bales of raw cotton to produce that amount of cloth. This would represent a consumption of perhaps 220,000 bales per year to replace the local industry that has been destroyed.

Production has decreased with every step in the increase of importation. Both the cultivation and the manufacture of cotton have disappeared from the fertile lands of Bengal. The fields formerly occupied by this most useful plant have returned to jungle. If we now wish to find the poor cotton planter, we must seek him among the hills. There, he obtains small crops in return for a great deal of labor and then spends months transporting his goods to the Ganges River. At the river, his meager product is shipped to Calcutta on its way to England. It returns to him perhaps at the close of the second year, providing him with a few yards of poor cloth—a combination of cotton and flour <note>original: "cotton and flour" — Referring to the practice of "sizing," where British textile mills used starch or flour to add weight and a smooth finish to cheap exported cloth.</note>—in return for the cultivation of an entire acre of land.*

Under this system, the value of labor diminishes steadily and regularly, and with it, the quantity and quality of the cotton produced.† Yet, the English are accustomed to regarding the low price of labor as an essential element of cheap production; they look to these low wages as a reason to hope for large supplies in the future. For example, Mr. Porter informs us that:

> “In the level plains of Candeish <note>Modern: Khandesh</note>, and in many other parts of Hindostan <note>Modern: India</note>, cotton wool, freed from the seed, could be sold with a profit to the cultivators at one penny per pound. This cost is trebled or quadrupled by the expense of conveyance to the ports of shipment.” —**Porter’s *Progress of the Nation.***

The price remaining for the cultivator is one penny per pound. However, it is difficult to imagine where "the profit" is to be found when his total wages consist of an insufficient supply of the poorest food and clothing—followed by famine and pestilence every time a crop fails.
