* The produce of the great cotton-growing districts on the Nerbudda <note>Modern: Narmada River</note> is carried on the backs of oxen. Each ox carries 160 pounds at the slow rate of seven miles a day in fair weather. The distance to Mirzapore on the Ganges is 500 miles, and the cost of transport is two and a half pence (five cents) per pound. From there, it goes to Calcutta—a distance of 800 miles—by water, without the aid of steam power, I believe. 

From another part of the cotton-growing districts in the Deccan, the transport involves a continuous journey of two months; during the rainy season, the road is impassable and the country's trade comes to a standstill. *In the absence of even a defined road*, the carriers and their pack cattle are forced to travel only by daylight to avoid losing their bullocks in the jungles they must pass through, all under a burning sun ranging from 100 to 140 degrees. 

If the herd—sometimes numbering as many as a thousand—is caught by rain, the cotton becomes saturated with moisture and turns heavy. The black clayey soil <note>This refers to "Regur" or Black Cotton Soil, which is fertile but becomes a sticky mire when wet.</note>, *which makes up the entire line of road*, sinks over a man's ankles and up to a laden ox's knees. In this predicament, the cargo sometimes lies on the ground for weeks, and the merchant is ruined! These "black clayey soils" are rich and fertile, yet they are superabundant and unused. The poor wretch who raises the cotton must cultivate the high lands that require neither clearing nor drainage, and his masters take half the product of those poor soils while refusing even to build a road *through* the rich ones. Instead, they force him to send his cotton to market to be exchanged for cotton cloth manufactured thousands of miles away. A system better designed to force men to continue cultivating the poorest soils using nothing but sticks could not be imagined.

# THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.

The lower the price of unproductive labor <note>original: "unproductive labour" — In Carey’s economic theory, this refers to the labor spent on transportation and middleman trade rather than on creating goods.</note> can be made, the lower its price will be. This leads to a more confident hope of using it profitably, and larger sums will be spent on an effort that must forever remain useless, so long as the people continue to be prevented from consuming the products of the land upon that very land.*

The deterioration of quality is due to farming retreating from the lower and richer lands. That retreat is a consequence of the system that ruined the manufacturers of India and destroyed the power of collective action. We know the superiority of Sea Island cotton. In Demerara <note>Modern: Guyana</note>, cotton plantations have always succeeded better on the seacoast than in the interior. It was the same in India. Salt manure is considered absolutely necessary if superior quality is desired, as it produces a fiber <note>original: "staple"</note> that is both strong and silky. Since this is the case, it is useless to attempt improvement when farming moves further from the sea every day. This shift has created a strong desire in England to build railroads, hoping to move cotton from the hills without spending more on labor for transport than was spent on growing it. Every such effort must fail. Free trade with England drove the industry to the hills. Even freer trade will drive it to hills that are even more distant. In some cases, it is thought that if the poor could be provided with carts, they could expand cultivation profitably. However, using such vehicles requires the existence of established roads—luxuries that most of India still lacks.

Like the people of India, those in the Southern United States have, until now, had a bulky export trade. This trade, of course, had to bear all the expenses of the voyage out and back. For a time, this arrangement was prosperous. India was far from the manufacturing centers <note>original: "machinery of conversion"</note>, while South Carolina was near. As long as it was still necessary to rely on India for supplies, the price of cotton raised in Carolina was the Indian price *plus* the difference in transportation costs. England acted as a kind of home market where the planter earned twenty or thirty cents per pound. Gradually, however, the nearby supply grew larger than the nearby demand, and it became necessary to seek...

---

If the manufacturing population of that country <note>England</note> increases during the next ten years at the same rate it has during the last, it will become necessary, in order to employ them, to secure a permanent and cheap supply of cotton. This can be done, he thinks, by cultivating it in British India, where, on the authority of Major-general Briggs, Sir Charles Forbes, and others, a supply can be produced that is sufficient for the wants of the entire world, equal in quality to the article supplied from New Orleans, and *cheaper by half*. He states the wages of American slave labor to be equal to about 1 shilling 6 pence <note>about 36 cents in 1850</note> per day, while that of the free Hindu <note>original: "Hindoo"</note> is only *about two pence* <note>about 4 cents</note>. The advantages to be derived from such a course, he stated, would be the certainty of a good and adequate supply at a cheap rate, the strengthening of our Indian possessions through commerce, and the emancipation of American slaves by making their labor unprofitable to their owners.

* The *London Chronicle*, in a recent article, shows that the efforts made during the last few years to make India a cotton-growing country that might rival the United States have entirely failed. It notes the failure and abandonment of the experiments in cotton cultivation carried on under Dr. Wight’s supervision at Madras. This project, which aimed to produce a product less obviously inferior to American cotton than the current badly picked and mediocre Indian variety, was zealously and even lavishly supported by the local government. However, the recent failure of a similar experiment in Bengal, after an expense of about 100,000 pounds <note>original: "£100,000"</note>, had already given fair warning of the likely outcome of Dr. Wight’s efforts in the neighboring province. Its abandonment would seem to settle the question: India will not again become, as it once was, a great cotton-growing country. In 1796, America did not export a single pound. In 1834, she exported as much as all the rest of the world put together. And in 1846, out of 467,856,274 lbs. imported into England, 401,949,893 lbs. came from the United States, while only 34,556,143 were supplied by the East Indies and Ceylon! The total value supplied from India in 1845 did not exceed 600,000 pounds.

# THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.

...markets for cloth and yarn in India and China. In these markets, the price the producer received could not exceed the local selling price *minus* the cost of transportation. The inevitable result was a decrease in the productivity of Indian labor and a reduced ability to consume cotton. This, of course, increased the quantity of cotton forced onto the global market. With every step of this process, there has been increased competition from the American grower. The result is that the Indian producer is ruined, while the American producer is saved from ruin only by natural disasters—frosts, floods <note>original: "freshets"</note>, and levee breaches <note>original: "crevasses" — specifically referring to breaks in the Mississippi River levee system</note>—which keep the supply within the limits of demand.

Average consumption in the United States is at least thirteen, and likely fifteen, pounds per person. This is at least half of what it would be if not for the heavy cost of labor for the consumer. Average global consumption outside the United States is just over one pound per person—about one-thirtieth of what it should be. Yet cotton has become almost like a weed in the world market <note>meaning it is overproduced to the point of being devalued</note>, and people everywhere want to replace it with crops that could be better grown elsewhere. In the uplands, they substitute wheat, which would grow better farther north. In the lowlands, they raise sugar, which would be much more productive farther south. These are serious economic discords, and it is important that we trace their cause to provide a remedy for such an unnatural state of affairs.

With a view to doing so, I provide the following:

The portion of Europe that has most fully adopted the system of protection being the **Zollverein** <note>original: *Zoll-verein* — the German Customs Union, an agreement among German states to create a free-trade area with a common external tariff</note>, it will be useful to compare the growth in their consumption with that of Great Britain and Ireland.

The imports of raw cotton into **Prussia** before the formation of the tariff league, or *Zollverein*, remained stationary from 1827 to 1835 at 44,000 hundredweights <note>original: "cwts." — a unit of weight equal to 112 pounds</note> per year. The import of yarn increased from 1823 to 1835, rising from 61,000 to 115,000 hundredweights. The total increase over 12 years was from 105,000 to 159,000 hundredweights, or from 30,000 to 45,000 bales. The quantity has more than doubled, and home consumption has increased about 75 percent <note>Reference from *Merchants’ Magazine*, Vol. XIII. p. 286.</note> during a period in which our own consumption in the United States had mostly remained stationary. The quantity of cotton yarn <note>original: "twist" — yarn spun for weaving</note> and wadding imported from Great Britain had increased 135 percent in a shorter period than was required for Great Britain to increase her own combined home and foreign consumption by only 21 percent. The power to import thus grew along with the power of production. 

It is obvious that consumption tends, and must tend, to increase most rapidly where there is the least intervention <note>Carey refers to "intervention" by middlemen, transporters, and distant markets that add cost without adding value.</note> between the producer and the consumer. Equally obvious is the fact that the English demand—which is based on the principle of intervening between the two and consequently increasing the cost to the consumer—cannot be largely and permanently increased. The demand in 1846–1847 was less than that of 1837–1838. Even with the great fall in prices, the difference between the demand in 1839–1840 and that of 1847–1848 was only 171,000 bales.

The great increase in the consumption of the *Zollverein* is due to protection... <note>The increase of consumption after the formation of the Union was very rapid. As early as 1838, it was said that "the cotton manufacture of Saxony had already become twice the size it had reached before the Union." — See Porter’s *Progress of the Nation*, Vol. II. p. 198. The quantity of cotton hosiery made in Saxony has increased immensely lately; due to its cheapness, it has not only secured a monopoly of the markets within the Union, but has also been shipped in large quantities to the United States.</note>

In the first case, England took 846,000 bales at 7 pence <note>original: 7d.</note>, totaling **$53,000,000**.
In the second case, she took 958,000 bales at 5.5 pence <note>original: 5 1/2 d.</note>, totaling **$48,000,000**.

In both instances, the price was fixed in her own ports and regulated by her own purchasing power. If our domestic consumption in the United States had absorbed an additional 200,000 bales—thereby reducing the global supply to 750,000—the price would have risen to 8 pence, and the total value would have reached **$54,000,000**. Consequently, the profit of the entire crop would have almost doubled.

The result of this inability to expand her foreign market is, naturally, the accumulation of large quantities of cotton in English ports. This is accompanied by a fall in prices, which allows the English consumer to obtain more clothing materials for the labor he can afford to give in exchange. However, this advantage tends to decrease as his labor becomes less productive and as the tendency to "fly from ills they know" <note>This is an allusion to Shakespeare’s *Hamlet*, suggesting that the population is increasingly desperate to escape their current hardships, often through emigration.</note> increases. This is illustrated by the following table:

The total home consumption by the 27,500,000 people living in the United Kingdom was thus only 1,200,000,000 pounds over ten years. This averages 120,000,000 pounds per year, or 4 1/3 pounds per person, supplied at a price so low it ruins the producer. The average of the first two years was 122,500,000 pounds, while the average of the last two years was only 102,500,000 pounds—despite a population increase that should have raised consumption to 140,000,000 pounds.

From this data, it is clear that the ability of the people of Great Britain and Ireland to be customers for the world's cotton planters cannot exceed $10,000,000. Instead of growing with the population, this power clearly tends to diminish. The reason for this seems obvious to me: the people of England are constantly trying to sell the products of their labor in distant markets by competing with low-priced labor, and therefore at the *lowest* possible price. In return, they receive payment in food and other goods produced in distant markets, which come to them burdened with enormous transportation costs, and therefore—

# THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.

...obtained at the cost of much labor. The natural growth of production elsewhere tends to increase the supply of raw materials, but the power to pay for them does not increase. This is because the labor of British subjects, both at home and in the colonies, instead of becoming more productive of goods to be given in exchange, is becoming less productive from month to month and from year to year. Yet, into that constantly diminishing market are thrown all the surplus products of the world, so that the price of the entire global product may be fixed there. The effect of this is to shift the loss onto the planters—a loss that should belong to the British—and thus enable the British to supply themselves at the *lowest* price. Conversely, whenever the cotton planter ceases to be dependent upon them for his market, the British will again, as they did formerly, be obliged to buy at the *highest* price. The product of British labor, when measured in the first necessity of life—food—is small. Therefore, the remaining surplus to be spent on clothing is very small indeed. They are incessantly engaged in supplying low-priced, and often worthless, clothing to the rest of the world, and are therefore unable to clothe themselves.

That the trend is downward seems scarcely to admit of a doubt. A few years ago, through a great effort, the <term>poor-rates</term> <note>original: "poor-rates"; taxes levied at the parish level to provide relief for the local poor</note> of England were reduced to less than £4,000,000. They have since risen gradually, and those of 1848 were £7,817,000, or $38,000,000. Every ninth person is a pauper. In Scotland, the destitution of a large portion of the population is frightful. The people of the Northern and Western Highlands are in a state of pauperism, and Glasgow and its vicinity present a scene of wretchedness scarcely, if at all, to be exceeded in the world. Ireland is exhausted. Since there are no separate accounts of the imports into that kingdom, it is not possible to determine the current consumption of cotton, but the condition of the people is now far lower than at the dates of the following returns:

The total import of cotton into Ireland from all parts of the world, in the twenty years from 1802 to 1821 inclusive, amounted to 538,542 <term>hundredweights</term> <note>original: "hundred weights"; a unit of weight equal to 112 pounds in the British system</note>, or about 150,000 bales. This is an average of 7,500 bales per year. The total import of cotton yarn was 19,995,350 pounds, or about 1,000,000 pounds per year (the product of about 4,000 bales), making a total of 11,500 bales.* The amount of cloth imported is not provided.

In 1825—a year of great economic expansion everywhere—with an export of agricultural products to Great Britain amounting to almost $35,000,000, we find the import of raw cotton <note>original: "cotton-wool"</note> to have been 4,065,930 pounds, and the import of cotton cloth to have been 4,996,885 yards. This makes a total of about 6,000,000 pounds, or about 18,000 bales of cotton in all its forms, required for the supply of almost 8,000,000 people. This amounts to about three-quarters of a pound per person.

In subsequent years, no information can be obtained due to changes in the way the <term>custom-house</term> <note>the government office responsible for collecting duties and regulating imports/exports</note> accounts were kept. However, in a general report on the state of Irish trade made by a committee whose goals would not have been helped by underestimating the numbers, it is stated that the import of cotton cloth into that kingdom in 1835 was 14,172,000 yards. This is equal to about 4,000,000 pounds of cotton, or half a pound per person. What quantity of raw cotton or yarn was imported at that time cannot be determined, but it is shown elsewhere that some of the largest manufacturing establishments from a slightly earlier period had disappeared, and that the <term>calico printers</term> <note>businesses that printed decorative patterns on cotton cloth</note> were in a state of bankruptcy.†

Large quantities of cotton were sent to Gibraltar, Malta, Jamaica, and other locations to be smuggled into Spain, Mexico, and various other countries. The actual consumption within the British colonies themselves could not have exceeded 70,000,000 pounds—or about 170,000 bales—for a population of more than 100,000,000 people. During this period, the average price was a fraction over seven cents per pound. It follows that $5,000,000 is the maximum amount of trade maintained through England by the American cotton-planting states with a large portion of the world's population, despite those states producing two-thirds of the world's supply of this necessary commodity.

| | 1845 | 1846 | 1847 |
|----------|----------|----------|----------|
| **Millions of pounds** | 239 | 234 | 144 |

Is there any better evidence of the poverty inflicted by this system upon the people subject to it than the fact that a price increase of just one cent per yard reduces consumption by almost half?

Compare this with the growth of consumption in the protected markets of Germany and the United States. It becomes clear how steady the protected system (which is true free trade) is, compared to the perpetual instability of the monopoly system. Consider, too, the massive difference in consumption per person!

While England and all her vast global possessions consumed only 144,000,000 pounds, the consumption of the <term>Zollverein</term> <note>original: "Zoll-verein"; The German Customs Union, a coalition of German states formed to manage tariffs and economic policies within their territories.</note> (with a population of 25,000,000) had grown in nine years from 45,000,000 to 115,000,000 pounds, and the consumption in the United States was 243,000,000 pounds.

We have seen how slow the growth of English demand has been, and it is now worth examining the wasteful and exhausting process by which even this demand was achieved. "The extremely low price of cotton," say Messrs. Rathbone, Brothers & Co. in their circular,* "has encouraged the manufacture of a very inferior class of goods. These require a great weight of cotton compared to the labor spent on them, and *the production of these goods ceases entirely when cotton prices are even moderately high.*" They continue, "The demand for very coarse yarn is always large when prices are very cheap, but in the year just closed, it has exceeded all precedent,† particularly for export—chiefly to the <term>Levant</term> <note>A historical term for the Eastern Mediterranean region, including modern-day Turkey, Syria, Lebanon, Israel, Jordan, and Palestine.</note>. In some instances, to speed up its production, *it has not even passed through all the usual manufacturing processes.* It is the consumption of cotton for these low-quality goods," they add, "that is most immediately affected by even a moderate increase in prices." 

The cotton thus forced into the Levant goes to the same countries that were previously supplied by India. Consequently, the poor Indian producer is deprived of another portion of his market. The necessary result of this must be a further collapse of prices and an increased inability for Indian producers to continue their work. The decline in the trade of Western India is remarkable and is likely the result of flooding Asiatic markets with these half-made cotton goods.‡

<meta>This page continues Carey’s argument that the British "monopoly" system creates economic instability. # THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.

It has already been shown how large the export to India was in the first six months of the year, and now we see the consequences reported in the newspapers of the day. Even with the low price of cotton, the speculation has not paid off. The markets are glutted <note>oversupplied</note>, and the prices are unprofitable. "Great caution," it is said, "must now be exercised, or the exporting houses will suffer exceedingly."* The small rise in price has already caused many mills to begin working "short-time" <note>reduced hours</note>, and the factory workers are thus deprived of the money they need to purchase clothing. It is a highly speculative and extraordinary system—the most destructive to the interests of the world’s agricultural population ever devised. Feverish growth and chilling decline follow each other so rapidly that we are barely notified of the arrival of one before we see signs of the other’s approach. 

The reason it is so difficult to expand the sale of cotton in distant markets is that the **labor-cost** <note>the amount of work a person must do to afford the product</note> of the cloth obtained that way is too high. We have seen that the expansion of manufacturing in this country was rapid for a few years following the passage of the Tariff of 1828. Manufacturing then became almost stationary under the Compromise Tariff <note>The Compromise Tariff of 1833, which gradually reduced protectionist duties</note>; during that time, imports not only failed to increase but actually decreased until they reached their lowest point in 1842–43. The labor-cost of clothing was steadily increasing during that period. However, as the Tariff of 1842 came into operation, the labor-cost diminished. This created the power to pay for finer cloths from abroad, and thus both domestic manufacturing and imports increased together. 

To see how this works, we need only look at a single farmer in Tennessee or Kentucky. He might harvest 30 or 40 bushels of corn for the labor spent on one acre of land. He is happy to sell it at 20 cents per bushel,† even when the price in Liverpool is 75 or 80 cents. Thirty-five bushels yield him $7, which is roughly the cost of 70 yards of decent cotton cloth (both plain and printed) by the time it reaches his farm. To produce those 70 yards of cloth requires only 20 pounds of cotton—about one-twentieth of the yield of a well-cultivated acre. Converting those pounds of raw cotton into yards of cloth requires far less than half the capital and half the labor that was required to grow the cotton in the first place. 

However, even if we estimate the processing cost at one-half and add that to the weight of the cotton, we see that the farmer is essentially giving 35 bushels of corn in exchange for the equivalent of 30 pounds of raw cotton. Yet that same corn sells, at the place where it is consumed, for enough money to purchase almost a whole bale of cotton. It is obvious that although the *money-price* of the cloth is low, the *labor-price* (what the farmer must do to get it) is high. It is this labor-price that determines how much people can consume. Furthermore, the cloth itself is often of poor quality. As far back as 1832, the amount of flour <note>used as "sizing" or starch to add weight and stiffness to fabric</note> required for use in English cotton factories was stated at *forty-two million pounds*,‡ or almost the weight of 100,000 bales of cotton. All of this flour is sold as if it were cotton to poor consumers in distant lands, who are thus defrauded and impoverished.

Bad as this is, the total loss is even greater. When corn is sent away from the land, the farmer loses the organic refuse (manure). The soil is impoverished, and the farmer is eventually compelled to move to other lands, only to impoverish those as well. *The loss from this soil depletion alone is worth far more than the value of every single import brought into the United States from all the manufacturing nations of the world.* This apparently "cheap" clothing is actually very expensive. It is obtained at the cost of immense labor, and it has little value once it is finally acquired.

He replied that it was worth ten cents, and wheat was fifty cents a bushel."—*Augusta Chronicle*, May 1849.

# THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.

What is true of Tennessee and India is equally true for the rest of the world that is compelled to depend on England for supplies of cotton cloth. The poor Russian obtains less than a pound of cotton for a bushel of wheat; he essentially gives ten days of labor for one. In contrast, if he could have that cotton converted locally by the same person who ate his food, he would trade one day of labor for another. This is also the case for the German, the South American, the Mexican, the Italian, the Spaniard, and the Turk. The system tends to prevent people from concentrating and working together, which diminishes the value of labor throughout the world. It is because of this that almost all nations are trying to block the manufactured goods of Great Britain.

Everywhere these nations turn, however, they are met by the smuggler—someone now regarded by the highest authorities in Great Britain as the "greatest of reformers." Gibraltar is maintained as a base for the purpose of smuggling goods into Spain. Exhausted Portugal receives millions of pounds of cotton goods, also to be smuggled into Spain. Thus, that unfortunate country is kept in a state of poverty because the people of England believe it is profitable to buy cloth produced abroad, even while their own laborers sit idle for lack of work and food rots in the fields for want of mouths to eat it or roads to transport it.

If the system tends to exhaust the people who have to buy cotton at such high prices, it exhausts those who produce it just as much. These producers are compelled to sell at whatever price the people of England think proper to set. Why that is so may be understood by examining the following table:

The price quotes for the latter part of last year were below the average, being about 4d., and they remained at that point for several months until the main portion of the crop had been shipped. Unfavorable prospects for the new crop prevented a further fall, but it is impossible to tell what the price would have been if this year's production had increased in proportion to the population engaged in producing it. It certainly would have fallen much lower than four pence. 

An examination of this table will, I think, enable us to understand the cause of the present extraordinary state of things. A large portion of this year's crop has been destroyed by frosts and floods <note>original: "freshets"</note>. Surprisingly, instead of bringing distress and ruin, that fact has brought increased activity and life to the planters, and an increased power to consume cloth, sugar, coffee, and other goods. Why is this? I believe the answer is easily found.

The total amount that Great Britain can collect in payment for American cotton—whether consumed at home or abroad, including freights and commissions—appears to be limited to somewhere between $45,000,000 and $57,000,000.

# THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.

...with a clear tendency to decrease. Of the crops from the past four years, the quantity consumed here in the United States and exported by us directly to foreign ports has stayed fairly consistent at about 1,000,000 bales. The rest has gone to England, which has $57,000,000 available to pay for 900,000 bales—roughly $63 per bale. However, when the total crop reaches 2,400,000 bales and we send England 1,400,000, that entire larger quantity must be paid for with a sum smaller than $57,000,000. This is because there are now massive expenses for storage, interest, risk, and other costs. Consequently, the total amount available to the planters falls to $50,000,000, leaving the planter with only $36 per bale. Out of this, he must also pay the high shipping rates <note>original: "freights"</note> that come with large crops, rather than the moderate shipping rates that would have applied to a smaller number of bales. The price obtained in England sets the price for the entire crop, and the result is as follows:

1,900,000 bales at $63 each: $120,000,000
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Minus the low shipping costs, at home and abroad, for a small quantity.
2,400,000 bales at $36 each: $86,000,000
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Minus the high shipping costs, at home and abroad, for a large quantity.

It is obvious that it would have been far better if those extra 500,000 bales had been burned or destroyed by frost before they were even picked.
The crop of 1844 was 812,000,000 pounds, and the value was estimated at $65,772,000.
In 1845, it rose to 958,000,000 pounds, and the value fell to $56,000,000.
In 1847, it fell to 711,000,000 pounds, yet it was worth $72,000,000.
In 1848, it rose to 1,100,000,000 pounds, and until the occurrence of frosts and <term>freshets</term> <note>freshets: sudden floods in a river from heavy rain or melting snow</note>, the prospect was that it would not average more than 5¼ cents in New Orleans, or about $60,000,000.

The gradual but steady subjugation of the planters to this system can be seen from the following facts: From 1830 to 1835, the price of cotton here was about eleven cents. We can assume this is roughly what it would yield in England, after shipping and charges. In those years, our average export was about 320,000,000 pounds, yielding about $35,000,000. At that time, the average price of a piece of cotton cloth (24 yards long, weighing 5 lbs. 12 oz.) was 7 shillings and 10 pence ($1.88), and the price of iron was £6 10s ($31.20). Therefore, our exports, when delivered in Liverpool, would have bought us 18,500,000 pieces of cloth, or about 1,100,000 tons of iron. 

In 1845 and 1846, the amount of cotton consumed by the people of England was almost the same quantity—about 311,000,000 pounds—but the average price here was only 6½ cents, making the total value $20,000,000. The price of cloth then was 6 shillings and 6⅛ pence ($1.57½), and iron was about £10 ($48). The result was that for nearly the same quantity of cotton, we could only get about 12,500,000 pieces of cloth, or about 420,000 tons of iron, delivered in Liverpool. If we divide the return between the two commodities, the loss looks like this:

| | Average from 1830 to 1835. | 1845–46. | Loss. |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Cloth (pieces) | 9,250,000 | 6,250,000 | 3,000,000 |
| Iron (tons) | 550,000 | 210,000 | 340,000 |

The labor required to turn cotton into cloth had been greatly reduced by technology, and yet the proportion of the crop kept by the manufacturers had greatly increased, as shown here:

| | Weight of Cotton used (lbs). | Weight of Cotton given back to planters (in goods). | Retained by the manufacturers (lbs). |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| 1830 to 1835 | 320,000,000 | 110,000,000 | 210,000,000 |
| 1845 and 1846 | 311,000,000 | 74,000,000 | 237,000,000 |

# THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.

In the first period, the planter would have had 34 percent of his cotton returned to him in the form of finished cloth, but in the second period, he received only 24 percent. The grist miller <note>original: "grist miller"; a miller who grinds a farmer’s grain into flour, usually keeping a small portion as payment</note> gives the farmer a larger proportion of the grain’s product from year to year; thus, the farmer gains all the profit from every technological improvement. In contrast, the cotton miller gives the planter a smaller portion of the produced cloth every year. The grain miller moves closer to the producer every day, while the cotton miller moves further away, because as the volume of product increases, the cost of transportation also increases.

We may now investigate the cause of the surplus of stock in the English market. If that can be determined, we will be able to see why the price of cotton has fallen to such ruinously low levels.

Of the crop of 1828–29, our own domestic consumption was . . . 118,000 bales.
Of the crops of 1832–33 and 1833–34, the average was . . . 195,000 bales.
Of the crop of 1834–35, it was . . . 216,000 bales.

Our consumption almost doubled in six years, with a trend toward even faster growth. This increase occurred without any decrease in our consumption of foreign-made cloth.

Of the crop of 1841–42, we consumed only . . . 268,000 bales,
accompanied by a great decrease in the consumption of foreign cloth.

Of the crop of 1847–48, we consumed . . . 607,000 bales,
accompanied by a large increase in the consumption of foreign cloth. Total consumption more than doubled in a similar period of time. In the intermediate period between 1835 and 1843, our consumption remained stagnant. If it had not been disrupted by the effects of the Compromise bill <note>original: "Compromise bill"; the Tariff of 1833, which reduced protective duties and was blamed by Carey for stalling American industrial growth</note>, it certainly would have doubled in that period, and likely much more than doubled. However, if we assume an increase of only 12.5 percent per year—which is four times the rate of population growth—the home demand would have been as follows:

No one can doubt that progress would have been greater than what is recorded here. Yet, even with these conservative estimates, we would have used over 3,000,000 more bales than we actually did. If we had used them, the producer of the cotton would have set the price, rather than the buyer. Under those circumstances, would the price have fallen below ten or twelve cents per pound? On the contrary, would it not have risen to fourteen or fifteen cents, unless the total crop had significantly increased? I believe it would have, and I am certain that it will do so shortly after we fully adopt a system—

<meta>This page continues Henry Charles Carey’s argument that a strong domestic "home market" is the only way to ensure high prices for American cotton and fair wages for labor. He contends that protective tariffs create the industrial infrastructure necessary for this consumption.</meta>

-># THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.<-

...that will establish a market for labor here that will enable us to consume the products of the land directly on the land itself. My reasons for believing this are as follows:

The good cotton lands of India are currently unused. To make them productive requires both labor and capital. To encourage the use of either, the laborer must receive wages and the owner of capital must see a profit. Both wages and profits must increase in price as demand for them grows. Such a demand will inevitably arise when England finds herself forced to look to India for an increased supply of cotton. This must happen as soon as our domestic American demand rises to **1,000,000** bales per year—which will occur within the next three years, if the economy is permitted to grow.

It will be asked, what should we do with all this cloth? In reply, I say again—and I repeat it because it is essential to remember—*every person is a consumer to the full extent of what they produce, whatever that may be.* If the Tariff of 1828 <note>original: "tariff of 1828"; a protective tariff designed to protect northern industry, which Carey argues benefited the whole economy</note> had remained unchanged, coal production in the same period would have reached **15,000,000** tons. This is because furnaces and rolling mills would have been built throughout the country, and railroad tracks would have been manufactured by the hundreds of thousands of tons. Triple the amount of railroads would have been constructed without causing financial bankruptcy. The demand for railroads, mills, furnaces, and steam engines of every kind would have created a massive demand for labor that was otherwise wasted. Those surplus earnings would have been spent on clothing and other comforts of life. This would have created a market on the land for the products of the land worth hundreds of millions of dollars, enabling both the farmer and the planter to improve their tools for production and transportation—growing rich instead of remaining poor as they have done. With every such step, immigration from Europe would have increased, and since every person would have immediately become a producer, everyone would have been a consumer. The Englishman would consume twelve pounds of cotton where before he consumed only four; the Irishman would consume twelve where before he consumed only one. Meanwhile, shipping costs to Europe would be so reduced that the price of cotton in New York would be nearly as high as in Liverpool.

It should be noted that the quantity set here for 1846–1847 exceeds what we actually consumed by only one-third. If immigration had continued to increase from 1834 to the present at the rate it was then advancing, our population would be **20** percent larger than it is now. This would account for nearly the entire quantity of cotton, even without accounting for increased consumption by the existing population. All these people would have required large supplies of coffee, silk, and a thousand other foreign goods, much of which we would have paid for with finished cotton products. The ease of obtaining iron would have provided roads to the farmer and planter, and everyone would have had more profit from their labor to spend on clothing. The planter himself and his people <note>original: "his people"; in the context of the 1850s American South, this refers to enslaved laborers</note> would now be consuming three yards of cloth where they now consume only one, and the home market would now be absorbing **1,200,000** bales instead of a million. What then would be the price of cotton, even with a total crop of **3,000,000** bales? Would it not be **$60** a bale, yielding the planter **180 million dollars** instead of **80 million**? I believe it would.

In 1845 and 1846, the planter supplied **311,000,000** pounds of cotton. In exchange for this, delivered at the coast, he could have received **74,000,000** pounds of finished cloth delivered in Liverpool, with him paying the freight and commissions for the return trip. In reality, he gave **156,000,000** pounds of raw cotton for **37,000,000** pounds of cloth; the shipping charges on this, even without taxes, would have reduced his share to **30,000,000** pounds at the plantation, and probably less. That **30,000,000** had, however, been spun and woven <note>original: "twisted and woven"</note>, and the difference...

->### THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.<-

The 126 million pounds of cotton was what the planter gave in exchange for the spinning <note>original: "twisting"</note> and weaving of *30 million* pounds. The average annual work of factory workers—men, women, boys, and girls—amounts to converting 3,000 pounds of cotton into cloth. Therefore, the planter gave 126 million pounds of cotton to pay for the labor of 10,000 people (mostly boys and girls), and he had to transport 156 million pounds to the market. If he calculated the cost of shipping from the plantation to Nashville or another shipping point, he would find that transport alone cost more than the value of the labor he received in return. In fact, he had essentially given the cotton away, receiving nothing of equal value in return.

If all 156 million pounds had been converted into cloth within the country, it would have provided about seven additional pounds of cloth for every person in the United States. This cloth would have then been consumed at home. Consumption in the South would have risen to match the current levels in the North, and Northern consumption would have increased significantly because of the high demand for labor that would have existed. If this had happened, the price for the entire crop would have been 8 pence <note>The "d" stands for denarius, the symbol for a British penny</note> instead of 4.5 pence. The planter would have received an *additional* seven cents per pound on 900 million pounds—a total of *63 million dollars*. As large as that sum is, it represents only a fraction of the benefits that would have resulted from this approach.

Some will argue that high prices would stop people from buying cotton. If that is a concern, it is vital for the producer to eliminate the massive fees charged by the many middlemen who now stand between him and the consumers. High prices caused by the current system do stop consumption because they act as a tax on both the producer and the consumer. However, if the planter received higher prices because it became easier to trade directly with the consumer, it would have the opposite effect. It would increase consumption because we would receive more from the rest of the world for what we sell, and our domestic consumption would grow more quickly. The increasing immigration to the United States would raise the value of labor abroad. Landlords in Europe, who are currently evicting people from their lands and burning their houses so they cannot return, would then be forced to offer them incentives to stay. Agriculture would improve, wages would rise, and the ability to buy cotton would grow on both sides of the Atlantic, greatly benefiting the planter. With this increased demand, he would finally find some stability instead of the current "gambling" system that often leaves him nearly ruined. The following diagrams, taken from the circular of Messrs. Rathbone, Brothers, & Co. (mentioned previously), show how little stability currently exists.

The middle line shows the fluctuations of cotton "long cloth" <note>A plain cotton fabric made in long pieces.</note>; the prices are listed per piece on the right side of the charts.

***

Here we see that the price of cotton is lowest when the price of cloth is highest. The manufacturers are making fortunes while the planter is being ruined. These are the inevitable results of a system that forces almost all the world's cotton into a single market (England). In that market, there is only a fixed amount of money to be exchanged for cotton. Consequently, the price of every pound of cotton depends entirely on how the total supply relates to the constantly shrinking amount of money available to pay for it. It is a constantly shrinking <term>Procrustean bed</term> <note>original: "Procrustean bed." A reference to a Greek myth about a man who forced travelers to fit into a bed by either stretching them or cutting off their legs; here, it means a system that forces everyone to fit into an arbitrary and harmful standard.</note>. 

While the system destroys the planter and lessens his ability to provide for his people, the manufacturers continually criticize him for being a slave owner. They also constantly threaten to replace his cotton with the "free" labor of the impoverished <term>Hindoo</term> <note>A term used in the 19th century to refer generally to the people of India.</note> rather than the well-fed, well-clothed, and well-housed laborer of the American South. The lower the price of cotton falls, the more determined the British are to keep it low. They plan to build railroads in India so that Indian cotton can reach the market cheaply and British cotton cloth can be sent more easily to that country. Yet, with every increase in the export of cotton goods to India, the poor Indian laborer becomes more enslaved and falls further victim to famine and disease.

The difference between twelve cents and eight cents per pound for cotton amounts to about one cent per yard of fabric. People in Great Britain and Ireland consume about fifteen yards of fabric per person, while the average in the British colonies is only about three yards. It is absurd to think that this tiny price difference would significantly change how much cloth people buy under normal circumstances. 

However, imagine how much our own home consumption would increase if we adopted a system that allowed the farmers of Tennessee and Ohio to exchange their produce directly with the Southern planter—food for cotton. They could trade on an equal basis—acre for acre—instead of the current system where they must trade many bushels of food for just a few pounds of cotton. Currently, the value of that exchange is swallowed up by the cost of transporting food and cotton to and from Liverpool and Manchester.

The harmony of interests throughout every part of the United States <note>original: "the Union"</note> is perfect; all that is needed is for everyone to understand it. What injures the farmer also injures the planter, and the reverse is also true <note>original: "vice versa"</note>: the planter cannot suffer without the farmer being hurt as well. Throughout the South, planters are currently abandoning cotton and planting wheat instead. They are doing this at the very moment when the European market—

->### THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.<-

...for food is to be closed off from the hundreds of millions of people for whom, it is claimed, we now need a market.

Since some might doubt that this harmony exists, I intend to show how our current course of action regarding food production tends to destroy the market for cotton.

The people of Germany and Russia have food to sell after they have fed themselves. They wish to use the proceeds from that food to buy cloth. The higher the price they receive for the food they sell, the more cloth they can afford to buy. Currently, the primary food market is England. If we flood that market with our products, the price of food will be low, and the German people will be able to buy very little cotton. If we do not flood it, the price may remain high, and they may buy a great deal of cotton. We are currently turning laborers, miners, and mechanics into farmers; this reduces the number of consumers and increases the number of producers. The more consumers we have at home, the less surplus food we will have to spare. This makes the price of food in England higher, which increases the amount of cotton that can be purchased by the Germans and the Russians. Conversely, the more producers we have, the more food we will have to sell; this lowers the price and reduces the amount of cotton that can be purchased <note>original: "produced"</note> by the Germans and Russians. 

All of this seems so obviously true to me that it only needs to be stated. We have seen that the price of food here is maintained by domestic demand resulting from the massive immigration currently taking place. We know that if we could increase next year's immigration to half a million people—by creating a demand for labor to build furnaces, mills, and other similar works—there would be an even greater demand for grain. This would drive prices even higher. 

Let us now suppose that next year's immigration reaches 600,000 people, producing a further increase in food demand worth twenty or thirty million dollars, and see what the effect would be on the <term>planter</term> <note>In this context, a large-scale farmer, typically in the South, who grew cash crops like cotton or tobacco.</note>. The Canadian farmer would find a market for his grain within the United States <note>original: "the Union"</note>, because the price would be high enough to allow him to pay the import <term>duty</term> <note>A tax paid on goods brought into a country.</note>. The value of agricultural labor everywhere would rise along with the increasing price of food. Every farmer, both at home and abroad, would consume more cloth because he could sell the products of his labor at a higher price; that is, he could obtain more cloth and iron in exchange for his crops. The German, the Russian, the Irishman, and the Englishman would be better customers than they are now. Meanwhile, the domestic demand would absorb enormous quantities of goods that would otherwise go to England to increase the "stock on hand"—the measurement used to determine the price paid for the upcoming crop.

Our present policy tends to destroy both the domestic and the foreign markets. It reduces the productivity of labor on both sides of the Atlantic. Everything taken from the surplus that remains after the laborer is fed is also taken from the fund that would otherwise be spent on cloth or iron.

### THE TOBACCO PLANTER.

A brief examination of the tobacco trade will show exactly the same results. In 1822, we exported 83,000 <term>hogsheads</term> <note>A large wooden barrel used to ship tobacco, typically holding about 1,000 pounds.</note>, and the price was $74.82, yielding about $6,200,000. In 1845, we exported 147,000 hogsheads, and the price was $50.00, yielding $7,350,000. After subtracting the extra cost of transporting the larger quantity to the shipping port, the producers actually received less for the larger shipment than they had for the smaller one. From 1830 to 1835, the average export was 90,000 hogsheads, bringing in $6,200,000—which gave the producer at his plantation as much money as the much larger quantity exported in 1845. The sum of $6,200,000, during these two periods, would have purchased in Liverpool—

The planter is giving almost two-thirds more tobacco for only twenty percent more cloth, even though his fellow planter is almost ruined by the low price of cotton. However, in the case of iron, the situation is even worse, for he gives two-thirds *more* tobacco for thirty-five percent *less* iron. In the first period, he could obtain two and one-fifth tons for a <term>hogshead</term> <note>original: "hogshead"; a large wooden cask used to ship tobacco, weighing roughly 1,000 pounds</note>; whereas in the latter period, he receives little more than one-third of that quantity, or seven-eighths of a ton. 

It is obvious that he is being taxed by someone—that he is giving more and receiving less—and the cause of this is that the productive power enabling people outside of the United States <note>original: "the Union"</note> to pay for tobacco does not keep pace with the power of those inside the country to produce it. What is his remedy? It is to increase the number of people inside the United States with whom he can have perfect freedom of trade. The Englishman would consume six pounds of tobacco for every one pound he consumes now if it were not burdened with a tax of three shillings per pound; the German would do the same, as would the Frenchman, once he can free himself from the tax imposed on him by the government monopoly. 

The more people who are brought into the country through immigration, the more will be moved from the list of small customers to the list of large ones. Consequently, the cost of transportation from the place of production in Maryland, Virginia, Ohio, or Kentucky to the place of consumption in Philadelphia, New York, Berlin, or Vienna will decrease. This is because the larger the volume and value of the goods transported west, the lower the charges will be for transporting goods eastward. Therefore, there is perfect harmony between the interests of the tobacco planter, the manufacturer, and the ship-owner.

### THE SUGAR PLANTER.

The sugar trade presents the same state of affairs. The farmers <note>original: "agriculturists"</note> of the world are giving a constantly increasing quantity of labor in exchange for a constantly diminishing return. The following record of the movement of the great sugar market since the start of the 19th century shows that the total amount paid for sugar has been constantly decreasing. Meanwhile, the price of the English goods given in exchange has varied so little that while in 1801 the consumption of 14.2 people paid for one ton of iron, by 1831 it required the consumption of 24 people, and that proportion has been steadily increasing. The total sum paid in 1847 for this important food item by *twenty-nine million* people was less than what was paid in 1801 by sixteen million people, and the contribution per person was less than half. Yet, the difference in the price of iron was, by comparison, insignificant.*

I am not extending this table further because Mr. Tooke’s list of prices <note>Tooke’s *History of Prices*, a famous 19th-century economic reference</note> does not reach the end of the next ten-year period, and I have no other list that seems to match it. However, enough information is provided to show that the people of the United Kingdom were steadily giving less iron in exchange for more sugar. In 1801, the sugar planter could have obtained 1,100,000 tons of iron as the equivalent of 180,000 tons of sugar; but by 1831, he could only get a million tons of iron as the equivalent of 210,000 tons of sugar. From that time to the present, there has been a constant effort to make sugar cheaper. Yet, in the years 1845 to 1847, only 15,900,000 hundredweights were taken for consumption (including the large quantity exported after being refined). This averages 5,300,000 hundredweights per year—only 45 percent more than in 1801, even though the population had increased by 90 percent. It is obvious that the ability to consume sugar is diminishing, yet the prices for the entire world are set in England. The result of this is seen in the fact that 5,800,000 tons in 1847 would only buy £7,200,000 worth of goods, while 3,600,000 tons in 1801 would buy about £8,200,000.

The profit on labor used to grow cotton has fallen so low that the Carolinian planter is trying to grow wheat, and the Mississippian is trying to grow sugar. Sugar prices fall so low that the West Indian planter turns his attention to coffee. By the time his coffee trees have become productive, the price of coffee has fallen so much that he cuts them down—and then the price rises again, while the price of sugar falls.§ This happens everywhere and at all times. The producers are dominated by the <term>exchangers</term> <note>middlemen, merchants, and shippers</note>, and they will continue to be as long as the price of their entire crop is determined by whatever price can be obtained for a small surplus in the constantly shrinking market of England.

The global production of sugar is roughly one million tons, and the total earnings for the planters may be about $70,000,000. Taking the cotton crop at $80,000,000, we have a total of $150,000,000 as the value of the labor for that large portion of the world's population employed in producing these two articles, which are so essential to the comfort of everyone else. The equivalent of this sum in 1845 and 1846 (delivered at the plantation) might have been about 2,500,000 tons of iron—the article that is more essential than any other for maintaining or increasing productive power.

A ton of <term>bar iron</term> <note>raw iron processed into bars for blacksmithing or manufacturing</note> is not even worth twenty-five days of labor when that labor is properly applied in the coal and iron fields of the United States <note>original: "the Union"</note>. But even at that rate, one man would produce more than twelve tons per year. To produce the entire quantity of iron required to pay for the cotton and sugar crops of the whole world would, therefore, only require the labor of 200,000 men. Is it not obvious that the world's farmers are being taxed a massive amount to support...

These men are fleeing the rich, unused soils of lower South Carolina and southern Alabama for the highlands of Arkansas and Texas. In doing so, they increase their need for transportation while diminishing their ability to pay for it. No matter how fast they flee, they cannot run fast enough to stop the increase of the cotton crop, the average of which must soon reach three million bales. But where will the planter find a market then? Among the world's sugar planters? Like him, they are ruined for lack of a market. Among the coffee growers? They, too, are ruined for lack of a market. Among the wheat growers? The Russian farmer wastes his crop for lack of a market, and the American farmer is competing with him for the English market, while the Englishman is ruined by competing with both.† Are they among the factory workers of England? Wherever one looks, he must see that the producers of the world want markets. Because they lack them, they are becoming poorer instead of richer. Their ability to even buy the machinery of production is daily diminishing. The price of iron—when measured in sugar, coffee, cotton, wheat, indigo, or any other product of the earth—is tending steadily upward. Yet, there is no single commodity in the world that would tend to fall in price so steadily if it were not for the existence of *the monopoly system* <note>The author refers to the British system of centralized manufacturing, which forced the rest of the world to sell raw materials cheaply and buy finished goods at high prices</note>. The supply of iron could be increased to an indefinite amount, and with a rapidity far exceeding that of any agricultural product. If we created a market requiring 10,000,000 tons annually, this country could supply it within ten years. Double or triple that amount, and we could supply the whole requirement in a reasonable time; our capacity is limitless, and we could employ half the laborers of Europe. 

It is here, *and here alone*, that the cotton planter can look for a market capable of expanding at the same rate as his power to produce. Here, and here alone, can the market for coffee, silk, indigo, and all other products be so enlarged that the coffee planter and the silk grower can quadruple their own consumption of cotton.

## CHAPTER ELEVENTH.

### HOW PROTECTION AFFECTS THE LANDOWNER.

**THE** great savings fund is the land. It acquires value through the almost imperceptible contribution of labor. The first object of a poor farmer working thin soils is to obtain food and clothing for himself and his family. He gives his leisure time to the work of improvement. In one place he digs a small drain; in another, he roots out a stump. At one moment he cuts fuel for his family—thereby clearing his land—and at another he digs...

<note>The following passage discusses how British economic policy and the repeal of the Corn Laws (tariffs on imported grain) affected English and Irish farmers.</note>

> "The prospect of an Irish demand for grain <note>original: "corn"</note> is improving, and the dependence of England on foreign supplies will gradually increase. The land monopoly of England, by adding the cost of rent to be paid by the tenant farmer, required a tax on foreign imports. This tax protected the English farmer against foreign producers who had no rent to pay. The removal of this tax [the repeal of the Corn Laws] has now thrown the entire burden of the rent directly onto the English farmer; previously, that burden was shared by all consumers of bread. This burden will be made even worse by the repeal of the Navigation Laws <note>Acts that restricted the use of foreign ships for trade between Britain and its colonies</note>. By diminishing shipping costs, these changes will make the competition between the cheap, rent-free lands of other countries and the high-rent soil of England more severe. As a consequence, much of the poorer soil will be abandoned. The expensive farming methods previously used to increase the quantity of protected grain must be given up as unprofitable. We can expect a considerable decrease in the yield of a *good* English harvest compared to former years. We have provided an official table above showing the quantity of food consumed in England for the year ending August 1849. That food supplemented the harvest of 1848, which was 'good,' but the yield per acre could not have been as large as usual due to the reasons mentioned. The result is that small farmers, with small crops and low prices, cannot afford tithes, taxes, poor rates, and rent—the last being the most burdensome. Their capital and their numbers are shrinking annually, which increases the number of people looking for work in other industries where they must buy bread rather than grow it."

<meta>This page continues the argument that the earth acts as a "machine of production." It transitions from discussing international trade and markets to the fundamental principles of land cultivation and political economy, specifically challenging the prevailing theories of the time regarding how human societies settle and use the land.</meta>

-># THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.<-

...as well as to make it easier to water his cattle, and thus keep his manure in the stable-yard. He knows that this "machine" <note>The author uses the "machine" as a metaphor for the land itself.</note> will feed him better the more perfectly he develops it, and that there is always a place for his time and his labor to be spent for his own benefit.

The land was given to man for his use, and the basis of the entire science of political economy <note>original: "political economy"; the study of how a society manages its resources and creates wealth.</note> is found in the law that governs his relationship with this great and only machine of production. David Ricardo <note>David Ricardo (1772–1823) was an influential British economist. His "Theory of Rent" suggested that people first cultivate the most fertile land, and as population grows, they are forced to use poorer land, leading to economic hardship.</note> taught that in the early stages of society, men could take control of rich soils from which they could obtain an abundant supply of food. He argued that as the population grew, food became scarcer, creating a necessity for people to scatter in search of those rich soils. However, the common sense of mankind teaches the exact opposite. In this case, as in all others, the common sense of the many is right, while the "uncommon sense" of the few experts is wrong. This will be clear to anyone who takes the trouble to follow this sketch* of how the earth was gradually occupied:

> “The first farmer begins his work on the hillside. Below him are lands where the water has carried the richest portions of the soil from above, along with fallen leaves and trees. For ages, all of these have rotted and merged with the earth, creating soils capable of yielding the largest harvests. Yet, for this very reason, they are inaccessible to the beginner. Their richness is shown by the enormous trees covering them and by their power to hold the water needed for decomposition. The poor settler lacks the power either to clear them of their heavy timber or to drain them of their excess moisture.

> He begins on the hillside, but in the next step, we find him descending the hill and obtaining a larger return for his labor. He has more food for himself, and he now has the means to feed a horse or an ox. Aided by the manure produced by these better lands, we see him next retracing his steps, improving the hillside, and forcing it to yield double the harvest he first obtained. With each step down the hill, he obtains a larger reward for his labor; at each step, he returns with increased power to the cultivation of the original poor soil. He now has horses and oxen. While he uses them to extract the manure that has accumulated for ages from the new soils, he also has carts and wagons to carry it up the hill. At each step, his reward increases while his labor decreases. He goes back to the sandy soil and digs up marl <term>a soil made of clay and lime, often used as fertilizer</term> to cover the surface, or he returns to the clay and digs down to the limestone, which helps him double the land’s product. He is constantly building a machine that feeds him while he makes it—a machine that increases in power the more he takes from it. At first, the land was worthless. It has fed and clothed him for years, and now it has great value; those who might want to use it would pay him a large rent.

> “The earth is a great machine given to man to be shaped to his purpose. The more he shapes it, the better it feeds him, because each step is merely preparation for a new step that is more productive than the last—requiring less labor and yielding a larger return. The labor of clearing land is great, yet the initial return is small. The earth is covered with stumps and filled with roots. With each year, the roots decay and the ground becomes richer, while the labor of plowing is reduced. Eventually, the stumps disappear and the harvest doubles, while the labor required is half of what it was at first. To move this process along, the owner has done nothing but plant and harvest; nature has done the rest. The help he obtains from nature yields him...”

---

* Originally published in my book, *The Past, the Present, and the Future.*

<summary>This page challenges David Ricardo's economic theory of land use, arguing instead that farmers start on poor hillsides and gradually move to richer valley lands as they gain the tools and power to clear them.</summary>

--- Page 137 ---
<meta>This page continues the argument that the earth is a "machine of production." The author is refuting David Ricardo's theory of rent by arguing that humans actually begin cultivation on poorer, easier-to-clear hillside soils and only move to richer, more difficult-to-manage valley lands as their technology and collective labor power increase.</meta>

...as much food as was originally obtained by the labor of cutting down and clearing away the trees. This, however, is not all. The surplus produced this way has given the farmer the means to improve the poorer lands by providing manure to enrich them. In this way, he has tripled his original yield without additional labor, because the effort he saves while working the newer, easier soils is enough to cover the cost of transporting manure to the older ones. He is gaining a daily increase in power over the various resources <note>original: "treasures"</note> of the earth.

In every task related to shaping the earth, the result is the same. The first step is always the most expensive and the least productive. The first drainage ditch <note>original: "drain"</note> begins near the stream, where the labor is hardest. It clears only a few acres of water. Slightly higher up, the same amount of labor—benefiting from the work already completed—clears twice as many acres. Then that number is doubled again, until a perfect system of thorough drainage can be established with less labor than was originally required for even the crudest attempt. Applying lime to clay soil across fifty acres is easier work than clearing a single acre of forest was, yet this process doubles the harvest for every one of those fifty acres. 

A man who needs a little fuel for his own use spends a great deal of labor opening a nearby vein of coal. Enlarging this mine to double its output requires relatively little labor; the same is true for the next expansion, which allows him to use a mining wagon <note>original: "drift wagon"; a wagon used in a horizontal mine passage or "drift."</note>. This gives him a return fifty times greater than what he achieved when he used only his arms or a wheelbarrow. Digging a shaft to the first coal vein below the surface and building a steam engine are expensive operations; however, once these are finished, every future step becomes more productive and less costly. Digging to the next vein below or tunneling to another are minor tasks <note>original: "trifles"</note> compared to the first, yet each provides a yield just as large. 

The first railroad line passes houses and towns inhabited by one or two hundred thousand people. A half-dozen small branch lines, which together cost far less labor than the first, connect another three hundred thousand or perhaps half a million people to it. As trade increases, a second, third, or fourth track may be needed. The original track makes it easier to transport materials and remove obstacles, so three new tracks can now be built with less labor than was required for the very first one.

All labor spent shaping this "great machine" <note>The author uses the "machine" as a metaphor for the earth and its infrastructure.</note> is merely the introduction to applying even more labor with even greater returns. With each application, wages rise. Because of this, parts of the machine, as it currently exists, always trade on the market for far less labor than they originally cost to build. 

The farmer who worked the thin, poor soils was happy to get a hundred bushels of grain for his year’s work. As he and his neighbors progressed "down the hill" toward more fertile soils, wages rose, and two hundred bushels are now the standard pay. His farm might yield a thousand bushels, but it requires the labor of four men who must each receive two hundred bushels. This leaves a surplus of only two hundred bushels. Valued at twenty years' profit <note>original: "At twenty years' purchase"; a historical method of calculating the capital value of an asset based on 20 times its annual yield.</note>, this gives a capital value of four thousand bushels, or the equivalent of twenty years' wages. Yet, to create that farm, the labor of the owner, his sons, and his assistants likely totaled a hundred years of work, or perhaps even more. During all this time, however, the land has fed and clothed them all. The farm has been created through gradual <note>original: "insensible"</note> contributions made year after year, often without them even noticing the effort.

The farm is now worth twenty years’ wages because its owner has successfully harvested a thousand bushels a year for a long time. But while it lay idle for centuries, accumulating natural wealth, it was worth nothing. This is true of the earth everywhere: the more we take from it through intelligent labor, the more it has to offer. When the coal mines of England were untouched, they were worthless.

He concludes that the value of land and resources is derived from the labor invested in them, rather than their mere existence.</summary>

### THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.

Now their value is almost beyond calculation; yet the land contains abundant supplies for thousands of years. Iron ore, a century ago, was a drug <note>original: "a drug"; an item in such oversupply that it is difficult to sell and has little value</note>, and leases were granted at almost nominal rents. Now, such leases are considered equivalent to the possession of large fortunes, despite the great quantities that have been removed, and even though the amount of ore now known to exist is probably fifty times greater than it was then.

> " *The earth is the sole producer.* Man shapes and exchanges. A part of his labor is applied to the shaping of the great machine <note>The "great machine" refers to the earth or the land itself</note>, and this produces changes that are permanent. The drainage ditch, once cut, remains a drain; and the limestone, once reduced to lime, never again becomes limestone. It passes into the food of man and animals, and ever after takes its part in the same cycle with the clay with which it has been incorporated. The iron rusts and gradually passes into the soil, to take its part with the clay and the lime. That portion of his labor gives him wages while preparing the machine for greater future production. That other portion which he spends on shaping and exchanging the *products* of the machine produces temporary results and gives him wages alone. Whatever tends, therefore, to diminish the quantity of labor necessary for the shaping and exchanging of products, tends to increase the quantity that may be given to increasing the amount of products and to preparing the great machine; and thus, while increasing the present return to labor, it prepares for a further increase in the future.
>
> " The first poor cultivator obtains a hundred bushels for his year's wages. To pound this between two stones requires twenty days of labor, and the work is not half done. Had he a mill in the neighborhood, he would have better flour, and he would have almost his entire twenty days to bestow upon his land. He pulls up his grain by hand. Had he a scythe, he would have more time for the preparation of the machine of production. He loses his axe, and it requires days for himself and his horse to be on the road to obtain another. His machine loses the time and the manure, both of which would have been saved had the axe-maker been at hand. The real advantage derived from the mill and the scythe, and from the proximity of the axe-maker, consists simply in the power which they afford him to devote his labor more and more to the preparation of the great machine of production; and such is the case with all the machinery of preparation and exchange. The plow enables him to do as much in one day as he could do with a spade in five. He saves four days for drainage. The steam engine drains as much as could be drained by thousands of days of labor without it. He has more leisure to apply marl <note>marl: a soil nutrient consisting of clay and calcium carbonate</note> or lime to his land. The more he can extract from his machine, the greater is its value, because everything he takes is, by the very act of taking it, shaped to aid further production. The machine, therefore, improves by use; whereas spades, plows, steam engines, and all other machines used by man are but the various forms into which he shapes parts of the great original machine, only to disappear in the act of being used—just as much as food does, though not so rapidly. The earth is the great labor savings bank, and the value to man of all other machines is in the direct ratio of their tendency to aid him in increasing his deposits in the only bank whose dividends are perpetually increasing, while its capital is perpetually doubling. That it may continue forever to do so, all that it asks is that it shall receive back the refuse of its produce—the manure; and so that it may do so, the consumer and the producer must take their places by each other. Once that is done, every change that is effected becomes permanent and tends to facilitate other and greater changes. The whole business of the farmer consists in making and improving soils, and the earth..."
