# THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.

...rewards him for his kindness by giving him more and more food the more attention he bestows upon her.

The isolated settler must occupy the spots that he can cultivate with his basic tools. Having neither horse nor cart, he carries his crop home on his shoulders, as is still done in many parts of India. He carries a hide to a place of trade, perhaps fifty miles away, just to obtain leather or shoes in exchange. As the population increases, roads are built. More fertile soils are brought under cultivation. The store and the mill move closer to him, and he can obtain shoes and flour using less <term>machinery of exchange</term> <note>original: "machinery of exchange"; the systems of transportation, shipping, and middlemen required to move goods from producer to consumer</note>. He has more leisure time to prepare his "great machine" <note>The "great machine" refers to the land or the soil itself</note>, and the returns on his labor increase. More people can now obtain food from the same area of land, and new places of trade appear. Wool is converted into cloth right on the spot, and he exchanges goods directly with the clothier. The sawmill is nearby, and he exchanges with the sawyer. The tanner gives him leather for his hides, and the papermaker gives him paper for his rags. 

With each of these changes, he has more and more time and <term>manure</term> <note>original: "manure"; used here in the broader sense of organic fertilizer and soil nutrients that are returned to the land</note> to devote to the preparation of the great food-making machine. Every year, the yields become larger. His power to command the use of trade systems increases, but his *actual need for them* diminishes. Every year, there is an increasing tendency for the consumer to be placed side-by-side with the producer. This allows him to devote more of his time and mind to the business of improving that great instrument, the earth; thus, an increase in the consuming population is essential to the progress of production.

> "The loss caused by using the machinery of exchange is determined by the bulk of the article being traded. Food ranks first in bulk; fuel is next; stone for building is third; iron is fourth; cotton is fifth; and so on, diminishing until we come to small items like lace and nutmegs. Raw material is the product in which the earth has cooperated the most, and its production improves the land the most. The closer the place of exchange or processing can be brought to the place of production, the less value is lost in the process, and the greater the power to accumulate wealth for the production of even more wealth.
> 
> "The man who raises food on his own land is building up his 'machine' to work to better advantage the following year. However, his neighbor, to whom food is *given* on the condition that he sits still, loses a year’s worth of work on his own machine; all he has gained is the pleasure of doing nothing. If he has employed himself, his horses, and his wagon in bringing that food home—taking the same number of days that would have been required to grow it himself—he has misspent his time, because his farm remains unimproved. He has wasted both labor and fertilizer. Since nobody actually gives food away for free, it is obvious that a man who owns a farm but obtains his food elsewhere must pay for it to be grown and pay to have it transported. Even if he earned good wages in some other pursuit, his farm—instead of being improved by a year of cultivation—is worse off due to a year of neglect. He is a poorer man than he would have been if he had raised his own food.
> 
> "The next bulkiest article is fuel. While a man warms his house, he is also clearing his land. He would lose out by sitting idle even if his neighbor brought the fuel to him—and he would lose even more if he had to spend his own time hauling it—because he would be wearing out his wagon and losing the potential fertilizer for his fields. If he were to hire himself and his wagon out to another person to earn the same amount of fuel he could have cut on his own property, he would be the loser, for his own farm would remain uncleared of timber.
> 
> "If he takes stone from his own fields to build his house, he gains twice over: his house is built, and his land is cleared of stones. If he sits still and lets..."

<meta>This page continues Henry Charles Carey's argument that the value of land is tied to its proximity to markets. # THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.

...if his neighbor brings him stones, he loses, because his fields remain unfit for cultivation. If he works just as hard for a neighbor and receives the same apparent wages, he still loses because he still has to remove the stones from his own land. Until they are removed, he cannot cultivate his land.

> “With every improvement in the <term>machinery of exchange</term> <note>original: "machinery of exchange"; the systems of transport, shipping, and middlemen used to move goods from producer to consumer</note>, there is a decrease in the proportion that those systems take from the total amount of production. This is because of the extraordinary increase in products resulting from the increased ability to use labor to build up the 'great machine' <note>Carey uses "the great machine" to refer to the land or the soil itself</note>. It is observed daily that the demand for horses and men increases even as railroads replace them on the <term>turnpikes</term> <note>original: "turnpikes"; main roads or highways, often where tolls were collected</note>. The reason is that the farmer’s ability to improve his land grows faster than the supply of men and horses available for his work. The man who previously sent half-fed cattle to market—accompanied by horses and men to drive them, and wagons and horses loaded with hay or turnips to feed them on the road and fatten them at the market—now fattens them on his own ground. He sends them by railroad, ready for the slaughterhouse. His use of the machinery of exchange is reduced by nine-tenths. He keeps his men, his horses, and his wagons at home, along with the leftovers of his hay or turnips. The former are employed in ditching and draining the fields, while the latter fertilizes the soil he already cultivates. His production doubles, and he accumulates wealth rapidly, while the people around him have more to eat, more to spend on clothing, and accumulate more wealth themselves. He needs laborers in the field, and those workers need clothes and houses. The shoemaker and the carpenter, finding a demand for their labor, now join the community, eating the food right where it is produced. Thus, the systems of trade are improved while the amount of transportation required is reduced. The amount of flour consumed locally encourages the miller to come and eat his share while preparing flour for others. The labor spent on trading is reduced, more is given back to the land, and the lime is now used for fertilizer. *Tons of turnips are harvested from the same area that previously only produced bushels of rye.* The quantity of goods to be consumed increases faster than the population, so more people are needed on the spot; next, the wool mill arrives. The wool no longer requires wagons and horses for transport; those animals are now used to haul coal. This allows the farmer to stop using his woods for fuel and instead clear and cultivate the rich soil that has produced nothing but timber for centuries. Production increases again, and the new wealth is invested in a cotton mill. With every step of progress, the farmer finds new demands for the 'great machine' he has built, accompanied by an increased power on his part to make it stronger and to sink its foundations deeper. He now supplies beef and mutton, wheat, butter, eggs, poultry, cheese, and every other comfort and luxury of life that the climate allows. He gets all of this from the same land that—when his father or grandfather first began farming the thin soil of the hills—yielded barely enough rye or barley to support life.”

If we study the cause of land value anywhere, we will find it results from a decrease in the cost of transportation. The newspapers of the day, speaking of the operations of the railroad recently built from Springfield, Illinois, to the Illinois River, tell us that:

> “One week before the railroad was finished, corn could be had here in any quantity at 15 cents a bushel. Now,” says the *Sangamon Journal* <note>original: "Saugamon Journal"; refers to the *Sangamon Journal*, a prominent 19th-century Illinois newspaper</note>, “not a bushel can be had for less than 25 cents. This,” it adds, “is the effect of the completion of the railroad on the price of one article produced by our farmers.”

The first expense that must be paid by land is transportation. When that cost is so high that it consumes all the profits, the land will remain uncultivated.

<meta>This page continues Henry Charles Carey’s argument regarding the relationship between land value and population density. # THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.

Reduce the cost of transportation enough to leave enough to pay the wages of labor, and the land will be cultivated, but it will yield no rent. Reduce it further, so as to leave a surplus beyond the worker's reward, and the land itself will gain value. Reduce it even further by completely removing the need for transportation—creating a market on the land for all its products and allowing the farmer to easily return all the waste <note>original: "refuse of its products"; organic matter and manure used as fertilizer to maintain soil fertility</note> back to the soil—and the land will reach the highest value of which it is capable. 

The primary "commodity" that the government and people of the Union <note>the United States</note> have to sell is land. In quantity, it is practically unlimited; long before our current territory is even surveyed for sale, vast new regions will have been brought within the borders of the Union. In quality, it deserves to be ranked first in the world. The coal region covers 133,000 square miles. Iron ore is found everywhere, untouched. Copper, zinc, and almost all other metals are abundant. South Carolina has millions of acres of the finest unoccupied meadowland, along with lime and iron ore in unlimited supply. Virginia is in a similar state, yet people are leaving both states, even though population is the only thing needed to make them leading states in the Union in terms of wealth. In Alabama, Louisiana, and Mississippi—which have unrivaled advantages for producing the world's primary clothing material <note>original: "clothing material"; referring to cotton</note>—two-thirds of their total area, or 83,000,000 acres, remains unsold. The land controlled by the government is measured in hundreds of millions of acres, and to give all of this value, we only need more people.

In Europe, by contrast, the population is considered excessive. Marriage is seen as a luxury that should not be indulged in, for fear that it will result in an increase in numbers. It is said that "everyone has a right to live," but once that is granted, it is added that "no one has a right to bring creatures into life to be supported by other people."* Poor laws <note>original: "Poor laws"; the system of social relief for the impoverished in England</note> are denounced for supposedly encouraging population growth—acting as a machine for supporting those who do not work "out of the earnings of those who do."† It is thought that no man has a "right" to claim a seat at the great table provided by the Creator for all mankind, or that "if he is willing to work, he must be fed." Labor is held to be a mere "commodity," and if the laborer cannot sell it, he has no "right" but to starve—himself, his wife, and his children. 

A "particular tendency to error in the current social philosophy of the day," to which it is deemed necessary to direct special attention, is the "unsound, exaggerated, and somewhat <term>maudlin</term> <note>original: "maudlin"; tearfully or weakly emotional</note> tenderness with which it is now fashionable to regard <term>paupers</term> <note>original: "paupers"; people receiving public charity</note> and criminals."‡ These are the doctrines of the English free-trade school, in which Political Economy is limited to an examination of the laws that regulate the production of wealth, without any reference to either morals or intellect. Under such teaching, it is no surprise that poverty and crime are increasing so rapidly.§

Throughout Europe, human beings are held in low regard. They are considered "surplus," and it is believed the sooner they can be expelled, the better it will be for those who can afford to stay behind. To achieve this goal, Colonization Societies are formed, and petitions are sent to Parliament by men who desire to export their fellow citizens by the hundreds of thousands every year. Both Whig and Tory journals|| <note>the primary opposing political factions in 19th-century Britain</note> unite in urging the necessity of driving people from the—

<meta>This page continues Henry Charles Carey’s critique of the British "free-trade system," arguing that it leads to the depopulation and economic ruin of colonies and neighboring nations. # THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.

The land of Britain. Secretaries of State provide clever calculations regarding the amount of money required to carry out the work of expulsion <note>original: "expulsion"; refers to state-sponsored emigration or the forced removal of tenants during the Highland Clearances and Irish Famine</note>. On all sides, it is agreed that people are too numerous and that their numbers grow too fast; and yet, there is not a country in Europe that can justly complain of over-population. Ireland—the prime example of this *free-trade system*—has millions of acres of her richest lands as yet untouched. If drained, these lands alone would yield food in abundance for the entire population.

It is not, however, the laborer alone who stands in need of aid. The condition of the landowner is little better. This system of universal discord is described in one of the journals of the day:

> "The state of the country is frightful. Assassinations are estimated at more than ten per week, fifty per month, which, added to the systematic starvation of almost another hundred in the same timeframe, presents a situation without parallel in modern civilization. Despite this decrease in the population, the million of workhouse inmates and dependents continues to increase. In less than a month, it will be more than a proprietor's life is worth to be seen by his tenants. Rents, which are now merely nominal in their collection <note>meaning they exist on paper but cannot actually be collected</note>, have recently sunk to a fourth of their previous amount. Lands previously leased at £2 10s. per acre are being offered at less than 15s.; such is the desperation of the starving millions that landlords are afraid to further aggravate their sufferings."

The Parliament of England is now engaged in passing laws to transfer—for the fourth time in little more than two centuries—the bulk of Irish property to English "undertakers" <note>original: "undertakers"; speculators or contractors who were granted land in Ireland to "plant" it with loyal subjects</note>. The small-scale farmer has been ruined. Labor has become utterly worthless, even though labor is the only thing needed to bring 7,000,000 acres of the world’s richest (but currently unproductive) soil into cultivation.

The landowner of India has been ruined. The massive body of village proprietors that existed in that country only half a century ago—helping and governing themselves—has disappeared.

The landowner of the West Indies—of Demerara and Berbice <note>regions in modern-day Guyana</note>—has been ruined, and the condition of the laborers there has not improved.

The landowner of Portugal—which acts as a continental colony of Great Britain—has been ruined. Along with the diminished value of land, there has been a steady decay of civilization, until the name of Portugal has become almost synonymous with weakness and barbarism.

If we look to Canada, Nova Scotia, or New Brunswick, the same picture meets our eyes. Land of the same quality, located just one minute north of the imaginary line dividing the British provinces from the Union <note>the United States</note>, is worth less than half as much as land situated one minute south of it. Lord Durham <note>John Lambton, 1st Earl of Durham, who authored a famous 1839 report on the affairs of British North America</note>, in his report made only a few years ago, says that "land in Vermont and New Hampshire, close to the border line, is five dollars per acre, while in the adjoining British townships it is only one dollar." He adds that on the northern side of the line, despite having superior fertility, the land is "wholly unsaleable even at such low prices." Canada has no local market for its products, and the cost of transportation consumes the entire profit. Much of the harvest is absolutely wasted because it cannot be brought to market at all. The labor of men, women, and children—as well as that of wagons and horses—is being wasted everywhere. This is why the Canadian desires a change of government that would allow him to adopt a protective tariff. Give him that—annex him to the Union—and his land will gain a value similar to that found in the United States. Farmers will then grow rich, laborers will grow rich, and the power to consume cloth and iron will grow with the same speed that it recently did with us.

Every colony of England would gladly separate from her, feeling that a connection with Britain is synonymous with a worsening of their condition. Every one of them would gladly unite its fortunes with those of our Union, feeling that—

<meta>This page continues Henry Charles Carey’s argument that the British economic system relies on the exploitation of "cheap labor," contrasting it with the American protectionist model which he believes increases the value of the individual and promotes global harmony.</meta>

# THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.

Connection with us is synonymous with improvement. The reason for all this is that the British system is based upon cheap labor and tends to oppress the many for the benefit of the few. In our system, it is the many who govern; and since experience has taught them that prosperity and free trade with England are incompatible with each other, we have "free trade" tariffs with protective duties of thirty percent, which are likely to be increased. The colonies are ruined by free trade, and they desire annexation [to the United States] so that they may enjoy protection.

This idea of "cheap labor" is universal among British colonists. It is found in all their books. If they fail to succeed, they claim it is because labor is "too high." They are willing to receive convicts because they can be obtained "cheaply." They tell their correspondents that men can be brought from continental Europe who will work for small wages, while Englishmen must have large ones—that is <note>original: "i. e."</note>, enough to feed and clothe themselves comfortably. They emancipate the enslaved, and then, finding their labor "too expensive," they send to India or to the coast of Africa for "cheap" laborers <note>This refers to the "coolie" trade and indentured servitude programs that replaced chattel slavery in British colonies</note>. The *Times* [of London] informs us that the great works of England are based upon an ample supply of "cheap labor." The whole system aims for the degradation of the laborer by requiring him to underwork and replace the laborers of other countries, despite the disadvantages of distance and the heavy cost of transportation. 

Protectionism, however, aims to raise the value of labor, thus promoting the "annexation" of individuals—by inducing the people of Europe to transfer themselves to our shores—and establishing true free trade between ourselves and them. It is a bounty on the importation of the machine we need—man—to give value to the machine we have in such abundance—land. It leads to perfect free trade—the annexation of nations—by raising the value of human life throughout the world.

It has been, at times, a matter of surprise that the hundreds of thousands of people who have arrived in this country have been so instantly absorbed that their presence has been unfelt. Indeed, the more people we received, the larger was the quantity of food, fuel, cloth, and iron given in exchange for labor. Such is the natural result of a system which allows the miner, the ironworker, the spinner, and the weaver to combine their efforts with those of the farmer and planter. Had the policy of 1828 <note>The Tariff of 1828, a high protective tariff supported by Carey</note> remained unchanged, and were we now receiving a million men a year, the only effect observed would be that wages, profits, and the ability of the laborer, landowner, and capitalist to afford the good things of life would be steadily increasing. With each step forward, the tendency toward immigration and the increase in land value would grow at an accelerated pace. We need population.

By the people of the Union thoroughly adopting this course, we will find the remedy for the ills of both the landowners and the laborers of the rest of the world, and the removal of the discords that are now so universal. So that we may clearly see how this would contribute to producing harmony, we must first inquire into the causes of discord.

The laborers of the world have one common interest: that labor should become everywhere productive and valuable. The more wheat produced in return for a given amount of labor, the more of it the shoemaker will obtain for his work; likewise, the more advantageously the shoemaker can apply his labor, the more readily the farmer can provide himself and his family with shoes. This is also the case with nations. It is in the interest of everyone that labor in all nations becomes productive. If the labor of a cotton-growing nation becomes unproductive, the sugar-growing or wheat-growing nations feel the effect through the increased difficulty of obtaining clothing.

<meta>This page continues Henry Charles Carey’s argument in "The Harmony of Interests," moving from a critique of British "cheap labor" to an explanation of how the interests of landowners and laborers are naturally aligned, and how the "middleman" system of trade disrupts this harmony.</meta>

# THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.

The landowners of the world share one common interest: that land everywhere should become productive and valuable. Land becomes more valuable as the skill and intelligence of the laborer increases. This can be seen by comparing the present with the past in any developing country, or by comparing different countries today. In Russia, the land itself has little value. In Belgium, however, where farming is practiced with a level of intelligence unknown elsewhere, land is very valuable.

Every improvement that makes it easier to trade food for cloth, or cotton for food, reduces the amount of labor required to obtain basic necessities. This enables the producer to acquire other goods and resources needed for mental improvement or to apply his labor more effectively. Therefore, a landed proprietor in England has a direct interest in improving cotton cultivation in the United States, because it improves the condition of the man working his own land. Similarly, the cotton grower has an interest in the success of the Russian wheat grower, because the Russian is then able to purchase more clothing.

Among the landowners and laborers of the world, there is a perfect harmony of interests. Standing between them, however, are the men employed in <term>transportation, conversion, and exchange</term> <note>original: "transportation, conversion, and exchange" refers to the middlemen: shippers, manufacturers (who "convert" raw materials), and merchants</note>—namely, ship owners, manufacturers, and merchants.

The goal of prohibiting manufacturing in the colonies was to force colonists to use ships they would not otherwise need, and to pay manufacturers and merchants for services they could have performed better themselves. The inevitable result was discord, which in our case led to war and a massive waste of time and money. Another result was that the number of people involved in transportation, manufacturing, and trade increased faster than the number of actual producers. England shifted from being a seller of food to a purchaser of foreign food. 

Next came the <term>Corn Laws</term> <note>The Corn Laws (1815–1846) were tariffs and other trade restrictions on imported food and grain ("corn") designed to keep prices high for domestic landowners</note>, which were intended to block food imports for the benefit of landowners. Other laws prohibited the export of machinery to benefit the owners of ships and factories. Through the former, landowners were able to tax the laborer and the mechanic; through the latter, the mechanic was able to tax the rest of the world in return. The effect has been to discourage English labor and capital from productive work, driving it instead into the much less profitable sectors of transportation and trade. This has happened to such an extent that the "converters" (manufacturers) have finally gained power over the landowners. They have abolished the restrictions on food imports that the landowners had established for their own protection. Since revolutions never go backward, we can safely conclude that the Corn Laws will not be restored. So far, the result has been the ruin of Irish landholders; the next result, if this system continues, must be the ruin of those in England.

We are told that the people of Russia have been forced to waste food because they lack a market. They would rather trade a bushel of wheat for a yard of cloth than let it go to waste. We are told they cannot afford this trade, but what else can they do? If they cannot manufacture cloth themselves, they must buy it and give something of equal value in return—even if that means trading many bushels for a few yards. Until Russia can create a local market for this surplus food, it will seek any market at any price. The price in England will not much exceed the cost of transporting the food from the farm to the town where it is eaten. Almost the entire price goes to the <term>exchanger</term> <note>the merchant or middleman</note>, resulting in a loss for both the land and the laborer.

<summary>Carey argues that landowners and laborers worldwide share a "harmony of interests" that is disrupted by the British system of middlemen (shippers and manufacturers). He illustrates how trade restrictions like the Corn Laws and colonial prohibitions create economic discord and benefit merchants at the expense of producers.</summary>

# THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.

Both of these must tend toward the Russian level—which is currently very low—because there is no local market on the land for the products of that land.

The goal of the currently dominant class in England is to bring about universal free trade. If such a measure were adopted by the United States, it would close every furnace, rolling mill, and every cotton and wool factory in the country. This would decrease the value of both labor and land by forcing food producers to look for a market in England. If the <term>Zoll-verein</term> <note>original: "Zoll-verein"; the German Customs Union, a coalition of German states formed to manage tariffs and economic policies.</note> adopted similar measures, it would force the people of Germany to do the same, leading to similar results. The English market would be overwhelmed by the weight of these goods, and prices would fall so low that they would utterly destroy the laborer's ability to pay rent for the land and the owner's ability to improve it. The class of people who stand between the producers across the world—the middlemen—would grow daily in number and strength. Meanwhile, the productivity of labor and land would daily decrease, leading to a steady decline in the value of both.

On the other hand, let us suppose the people of the United States, Russia, and Germany were to adopt measures that enabled them to consume all the food produced on their land right there at home. This would put a stop to the massive imports that are currently crushing the English farmer. The immediate effect would be that the value of labor and land in all those countries would rise. Consequently, the value of both would also rise in England. The demand for labor in those countries would quickly drain off the surplus workers currently employed in English factories. The increased demand for home-grown food in England would then encourage people to invest labor and capital into farming, and the value of both would rise. Consumption would increase as labor became more productive. The power of the producers would be restored, while the power of the mere "exchangers" (middlemen) would be diminished.

To improve the condition of labor and land in the United Kingdom, it is essential to abolish the colonial system. Maintaining this system involves paying a terrifying amount of taxes, all of which must be paid by the producers and those who own the <term>machine of production</term> <note>Carey uses "machine of production" to refer to the land itself or the industrial infrastructure.</note>, whether abroad or at home. Although the tax is officially paid by the person selling the wheat or the person transporting it, it is actually paid by the person who produces it and the person who consumes it. Three-fourths of the British nation are currently engaged in transporting, manufacturing, or exchanging the products of others. They add nothing to the actual quantity of goods produced, yet they live off of them. In doing so, they worsen the condition of landowners and laborers in England and throughout the world.

The landowners of England have been the country's lawmakers. They created the system that caused the American Revolution—the same system that has depopulated India and must eventually ruin every country subjected to it—and they are now paying the price. Every step they took to degrade the people around them has resulted in a loss of their own power. Their policy has turned the small, independent farmer into a hired laborer, and has driven farm laborers into the crowded lanes and alleys of Liverpool and Manchester. Throughout much of Scotland, they have replaced people with sheep, driving the former inhabitants to seek refuge in Glasgow. With every step, they have weakened themselves by converting...

The middleman <note>original: "exchanger"</note> has set his foot upon their necks. *Commerce is King.* They are prostrate, and so they must remain until they receive help from abroad. Their natural allies are the landowners of the rest of the world. The East India Company, as the great landowner of India, is greatly interested. That country is becoming daily less and less able to pay taxes, and the power to do so must diminish as long as this system continues. If the machinery now employed in converting cotton into cloth *for* India were instead employed in making cloth *in* India—thereby creating a market on the land for its own products—the cultivation of cotton would revive. The demand for food would increase, the population would grow, the jungle would be cleared, and the Company might then obtain a constantly increasing revenue from taxes that are constantly decreasing in their weight, paid by a people whose condition is constantly improving. The price of labor would rise, the necessity for standing armies would diminish, and the Company might then, at some point in the near future, sell its assets to a people who would thereafter govern themselves.

It is to the people of the United States, however, that they must chiefly look for help. Already owners of the main part of North America, Americans are likely soon to own the whole of it. The *national* adoption of a protective policy <note>The "protective policy" refers to protectionism—using tariffs to encourage domestic manufacturing.</note>—rather than a partisan or sectional one—would at once raise the value of land throughout the Union. This is because it would be understood that a market would be created everywhere on the land for the products of that land. The British provinces <note>Referring to Canada and the Maritimes.</note> would then quickly be incorporated into the Union, and the supply of food to British markets would cease; Cuba and Mexico would follow, and thus a market would be created for the population of all Southern Europe. With each such step, the value of labor would rise. This would be followed by an effort on the part of landholders everywhere to retain their tenants <note>original: "rent-payers"</note> if they wish to preserve the value of their land. Spain and Italy would become manufacturers for themselves, and thus the colonial system would gradually fade away, and with it the power of the middlemen over the laborers and landowners.

It is not by immigration alone that the population of the Union would be augmented and increased value given to the abundant land. The present system degrades the countryside to build up great cities. These cities become the resort of tens of thousands who would have remained at home among parents and friends if furnaces, rolling mills, or cotton and wool mills had afforded them employment for their time and minds. The same cause forces another portion of the people to flee to the West. While in the first case we see the poverty, vice, and disease of crowded cities, in the second we see the hardships of a scattered population. Men, women, and children starve in New York, while other men, women, and children perish from fevers common to the occupation of new territories before the infrastructure <note>original: "arrangements"</note> is in place that would have resulted from a more gradual expansion of settlement. 

It will be said that there is a conflict here. If the city population did not grow, what would become of the owners of city lots? Yet the harmony of interests is here, as everywhere else, perfect. Towns and cities would grow more rapidly than ever, but they would grow more healthily, maintaining a closer relationship to the population of the country whose trade they wish to conduct. New York would stop being, as it is now, a great wen <note>original: "wen"; a sebaceous cyst or an unhealthy growth, used here metaphorically to describe an overgrown, parasitic city.</note>, absorbing all the profits of hundreds of thousands of poor farmers—her customers—who must give ten days of labor spent raising corn in exchange for the labor of one day spent producing British iron. The country and the city would grow together, and the jealousy of the country toward the city would quickly pass away.

The people of China constitute a world of themselves. They have little...

Interaction with the outside world, nor is the example of Hindustan <note>original: "Hindostan," a historical name for northern India, often used then to refer to the whole subcontinent.</note> likely to produce any desire for its extension—certainly not while they still remember that their desire to prohibit the importation of opium involved them in a war that resulted in the destruction of cities and the ruin of hundreds of thousands of innocent people <note>The First Opium War (1839–1842), where Britain forced China to accept opium imports.</note>. The system of that country is the direct opposite of ours, in the fact that their government is in the hands of one person, while here it is in the hands of all. In this respect, it suffers under an infinite disadvantage; yet the spectacle presented there of the results of combined action puts our boasted civilization to shame. A recent writer <note>Robert Fortune, a Scottish botanist famous for introducing Chinese tea plants to India.</note> thus describes the condition of the people:

> “The farms are small, each consisting of from one to four or five acres; indeed, every cottager has his own little tea garden, the produce of which supplies the wants of his family, and the surplus brings him in a few dollars, which are spent on other necessaries of life. The same system is practiced in everything relating to Chinese agriculture. The cotton, silk, and rice farms are generally all small and managed upon the same plan. There are few sights more pleasing than a Chinese family in the interior engaged in gathering tea leaves, or, indeed, in any of their other agricultural pursuits. There is the old man—perhaps the grandfather, or even the great-grandfather—patriarch-like directing his descendants, many of whom are in their youth and prime, while others are in their childhood, in the labors of the field. He stands in the midst of them, bowed down with age. But, to the honor of the Chinese as a nation, he is always looked up to by all with pride and affection, and his old age and gray hair are honored, revered, and loved. When the labors of the day are over and they return to their humble and happy homes, their fare consists chiefly of rice, fish, and vegetables, which they enjoy with great zest, and they are happy and contented. I really believe there is no country in the world where the agricultural population is better off than in the north of China. Labor with them is pleasure, for its fruits are eaten by themselves, and the rod of the oppressor is unfelt and unknown.”*

Let this be compared with the results of the system that has desolated Ireland and India, and that drives our people to Oregon and California, while men everywhere among ourselves are half-cultivating large farms when they might obtain triple the result from half the surface. Let it then be determined which system tends most to promote the prosperity and happiness of the laborer, and to improve the condition of the landowner.

The policy of England tending toward dispersion <note>In Carey's view, "dispersion" is the forced spreading out of people to find new land because the old land has been exhausted by an export-only economy.</note>, she desires to facilitate the making of roads by which all the commodities of the world may be brought to her, only to be returned to the places they came from. In this process, she retains so large a portion of the value that it causes the destruction of both the land and its owner. Lower India is utterly exhausted, and England desires railroads to more distant points, which will then be exhausted in their turn. From 1834 to 1840, she lent us iron to make roads in new countries, and we were ruined by dispersion. From 1843 to 1847, we filled up the empty spaces—the policy being that of concentration—and we grew rich. 

The present policy is that of dispersion. It is proposed to make a railroad to the Pacific so that men may scatter themselves more widely, even though we now occupy a space that would be sufficient for almost the entire population of the world if it were properly cultivated. The more roads we make in the already settled States, the richer and stronger we shall grow, and the greater the value of land will become. The more roads we make in yet unsettled lands, the poorer and weaker we shall grow, and the less the value of land will be. It is necessary for the farmer, then, to look carefully at every scheme that promotes dispersion.

The value of labor and of capital is dependent on the quantity of both that can be given to the work of production. Every increase in the quantity...

<meta>This page continues Henry Charles Carey’s argument for economic "concentration." He argues that bringing producers and consumers closer together reduces the wasted effort of transportation and increases the value of both labor and land.</meta>

# THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.

The quantity of either labor or capital required for the <term>conversion</term> <note>original: "conversion," referring to the industrial process of turning raw materials into finished goods</note> and transportation of goods tends to diminish the value of everything. Conversely, every reduction in the amount of labor and capital needed for these tasks tends to increase the value of everything. The closer the consumer and the producer can be brought together, the more capital and labor can be dedicated to actual production. Consequently, less is required for transportation, leading to a more rapid increase in the value of both labor and land.

Currently, we are separating the consumer from the producer, and as a result, five percent stocks are trading at their face value, land is cheap, and wages are low. If the **Tariff of 1842** <note>A protectionist law that raised taxes on imported goods to encourage American manufacturing.</note> were re-enacted, interest rates would rise to six percent and labor would earn a larger return. This would result in a significant increase in the consumption of food, wool, and cotton, and the value of land would rise.

The addition of a million people to our community through European immigration establishes free trade with them. Similarly, the annexation of the land and people of Canada and other British possessions would enlarge the region of perfect free trade. This would also be true for the annexation of Cuba, Mexico, Ireland, or even England,* and free trade established in this way would benefit everyone—both those doing the annexing and those being annexed.

The people of the North would not object to the annexation of Canada, even though such a measure would profit them very little. Both the North and the Canadians are sellers of food; it is the higher value of wheat and flour on the American side of the border that makes Canadians want to join the Union. On the other hand, the people of the South would oppose admitting Canada, even though it would turn Canadians into large-scale customers instead of small ones.† Once within the Union, the consumption of cotton in the British provinces would quickly rise from 20 million yards (weighing 5 million pounds) to 30 million pounds. In this way, the Southern planter would gain a market for 50,000 bales of cotton. While the material interests of the South would be improved by annexing Canada, the South would still oppose the measure because of perceived dangers to their political interests.

The South would advocate for the admission of Cuba into the Union, even though the effect of such a measure would currently ruin sugar cultivation—the only resource the Southern planter can now look to with hope, and the only one that has allowed him to survive the current hopeless state of cotton farming. Conversely, a person from the North would oppose the measure, even though it would provide sugar at a much lower cost than today and create a massive market for Northern grain and cloth. In these cases, political interests are at odds with material ones. In both instances, however, the discord is only on the surface, while the harmony of interests is real. Establishing the true freedom of trade that comes from the immigration of individuals or the annexation of entire communities will always benefit everyone.

The cotton planter, as we have seen, now sells his product in the cheapest—

# CHAPTER THIRTEENTH.

## HOW PROTECTION AFFECTS THE MANUFACTURER.

The shipowner stands between the producer of cotton and his customers; the larger the quantity of goods to be transported compared to the number of ships available, the higher the shipping rates (freights) will be. We might suppose from this that his interests would be served by a policy that forces cotton to travel to the loom, and that he would be harmed by a policy that requires the loom to come to the cotton. However, as we have seen, the opposite is true. The more the loom is brought to the cotton, the more valuable human labor becomes. This leads to more people being imported (immigrants), a larger variety of goods being exported, and a greater volume of business for ships.

The manufacturer, in the same way, stands between the producer and the consumer of cotton. The larger the quantity of cotton to be <term>converted</term> <note>Processed or manufactured into finished goods.</note> compared to the amount of machinery available for that conversion, the higher his fee for using that machinery will be. It might therefore be supposed that he would be harmed by measures that place looms in the cotton fields of the South or on the coal fields of the West. But again, the reverse is true. The more people who make coarse cloth in the South and West, the more people there will be who require fine cloth and silks from the East.

The greater the demand for labor in one region, the greater the demand will be in another for the skills already acquired there. This leads to a constant increase in wages and a matching increase in the power to consume food, cloth, and iron. The more people can trade at home with neighbors whose labor is valuable, the more they will receive in exchange for their own labor. Every measure that tends to break down the **monopoly of machinery** <note>The concentration of industrial power in Great Britain, which forced the rest of the world to send raw materials there for processing.</note> increases the value of human beings throughout the world. Nothing would have that effect more than transferring the machinery of **Lowell** <note>A major textile manufacturing center in Massachusetts.</note> to the cotton fields, where it would eventually be replaced by even more advanced machinery.

But some will say, "The people of the South need no further protection than they already have. They are satisfied with a 30 percent tariff. If they can manufacture without a duty increase, why should they impose higher duties on fine cloths and silks just to benefit the North and East? We know the North cannot make fine muslins at the current duty rate, nor can they manufacture silk goods in competition with France. The South will process its own cotton and conduct its own trade while leaving the tariff as it is; then Lowell, **Lawrence, and Providence** <note>Key industrial cities in Massachusetts and Rhode Island.</note> must collapse, because competition with the South will be impossible." Such are the views constantly spread by journals whose editors claim to have great knowledge of political economy.

<summary>Carey argues that moving manufacturing (the "loom") closer to raw materials (the "cotton") benefits everyone—shipowners, manufacturers, and laborers alike—by increasing the value of labor and creating new markets for high-end goods.</summary>

...economy, and whose theories are accepted as authoritative by their readers. However, nothing could be less in line with the true interests of the planters.

The more machinery there is available for turning cotton into cloth, the lower the cost will be for using it. The planter needs to free himself from a **monopoly** that limits the growth of that machinery. Currently, this monopoly forces him to give the owners of the few existing machines—whether they are English or American—a share of his product that is far too large compared to the value of the equipment he uses to grow the cotton. Breaking one monopoly just to start another would not help him. That would be the result if he simply tried to replace the factories in Lowell or Lawrence <note>Major textile manufacturing centers in Massachusetts.</note> with factories in Augusta or Graniteville <note>Rising industrial centers in Georgia and South Carolina.</note>. 

A Southern manufacturer would inevitably do exactly what the Northern one does now: buy his cotton at the market price **fixed in England**, and sell his finished goods at the market price **also fixed in England**. Until we have enough machinery to prevent large amounts of unsold cotton from piling up in England, the English market will continue to set the price for the whole world. As long as we are forced to go to England for any part of our cloth supply, the price of all cloth will be determined by the cost of obtaining that last small portion. What the planter actually needs is for the price to be set here in America for both cotton and cloth. To achieve this, he needs an *increase* in the total amount of machinery ready to work for him, not just a shift in ownership from Northern men to Southern men.

It is absolutely necessary for them to do this, as is clearly shown in the diagram on page 75. It illustrates how enormous the manufacturers' charges become when the amount of cotton needing processing is much larger than the capacity of the machinery available to process it. |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **1847-8** | 940,000,000 | 4 pence | 8 pence | £28,000,000 | £15,600,000 | £12,400,000 |

The amount of machinery had increased, but the market was gone. Wars, revolutions, and the threats of further unrest had destroyed it. The planter received only 4 pence per pound, a large portion of which was consumed by the cost of transportation. Meanwhile, the manufacturer received just as much for spinning the fiber into yarn as the planter received for the entire process of growing, ginning, and baling it—including the costs of transporting it to the shipping port and then to Liverpool, as well as all the fees paid to the numerous middlemen who handled it along the way.

The planter requires machinery capable of processing his crop, and he also needs a reliable market for it once it is processed. The failure of either is equally disastrous for him.

He cannot obtain the necessary machinery under the current monopoly system. It is a system of mere gambling; while a few people make fortunes, the majority are ruined. The distant, wealthy elite—the "cotton-lords" <note>Powerful British textile magnates who dominated the global market.</note> of England—are not the people he should look to for this equipment. He must look to himself and to others like him at home in America. Fuel and iron ore are abundant in the South, and cotton fields provide cheap locations for building massive factories. In these factories, the product of thousands of acres of cotton could be processed using labor that is currently wasted, utilizing coal and iron ore that sit untouched, and harnessing water power that remains undeveloped. With these resources, every pound of cotton produced in the South—not counting what Great Britain and others need for their own immediate use—could be converted into yarn or cloth and sold cheaply to the world. The planter would then receive a yard of cloth in exchange for only a pound and a half of cotton, instead of having to give five pounds of cotton for that same single yard.

The difference between the price of the cotton crop in Liverpool and the price of the finished yarn—also in Liverpool—in 1844–1845 would have exceeded one hundred million dollars. This sum is twice the amount* it would cost to build enough spinning machines <note>original: "spindles"</note> right in the Southern cotton fields to convert the entire crop that is currently sent outside the borders of the United States.

If this were done, the planter would have yarn or cloth to sell instead of raw cotton. His crop yields would quickly rise to five million bales, because the labor and fertilizer <note>original: "manure"</note> currently wasted on long-distance transportation would instead be invested back into the land. Capital that is now swallowed up by brokers, ship-owners, and distant manufacturers would be used to build railroads, improve farming equipment, spread education, and in a thousand other ways that make labor more productive. But where, however, is he to find a market for these increased products?

Commerce is essentially an exchange of equal values. If the supply of iron, silk, coffee, tea, and other goods the planter needs does not keep pace with the increase in his cotton supply, he will find himself constantly giving more for less.

* See *The Plough, the Loom, and the Anvil*, No. XIX., page 421.

### THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.

...more cotton for less iron or silk, and thus others will enjoy the whole advantage resulting from his increased exertion. For the advantage to be his, as it justly should be, the production of the goods he wants to *receive* in exchange must increase at the same rate as the goods he wants to *give*. If this happens, he exchanges labor for labor. If it does not, he gives more labor for less labor.

The question now arises: Can global production, under the existing system, increase in such a way as to give the planter a fair equivalent for his crop? The answer is found in the fact that the system has already failed to do so. Even now, the planter is forced to abandon cotton in favor of wheat and sugar. How, then, can we expect it to succeed in the future? The average crop will soon reach 3,000,000 bales <note>A prescient estimate; the U.S. cotton crop reached 3 million bales by the early 1850s.</note>. When it does, the planter's condition will be worse than it is now. Global production is not growing as fast as our own. Until it does, we must work at a disadvantage, giving a lot of labor for very little in return.

Despite its vast amount of rich and unimproved land, the United Kingdom produces little. It cannot even feed its own people. It has a little iron and coal to sell, but a demand for an extra hundred thousand tons of iron would greatly drive up the price of all iron without significantly increasing the demand for cotton. This is because the wealthy iron-master would get richer, while the poor miner would remain as poor as he is now. Great Britain has almost nothing to sell but *services* <note>original: "services—not products"; Carey means the labor of manufacturing, transporting, and selling goods, rather than the raw materials themselves.</note>—not *products*. We cannot look to her for a market.

In France, almost half a million of the men most capable of working are instead carrying muskets in the army. A large portion of the remaining population's labor is spent growing food for these soldiers and other non-producers, making clothes for them to wear, and manufacturing gunpowder for them to burn. Therefore, they have few products to sell. Like Great Britain, they have little to offer in exchange except for services.

The people of Italy and India raise some silk, but most people in both countries are occupied with things other than productive labor. This is unlikely to change, and they cannot increase their production to keep pace with ours. Germany maintains large armies and produces little to sell. The same is true for Spain and Portugal. Mexico has a little silver and cochineal <note>A red dye produced from insects found on cacti.</note>, but the quantity is not increasing, nor is it likely to. Wherever we look, the power of production is not only small but unable to grow under current circumstances. Unless a change is made, we cannot find markets for the products of our constantly growing population. 

What is the remedy? It is to bring the people to the place where *alone* their labor can be made productive, and thus establish perfect free trade with them <note>Carey uses "perfect free trade" here to mean bringing manufacturers to the United States so that farmers and manufacturers can trade directly without the costs of international shipping and middlemen.</note>.

If fifty thousand English miners and furnace workers were distributed among the coal and iron-ore fields of Pennsylvania, Ohio, Indiana, Tennessee, and Alabama, they would produce 600,000 tons of bar iron. This iron would be exchanged with the farmer for his wheat and the planter for his cotton. The planter would then receive a ton of iron for a single bale of cotton, instead of giving two or three bales for one ton. He could then afford to build roads to reach his markets. His people's labor would become valuable, and they would consume five times as much cloth as they do now. This would create a massive new market for his cotton.

The same number of Italians living here would raise four times the silk we currently consume, and they would also be large consumers of our food and cotton. If a market for silk were established here, we would soon raise as much as the rest of the world combined and consume almost all of it ourselves.

The planter and the farmer *must* create a market on their own land for the...

He argues that the United States should bring manufacturing to its own shores to create a local market for its agricultural products, rather than relying on distant foreign markets like Great Britain.</meta>

# THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.

...products of the land, by bringing the people they want to employ here to produce the goods they need to consume; otherwise, they *must* continue to give an ever-increasing amount of labor for an ever-decreasing return. By choosing the first path, they would turn someone who consumes only one pound of goods into someone who consumes twenty, and those who consume twenty pounds into consumers of forty. By adopting the opposite policy—what is currently called "free trade"—they will instead turn a twenty-pound consumer into a one-pound consumer.

If it were known in Europe today that this was the *fixed and permanent policy of the nation*, this year would see a migration of half a million people, along with an incalculable amount of capital in the form of machinery. Once here, they would stay, immediately and immensely expanding the market for both food and cotton. In less than five years, that migration would reach a million people per year. With every passing year, the ability to obtain food, clothing, and the machinery needed to make labor profitable would increase, offering new incentives for both workers and investors to move here. Each year, the desire of our neighbors to the north and south to join the Union <note>Carey is referring to the United States and the 19th-century idea of "Manifest Destiny," suggesting that Canada and Mexico might eventually join the U.S. for economic reasons.</note> would grow. Before long, the Union would encompass all of North America and a population of forty or fifty million people—who would themselves consume far more cotton than we currently grow. 

A Canadian, once inside the Union, would find his labor three times more profitable, for he would receive three times the iron and cloth in exchange for less effort. The mines of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick would yield their treasures to workers who currently can afford very little food or clothing, but who would then have the power to consume much more. The mines of Mexico would be made to produce three dollars where they now produce only one. Everyone would obtain silver, gold, iron, lead, cloth, and all other necessities, comforts, and luxuries of life at a much lower cost of labor.

With every step of this progress, there would be an increased demand for both the physical and mental labor of Northern manufacturers. The demand for fine cloth and silk would grow as the ability to produce basic cloth and iron increases; the demand for fine books would grow alongside the increase in schoolbooks and newspapers; and the demand for cotton and wool-processing machinery would grow as people gain the ability to afford iron for railroads.

There is, therefore, a perfect harmony of interest between the manufacturer and the planter <note>original: "planter" — specifically referring to Southern cotton plantation owners.</note>. Everyone shares an interest in trying to throw off the burden imposed on them by the current monopoly on machinery <note>Refers to Great Britain's 19th-century dominance in industrial manufacturing, which Carey argues forced other nations to remain purely agricultural.</note>; however, the farmer has the greatest interest of all. The current system tends to reduce production throughout the world, diminish the power to consume, and thus destroy the customers of both the planter and the farmer. The goal of protection <note>The policy of using tariffs to encourage domestic industry.</note> is to raise the value of labor throughout the world by increasing the respect with which people are treated abroad, thereby boosting both production and consumption. As the desire to flee Europe increases, foreign governments will feel it is more necessary to try to keep their people at home by improving their conditions. Through that process, and that alone, will the workers of the world be raised to the same level as our own.

<meta>This page continues Henry Charles Carey’s argument, moving from the benefits of migration to the specific impact of protectionist policies on the capitalist or investor. # THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.

### CHAPTER THIRTEENTH.

### HOW PROTECTION AFFECTS THE CAPITALIST.

If protection is a "war on labor and capital," as some claim, it must work by reducing how productive labor is. This would prevent labor from being used effectively and decrease the ability to accumulate wealth through clearing, draining, and fencing land; building houses; constructing roads and bridges for transportation; and creating machinery to turn raw materials into goods for human use. If, on the contrary, protection truly does what its name implies—protect the laborer—then it must increase the power to accumulate wealth. This wealth can then be used to increase productivity, making it even easier to accumulate more wealth in the future.

The primary engine of production is the land. The more time and thought that can be dedicated to its cultivation, the faster production will grow, the higher the returns on capital will be, and the more quickly the human condition will improve.

Conversely, the more time and thought that *must* be spent on building transportation infrastructure, the slower the increase in production will be. This results in smaller returns on capital and slower social progress. The goal of protection is to bring the consumer to live right next to the producer. This saves on transportation costs and makes it easier to apply labor directly to production, while reducing the number of people <note>The author refers to "middlemen"—merchants and shippers—who take a share of the value without adding to the physical product.</note> among whom the product must be divided.

For example, an iron furnace capable of producing 5,000 tons of iron per year can be put into operation for about $30,000. In Ohio, those 5,000 tons of iron would be worth 150,000 bushels of wheat. That wheat is the product of 12,500 acres of land that cost $40 per acre—totaling $500,000 for the labor of clearing and draining it, building fences, barns, and houses, and everything else needed for farming. Even if we assume the furnace, worker housing, and mine preparation cost $100,000, the capital required to produce the wheat is still five times greater than the capital needed to produce the iron, yet both yield the exact same economic return. 

But that is not all. The wheat weighs 4,000 tons. Transporting this to New York and then to Liverpool requires more capital in wagons and canal boats than would have been needed to produce the iron at home. It also requires far more capital in shipping than domestic production would have. Thus, we end up using seven, eight, or even ten times the capital necessary to get the same result: 5,000 tons of iron.

The capital invested in building the furnace, the houses, and preparing the mines would have been a permanent investment. It would have increased the value of every surrounding acre because it created a local market for the land's products. In contrast, wagons, ships, and canal boats disappear over time as they wear out. Meanwhile, the land, because it is constantly harvested for export, becomes exhausted and is frequently abandoned by its owners. In this way, the entire investment is wasted.

The farmer might say that he could not have obtained any more iron locally for his crops—that the local iron-master paid him for his wheat and charged him for his iron based on the prices in Liverpool. He might feel he profited just as much by trading in one place as the other. Unfortunately, this is nearly true. As long as he is *compelled* to compete with the low-paid labor of Europe, he must accept this consequence. As long as he is *dependent* on England to buy even a million bushels of his wheat, England will dictate the price for all the wheat produced. And so long as he is *dependent* on her for the last few thousand tons of iron, she will fix the price for all the iron.

<summary>Carey argues that protectionist policies benefit capitalists by reducing the massive waste of capital spent on international transportation. He illustrates how local manufacturing creates permanent land value, whereas export-heavy agriculture exhausts the soil and relies on volatile foreign prices.</summary>

...is consumed. The producer needs to increase domestic food consumption to match production, and domestic iron production to match consumption. If he does this, the prices for both will be determined locally. With this approach, a small amount of capital will produce a large amount of iron. Currently, a large amount of capital is required to produce very little iron.

It has been shown (on page 74) that the total amount of cotton—311,000,000 pounds—consumed by the people of Great Britain and Ireland in 1845 and 1846 could have been paid for with 6,250,000 pieces of plain cotton cloth and 210,000 tons of iron delivered in Liverpool. However, by the time this cloth and iron reached the plantation in America, the quantities would have shrunk to 5,000,000 pieces of cloth (120,000,000 yards) and 160,000 tons of iron—and perhaps even less, even assuming they were imported tax-free <note>original: "duty free"</note>. Producing those 120,000,000 yards of cloth during those two years would have required only 20 moderate-sized mills, each capable of processing 2,000 bales of cotton into cloth. Producing the iron would have required little more than two factories similar to the one described on page 42 in the Lehigh region of Pennsylvania.

To transport 700,000 bales of cotton would require 60 ships, each carrying 2,000 bales and making three trips a year. When you add the cost of steamboats, warehouses, packing machinery, and other infrastructure on the American side, along with the docks, carts <note>original: "drays"</note>, warehouses, railcars, and railroads on the British side, you find that the capital required just to transport those 311,000,000 pounds of cotton *after* they reached the shipping port was three times greater than the capital needed to provide the machinery for the planter to manufacture them into cloth on-site. *The planter pays for all of this*. This is why we see the planter sending away 311,000,000 pounds of cotton only to receive 74,000,000 pounds back in the form of cloth at Liverpool—which then shrinks to 60,000,000 pounds by the time it reaches the plantation. Essentially, he is giving five pounds of raw cotton for just one yard of cloth. It is clear that, in this system, a massive amount of capital is required to obtain a very small result.

Let us now look at the amount of capital the planter used to produce those 250,000,000 pounds of cotton at the shipping port—the same cotton he gave to the English in those two years just to have 60,000,000 pounds spun and woven. On average, 155,000,000 pounds are sent out annually, and 30,000,000 are returned; 125,000,000 pounds are lost to costs along the way. Since cotton land produces an average of less than 300 pounds per acre, it would take 416,000 acres to produce those 125,000,000 pounds—not counting the rest of the land on the plantations left uncultivated. The average amount of labor required to prepare this land for production—including fencing, housing, machinery, cotton gins <note>original: "gin-houses"</note>, and roads—is at least 100 days of work per acre, and that is a conservative estimate. If we value that labor at only 50 cents a day, we reach a cost of $50 per acre. At this rate, the capital invested in land would be $20,800,000. If we estimate the value of the workers <note>The author uses "hands" to refer to enslaved labor, which was the basis of the cotton economy in the mid-19th century South.</note> at the same amount as the land, we add another $20,800,000. Finally, there is the capital used for transportation to the shipping port. To give you an idea of that cost, here is a statement from an eyewitness:

> "Some idea of the expense of this initial movement can be gained by those who have seen cotton coming over terrible roads, buried up to the wheel hubs <note>original: "up to the hub"</note>, and dragged slowly for 20, 30, or 40 miles. We have seen it arriving in Natchez and Vicksburg, hauled by five pairs <note>original: "yoke"</note> of oxen carrying 2,800 to 3,000 pounds. They move so slowly that the motion is barely visible. So many oxen die in their harnesses <note>original: "perish in the yoke"</note> during the winter and spring that it has been said, with some exaggeration, that you could walk from Jackson to Vicksburg on the bodies of dead oxen. That was before the railroad was built. A wagon is loaded, say 14 miles from Natchez, and..."

This is a very low estimate of the "fixed labor"—which we call capital—invested to bring **125,000,000** pounds of cotton to the place of shipment. Now, let us see how much fixed capital is provided by distant manufacturers in exchange for all of this. A mill that can process **2,000** bales of cotton can easily be built for no more than **$100,000**. Those **2,000** bales contain 900,000 pounds of cotton. It would take thirty-four such mills to process **30,000,000** pounds, and the total cost of all these mills would be **$3,000,000**. This is only about one-fifteenth of the capital employed by the planter. Is it any wonder, then, that the planter’s capital yields him such a small return?

Power is most effective when it is applied directly. The more machinery or intermediaries that come between the producer and the consumer, the weaker the power and the smaller the result. The planter obtains his cloth and iron indirectly by growing cotton and food to send abroad. However, if he applied his resources <note>original: "power"</note> directly to producing both cloth and iron, his total production would double and his ability to accumulate wealth would quadruple.

If the planters of 1845 and 1846 had provided themselves with the machinery needed to convert the **155,000,000** pounds of cotton consumed in England into cloth, they would have seen iron furnaces spring up around them. These furnaces would have been capable of producing three times the amount of iron they actually received for that cotton. This would have created a local market for the products of the land. As a result, they would have earned far more for the remaining portion of their crop than they actually received for the entire harvest. 

The proceeds from those **155,000,000** pounds would have bought enough iron to build hundreds of miles of railroad. This would have decreased their need to rely on distant markets while simultaneously increasing their power to reach them by growing their capital. It will be argued, however, that while I have accounted for the labor of producing the cotton, I have not accounted for the labor required to turn it into cloth. No such allowance is needed. The labor of men, women, and children that is currently completely wasted in *every county* of the South is more than enough to run five such mills. Furthermore, the cotton that is currently lost for lack of workers at harvest time would pay for the mills twice over.

The planter currently receives only one pound of finished cloth in exchange for five pounds of raw cotton. If the costs that currently exist between the planter on one side and the spinner and weaver on the other could be saved, he would instead receive two pounds of cloth for every three pounds of cotton. To accomplish this, there is only one way to proceed: we must *persuade the machinery to come to the cotton*. This removes the necessity of sending the cotton to the machinery. 

At present, we seem to be following the same path as a man who spends hundreds of thousands of days of labor clearing and farming land to produce wheat, only to waste two-thirds of that wheat on the road to and from a distant mill—all because he refuses to apply three or four thousand days of labor to build a mill on his own land. A gristmill <term>gristmill: a mill used for grinding grain into flour</term> costing 5,000 days of labor will grind all the grain produced on land that cost 300,000 or even 500,000 days of labor to develop. Yet, the man mentioned above would waste more days on the road annually than it would take to build such a mill. 

So it is with our planters and farmers. We see in every small community that flour mills quickly appear to convert grain into flour, and they are satisfied with a one-eighth share as a fee <note>original: "one-eighth toll"</note>. We see that in every neighborhood where there is timber and a little water power, sawmills are built to convert logs into boards. With each of these operations, flour and boards are obtained at a lower cost of labor; the farmer has to give up less of his wheat and timber to have them processed. What would the wheat-grower say if he had to give away five bushels of grain just to get one bushel of flour back?\* And what should the cotton-grower say to receiving back only one bale of cotton in the form of cloth for every five he sends away? Let him reflect on this question, and then answer the following: Why should not every reasonably sized community have its own place for converting cotton into cloth? If that could be done, the planter would receive half of the cloth produced from his cotton.

The planter will likely deny this at first glance. He will say: "If I sell my cotton to go to Manchester <note>A major center of the British textile industry in the 19th century</note>, it will earn me five cents. If I sell it to a manufacturer right here, he will give me no more. If I buy English cloth, it will cost me ten cents. If I had a manufacturer right here, I would pay the same." 

This must be the case as long as he finds himself *compelled* to compete in the English market with the poor Indian <note>original: "Hindoo"; referring to the low-wage competition from cotton workers in British-colonized India</note> for the sale of his cotton, and is compelled to purchase his supply of cloth there; for as long as that lasts, the prices of both will be fixed in Liverpool. 

However, with every step toward economic independence <note>original: "emancipation"; here referring to the South's potential freedom from volatile foreign markets</note>, he would find himself a winner. Let him look around and see how much of the labor in his neighborhood and on his own plantation is wasted for want of the demand that would be created by a nearby factory. Then, let him reflect on the advantage of having a place of employment in that factory throughout the year for people who could, if needed, help him with his harvest <note>original: "picking"</note>. This would save him the labor that is currently lost on cotton wasted in the field or ruined by early frost. Let him consider these things, and he will probably find that the loss in these areas alone is equal to the value of the labor required to convert all the cotton of the neighborhood into yarn. If these things could be saved, and if he could thus, with—
