If he were to apply the same labor and send yarn to market instead of raw cotton, he and his neighbors would benefit greatly from the change.

Having done this, let him look at the price he receives for his corn. Consider the difference it would make if he had a local market <note>original: "market on the ground"</note> because some of his neighbors had become skilled tradespeople or factory workers <note>original: "mechanics, mill operatives, &c."</note>. Instead of remaining poor while farming small plots of land, these neighbors would earn good wages and consume twice as much food as they do now, all while producing none themselves. The farmer would immediately save much of the cost of transportation. He would sell food at home instead of having to buy it back from Manchester or Lowell—with the added costs of commissions and shipping from his own neighborhood driving up the price. Everyone would benefit greatly from this change.

Next, let him look at his cleared land. Consider what its value would be if all the manure produced by his hay, oats, corn, and fodder went back into the soil, rather than being wasted on the road. Imagine if the nutrients from his wheat and corn stayed on his land instead of being shipped to Lowell or Manchester. See if he would not be a gainer by this change.

Then, let him look at his uncleared land and calculate how much it would cost him simply to destroy the timber. Now, calculate the value of that same timber if there were a factory nearby—if the blacksmith, shoemaker, hatter, tanner, bricklayer, and carpenter all needed houses. Imagine a town growing up around the mill, with inhabitants wanting pork, meal, milk, beef, flour, potatoes, and mutton. See if he would not benefit greatly from this change.

Let him look at the amount of land where this timber stands, for which he is currently paying—or losing—interest. Then, look at the quality of that land and compare it to what he currently cultivates. Calculate how many bushels of potatoes it would yield. Compare their value—when consumed locally—with the value of the 300 pounds of cotton currently produced by an acre. See if he would not benefit from the change.

Let him add all these factors together. He would save all the costs of freight and commissions, even if he received no more for his cotton and paid just as much for his cloth. See if he would not receive the full value of his cotton, rather than only one-third of it as he does now.

The great cities and towns of the world are built at the expense of the farmer and the planter. Looking around New York, Philadelphia, or Boston, it is impossible not to be struck by the number of people who live merely by exchanging goods—passing them from the producer to the consumer—while producing nothing themselves. Wagons and wagoners, carts and cartmen, boats and boatmen, ships and sailors are everywhere, hauling cotton, wool, corn, wheat, and flour as if for the sheer pleasure of moving them. 

The farmer in Tennessee sends his cotton to Manchester to be spun. His corn goes along with it to feed the man who spins it. When the corn leaves the farmer, it is worth twenty cents. By the time the Manchester spinner eats it, it is worth perhaps a dollar. The laborer buys it at that price; the manufacturer pays him a dollar for it and then adds that cost—plus a ten-cent markup—to the price of the cloth. The corn and cotton are transformed into cloth, and the Tennessee man buys it back, paying five bales of raw cotton for every one bale's worth of finished cloth! He can sometimes afford to send his corn away, but he can never send his potatoes. This is because potatoes are among the class of commodities that the earth produces so abundantly that they are too heavy and bulky to pay for the cost of shipping <note>original: "will not pay freight"</note>. The only things he can raise for a distant market are those of which the earth yields very little, and which can therefore afford to pay...

<sig>19</sig>

He demonstrates that establishing local manufacturing would save on transport, preserve soil fertility, and allow farmers to sell high-yield, bulky crops like potatoes that are otherwise impossible to export.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Henry Charles Carey’s argument for local manufacturing. He previously explained that transporting raw goods over long distances wastes resources and depletes the soil. Here, he argues that bringing the factory (the "mill") to the farmer creates a "profitable consumer" and protects the local economy from the volatile shifts of foreign markets, specifically criticizing the lower tariffs of 1846.</meta>

# THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.

The farmer pays for the transport of his goods. He grows three hundred pounds of cotton, all of which goes to market, yet he receives back only sixty pounds of it fashioned into cloth. This process returns nothing to the soil that was originally drawn out of it. However, if he had consumers living near him, he would grow almost as many bushels of potatoes instead. The manure from that crop would go back onto the land to enrich it, making the farmer himself wealthy. He could then afford to clear the timber, dig ditches, drain the soil, and cultivate the richest land, which is currently covered with trees or water.

Why does he not do these things? Why does he not convert the "unprofitable consumers" <note>By "unprofitable consumers," Carey refers to people living in poverty who consume very little and produce no surplus for the market.</note> everywhere around him into profitable ones?* Why does he continue, year after year, to send his grain or cotton to a distant mill, instead of bringing the mill to him *once and for all*? 

The reason can be found in the newspapers every day. Two years ago, cotton, wool, and iron manufacturers were prosperous. Now, they are all stopping work. Many are already ruined, and many more are likely to be. Why is this? Does it happen because of any change in our own domestic affairs? It does not. It happens because of changes abroad. Two years ago, England was building railroads, and their consumption was large. This year, England is not building roads, and their consumption is small. Two years ago, we built factories and furnaces. This year, the manufacturers and furnace-builders are ruined. All of them would be ruined if they did not have a protective tariff—inadequate as the **Tariff of 1846** <note>The Tariff of 1846, or the Walker Tariff, lowered trade barriers, which Carey argued left American industry vulnerable to foreign competition.</note> is—to give them the protection needed to secure them against such global changes. They would be prosperous now if the **Tariff of 1842** <note>The Tariff of 1842 was a highly protectionist measure that Carey championed.</note> had remained unchanged. Furthermore, the thousands of people employed in those industries would have remained profitable customers for the farmers, instead of being driven across the country to become the farmer's rivals, increasing the supply of food for which there is already more than enough <note>original: "redundance"</note>.

The capital used just to transport cotton is more than what it would cost to build the mills to convert the entire crop into cloth. The mill represents "saved labor." Transportation is "lost labor," which can never be regained. Once the mills are built, all that labor could be applied to actual production.

* The following description of some of these "unprofitable consumers" is from a letter to a correspondent of the *New York Herald*:

> "Yesterday, I traveled twenty miles over a public road and stopped at nearly every house. They were occupied by those called 'the poor white people.' I found fifty log houses on my route. You pass through a forest and come to cleared land. On one side of the road, you see a field of corn, perhaps five to ten acres. A few rods back from the road, standing amid this corn, is a log cabin with smoke curling up in blue wreaths even on these hot days. A wicket gate opens from the road; you pass through it and follow a footpath to the entrance of the cabin. 
> 
> There is a stone for a step, and you enter. A woman is spinning. She asks you to take a seat made of hickory—both the frame and the seat itself. There are two or three more like it. In the corner of the room is a bed. The fireplace is very large, and the chimney is built of mud on the outside of the hut. There are some nails for hats and clothes. There is a rifle resting on wooden pins, and a shelf holding a few items: a broken comb, a Bible printed by the American Bible Society, and a basic utility knife <note>original: "case-knife"</note>. In a corner is a barrel. If you look inside, you will find half a bushel of cornmeal, and hanging over it on a string is a piece of bacon. There is a cupboard in the corner; if you open it, you might find a cup, a saucer, and a plate—or perhaps you won't. 
> 
> This is a true-to-life description. You ask about the family—'My husband is pulling fodder' <term>pulling fodder: the practice of stripping the leaves from standing corn stalks to use as animal feed</term>. 'How many children do you have?' 'Six.' By and by, you see all six fair-haired <note>original: "flaxy-headed"</note> children peeping through the cracks in the hut. In the summer, because there are no windows, the 'chinking' or filling between the logs is removed for air. You wonder how people can live in such a one-room den. Yet they do live and get on very well. They sometimes keep a cow and a few pigs to make ham and bacon, and they grow corn, wheat, and oats. The cabin would be worth twenty dollars if it were for sale."

# THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.

The wasted labor of workers on the plantations, and that of the "poor white people" throughout the South, is more than what would be required for the work of conversion <note>original: "conversion"; here meaning the industrial processing of raw materials like cotton into finished goods like cloth.</note>. Protectionism seeks to enable the planter to save this labor and build up capital.

It is often called "a war upon labor and capital," but in this case, it certainly seems to be exactly what its name implies: protection for the producers of food and wool against a system that forces them to give up fifteen dollars of capital in exchange for only one. Its goal is to promote concentration <note>Carey uses "concentration" to mean keeping people and industry close together to reduce transport costs and improve the land.</note>. In contrast, the goal of the system falsely called "free trade" is to promote dispersion—the scattering of people and resources. The last twelve months have seen the departure of many thousands of men and many millions of dollars in capital to California, not one-tenth of which will ever return. One of the newspapers of the day states that:

> "Considerable excitement has been created here (New York) among those who have made shipments of merchandise to California by the receipt of letters from commission houses in San Francisco containing accounts of sales. It appears that the charges have, in several instances, entirely used up the proceeds of the sales. We hear it stated in dry-goods circles that one of our largest auction houses sent out over two hundred thousand dollars' worth of dry goods last winter, for which they have received no payment up to this time."

Hundreds of ships are now sitting in the Pacific, doing nothing and earning nothing, when they could be carrying cotton; meanwhile, we are building other ships to replace them. The capital now invested in those ships and in California could have built mills to process half the cotton of the South, and furnaces to produce as much iron as is made in Great Britain. For all this waste of capital, the farmer and the planter pay the price. The *harmony of interests* is so complete that the losses of the shipowner and the manufacturer are always borne, in the largest proportion, by the farmers and planters.*

---

* The following estimate of the amount of labor and capital *lost by ourselves* and wasted in California is from the *New York Herald*, and it is not far from the truth:

> "It is estimated that about 500 vessels had arrived at San Francisco from the United States and Europe by the 1st of November, and that at least 100,000 people were in California at that time. The average cost of an outfit for each person cannot be less than $200, which totals $20,000,000. It will cost an average of at least $300 per year for each person to live there. This amounts to $30,000,000. This makes a total of $50,000,000 for just the basic outfit and provisions for one year. The 500 vessels that had arrived by the latest date, and the 500 currently on the way, are worth an average of about $10,000 each, totaling $10,000,000. We estimate the value of each individual’s time to be worth an average of $200—a total of $20,000,000. The grand total for the outfit, the cost of living for one year, the cost of vessels involved in the trade, and the value of time for one year is $80,000,000. This is a conservative calculation, as the actual spending and absorption of capital up to this time will probably reach a full $100,000,000. 
>
> As a balance against this, we have so far received about six million dollars ($6,000,000) in gold dust from California and the entire Pacific coast. It is clear that there is still an enormous balance against California. At the current rate of return, it will be a long time before we even recover the sum spent, let alone see any profits. It is our impression that most of those involved in the trade would be satisfied with merely getting back the cost of their shipments. Most have abandoned any idea of profit, and many will never see a cent: costs such as freight and storage will eat up every penny of the original cost. The only product of California to pay for this immense amount of property is gold. At present, it has no other resources, and we know of none but its minerals. It is now a little more than twelve months since the migration to California began, and the history of the world has never seen such a massive movement of people. In addition to the hundreds of vessels departing from all parts of the world for California, we have nearly a dozen of the finest steamships in the world regularly employed in carrying passengers and mail between this port and San Francisco, via Chagres and Panama <note>Before the Panama Canal, travelers crossed the Isthmus of Panama by boat up the Chagres River and then by land to the Pacific coast.</note>. Several large steamers are now on their way around the continent to join the line from Panama to San Francisco, and shortly we shall have two or three more on the line between this city and Chagres."

# THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.

The world's landowners are the great capitalists. The "exchangers" <note>original: "exchangers"; middlemen such as merchants, shippers, and wholesalers who facilitate trade.</note> are the small ones, yet they and their machinery absorb the majority of what the land produces. Therefore, land yields only a small return for the labor spent preparing it for production. In almost every part of this country, land has little value, rarely worth more than the cost of its fences and buildings. For this to change, and for landowners to prosper, they must "bring the loom to the cotton and the anvil to the food" <note>Carey’s central metaphor for establishing manufacturing (the loom and anvil) close to the sources of raw materials and food to eliminate transport costs.</note>, instead of sending massive amounts of cotton and food away, year after year, in search of a loom and an anvil elsewhere.

The farmers and planters of the Union have yet to learn how rapidly their capital is capable of growing. Settling land for the first time requires a great deal of labor; however, as in many other cases, the first step is the most expensive. Once the land is cleared, the farm enclosed, the house built, and the road made, the cost of transportation still eats up so much of the product that the property as a whole has little value. Building a railroad doubles that value, but the amount of cloth or iron that can be obtained in exchange for wheat or cotton is still so small that the land remains worth very little. Bringing a furnace or a cotton mill to the area—thereby creating a market on the land for the products of the land—requires an amount of labor that is absolutely insignificant compared to the amount already spent. Yet, it doubles the value of everything nearby. The only reason for a difference in the value of land anywhere—assuming quality is equal—is proximity to, or distance from, a market.

Let us now suppose that during the last twenty years we had annually set aside a small part of the labor wasted on transport, and a small portion of the food and cotton lost in distant markets, to build furnaces and erect cotton mills. Imagine if the Southern States now possessed one hundred furnaces, each capable of producing 5,000 tons of iron, along with rolling mills to convert it into bars. Imagine if they had mills capable of converting 500,000 bales of cotton into cloth, and if the spare labor of their workers had been used to grade roads upon which they had been laying iron bars produced in their own furnaces and mills for years. Consider what the result would be.

Throughout the entire South, there would have been a nearby market for a large portion of their products. Every region would enjoy the facilities to transport its surplus food or cotton to distant markets at one-fifth of the current cost. Thus, the land in every part would have increased in value to an almost incalculable degree. The planting states have 400,000,000 acres; adding just ten dollars per acre to the current value would total four billion dollars. Meanwhile, the cost of building furnaces, rolling mills, and all the other machinery necessary to cover those states with roads—filling them with the equipment needed to process enough cotton to free them from dependence on distant markets—would not have cost fifty million dollars. As large as that sum may seem, the return would have been an increase in capital measured in the thousands of millions.

An addition of one dollar per acre in the annual value, or rent, of a plantation would add more than ten dollars per acre to its total value. Currently, a farmer sends his corn to market and receives twenty cents, yet the consumer pays fifty. He buys back iron that costs him 300 bushels of corn per ton, yet the producer of that iron receives only 25 bushels. If iron and cotton manufacturing had been allowed to develop throughout Virginia, Tennessee, Alabama, and other Southern states, today 60 bushels of corn or half a bale of cotton would pay for a ton of iron. If that were the case, what would the land be worth now? Would it not be much greater—

->THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.<-

...than at present by more than twenty dollars an acre? If so, would that not total eight billion dollars? It is almost inconceivable how small an amount of capital is required to double, triple, or quadruple the value of land after the first and most expensive process—the initial settlement and occupation—has been finished.

Let us now look at the state of things in England. The greatest opportunity for employing capital <note>original: "capital"; in this context, the money or resources available for investment.</note> is the land. There are sixty-four million acres in the United Kingdom. Spending only twenty shillings worth of labor per acre would absorb the enormous sum of three hundred million dollars. An average investment of three guineas <note>original: "guineas"; a British gold coin worth 21 shillings.</note> per acre would absorb one billion dollars. In contrast, the entire capital employed in cotton manufacturing is only thirty-four million pounds* (about one hundred and sixty million dollars), and the capital invested in shipping is only slightly more than that. 

Now, let us assume that half of the cotton machinery is for domestic trade and the other half for foreign trade. Suppose also that half of the shipping is for home purposes—including importing tea, coffee, sugar, and silk for the local market—and the other half is for other purposes. The result is that the market for capital provided by foreign trade is only one-sixth of what would be required for agriculture, even at a rate of only three pounds per acre. If we assume that ships and machinery last about ten years, the annual demand created by foreign trade is only three million pounds. This is equal to less than one shilling per acre invested annually in land improvement. 

No one familiar with the condition of Irish agriculture, or a large portion of the land in England and Scotland, can doubt that spending twenty times that amount on gradual improvements in farming and transportation would yield a large return. However, land everywhere is centralized in the hands of great owners and worked by large-scale farmers. Consequently, capital does not find a way to be invested in land improvement. Instead, it must seek an outlet <note>original: "vent"</note> in manufacturing and commerce. Together, these fields are so small that competition is fierce and the rate of profit is very low.

The savings of Ireland are forced into England because there are no ways to invest locally. From 1821 to 1833, no less than ten million pounds were transferred in this way; more recent reports show that this trend has continued to the present day.

A large portion of the deposits in Scottish banks is habitually invested in "the funds" <note>original: "the funds"; government bonds or national debt.</note>. Because local investment is prevented, there is a constant pressure on the financial center in London. This deprives both large and small capitalists of a fair return on their money.

The natural result of this lack of local investment is the accumulation of large amounts of money in London, where it seeks a market at low interest rates. Foreigners are then invited to borrow this money—which is to say, they are invited to buy English cloth and iron on credit. Once this unemployed capital has been scattered across the world through this process, a crisis inevitably occurs. The debts are called in, leading to bankruptcy for England’s debtors and widespread ruin among English merchants. This is the history of the period from 1835 to 1842, which ended in bankruptcy and the refusal to pay debts <note>original: "repudiation"; specifically referring to several U.S. states defaulting on their debts to British creditors in the early 1840s.</note>. This is also the history, so far, of the Tariff of 1846 <note>original: "tariff of '46"; the Walker Tariff, which lowered U.S. import duties and was criticized by Carey for encouraging debt and harming local industry.</note>. We have bought thirty to forty million dollars worth of goods on credit, and the day of payment must eventually come.

By a series of operations like this, all of England's customers...

...had been ruined, and by 1842, no foreign country remained that could be trusted. Capital <note>original: "capital"; here meaning the money and resources available for investment.</note> seemed more than sufficient. Interest rates were very low, and there appeared to be no prospect of improvement. Everything was prepared for a massive wave of domestic speculation, and the railroad soon became the obsession of the day. It was a great lottery in which nobles and the poor, bankers and retired military officers, clergymen and pickpockets, all bought tickets, certain that they would draw a winning prize. Five thousand miles of road have been built at a stated cost of £148,000,000,* but the larger portion of this vast sum has merely been a transfer from the pocket of one gambler into that of another, as can be seen from the following statement:

| | | **Per mile**, | |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| The mere parliamentary expenses† of the Blackwall railway amounted to | . . . . | | $70,000 |
| Those of the Manchester and Birmingham to | . . . | “ | 25,000 |
| And those of the Eastern Counties' road to | . . . | “ | 23,000 |
| The amount allowed for land by the Manchester and Birmingham was | . . . . . . | “ | 80,000 |
| Eastern Counties | . . . . . . | “ | 75,000 |

<margin>† Parliamentary expenses: The legal and lobbying costs required to obtain an Act of Parliament to authorize a railway's construction.</margin>

In this manner, the cost of the projects was inflated to $250,000, $300,000, $400,000, and in one case to $1,400,000 per mile. The consequence of this has been that while the few who designed these schemes have been enriched, the many have been ruined. England is covered with the wrecks of this disastrous speculation. This crisis owed its existence to the fact that the whole policy of the country tended to force capital into commerce and manufacturing—which offer the smallest field for its employment—and to drive it away from agriculture. Agriculture is the only field that is constantly enlarging, and in which an almost unlimited amount of labor and capital might be employed at a steadily increasing rate of return.

The way in which this system operates upon the wealthy investor here is now to be examined. In 1835, as we have seen, the natural outlets for capital were closed. We stopped building mills, furnaces, or metal refineries <note>original: "rolling-mills"; factories where metal is rolled into sheets or bars.</note>, and the building of ships and houses decreased. The necessary consequence of this blocking up of capital was that the price of stocks that pay dividends rose, and this produced a desire to create new stocks using the then-idle capital. Roads and canals were started in the West and Southwest, banks were created, and the investor was led to believe that he would receive ten or fifteen percent per year for the use of the funds he placed under the control of strangers. 

The day of settlement, however, arrived. England claimed payment for the cloth and iron she had provided; but the money that should have paid her was scattered to the four winds. It was invested in unproductive roads and in banks that were ruined by the failure of their debtors. In this way, as many millions were wasted as would have been needed to build enough furnaces to produce four times the iron we have ever used, and to turn all the cotton we then produced into cloth. The mass of smaller investors were ruined, but the few were made rich.

We are now moving in the same direction. Money is said to be "cheap"—that is, there is much sitting in banks to the credit of depositors for which they are receiving no interest. The newspapers of the day inform us that stocks and bonds from Western cities are coming into demand; here we have the beginning of a movement similar to that of 1836. In a little while, it will be thought sensible to create banks in distant places; then, after a short while, England will claim payment for the cloth and iron we are now buying on credit, and then the scenes of 1842 will be enacted all over again.

<meta>This page transitions from Carey's critique of British financial speculation to his broader theory of economic harmony. He argues that the British "colonial system" artificially depresses global labor and capital. He then begins a new chapter explaining how protectionism—far from being a burden—actually benefits the worker by increasing the productivity of labor through machinery.</meta>

->THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.<-

If we want to know who is responsible for the power to disrupt global economic stability in this way, we only need to look at the prices of cotton and yarn between 1844 and 1848, as shown in a previous chapter. The farmers and planters of the world first give away their products for almost nothing, then borrow a portion of those same products back in the form of cloth and iron; when they are eventually ruined by this process, they are denounced as bankrupts and swindlers.

The true interests of capitalists in all nations are in perfect harmony with one another. Whatever tends to decrease production in one country also tends to decrease the return on capital in all others. The British system is "a war against the labor and capital of the world," harming its own people as much as those of other nations. Its effect is to keep the returns for the capitalist very low, and often to deprive him of any return at all. This happens because the system tends to force the worker to underbid the Indian <note>original: "Hindoo"; here referring to workers in colonial India.</note> and the Russian worker, sinking him to their level of poverty. Therefore, the workers and capitalists of other nations are forced to turn to protective measures. 

The immediate effect of adopting efficient and complete protection as a national policy would be the transfer of a massive amount of capital to this country in the form of machinery. This would be followed by a gradual rise in the rate of profit abroad, which would eventually level out with our own. Once that capital is here, it cannot be taken back. Like the immigrants we welcome, it would stay; the necessary result of this transfer of capital would be an increased arrival of people—who are the most valuable form of capital, though currently the most despised in Europe.

To achieve true freedom of trade, we must raise the status of the workers and capitalists of Europe to a level equal with our own. The colonial system <note>original: "colonial system"; the economic policy where a mother country extracts raw materials from colonies and sells back manufactured goods.</note> tends to depress and destroy both.

## CHAPTER FIFTEENTH.

### HOW PROTECTION AFFECTS THE WORKER.

Whenever there is a surplus of any commodity in the market—whether caused by natural or artificial factors—the price of the entire supply tends to fall to the price at which the very last portion can be sold. Conversely, whenever there is a shortage, the price of the entire supply tends to rise to the point at which the last needed portion can be obtained. Labor is a commodity, the owners of which seek to exchange it with others—giving it in the form of sugar or cotton and receiving it back in the form of cloth and iron. As such, labor is subject to the same laws as all other commodities. As long as there is a surplus of labor anywhere, the price of labor everywhere tends to fall to the lowest possible level. As that surplus diminishes anywhere, the price everywhere will tend to rise to meet the highest level.

Raw labor, unaided by machinery, can achieve very little. A man without an axe cannot fell a tree, nor can a man without a spade dig the earth. A man without a sickle <note>original: "reaping-hook"</note> must pull up grain by hand, and he who has no horse or cart must carry his load on his own back. Such is the condition of the people of India, and it is nearly the same for the people of Ireland. Consequently, labor is unproductive and its price is low.

To make labor productive, people require machinery, which consists of three types:
1.  **Machinery of production**, consisting of land that has been cleared, drained, and otherwise prepared for cultivation.
2.  **Machinery of conversion**, such as sawmills (which turn logs into planks), gristmills (which turn wheat into flour), cotton and woolen mills (which turn raw fiber into cloth), and furnaces (which turn fuel and ore into iron).
3.  **Machinery of transportation**, by which...

<meta>This page continues Henry Charles Carey’s argument regarding the "harmony of interests" between labor and capital. Having previously critiqued the British colonial system for devaluing global labor, he now explains the mechanical differences between "production" (agriculture) and "conversion" (manufacturing), arguing that localizing industry benefits the worker and the capitalist alike.</meta>

-># THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.<-

The man who raises food is enabled to place it where he can exchange it with the one who makes cloth or iron.

These two latter categories—manufacturing and transportation—make no addition to the actual quantity of food or wool that is to be consumed. The wheat or cotton that enters the mill comes out as flour or cloth. The barrel of flour that is placed on a ship comes out as a barrel of flour, neither more nor less. It will feed no more people when it arrives than when it first departed.

However, the bushel of wheat that is sown in the earth produces six, eight, or ten bushels, and a bushel of potatoes produces twenty or thirty bushels. These have been placed in the <term>machine of production</term> <note>Carey uses "machine of production" to refer to the natural productivity of the earth and agriculture.</note>, while the others have merely been placed in the machines of <term>conversion</term> <note>original: "conversion"; here meaning manufacturing or processing raw materials into finished goods.</note> or transportation.

The more labor that can be applied to the machine of production, the larger the supply of food and wool will be. Consequently, a larger quantity of both will be considered the equivalent of a single day's labor.

The nearer the place of conversion can be brought to the place of production—that is, the closer the factory is to the farm—the less need there will be for transportation. This makes the demand for labor more steady throughout the year and allows more labor to be dedicated to actual production. As a result, the laborer will be better fed and clothed, and wealth will accumulate more rapidly in the form of machinery to be used for even further increases in production.

Wealth tends to grow more rapidly than population because better soils are brought into cultivation. This growth occurs whenever people abandon swords and muskets for spades and specialized plows. Every increase in the ratio of wealth to population increases the power of the laborer compared to the power of landed or other capital. We can all see that when ships are more plentiful than passengers, the price of passage is low; conversely, when passengers are more plentiful than ships, the price is high. 

When plows and horses are more plentiful than plowmen, the workers set the wages. But when plowmen are more abundant than plows, the owners of the equipment determine how the products of labor are distributed. When wealth increases rapidly, new soils are farmed, and more plowmen are needed. This demand for plows creates a demand for more men to mine coal and smelt iron ore. Thus, the <term>ironmaster</term> <note>A manager or owner of an ironworks.</note> becomes a competitor for the laborer’s services, and the laborer receives a larger share of the constantly increasing returns. 

As the laborer wants more clothes, the manufacturer begins to compete with the ironmaster and the farmer for his services. His share increases again, and as he desires sugar, tea, and coffee, the shipmaster must then compete with the manufacturer, the ironmaster, and the farmer. 

Thus, with the growth of population and wealth, there is a constantly increasing demand for labor. The increased productivity of labor and the resulting ease of accumulating wealth lead necessarily to an increase in the laborer’s share of the product. His wages rise, and the capitalist’s proportional share falls. Yet, the capitalist still accumulates fortune more rapidly than ever because the total volume of production is so much larger. In this way, the interests of the capitalist and the laborer are in perfect harmony with each other. 

If we need evidence of this, it is seen in the constantly increasing total rental income in England, even though that income is derived from a constantly decreasing *percentage* of the land's total product. We see it also in the enormous total of railroad tolls compared to the old <term>turnpikes</term> <note>A high road or toll road; Carey is comparing the efficiency of the modern railroad to older, more expensive wagon transport.</note>. Even though the railroad transports the farmer’s wheat and brings back his sugar for less than one-fourth of the *proportion* charged by the old wagon and horse teams, the total profit is higher. The laborer's output has increased, and the proportion that goes to the capitalist has decreased. The power of the worker over the product of his own labor has grown, while the relative power of the capitalist has diminished.

<summary>Carey explains that wealth grows when manufacturing is local to production, reducing transport costs and increasing the laborer's share of profits. He argues that labor and capital interests are harmonious because as wealth increases, competition for workers raises wages even as total capital grows.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Henry Charles Carey’s argument that proximity between the producer and the consumer is essential for economic prosperity. He compares the economic conditions of India, the American South, and New England to show how high transportation costs and "surplus labor" reduce the wages and purchasing power of workers.</meta>

-># THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.<-

Wherever we look throughout this country, we find that where transportation machinery is most needed, the amount of labor that can be dedicated to production is lowest, and the return to labor—the wages of the laborer in food, clothing, and other necessities and comforts of life—is lowest. Conversely, where transportation is least needed, the amount of labor that can be given to production is greatest, and wages are highest. In other words, the closer the consumer and the producer can be brought together, the larger the return to labor.

For the past forty years, the cultivation of cotton in India has been gradually moving away from the lower plains toward the hills. This has produced a constantly increasing need for transportation and a constant decrease in the amount of labor that could be applied to production. With every such step, labor has become more of a surplus <note>In this context, "surplus labor" refers to workers who are unemployed or underutilized because their labor is no longer profitable or productive within the current system.</note>, and the reward for labor has been steadily diminishing.

For much of this same period, this has been the case with Southern labor in the United States. It has been gradually moving away from the lower lands of South Carolina and Georgia, producing a constant increase in the need for transportation. Meanwhile, the goods to be transported would command a constantly decreasing amount of cloth, iron, and other necessities of life in return. This tendency has been slowed to some degree by large domestic consumption and by the ability to apply labor to the cultivation of sugar. However, if we were to change our revenue system now and establish perfect free trade <note>original: "freedom of trade"</note>, the domestic manufacturing of cotton and the domestic production of sugar would cease. Raw cotton <note>original: "cotton wool"</note> would then fall to three cents per pound, because the planter would be reduced to that as the only thing he could cultivate for sale. Labor would become more and more of a surplus, with a constant decrease in the power of the laborer to obtain either cloth or iron.

This has been—and must continue to be—the case for sugar and coffee planters as well. Their products yield them a constantly diminishing quantity of either cloth or iron, with a constantly increasing difficulty in obtaining clothing or machinery in exchange for their labor.

In New England, wages—*that is*, the power to obtain food, clothing, and iron in exchange for labor—are high. However, they tend to rise with every increase in the productivity of Southern and Western labor. They will continue to do so as Southern and Western men become manufacturers, because those regions will then have more to offer in exchange for labor. With any decrease in the productivity of labor in the South or West, the wages of New England must fall, because there will then be less to offer them in exchange.

In England, the power to obtain food, clothing, or iron in exchange for labor is small, and it tends to diminish as a larger portion of the population becomes dependent upon transportation, and a smaller portion applies itself to production. This is because every such step creates a necessity for greater effort to undersell and replace the Indian worker <note>original: "Hindoo"</note>, whose annual wages even now are only six dollars, out of which he must provide his own food and clothing. With every step downward, labor is increasingly becoming a surplus, as seen in the growing anxiety to export the population <note>This refers to the 19th-century practice of encouraging "surplus" workers to emigrate to colonies to reduce poverty and competition for jobs at home.</note> at almost any immediate sacrifice. We may now inquire why this is so.

The great object of England is commerce.

Commerce among men tends to produce equality of condition, both moral and physical. Whether it tends to raise or lower the standard of living depends upon the character of those with whom it is necessary to maintain it. A person who is compelled to associate with the idle, the dissolute, and the drunken is likely to sink to the level of his companions.

The same is true of labor. The necessity of depending on commerce with men—

<meta>This page continues Henry Charles Carey’s argument that economic well-being is tied to the proximity of producers and consumers. He previously argued that moving labor away from production centers increases transportation costs and lowers wages. Here, he begins to argue that international dependency functions like a forced "communism" that drags down the standard of living for industrious nations.</meta>

-># THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS<-

In a community where the standard of living is low, there is a tendency to sink the laborer to the level of the lowest. Imagine placing half a dozen men on an island: if two are industrious and grow food, while the others—less inclined to work—are left to provide meat, fish, clothing, and shelter, the industrious men will be *compelled* to exchange their products with the idle ones. Since clothing and shelter are as necessary as bread, those who play will profit from the labor of those who work. When the workers realize this is the result, they will stop working with any spirit, and gradually all members of the small community will become equally idle. Here lies the error of <term>communism</term> <note>Carey uses "communism" and "socialism" here to describe any system that forces economic interdependence or the sharing of resources regardless of individual productivity.</note> and <term>socialism</term>. They seek to force a union and compel men to exchange with each other; the inevitable effect of this is to sink the entire group to the level of those at the bottom.

The same is true of nations. An industrious community that grows food but depends on an idle community to manufacture iron must give a large amount of food for a small amount of iron. A peaceful community that grows cotton but depends on a warlike one that produces silk must give much cotton for very little silk. Depending on others for necessities creates a "community of goods," where the sober and industrious must help support the idle and the immoral—this applies to nations as much as to individuals.

As long as this state of dependence exists, the condition of each nation is determined by the condition of the other. If the idle become even more idle, and the immoral even more immoral, those who continue to work must steadily give more of their labor for less in return. Their condition must deteriorate unless they take measures to gradually diminish and finally end their dependence on such companions.

The policy of England has tended to produce <term>communism</term> among nations. She has made herself dependent on other communities for supplies of basic necessities like food and clothing. She obtains her rice from the impoverished <term>Hindu</term> <note>original: "Hindoo"</note>, her corn from the <term>Russian serf</term>, and her wool from the <term>Australian convict</term>, while neglecting her own rich soils that only wait for labor to become productive.

The necessary consequence of this is a downward trend in the condition of the English people. Since the people of our own country are being invited to compete with them, it is worth showing the condition to which they have been reduced by competing with the low-priced labor of Russia and India.

*The Spectator*, a <term>free-trade journal</term>, informs us that "the condition of the laboring classes engaged in agriculture—long a disgrace to our advancement in civilization—has not improved; while wages exhibit a universal tendency to *decline beneath the lowest level of recent times*."

The *Morning Chronicle* has recently published a series of letters from a correspondent specifically sent to investigate the condition of the laboring classes in the agricultural counties. He informs us that in <term>Buckinghamshire</term> and <term>Oxfordshire</term>, average annual wages do not exceed 9 shillings ($2.16) per week. In <term>Berkshire</term> <note>original: "Berks"</note> and <term>Wiltshire</term>, they do not exceed 7 shillings and 6 pence ($1.79). It must also be remembered that "when a poor wretch is prevented from working for a day, or even half a day, his wages are stopped for that time." Sometimes a wife works in the fields and adds three shillings a week to the fund from which these unfortunate people must survive. Yet even this gain has its drawbacks, as will be seen by those who read the following account of the condition of the English <term>agricultural laborer</term> in the middle of the nineteenth century. Although it is long, it will be found interesting:

> "When a married woman goes to work in the fields, she must leave her children at home. In many cases, they are too young to be left by themselves, so they are generally left in the care of a young girl hired for that purpose. The sum paid to this <term>vicarious mother</term> <note>original: "vicarious mother"; meaning a substitute or surrogate caregiver</note>—who is usually just a child herself—is from 8 pence to 1 shilling per week. In addition to this wage, she is fed and housed. This is nearly equivalent to adding two more members to the family. Therefore, if a mother works in the fields for weekly wages equal to the cost of maintaining three children for the week, it often comes at the cost of having two additional mouths to feed.
>
> But these are far from being all the disadvantages of a mother performing outdoor labor. One of the worst features of this system is the cheerlessness it brings to the poor man's house. On returning from work, instead of finding his house in order and a meal comfortably prepared for him, his wife accompanies him home—or perhaps arrives after him. Then, everything that should have been done before his arrival must be done in his presence. The result is that home is made distasteful to him, and he hurries to the nearest ale-house. There, he soon spends the remainder of his wife's earnings for the week, as well as those of his children, if any of them have been working.
>
> A great deal is also lost through the wife’s lack of domestic skills. Her expertise at outdoor labor has been acquired at the expense of proper knowledge of her indoor duties. She is a mediocre cook and a bad housewife in every respect. In many instances, she is also lamentably deficient in the knowledge of ordinary needlework. She might acquire all these necessary skills if she stayed home more and spent less time in the fields. In addition to this, her children would have the benefit of being raised under her own eye, instead of being utterly neglected and left to themselves. The person left in charge of them—and someone is not always available—is generally a child herself, with no control over them. It is under these circumstances that the seeds of future <term>vice</term> <note>In this context, "vice" refers to immoral habits, idleness, or criminal behavior resulting from a lack of parental supervision.</note> are plentifully sown.
> 
> On the whole, regarding the system of married women working in the fields, I cannot help but see the balance as being disadvantageous when the children are young. In that case, I think it would be decidedly better for the poor man—considering only his physical comforts—if his wife stayed at home. This is the position of many a laboring man. In many cases where the family is large, some of the children are at work, adding their scanty wages of 1 shilling 6 pence to 2 shillings a week to the common fund. But I have known numerous cases of families with seven children where the eldest was not yet eight years old. Furthermore, when these children are old enough to work and earn their own wages, they soon become independent of the father and move out to support themselves. This provides some relief to him, unless his family is increasing at one end while diminishing at the other. There is no doubt that a family is frequently aided by the children's earnings, but in the vast majority of cases, the means of support are provided by the parents themselves. From what has already been said about the disadvantages the family faces when the wife works, it is evident that the husband's earnings are, after all, the true test and standard of his own condition and that of his dependents.

Moreover, in a very large proportion of cases, the wife remains at home, attending to duties more appropriate to her sex and position. In these cases, there is no other financial aid to be had, unless it is the small and inconsistent earnings of one or two of the children. We have seen that in the counties mentioned, there are about 40,000 married couples who, along with their children (totaling about 120,000), depend exclusively on agricultural labor for support. Of those 40,000 mothers, at least half stay at home. Some are compelled to do so because their children are so young; others—unless their families are older—prefer to do so as a matter of calculation, believing it is the best way to make the most of their limited resources. This can be considered the situation for half of the married couples, who, with their families, number about 100,000 individuals. 

As far as these people are concerned, the children are too young to add anything to the family's finances. Therefore, there is no other way to judge their condition or their standard of comfort than by the earnings of the husband. Let us, therefore, inquire into the condition of a family solely dependent on the average wages the husband has received during the past part of this year. I can best illustrate that condition with one of the many cases I studied in Wiltshire. The laborer in that case had previously earned 8 shillings a week, but he was then only receiving 7 shillings. He had seven children, the eldest of whom—a girl—was in her eighth year. Two of his children had attended a <term>dunce's school</term> <note>original: "dunce's school"; likely a "dame school," a very basic, low-cost private school for young children, often run by a local woman in her own home.</note>, but they were no longer attending. This was simply because he could not afford the 4 pence a week required for their education. To ascertain how far he was really...

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the economic conditions of the working class. Having established that women's labor often leads to domestic disorder and financial loss, the author now provides a specific case study of a laborer’s weekly budget to illustrate how 8 shillings are barely enough to sustain a family of nine.</meta>

-># THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS<-

Being unable to explain his circumstances in detail, I requested him to describe his household's weekly budget, assuming his earnings were 8 shillings <note>original: "8s."; 8 shillings was a common but very low weekly wage for an agricultural laborer in the mid-19th century.</note>. The following is the substance of the conversation, omitting the names of the individuals involved for the reader’s sake.

**When are your wages paid?** — On Saturday night, but often only once every two weeks <note>original: "fortnight"</note>.

**What do you do with the money upon receiving it?** — I first set aside my rent, which is 1 shilling a week. I then go to the grocer’s and buy supplies for Sunday and the rest of the week. I buy a little tea, getting two ounces for 6 pence. Sugar is cheap, but I cannot afford it. We sometimes sweeten the tea with a little molasses <note>original: "treacle"</note>, but generally drink it unsweetened.

**Do you purchase any meat from the butcher?** — Generally for Sunday, we buy a bit of bacon.

**How much?** — I can seldom afford more than half a pound.

**Half a pound among nine of you?** — Yes; it is a mere taste, but we do not even have that for the rest of the week. It costs me about 5 pence.

**Do you buy your bread, or make it at home?** — We buy it. We do not have enough fuel <note>original: "fire"</note> to bake at home, though it would be a great saving to us.

**Do you buy a large amount at once, or a loaf whenever you need it?** — We buy it as we need it.

**Have you a garden attached to your cottage?** — I have about fifteen <term>poles</term> <note>A pole is a unit of area equal to 30.25 square yards; 15 poles is slightly less than an eighth of an acre.</note>, for which I pay 1.5 pence per pole.

**What do you grow there?** — We grow some potatoes and cabbages.

**Do you grow a sufficient quantity of potatoes to last the year?** — No, not even if they were all healthy.

**In addition to the potatoes and cabbages you grow, how much bread do you require to support yourself, your wife, and seven children for a week?** — We require at least seven <term>gallons of bread</term> <note>A "gallon" loaf was a standard size weighing roughly 8 pounds and 11 ounces.</note>.

**What is a gallon of bread?** — It is a loaf which used to weigh 8 lbs. 11 oz., but now it seldom weighs more than 8 lbs. Those who supply bread to the <term>union</term> <note>The "Union" refers to the Poor Law Union, the local administration responsible for poor relief and workhouses.</note> seldom make it over 8 lbs.

**What is the price of the gallon loaf?** — Ten pence. It is cheaper than it was, but then there is not always as much of it. It is often short on weight.

**Seven gallons of bread at 10 pence a gallon would be 5 shillings and 10 pence, would it not?** — I believe it would be about that—you ought to know.

**Do you always get seven gallons a week?** — No, seldom more than six.

**Then you spend 5 shillings on bread, and make up for the shortage with potatoes and cabbages?** — Yes.

**You still have some money left; what do you do with it?** — Washing costs us something. For soap and soda, and for needles and thread for mending, we pay about 5 pence a week.

**Do you buy fuel?** — We sometimes get a <term>hundredweight</term> <note>A hundredweight (cwt.) is 112 pounds.</note> of coal, which would cost us about 1 shilling or 1 shilling 1.5 pence if we bought a large quantity with cash. When we can do neither, it costs us about 1 shilling 4 pence per hundredweight. If there is one poor man who can afford to buy it in bulk with cash, there are forty who cannot.

**How long would a hundredweight of coal last you?** — We make it last, one way or another, for two weeks.

**Your fuel, therefore, will cost you about 8 pence a week?** — It will.

**Is there anything else you have?** — We buy a little salted butter sometimes, which costs between 6.5 and 10 pence a pound. We are forced, of course, to take the cheapest; "and really, sir, it is sometimes hardly fit to grease a wagon with."

**But your money is already all gone: how do you pay for your butter?** — We do not always have it, and we can only get it by depriving <note>original: "stinting"</note> ourselves of other things.

**You have said nothing about your clothing: how do you get that?** — Were it not for the high wages we earn during the harvest season, we could not get it at all.

**How long does the period of high wages last?** — About ten weeks, and if not for what we earn then, I do not know how we could survive at all.

From this summary, it must certainly seem a mystery to the reader how they manage as they do. The weekly expenditure, in our view, is as follows for a family of nine with weekly receipts of 8 shillings:

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the household budget of a poor laborer’s family of nine. -># THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.<-

Clothing is provided for through the extra wages earned during the harvest. Meanwhile, the family cannot afford even the "luxury" of poor-quality butter without giving up their tea—two ounces of which must last an entire week—or their half-pound of bacon, which provides only a "mere taste" for each person on Sunday. To afford butter, they would also have to sacrifice some of their bread (which is already in short supply) or a portion of their fuel, the lack of which makes their home even more gloomy and miserable. Sugar, too, is out of the question without cutting into items that are even more absolutely necessary. Nor is there any money set aside for medicine, which is frequently needed by a family of nine living in such wretched conditions. 

What, in short, do we have here? We have nine people living for seven days on 60 pounds of bread—barely a pound a day for each person—half a pound of bacon, and two ounces of tea. The rest of their diet is made up of a supply of potatoes and cabbages grown in their garden, which in nine cases out of ten is far too small. Could they fall any lower into misery? This is especially true when we consider their limited supply of less nutritious food alongside the miserable shacks <note>original: "hovels"</note> in which they eat—either shivering in the winter frosts or breathing in the deadly smells <note>original: "pestilential odours"</note> created by the summer heat.

I could no longer be surprised that they felt 4 pence <note>original: "4d."</note> a week was too much to spend on the education of two children.

Since this was how his weekly wages were spent, I asked the same man to give me an account of his daily life, including his work and what he ate. In reply to my questions on this point, he answered essentially as follows:

> **At what hour do you go to work?** — Usually at six in the morning in the summer, but I have gone much earlier. In the winter, work begins at a later hour.
> 
> **Do you eat breakfast at home?** — When I do not go out very early, I generally do.
> 
> **What does your breakfast consist of?** — Mostly bread, and sometimes a little tea. Sometimes we also have a few boiled potatoes.
> 
> **When do you dine?** — About twelve o’clock.
> 
> **What does your dinner consist of?** — On Mondays, my wife gets a little flour and makes a pudding which, along with a few potatoes, serves as my dinner. Sometimes we have a pudding on other days, but usually our dinner is bread and potatoes, with a little cabbage now and then. When a family is not large, there might be a bit of bacon left over from Sunday, but that is never the case for us.
> 
> **Do you return to work again?** — I do, and when I come home at night, I might have a little tea again with the bread that makes up my supper. The tea is never strong for us, but at night it is very weak.
> 
> **Do your children get tea?** — We do not have enough for that.
> 
> **What do they drink?** — Water; sometimes we get them a little milk.
> 
> **What is your own drink?** — Water.
> 
> **Do you never drink beer?** — Never, unless it is given to me; I cannot afford to buy it.
> 
> **When your dinner consists of bread, potatoes, and water, do you have nothing to season it or make it taste better?** — Nothing but a little salt butter, and we can only afford that when the bread or potatoes happen to be of poor quality, or when we are feeling unwell <note>original: "ailing"</note> and our stomachs are a bit sensitive <note>original: "dainty"</note>.
> 
> **When your bread or potatoes are bad, or your stomachs are sensitive, you use the butter you said was "scarcely fit to grease a wagon with" as a treat?** — We have nothing better to eat.
> 
> **Suppose you had nothing but bread to eat; how much would you need to keep you going at work during the day?** — At least two pounds.
> 
> **And how much would one of your children need?** — About the same. A child, even if not working, will eat as much as a man; children are always growing and always ready to eat, and one does not like to refuse food to them when they are hungry. I would rather go without food myself than restrict <note>original: "stint"</note> my children, if I could help it.
> 
> **Then, at the rate of two pounds a day for each person, you would need about 126 pounds of bread for the week?** — I suppose about that much.
> 
> **And, as you only get about sixty pounds of bread a week, you have to rely on your potatoes, cabbages, half-pound of bacon, and two ounces of tea to make up for the sixty-six pounds of bread you cannot get?** — We have nothing else to rely on.
> 
> **Are those items enough to provide as much nourishment as there would be in sixty-six pounds of bread?** — Not nearly enough.
> 
> **Is what you have described your way of living every week?** — It is when I have work.
> 
> **And when you do not have work, how is it for you?** — In the winter months, we sometimes have scarcely a bite to put in our mouths.

-># THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.<-

Such is the substance of the statement regarding his own and his family's circumstances, made to me by a laboring man who has received the average rate of wages for the last nine months in Wiltshire. Commentary is scarcely needed, as the facts speak all too plainly for themselves. Had the family been smaller, or the wages a little higher, instead of a "taste," they might have had a meal of bacon once a week. But even then, it would be only once a week; potatoes and bread would still make up the staple of their diet, and even these are not provided in sufficient quantity. 

Furthermore, even if they had it more frequently, bacon is not the most nourishing food among various types of butcher meat <note>original: "butcher meat"; fresh meat such as beef, mutton, or pork, as opposed to preserved or salted meats.</note>; it is mostly fat. The little lean meat within it is almost destroyed by the curing process. However, it is greasy and quickly satisfies. "It fills us sooner than any other kind of meat," was the reply given to me when I asked why they preferred it to beef. But the problem is that it does not actually fill them; it satiates <note>original: "satiates"; to satisfy an appetite to the point of boredom or dislike, without providing true nourishment.</note> them without providing substance. Food requires bulk as well as nutrients. The stomach has a mechanical as well as a chemical action to perform. A man could not live on cheese alone, nor could he exist on pills containing the concentrated essence of beef. They buy bacon because it lasts longer than other meat—in truth, they buy it because it soon makes them feel too full to eat more. Nor is it always the case that they have even a "taste" of it once a week. I have seen several families who had not tasted any kind of butcher meat for weeks at a time. 

When French and English workmen labored together during the construction of some of the French railways, it was found that the Englishman could perform far more work than his French competitor. This was universally attributed to the superiority of his diet; everyone supposed it was reasonable to expect more work from a man who fed on beef and porter <note>original: "porter"; a dark, heavy style of beer popular among the working classes for its perceived strengthening qualities.</note> than from one whose fare was bread and grapes. But the diet of the man who is expected to develop the agricultural wealth of England through his labor, year after year, is, in many cases, little better than bread and water—the diet of a condemned cell! 

Contrast the condition of the English farm laborer with that of the farm laborer in Canada. In England, he eats butcher meat once a week, and not always even then; in Canada, he has as much of it as he wants at least once, and frequently twice, a day. Contrast his condition even with that of the enslaved people in the Southern States of America. In Virginia, the great slave state, a day seldom passes without an enslaved person eating some kind of butcher meat. In addition to this, when he is old and infirm, he has a claim on his master for support. But the English laborer, if he has a family to sustain, does not have the same nutritious diet as a slave, even during the days of his strength when he can and does work. Meanwhile, when he is disabled or loses his work, he must starve, or, as the alternative, become a vagrant <note>original: "vagrant"; a person without a settled home or work who wanders from place to place and survives by begging.</note> or the recipient of a formal and organized charity. In the words of one of the laborers themselves: "It is not a living, sir—it is a mere *being* we get." By this, he intended to convey that the only reward for their toil was being barely enabled to exist.

It may be said that the case presented is an extreme one. It is, however, the case for nearly one-half of those who are dependent upon labor in the fields. But it may be said that I have omitted to take into account some small privileges which the laborer has, and which, when he uses them, tend to improve his comforts. He may keep a pig, for instance, and his employer will sometimes provide him with straw for it, which, in time, will serve as manure for his little garden. This looks very well on paper, but that is mostly all. In the four counties being discussed, the number of laborers keeping pigs is about one in twelve. It is also a striking illustration of the condition of the laborers that even those who do raise a pig seldom get to eat any of it. Then we hear a great deal about the coal and clothing clubs (which I shall refer to more specifically later), the chief merit of which is that they tend to make life not pleasant, but barely tolerable for the poor.

### **The sleeping accommodations are thus described:**

> "These are upstairs, and are reached by means of a few greasy and rickety steps which lead through a type of hatchway in the ceiling. Yes, there is but one room, and yet we counted nine in the family! And what a room! The small window in the roof admits just enough light to enable you to see its character and size. The rafters, which are all exposed, start from the very floor, so that it is only in the very center of the apartment that you have any chance of standing upright. The thatch <note>original: "thatch"; a roof covering made of straw, reeds, or similar materials.</note> leaks through the woodwork that supports it, the whole place being covered with smoke and dust, and full of vermin <note>original: "vermin"; pests such as lice, bedbugs, or fleas.</note>. There are no cobwebs, for the spider only spreads his net where flies are likely to be caught. You look in vain for a bed frame; there is none in the room. But there are their beds, lying side by side on the floor, almost touching..."

The beds are placed next to each other, occupying nearly the entire length of the room <note>original: "apartment"; in this context, it refers to a single shared room in a cottage.</note>. These beds are large sacks filled with oat chaff, which the laborer sometimes receives for free and at other times purchases from his employer. The chaff from wheat and barley is used on the farm for other purposes. The bed next to the floor opening <note>original: "hatchway"; the opening in the floor through which the residents climbed into the sleeping loft.</note> belongs to the father and mother, who sleep with their infant, born only a few months ago in this very room. In the other beds sleep the children, boys and girls together. The eldest girl is in her twelfth year, and the eldest boy is nearly eleven; they are likely to remain for years in these same circumstances. Except for the youngest children, the family goes to rest at about the same hour, generally undressing downstairs and then ascending to crawl over one another to reach their respective sleeping places for the night. There are two blankets on the parents' bed, while the others are covered with a very diverse collection of materials. It often happens that the clothes worn by the parents during the day form the main part of the children's covering at night. This is the dormitory where the nine family members we just saw eating their wretched meal will pass the night, lying side by side. The only ventilation comes through a small opening that is called a "window" only out of politeness. In other words, there is almost no ventilation at all. What a miserable den in a time of sickness or death! What a den, indeed, at any time! And yet, when the dark goddess of night <note>original: "sable goddess"; a poetic personification of Night or Sleep. The "leaden sceptre" refers to the heavy, deep sleep she brings.</note> extends her heavy scepter over the soft, downy couches of Mayfair <note>Mayfair is an affluent district in London, home to the aristocracy and wealthy elite.</note>, these are the conditions in which she leaves a portion of her sleeping subjects in our rural parishes.

Let it not be said that this picture is exaggerated, or that it is a collection of rare hardships brought together for effect. As a representation of the extreme housing misery in rural districts, it is actually understated. The cottage in question has two rooms. Some have only one, with just as many inmates living in it. Others have three or four rooms, but with a different family occupying each room; in some cases, these families consist of nine or ten individuals. In some cottages, a lodger is also taken in, sharing the same room as the family. Fortunately, this is not the condition of all laborers in the agricultural districts; however, it is the condition of a very great number of Englishmen—not in the wilderness of a remote colony, but in the heart of Anglo-Saxon civilization in the year 1849.

> "Bad as all this is, it is likely to get worse. Everywhere, notices are being given of wage reductions and a decrease in the number of people employed. There is scarcely a district in any of these counties," says the writer, "where the work of reducing wages has not already begun." In one county, as early as last June, there was a reduction from 8 shillings to 7 shillings, and "fears are everywhere felt that they will be reduced to 6 shillings (equal to $1.44)." "Is it any wonder," he adds, "that with such a prospect before them, the agricultural laborers should brood over their circumstances with the ominous gloom of despair? What is that prospect? Winter is approaching—the season when we all require the most comfort. They are entering that season with only 8 shillings, 7 shillings, or even 5 shillings a week to support their families. How far will these pitiful amounts go in households of five, six, seven, eight, nine, or ten people? In estimating a laborer's comfort at any given time, we cannot look at his average wages. It is his current wages that determine his condition. If he ever had more than was necessary to provide basic comfort, he might save the surplus for hard times. But he never has enough for perfect comfort and is always tempted to spend everything he earns. He therefore begins this winter, as he does every winter, without any savings to fall back on. The fact is terrifying that, in this month of October, thousands of families in the very heart of England have no better prospect than living on 8, 6, or even 5 shillings a week in their cold, damp, cheerless, and unhealthy homes."

-># THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.<-

...a morsel of bacon on a Sunday is a luxury. Yet, by the simple process of expansion <note>original: "annexation"; here referring to the movement of people and markets into the American sphere</note> and economic protection, the planter could bring these same men to his side and convert them into large and valuable customers. The planter is currently invited to compete in the English market for the privilege of clothing men who lack the means to even buy bread. However, by an exercise of his will, he could instead bring millions of these same men to his own side every year. Each of those men would then require twenty pounds of goods a year; thus, two million of them would consume half as much as was consumed in 1847 by nearly thirty million people in England and Wales.

The English system demands that we establish a "community of goods" <note>original: "community of goods"; a shared global economic pool where resources and labor prices are leveled out</note> with people such as these. If this were allowed free play—if the people of the world were to establish what is called "free trade," and thus unite their efforts to maintain the *monopoly system*—wages everywhere would fall to the level of the poorest countries in the world. With every step, English wages would necessarily fall because they must be kept at a point that enables her people to underwork the rest of the world. Consequently, the trend everywhere would be downward, as it has been in Ireland and India. The adoption of perfect free trade by this country [the United States] would produce some temporary activity there, but a very short period would prove that we bought far less under free trade than we had done under protection. In the meantime, the imbalance of the English population would have largely increased, making the difficulty far greater than it is now, great as it already is. We now *pay for far less merchandise* than we did three years ago; if it were not for the fact that we are still able to buy on credit, we would make smaller demands on England than we have at any period since 1842. 

The greater the amount of capital lent to us, the lower the condition of the English laborer must fall. Every step England takes now is a step downward. If we do not want our laborers reduced to a level with theirs, we must use protection to try to raise their laborers to a level with ours. This will happen by relieving us of the necessity for *dependence* on trade with a people whose labor is valued lower than our own. Protection tends to raise the value of man both abroad and at home, enabling everyone to obtain more food, fuel, and clothing with *less* labor. Under protection, immigration has always increased, and it has declined whenever protection diminished. It is obvious that this must tend to raise wages abroad, because hundreds of thousands of people in Europe, who were considered "surplus," have sought our shores, thereby diminishing the number of workers competing for jobs there.

As we approach what is called "freedom of trade"—the system that maintains England’s monopoly on machinery—the value of labor here is falling toward the level of labor in England. The current diminished production of coal and iron is only maintained through a great reduction in wages. Labor is becoming surplus, and immigration is already falling off. This year will show a large decrease in immigration, and every step in that direction must be accompanied by a rise in freight costs, which diminishes our power to export either food or cotton. With the decrease of wages in the North, there is already a diminished *power* to consume either food or clothing, leading to an increase in the surplus that must be sent away. 

Thus, the same measures that increase the need to depend on the machinery of transportation actually diminish the *power* to obtain it. This leads to the worsening condition of the entire population: laborers and capitalists, farmers and planters, manufacturers and ship-owners alike. Conversely, the measures that diminish our need to depend on transportation tend to increase our power to obtain it, to lessen the burden currently pressing upon the landowners and laborers of Europe, and to bring about a state of things that shall give both us and them perfect freedom of trade. The harmony of all interests, whether individual or national, becomes more and more obvious the more this subject is examined.
