<meta>This page continues Carey's argument that free trade forces American workers to compete with impoverished foreign laborers, whereas protectionism encourages a domestic market that benefits everyone. He transitions here into a discussion of labor unrest and the economic impact of protectionism on slavery.</meta>

-># THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.<-

It may be helpful to review the last few years, with special focus on the conflicts that have occasionally broken out between employers and employees—including strikes, labor unions <note>original: "combinations"</note>, and so on—in order to show their cause.

It is within the memory of most of my readers that the years from 1836 to 1839 were marked by disturbances of this kind. The cause is obvious: production was decreasing, and the laborer found himself unable to obtain the quantity of food, fuel, and clothing to which he had been accustomed. He desired a rise in cash wages to meet the rising price of food, but the employer could not afford to give it. This led to the formation of unions for the purpose of compelling him to do so.

From 1844 to 1848, harmony was restored because production increased. The laborer found that each year his work enabled him to obtain more food, better clothing, and improved shelter.

The last year, however, has been marked by a series of labor alliances. In the coal regions of Pennsylvania, in Pittsburgh, Lowell, and various other places, there have been strikes and "turn-outs" <note>an archaic term for strikes where workers "turned out" of the factories</note>, some of them lasting a long time. Everywhere there have been demands for laws restricting the hours of labor; yet those who made these demands desired that their wages should remain the same. These things all result from one great fact: the productivity of labor is diminishing, and wages are trending downward toward the low levels seen in Europe.

That decline was also the cause of the jealousy toward foreigners which gave rise to the "Native" party <note>original: "native party"; referring to the Nativist or "Know-Nothing" political movement which was anti-immigrant</note>. In 1842, employment was almost impossible to find, and American-born workmen were unwilling to share the little work available with strangers. As the productivity of labor increased, wages rose, and the Nativist party almost died out, while the number of immigrants quadrupled. If the economic system of 1846 <note>the Walker Tariff, which reduced protectionist duties</note> is continued, the same jealousy will reappear; foreigners will be shunned, and immigration will decrease.

It is in the interest of American workmen that European wages should be raised to a level with our own. The only way to accomplish this is to follow a course that makes it profitable for every person in Europe who can afford passage to try to reach our shores. Everyone who comes will produce something, and will therefore become a customer for the products of others. Wherever we look, there is a perfect harmony of interests.

### CHAPTER SIXTEENTH.

#### HOW PROTECTION AFFECTS THE SLAVE AND HIS MASTER.

Protection tends to increase the productivity of labor. Many of the laborers in the Union are held as slaves, and protection must tend to make their labor more valuable to their owners, who might, therefore, be less willing to part with them. If this were the case, protection would tend to make slavery permanent, and everyone who opposes slavery should therefore advocate free trade.

According to all English writers, and many in our own country, the way to end slavery is to destroy the economic value of slave labor. With that goal in mind, the British government is urged to ban sugar grown by slaves and to encourage the expansion of cotton farming in India. The impoverished Hindu laborer—who works an entire month for two rupees (about one dollar) <note>original: "two rupees, (one dollar)"</note>, out of which he must feed and clothe himself—is held up as being a freer man than the well-fed, well-clothed, and well-housed laborer of Virginia or Kentucky.

Throughout history, men have become free as wealth and population have grown...

<meta>This page continues Carey's argument that land value is inextricably linked to human freedom, contrasting historical and modern examples from around the world to show how market proximity affects society.</meta>

-># THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.<-

...[as cities] have grown, and as land has increased in value. In the early days of Rome, when the region of Latium was filled with prosperous cities, land was valuable and men were free. With the gradual depopulation of Italy, land lost its value, and vast estates accumulated in the hands of great owners <note>original: "proprietors"</note> surrounded by slaves. It was the same in Attica <note>the region surrounding Athens, Greece</note>. In the days of Solon, land was valuable and men were free. In the time of Herodes Atticus, land was valueless and men were slaves. The richest lands of India have been abandoned and are now jungle, and the descendants of the small village landowners of the last century now sell themselves into slavery in Jamaica and Demerara <note>a region in modern-day Guyana; this refers to the "coolie" system of indentured labor that replaced African slavery</note>. In Russia, land has no value. The value of a property is estimated by the number of its serfs. In Belgium, land has great value, and the people are the freest in Europe.

With the gradual increase in the value of land in England, men became more free. Conversely, with every step that increases dependence on Poland and Russia for food, land is becoming less valuable, laborers are increasingly becoming inhabitants of parish workhouses and the slaves of parish beadles <note>church officials who managed the poor and enforced discipline</note>, and landowners are becoming more and more anxious to expel the population that would otherwise give value to the land. The land of Ireland has almost lost its value, and the Irish laborer has become a slave to the whims of masters who regard him as a burden <note>original: "encumbrance"</note> to be gotten rid of by any process, however cruel.

An increase in the value of land tends toward freedom; a decrease tends toward slavery. If protection <note>economic policies like tariffs that protect domestic industry</note> tends to add value to land, it tends to promote freedom; if it tends to diminish land value, it tends to maintain slavery.

The least valuable land is that where people are most scarce; the most valuable is that where they are most abundant. The cause of the difference between the two is found in the difference in the labor required to carry out exchanges. The hills of Limburg, the poorest part of Belgium, rent for six to eight dollars; and for flax land in Flanders, ten to twelve dollars per acre is a common rent. Meanwhile, cotton-producing land of the highest quality in the United States may be purchased outright <note>original: "in fee," a legal term for permanent and absolute ownership</note> for *one-eighth* of that annual rent. The Belgian land has a market nearby, and the American land does not; in this single and simple fact, one may find nearly the entire reason for this enormous disparity.

A man who lives in Arkansas must employ numerous men, horses, steamboats, ships, and warehouses to perform every exchange. As a consequence, he receives for the produce of his land little more than compensation for his manual labor, and his land has scarcely any value. He can raise little else for the market besides cotton, of which the earth yields relatively little, but which commands a price high enough to pay for transportation. His surplus corn is almost valueless; meanwhile, attempting to raise potatoes or turnips for the market—of which the earth yields hundreds of bushels per acre—would be ruinous because they are too heavy to ship profitably.

A man who lives near New York exchanges directly with the consumer of his products and the producers of the goods he wants to buy. He can raise potatoes, turnips, and cabbages—bulky articles—or strawberries and raspberries—delicate ones—none of which can survive long-distance transportation. He sells his milk directly and is not forced to convert it into butter or cheese to keep it from spoiling. He is not required to convert his corn into pork just to reduce its bulk so it can reach the market. His products are all consumed near him, and he can easily return the waste <note>original: "refuse," referring to manure and compost used to maintain soil fertility</note> to the land, increasing its productive power year after year. The amount yielded is far more than just wages for his labor; the entire surplus is the rent he derives from his land, and the market value of that land is fifteen or twenty times that annual rent.

<meta>This page continues Henry Charles Carey’s argument that land value is created by the proximity of markets and manufacturing. He contrasts the high value of land near industrial centers like New York with the low value of land in frontier or purely agricultural regions like Arkansas.</meta>

-># THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.<-

The value of that land is three, four, five, or six hundred dollars per acre, while land in Arkansas is now offered as a free gift <note>original: "in free gift"</note> to those who will come and pay the taxes. The only reason for this difference is that the owner of the New York land exchanges his products directly with the men who make hats and coats, shoes and stockings, plows and harrows, while the Arkansas landowner does not. To make the land in Arkansas as valuable as that near New York, it would be necessary for its owner to exchange his goods for hats, shoes, plows, and harrows as easily as the New Yorker does. In other words, he must create a market on the land itself for the products of that land. The return on labor would then be large, and the value of the individual would rise. Furthermore, all the profit returned above the worker's wages would be considered rent, and the value of the land would increase. Men would then become free for two reasons: first, because the cost of raising a slave would be far more than he was worth once grown; and second, because the land would be too valuable to be cultivated by slaves.

A man in Wisconsin can afford to raise hogs because corn costs only twenty cents a bushel. A man near New York cannot, because there corn is worth sixty cents. Similarly, a man in Arkansas can afford to "raise" slaves because they are worth as much as they cost to raise. A man near New York could not, because they would cost him more in upkeep than their services could ever repay. If Arkansas had a local market on its own land for all its products, hired labor would be found so much cheaper that no one would want to raise a slave.

An owner of expensive machinery cannot afford to employ poor-quality labor. The interest on his factory remains the same whether the looms produce only twenty-five yards per day or fifty. With the lower quantity, he would be ruined; with the higher, he would grow rich. A slave will provide the former, while a freeman provides the latter. To make the slave work as efficiently as the freeman, he must have an incentive <note>original: "inducement"</note>—that is, he must receive wages.

If a large landowner near New York were offered the services of men, their wives, and their families on the same terms a Southern planter has his slaves—simply to feed, clothe, and house them—he could not profitably accept the offer. This is true even though the cash price <note>original: "money-price"</note> of such labor is at least *twice* as high in the North as it is in the South. However, the price of their food would be *three times* <note>original: "thrice"</note> as high, they would require more clothing, and their children would need to be educated. To afford all of this, the landowner would need the intense effort of a man working for his own benefit and the careful saving of someone looking toward a future for himself and his family. If such an offer were accepted, the landowner would quickly find that his people produced less and wasted more than his neighbors' workers, and that the rent value of his land would actually decrease because of the arrangement.

If the Southern States were to install machinery to convert half a million bales of cotton into cloth and to produce half a million tons of iron bars <note>original: "bar-iron"</note>, it would create a massive demand for labor. The ease of obtaining iron in exchange for corn and cotton would lead to the construction of thousands of miles of railroad, creating even more demand for labor. The mills, furnaces, and roads would attract towns filled with tailors, shoemakers, hatters, blacksmiths, and manufacturers of plows, harrows, looms, spindles, and steam engines. This would create a new and large demand for labor, even while the number of available workers remained the same. It would then become necessary to use labor more efficiently because its value had increased. How could this be done? A slave will not do more than his usual amount of work without an incentive, and that incentive is found in wages. From that point on, the increased product of his labor would belong to the worker himself.

Large crops would then be produced instead of small ones, and one hundred bushels of corn or one hundred pounds of cotton would buy more cloth or iron than three hundred currently do. This increased value of crops would raise the price of land, and if that price should average even ten...

He suggests that industrializing the South would naturally transition slaves into wage-earners by making their labor more valuable and their upkeep more expensive.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Henry Charles Carey’s argument that creating local markets through industrialization would naturally lead to the end of slavery. He previously argued that if the South had local manufacturing, the cost of raising a slave would eventually exceed the slave's economic value, while the value of the land itself would skyrocket, making freedom more profitable for everyone involved.</meta>

-># THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.<-

If land values increased by even a few dollars per acre across the South, it would amount to four billion <note>original: "four thousand millions"</note> dollars, and in this way, the plantation owners would be made wealthy.

Here, then, are two commodities: man and land. Both increase in value, but the increase in the value of a man goes to the man himself <note>Carey refers here to the value of a free man's labor</note>, while the increase in the value of land goes to the owner. What would be the effect of this on their market value? Where property is steadily growing in value, it sells for twenty, thirty, or even more "years' purchase" of its rent. <note>“Years’ purchase” is an old method of valuing property; it means the sale price is equal to the annual rent multiplied by that many years.</note> Such would be the case with land.

When property is decreasing in value, it sells for only six, eight, or ten years' purchase of the rent that can be charged for its use. Such would be the case with the slave. As the productivity of his labor increased, he would be obtaining an increased portion of the profits for himself, leaving a smaller portion for his owner. Thus, the economic value of the slave would be transferred to the land.

Raising a slave would then become too costly. What then would become of the children? Everywhere, *parents* make sacrifices for their offspring, and children can only be raised by them in places where land is valuable. To encourage those sacrifices, parents must know that they are working for *their own* children, and not for *their master’s* slaves.

As land increases in value, it is inevitably divided. Large plantations would become small ones, each of which would produce more than the entire original plantation does now. Small farms would emerge, cultivated by Black tenants, and thus step by step, men, their wives, and children would become free—at the same time that their former owners were becoming rich.

To accomplish both these objects, it is necessary that the people of the South have mills and furnaces to create a market on the land for the products of the land. They cannot have these without protection <note>Carey is arguing for "protectionism," or taxes on imported goods, to encourage local industry.</note> against the monopoly system by which they are currently being exhausted. The abolitionist and the slaveholder should therefore unite in demanding the adoption of measures that would end the English monopoly on machinery.

The abolitionist might say, however, that this process would be too slow. On the contrary, it would be extremely rapid. Had the Tariff of 1828 remained in effect until now, the lands of the South would today be triple their current value, and the slaves of the South would be far advanced toward freedom.

The slaveholder might say that they would lose their property. The answer is that for every dollar of decreased value in a human being, they would gain five, ten, or twenty dollars in the increased value of their land. It is exactly as land becomes valuable that man becomes free.

The Union is now agitated by the question of whether or not slavery should be allowed to expand beyond its current borders. The agitators are determined to force the Wilmot Proviso <note>A proposed American law that would have banned slavery in any territory acquired from Mexico during the Mexican-American War.</note> upon the South, and the people of the South declare they will dissolve the Union rather than submit to it. Neither side is willing to look beneath the surface to understand the root cause of the problem.

If a demand for labor existed in the slave states because a market for products had been created on the land, the need to move elsewhere would disappear, and immigration would begin. The people of the South would not want to go to California, nor would the people of the North feel it necessary to pass laws to prevent them from doing so. All the discord between the different parts of the Union results from the existence of the colonial system <note>The "colonial system" refers to an economy that only exports raw materials and imports finished goods, which Carey believes keeps the South poor and dependent on Britain.</note>. The goal of protection is to end this system, thereby raising the value of both land and man—Black or white—throughout the world.

This question has so far been viewed merely as a matter of dollars and cents, and that is exactly the light in which it should be examined. When it can be shown to be in the *interest* of a group of men to follow a certain course, we can safely assume that a large portion of them will follow it; but

<summary>Carey argues that economic protectionism would end slavery by making land more valuable than slave labor, eventually enriching plantation owners while naturally transitioning slaves into free tenants. He claims the political strife over slavery's expansion, like the Wilmot Proviso, is a symptom of a flawed "colonial" trade system that exports raw materials instead of developing local industry.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Henry Charles Carey’s argument that economic prosperity is the key to ending slavery. He previously explained that when land values rise, the cost of maintaining an enslaved person eventually exceeds their economic output, making free labor and land ownership more profitable for the planter.</meta>

-># THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.<-

When we confine ourselves to showing that it is their *duty* to end slavery, and that in performing that duty they must ignore their own financial interests, we can safely assume that very few will follow that path. The agitators in the North are damaging property values and destroying the peace of the South, all while making life worse for the very people they claim to sympathize with. They do all of this just so *others* might be forced to perform what the North considers a "duty." It is time for reasonable men in both the North and the South to understand each other. They must decide to adopt a course that gives value to both labor and land, which would protect them from the dangers caused by activists who would destroy the value of both.

With every step of improvement in the value of land, there would be a corresponding improvement in the physical and moral condition of the landowner. Even now, throughout the South, there is a growing reluctance <note>original: "indisposition"</note> to hold people in slavery. How much more quickly and widely would that feeling spread if the owners of land and slaves felt themselves growing richer instead of poorer, as is currently the case? 

The cause of emancipation has actually been moving backward for the last twenty years. Those who want to know why only need to look at the facts: in 1845–1846, 600,000,000 pounds of cotton could not buy as much iron for a plantation as 100,000,000 pounds would have bought thirty years earlier, or as 275,000,000 pounds would have bought only twelve years earlier.* The result has been a growing tendency to abandon the land. Instead, people have placed a higher value on "property" that can be moved and sold (slaves), which land cannot be. 

Harassed and annoyed by abolitionists on one hand, and facing a constant decline in the value of the only crop he depends on the other, the planter is forced to switch from cotton to sugar or wheat. It is no surprise, then, that there is a state of "feverish excitement" throughout the planting states. This tension will only increase unless the factory <note>original: "the loom"; Carey argues that placing manufacturing near agriculture creates stable local markets.</note> can be brought to stand side-by-side with the cotton field.

There is a common impression that the people of South Carolina have exhausted their rich lands and are moving away because the soil is poor, but nothing could be further from the truth. They began by farming poor soils, as has been done in every country in the world, and they are now fleeing from meadowlands capable of producing the finest grasses. They have millions of acres of this land untouched, along with un-cleared river bottoms, undrained swamps, and deposits of marl <note>A lime-rich mud or rock used as fertilizer.</note>, lime, and iron ore—all of which exist in almost unlimited quantities. Nature has provided that state with everything it needs. However, man has so far done nothing but exhaust the thin, poor soils where cultivation first began. Therefore, their agricultural reports and newspapers repeat the same question year after year: "What shall the cotton planters do?"

> "This," says the editor of the *South Carolinian*, "is a question daily asked by our planting friends. There seems," he continues, "to be great anxiety at present regarding the strategy they should use when planning <note>original: "pitching"</note> their next crop. We hear the cry of 'less cotton and more grain' ringing from one end of the state to the other. We are not surprised that many planters who farm heavily say their current crop will leave them in debt if these ruinous prices continue much longer. No planter can make ends meet if he receives only four or five cents for his cotton but has to pay current exorbitant prices for bagging, bale rope, pork, mules, sugar, coffee, salt, and iron. Mules are expensive, pork is expensive, and bagging and rope cost as much as they did when cotton sold for twelve or fifteen cents. Meanwhile, the prices of sugar, coffee, iron, and salt remain steady at their old high rates. If the planter has to add the cost of clothes, shoes, hats, and blankets for his workers to these necessary expenses, he will have nothing left to reward him for his labor."

-># THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.<-

> "These are truly matters that they should consider carefully, and we reasonably think that a farming system which does not pay for the labor and capital invested in it would soon be abandoned. But it will not be. Our planters are taught no other systems; they do not know how they would fill the gap that would be created by suddenly abandoning the cotton crop. Even with the strictest budgeting, it would take several years before they could refine the arrangements that would make them entirely independent of cotton as a marketable crop. Therefore, the steps taken should be wisely considered before they are adopted. The utmost caution should be observed in making what we sincerely believe would be a radical change in our system of agriculture, if it were once begun. We therefore advise, for the coming year, a simple reduction of one-third of the cotton crop throughout the state. At the same time, the land taken out of cotton cultivation should be devoted to producing grain and increasing labor. This labor could then be used for proper manuring <note>Adding fertilizer, typically animal waste, to the soil.</note> and improved tillage of the remaining cotton, as well as the general improvement of the plantation. By this process, the cotton lands would become more fertile. The resulting increase in grain would make it much easier to raise mules, hogs, cattle, and sheep. In a short time, the entire state could make itself independent of the demands of our Kentucky neighbors, who kindly supply us with all such things, but only at the expense of our own farmers' prosperity; in practice, they annually drain the region of all the surplus cash in payment for their bacon and mules. If this system were adopted, we would soon be able to produce as much cotton on fifty acres as we do now on one hundred. Furthermore, investing agricultural profits at home, even if they are small, would have a wonderful influence on general prosperity. It would build infrastructure throughout our now desolate and almost unreachable state. This would not only keep our own sons within our borders but also encourage capitalists to come among us and put their money to work by teaching us a lesson in practical enterprise. We say to the planters: raise less cotton, more grain, more mules, and more hogs. Make your own clothes for the enslaved people; raise sheep and make your own blankets. Build tanneries and encourage shoemakers and hatters—in fact, encourage artisans of all kinds to settle permanently among you. Work at making your soil rich rather than devoting all your energy to wearing it out, and soon all things will go well for you. You will not produce as many bales of cotton; in fact, you might not look as impressive <note>original: "cut such a swell"</note> on your merchant-agents' <note>original: "factors"</note> ledgers; but, take our word for it, you will have happier slaves, richer lands, more success, fewer debts, and fewer worries to keep you awake at night."

It is impossible to read this without being struck by the fact that the state is a large importer of other agricultural products. This is because of the exhaustion of its naturally poor soil and its inability to clear and drain more fertile land; consequently, the state cannot produce cotton as competitively as its neighbors. Its main city is supplied with hay from the North, despite having an abundance of rich meadow land. It consumes pork from Ohio and uses mules from Kentucky. Thus, it sells its products at low prices—an inevitable result of being so far from the place where its food and cotton are converted into cloth—while it buys food, mules, and other goods from others at the highest prices because of its distance from the source of production. The state wastes labor and fertilizer on the road <note>By spending resources on long-distance transportation rather than local production.</note> and is then surprised by the exhaustion that necessarily results from such a policy.

It is suggested that the remedy for all of this is found, first, in reducing the quantity of cotton produced. However, production is already decreasing so rapidly that the great fear throughout the state seems to be that cotton cultivation must soon stop because they can no longer produce it. The state wants to reduce the supply of cotton, yet its people are fleeing to the West to produce even more cotton there. Second, the lands are to be manured, but we are not told where that fertilizer will come from. The state has almost no consumers of agricultural produce except for those who are already farming, and their consumption yields very little manure. Its horses are always on the road, wasting the manure that would have been provided by its hay, corn, rice, and cotton, which are instead consumed abroad. The consequence of...

The result is that nothing yielded by the land is returned to it, and both the land and its owner become impoverished together. Its population is shrinking. Everyone is looking elsewhere to find a better place to employ their capital and their labor. Under such circumstances, it is useless to talk about artificial fertilizers. Even the swamps and river bottoms, where natural fertilizer has accumulated for ages, will not pay the cost of clearing for the sake of raising only three or four hundred pounds of cotton per acre. 

Give the state a local population of consumers that will create a market on the spot for tons of potatoes, turnips, hay, milk, and veal—all of which would be yielded by rich soils—and the State will become one of the richest in the Union. It is population density that draws food from rich soils, as we see in Belgium, England, and New England. Conversely, it is depopulation that drives men back to poorer soils, as is shown in Ireland, India, South Carolina, and Virginia. The people of Ireland are fleeing from each other as if from a plague. Yet that unfortunate island, where men are restricted almost entirely to farming the land, now offers us the primary European market for our surplus food. Meanwhile, South Carolina, lacking its own consumers, serves as one of the main markets for the surplus products of populous Ohio. 

Whenever Ireland begins to consume the products of its land locally, it will have the manure <note>original: "manure"; here referring to animal waste used as fertilizer to restore soil nutrients.</note> necessary to maintain its poor soils and will gain the ability to clear and drain its rich ones. Then, it might export hay instead of importing it. Ireland, like South Carolina, abounds in untouched rich soils. It has millions of acres of bog <note>Peat wetlands.</note> that could be drained with far less labor and cost than was required for similar lands in England. It is estimated that three million of these acres would provide food for six million people. However, like South Carolina, Ireland is forced to waste the labor and fertilizer yielded by the poorer soils currently in cultivation on transportation costs. This makes the region too poor to clear and drain the rich lands, which have never paid—and never can pay—the cost of preparation without a local consuming population that needs the potatoes, turnips, and hay which the earth yields by the ton, rather than by the pound or bushel.

Had the people of the Southern States, during the last twenty years, been making their own iron from their own coal, ore, and limestone—at an average of only 250,000 tons per year—the total quantity made in that time would have been five million tons. All of that iron would still be there today in the form of agricultural and manufacturing machinery, railroads, cars, and locomotives. Furthermore, they would now be increasing that quantity at a rate of half a million tons annually.

Fifty thousand tons of iron would create almost 500 miles of single-track railroad. Let us suppose they averaged annually only half that quantity and now possessed—as they easily could—5,000 miles of railroad running through populous manufacturing villages. In these villages, they would be converting their cotton into cloth or yarn to supply the world. Let us then estimate the increased value of the landed property in those states. An average annual product exceeding current levels by only *one dollar per acre* in the states south of Mason and Dixon’s line <note>The boundary line that historically separated the free Northern states from the slave-holding Southern states.</note> would represent a capital of *six thousand millions of dollars*. This is perhaps five times the present "value" of their slave population. At such a point, the entire region would be on the highway toward freedom, just as the masters were making their way toward fortune.*

-># THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.<-

Despite the greatness of their position, the planters have allowed themselves to be taxed for the maintenance of the people of England. The English produce little themselves and therefore have very little to give in exchange for the vast mass of agricultural products they receive. The consequence of this is that their customers are becoming poorer every day. The planters themselves are fast passing toward a state of exhaustion similar to what the English have produced in Ireland, India, the West Indies, and every other country that has been compelled to submit to their most unnatural system. A writer, describing the present position of affairs, says:

> "As a disinterested spectator of events, I assure you that during a residence of nearly ten years in England, I have not seen the different branches of trade in so disastrous a position as they are at present. From the petty dealer to the wholesale tradesman, I have never heard so many complaints about the wretched state of trade, not only in the metropolis <note>original: "metropolis"; referring here to London.</note>, but generally throughout the country. I place more confidence in the statements of a dozen respectable tradesmen than I do in 'trade circulars' <note>original: "trade circulars"; newsletters or reports distributed among merchants providing market information, often accused of being biased to encourage investment.</note>, which are usually created to serve certain interests, to cover the real truth, or to incite speculation. If I were to give an impartial opinion, I should unhesitatingly say that the repeal of the corn-laws <note>original: "corn-laws"; British tariffs on imported grain that were repealed in 1846, marking a shift toward free trade.</note>, the repeal of the navigation laws <note>original: "navigation laws"; acts that restricted the use of foreign ships for trade between Britain and its colonies.</note>, and the railway mania <note>original: "railway mania"; a speculative bubble in the 1840s involving a frenzy of investment in British railways.</note> have together produced the present panic—for it is useless to say that there is not a panic. The leading men of nearly every class declare it by their looks, their words, and their actions.
> "The parish of St. Clement Danes, one of the richest parishes of the metropolis where I am now residing, shows the real condition of the general tradespeople of London. The churchwarden of this parish recently informed me that three applications had been made to the parishioners for the amount of their poor rates <note>original: "poor rates"; a tax levied at the parish level to provide financial relief for the local poor.</note> and other taxes, and not more than one in twenty had paid their bills; he intended to issue summonses against the delinquents. He also remarked that during a residence of eighteen years in this parish, he had never known trade to be so dull as it is now."

What prospect there is of improvement may be gathered from the following extract from a journal that is the highest free-trade authority in England:

> "We may not unreasonably fear, therefore, that as far as Ireland is concerned, a considerable source of the progressive increase of the population and wealth of the empire is much diminished, if not absolutely dried up. Other sources of increase have, at the same time, been opened to us; but whether these will balance, or more than balance, the loss occasioned by the condition of Ireland, is more than we can say. For many years the condition of the population there was gradually deteriorating while their numbers increased; that terrible process has at length reached its climax. The present generation has to sustain the deteriorated and, we fear, demoralized mass, without any immediate hope of their being restored to habits of productive industry. It seems right to put all classes at once on their guard, lest the decrease of population noticed in the last quarter may, from the causes we have mentioned, be an index to a permanently slower increase in population than has hitherto taken place." —*The Economist (London)*

With such a state of things, the consumption of our products cannot increase. The question to be answered is, "Can it even be maintained?" Whenever population diminishes in its ratio of growth, it is evidence of a deterioration of condition. When that is going on, the first effect is felt in the diminished demand for clothing, for food is the want that must be first supplied.

Let it but be known that the people of this country—North, South, East, and West—are *determined* that the seat of the cotton and iron manufactures of the world is to be here, and the transfer of men and machinery will be such as to exceed all present calculation. Every man that comes will consume three, four, five, six, or twelve times as much cotton as at present. Meanwhile, he will take all his food from our own farmers, who will then consume three pounds of goods where now they consume but one. The remedy for all the grievances of the planters is in their own hands. It lies in the pursuit of a policy advocated by the fathers of the Revolution, and by every chief magistrate <note>original: "chief magistrate"; a term for the President of the United States.</note> of—

<meta>This page continues Henry Charles Carey’s critique of the British economic system. He argues that the "monopoly system"—the British policy of centralizing manufacturing in England while keeping colonies purely agricultural—is the true cause of global poverty and the persistence of slavery in the United States.</meta>

-># THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.<-

In the history of the Union, from Washington to Jackson, nearly all the presidents were from south of the Mason and Dixon line. All except two were elected by the same party that now rejects protection <note>original: "protection"; referring to protective tariffs designed to encourage domestic industry and reduce dependence on foreign imports.</note>.

Of all the chapters in the history of the people of this Union, the most honorable to them, as I believe, is the one that records the history of the African race. The 300,000 people brought into this country <note>Carey is referring to the estimated number of people brought to the U.S. through the Atlantic slave trade before its abolition in 1808.</note> are now represented by almost four million people who have advanced far toward civilization and freedom. They have grown to that number because they have been well fed, well clothed, well sheltered, and reasonably worked. This case is totally without parallel in the world. History may be challenged to produce any group of men invested with as much power over their fellow men as has been exercised by the people of the South, who used it so moderately as to permit such a rapid increase in numbers and such a great improvement in their condition.

<margin>* Coleridge, *Six Months in the West Indies*.</margin>
Nevertheless, they are unceasingly stigmatized as "slave-drivers" and "negro-breeders" by the very nation [Britain] that lives off their labor. Of all the European nations possessing colonies, Britain has most misused its power over the African race, because it is the only one that has established laws prohibiting the consumer and the producer from living near each other. Many years ago, an intelligent English traveler* remarked that men went to the French islands to stay and practice trades, but they went to the English islands only to try to make fortunes and then return home. This has been the case everywhere, and what have been the results? In India, there is the most extraordinary poverty and a succession of famines and plagues without parallel. In the West Indies, there has been an equally unparalleled waste of life, requiring constant imports of new people just to maintain their numbers. From 1817 to 1829, a period of twelve years, the number of enslaved people in Jamaica was reduced by ten percent through death alone; whereas, had they been here, they would have increased by thirty percent. The number of people imported into that one island could not have been less than double the number imported into this Union; and yet, while that larger number is today represented by only 300,000 people, the smaller number here is represented by almost four million. The chapter on slavery in British history is as disgraceful as that of the Union is honorable.

The fact that slavery even still exists among us is due to the monopoly system <note>Carey’s term for the British mercantile system, which he argued forced the world into a state of "free trade" that benefited only British manufacturers while impoverishing agricultural producers.</note> which has destroyed the value of land in Ireland, India, the West Indies, and all other British colonies. Yet the nation that instituted that system now heads the crusade against slavery, even while it converts the free people of Ireland and India into slaves and denounces the Southern planters—at whose expense she lives—as unworthy to be received into the society of free-born Englishmen. Furthermore, those very planters are united in supporting the system that impoverishes them and the very people who denounce them!

On the increase of production in these lands, and on the proportion of that increase which is sent to this country, depends our capability of extending our cotton manufacture, or even of maintaining it at its present level. Let us therefore consider each of these sources of supply in turn, so that we may be able to form a fair estimate—"

**UNITED STATES.**—We may now turn our attention to our last and main source of supply, America, which has sent us:

->*American Cotton*<-

| | Imports in five years | Imports per year |
|:---|:---|:---|
| 1830—1834, inclusive | 3,241,958 | 648,391 |

It should be noted that the last five years include the three largest crops ever recorded, as well as one very poor harvest and one that was somewhat lacking.

Those familiar with these matters recognize that a price of 4 pence per pound <note>original: "4d. a lb."</note> for "middling uplands" <note>A standard grade of medium-length cotton fiber.</note> cotton, delivered in Liverpool, provides enough profit for American planters to encourage them to grow as much cotton as their enslaved labor force <note>original: "negroes"</note> can harvest. Therefore, since the average price has almost never stayed that low for more than a few weeks, the *possible* increase in the cotton crop will keep pace with the *actual* increase of the enslaved population, and it cannot exceed it. Currently, this population increases at a very steady rate of 3 percent per year. 

If these premises are correct, it follows that the cotton crop of each year will exceed that of the previous year—assuming **equally favorable conditions (such as good weather for planting and picking, late frosts, and freedom from pests or floods)**—by 3 percent. As the following tables show, this has been almost exactly the case. The years 1840, 1843, and 1845 were very favorable for growing and harvesting cotton. Let us see what crop each of those years would yield for 1849, if calculated based on the 3 percent annual increase mentioned above:

| | Actual crop | Number of years | Percentage | Estimated crop of 1849 |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| 1840 | 2,178,000 | 9 | 27 | 2,866,000 |
| 1843 | 2,379,000 | 6 | 18 | 2,807,220 |
| 1845 | 2,394,000 | 4 | 12 | 2,681,280 |
| **Average** | | | | 2,784,833 |
| **Actual crop** | | | | 2,730,000 |

The following table shows that, using the year 1838 as a starting point, the average increase of the American crop over the last 12 years has not quite reached 3 percent. In fact, any time this rate was exceeded over a short series of years, it was simply due to an unusual run of favorable seasons.

It is clear, then, that for any practical conclusions, we will be close enough to the mark if we assume the average increase of the American cotton crop is 3 percent per year, barring any *unusual* disasters or exceptionally good seasons. Let us now examine what portion of this increase will be available to us in Great Britain.

Consumption within the United States itself has been steadily rising and now increases at an average annual rate of about 35,000 bales. It is currently about 520,000 bales per year. Consumption on the European continent (of American cotton) now reaches about 700,000 bales. Therefore, America and continental Europe together require about 1,200,000 bales at present, and they will require more each year. Furthermore, they will always take priority over Great Britain...

Britain, as their profit margins are larger, and a small price increase affects their manufacturers less than ours and reduces consumption less. The following table will clarify this issue:

| 5-Year Period | American cotton crop | American cotton imported into Great Britain | American cotton exported from Great Britain | American cotton kept for domestic consumption |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| 1840—44 | 9,905,638 | 5,802,829 | 295,600 | 5,507,229 |

From this table, it appears that while the *production* of American cotton in the last five years exceeded the previous five by the unprecedented amount of nearly 1.5 million bales, only 385,000 of that increase reached this country. Furthermore, *we had to re-export more than three-fourths of that amount*, leaving an annual increase available for our domestic consumption of only 17,000 bales. To cover any increase in consumption beyond this, we have been using up our existing stockpiles.

We will now look at the *total* supply and the *total* consumption of *all types* of cotton in Great Britain during the last ten years:

| Years | Bales imported from all sources | Bales exported | Kept for domestic consumption | Annual supply for domestic consumption | Actual annual consumption | Actual weekly consumption |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| 1840—44 | 7,767,149 | 637,650 | 7,129,499 | 1,425,900 | 1,290,480 | 24,810 |
| 1845—49 | 7,852,454 | 992,850 | 6,859,604 | 1,371,920 | 1,477,360 | 28,410 |
| **Increase** | 85,305 | 355,200 | . | . | 186,880 | 3,600 |
| **Decrease** | . | . | 269,895 | 53,980 | . | . |

We have estimated the actual consumption of 1849 at only 1,650,000 bales, for reasons stated later.

Now, *keeping in mind that the figures in the tables above are almost entirely confirmed facts and not mere estimates*, let us summarize the conclusions they lead us to. These conclusions are enough to cause significant concern, if not alarm, and suggest that everyone involved—directly or indirectly—in England's great manufacturing sector should proceed with caution.

1. Our supply of cotton from various sources (*excluding the United States*) has for many years been steadily, though inconsistently, *decreasing*.

2. Our supply of cotton *from all sources* (including the United States) available for domestic consumption has lately been falling at a rate of 1,000 bales per week, while our consumption has been increasing during the same period at a rate of 3,600 bales per week.

3. The United States is the only country where cotton production is increasing. Even there, the increase does not exceed an average of 3 percent, or 80,000 bales annually. This is barely enough to meet the rising demand for its own domestic use and for continental Europe.

4. No price incentive can significantly increase this annual growth, as planters always grow as much cotton as the enslaved labor force <note>original: "negro population"</note> is able to harvest.

5. Consequently, if the British cotton industry is to grow at all *under its current structure*, it can only do so if a massive incentive is applied to grow cotton in *other* countries suited for its cultivation.

Within the memory of many people still living, a great change has occurred in the countries where we get the bulk of our cotton. When the industry was in its infancy, our main supply came from the Mediterranean, especially from Smyrna <note>Modern-day İzmir, Turkey.</note> and Malta. Neither of those places now sends us more than a few occasional bags. In the last century, the West Indies were our primary source. In 1786, out of 20 million pounds imported, 5 million came from Smyrna and the rest from the West Indies. In 1848, the West Indies sent us only about 1,300 bales. In 1781, Brazil began to send us cotton, and that supply continued to grow, though inconsistently, until 1830; since then, it has fallen by half. Around 1822, Egyptian cotton began to arrive in significant amounts, its cultivation having been introduced there two years earlier. Imports exceeded 80,000 bales in 1845, but the average of the last three years has been less than a third of that. Cotton has always been grown extensively in India <note>original: "Hindostan"</note>, but it did not send much to England until about thirty years ago. In the five years ending in 1824, the average annual import was 33,500 bales; in 1841, it reached 274,000, and it can now be roughly estimated at 200,000 bales a year.

Now, what is the reason why these countries, after having at one time produced so much and so well, have stopped or reduced their production within recent years? It is clearly a question of price. Let us consider a few of the cases:

| At the close of the years | Lowest price of Pernambuco <note>A region in Eastern Brazil famous for high-quality cotton.</note> | Percentage drop | Lowest price of Maranham <note>Now spelled Maranhão, a state in Northeastern Brazil.</note> | Percentage drop | Lowest price of Egyptian | Percentage drop | Lowest price of Surat <note>A city in Gujarat, India, which served as a major port for Indian cotton exports.</note> | Percentage drop |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1836—39 inclusive | 9 1/2d. | — | 8 1/4d. | — | 10 1/4d. | — | 4 5/8d. | — |
| 1840—43 . . | 7d. | — | 5 5/8d. | — | 7d. | — | 3 1/8d. | — |
| 1844—48 . . | 5 7/8d. | 36% | 4 7/8d. | 42% | 5 7/8d. | 43% | 2 3/4d. | 40% |

Here, surely, we can find the explanation for the deplorable decline in our miscellaneous supply. From the four years ending in 1839—when the great incentive was given that provided us with such an ample supply during the following period—to the <term>quinquennial</term> <note>original: "quinquennial"; meaning a five-year period.</note> period ending in 1848, there has been a fall in price of 40 percent on average. Unless, therefore, we assume either an enormous profit margin in the earlier period or an extreme reduction in the cost of producing the article in late years, such a fall in price would be quite enough to direct capital and industry into other channels. This prevents an article as bulky as cotton from being grown or shipped at all.

In both Brazil and India, freight and shipping costs make up an unreasonable proportion of the price of cotton. In both countries, the bales are carried great distances on the backs of mules or other beasts of burden. The lack of good roads, convenient vehicles, and safely navigable rivers in the cotton districts of both countries increases the expense of bringing the bales to the shipping ports to such an extent that, when prices are low in England, the final payment sent back to the planter is quite insufficient to repay the cost of growing, picking, and packing. In some years, the price of much of the Surat cotton sent to this country was so low that it only returned *one penny* a pound to the shipper at Bombay. By the time this reached the actual grower, it had probably dwindled away through the expenses of carriage to a sum inadequate even to pay the <note>original: "government rent"; this refers to the land taxes or rents collected by the British colonial administration in India.</note> government rent. 

Our supply from both these countries will depend entirely upon price. In Brazil, where we believe sugar cultivation is less profitable than it used to be, a range of prices 50 percent higher than those of the last few years would probably induce the planters to increase their cotton fields and would repay them for doing so. Regarding the East Indies <note>The Indian subcontinent.</note>, where large quantities are always grown, our supply from there depends on two things: first, the demand from China, which is usually supplied before Great Britain; and second, the question of whether the net price at Bombay or Madras will pay for picking, cleaning, packing, and transporting it to the coast. Under the incentive of high prices (such as those that prevail at this moment), we have no doubt that large quantities would be sent forward. The price required to secure such large supplies will decrease as the means of transportation are increased and made cheaper. If the prices of the last five years continue, we believe there can be no doubt that the supply will inevitably continue to fall off.

We do not, however, share the optimistic expectations held by many parties that even with higher prices, the quantity and quality of East Indian cotton sent to this country can improve fast enough to make us at all independent of the American supply. For, in the first place, the absence of good roads or navigable rivers in the cotton districts, the length of time and the spending of capital needed before these can be replaced by railroads, and the slow and unenterprising character of the people <note>This reflects a common 19th-century British colonial bias regarding the perceived industry of Indian workers.</note>, must necessarily cause any significant increase of supply (at least over 250,000 bales per year) to be a very slow and costly operation. And, in the second place, the *quality* of the cotton grown in India is unique. This peculiarity is still traceable, though to a lesser degree, regardless of the location or the seed used—even in the best specimens (which have unquestionably improved lately). We fear this unique quality will always prevent it from being a substitute for American cotton, except to a very limited extent.

Our hopes lie in a very different direction. We look to our West Indian, African, and Australian colonies as the regions from which we might soon draw such a supply of cotton—provided the government would only afford *every possible facility* (we ask and wish for no more). This would, at the very least, make the fluctuations of the American crop, and the varying portion of it that we receive, far less important to our prosperity than they are now.

The West Indies, as we have already seen, used to send us about 40,000 bales sixty years ago, which was three-fourths of our supply at the time. But the enormous profits realized on...

The cultivation of sugar—partly caused and significantly extended by our <term>prohibitive duties</term> <note>original: "prohibitory duties"; trade tariffs designed to block imports from other countries to protect colonial industries.</note> on all competing sugars—focused the colonists' attention exclusively on that crop. As in the similar case of protected wheat in Britain, other types of farming were gradually abandoned in favor of a single product. Sugarcane was grown in soils and locations utterly unfit for it, where nothing but the system of protective tariffs could have forced its growth, and cotton was soon completely neglected. Many parts of the West Indies—St. Vincent especially—which are poorly suited for sugarcane, are perfectly adapted for the cotton plant, which flourishes in light, dry soils, especially near the seacoast. 

Now that the artificial stimulus which our mistaken policy so long applied to sugar cultivation has been withdrawn, sugar must be abandoned in all unsuitable locations and would be well replaced by cotton. We cannot say exactly what price would be required to make its cultivation profitable there. However, considering how cheaply it could be loaded onto ships in all these colonies, and how large a portion of the total production expense this transport usually represents, we see no reason why cotton should not be grown in the <note>original: "Antilles"; another name for the islands of the West Indies.</note> Antilles as cheaply as in the United States—provided the Black laborers can be relied upon for steady and continuous work during the picking season. Currently, the price of West Indian cotton ranges higher than the bulk of the American crop because it has a longer <term>staple</term> <note>The length of the cotton fiber; longer fibers are generally stronger and more valuable.</note>. We believe that if our planters energetically focused on this crop, they might soon send us a regular supply of 100,000 bales per year, thus finding a use for many estates that must otherwise be abandoned.

The experiment of growing cotton has already been tried successfully in one of our most promising African colonies: Port Natal <note>Now part of the KwaZulu-Natal province in South Africa.</note>. We have already received over 100 bales from this colony. The main portion consists of indigenous cotton, very similar to that shipped from New Orleans; it is clean, fine, and strong, but of a light brown color. On the whole, it is an excellent product for ordinary purposes and is worth nearly 7 pence per pound in today's market. The rest of the shipments were grown from Sea Island seed and are of excellent quality. Cultivation is rapidly increasing, and about 500 bales are expected from the colony next year. A society has been formed to promote emigration there, and a ship full of emigrants sailed a few days ago. Mr. Byrne, the agent, says:

> "Natal is situated in a sunny and bright region. It has iron, lead, coal, and copper in abundance; with British industry, it might be made one of the finest and wealthiest countries on the globe. The country is admirably suited for the growth of cotton, some of which is of a superior variety. In America, cotton was chiefly cultivated by slave labor at a cost of about £35 a year for each slave. In contrast, at Natal, the labor of the <note>original: "Zooloos"; the Zulu people of Southern Africa.</note> Zulus could be purchased at a cost of 10 shillings a month. Furthermore, Natal, due to its proximity to the sea, is advantageously situated for carrying on trade with England in competition with the United States. I would not advise you to cultivate sugar; you will likely be able to get that product better from Mauritius, where you will find a highly profitable market for all other agricultural produce. I intend to send out a screw-propeller steamer at the beginning of the year to run between that island and Natal."

From Australia, we have not yet received a large supply, but several acres are under cultivation. The samples sent are of such fine quality that they prove beyond question that the soil and climate are adapted to produce cotton as good as any grown in America. We currently have samples before us—alongside the Port Natal cotton—grown from Sea Island seed at Bolwarra, in New South Wales, near Maitland, about 80 miles north of Sydney. It is long, fine, and silky.

We believe that, with proper encouragement, the cultivation of cotton in these regions might increase at a steady rate equal to our increasing demand. Let us now look at a summary of how the matter stands.

We have seen that our annual supply of the American cotton crop over the last five years has reached nearly 1,120,000 bales. Because the yearly increase of the crop is balanced by the increasing demand from the United States and continental Europe, there is little probability of our ever receiving more than this on average. Let us suppose that a proper increase in price raises the production of Brazil to what it reached in 1830, and that of India nearly to what it was in 1841, and that Egypt and our own colonies again send us significant and increasing imports:

This would provide us with a supply of 33,500 bales per week, which is the estimated consumption for this year. For any additional supply, we must rely on increased production from the colonies, or on the amounts that even higher prices will allow us to extract from India and Brazil. The clear conclusion from all of this is that, in order to secure the supply of <term>raw material</term> <note>original: "raw material"; unprocessed cotton used as the basic ingredient for manufacturing.</note> needed to meet our current consumption, *we must be prepared to pay a significantly higher range of prices than we have seen in recent years.* In fact, the average prices of the last five years have proven quite inadequate to bring enough cotton to this country to keep our existing machinery working full-time, despite large harvests in America. Therefore, higher prices *must* prevail in the future. Spinners and manufacturers should not wish for anything else; experience has clearly shown them that no circumstance causes as great or as certain a loss as an inadequate supply of cotton, and only higher prices can prevent this ultimate disaster.

This covers the likely sufficiency of the cotton supply to this country, *assuming that consumption is what it appears to be and will continue at its current rate.* But are we justified in making these two assumptions? Let us look at a few facts regarding this question.

First, let us determine what the actual consumption has been over the last ten years. We have accurate data for nine years and for the first ten months of this year. During these ten months, deliveries to the industry reached 1,495,000 bales. However, we know that during the latter part of this period, manufacturers have been purchasing far more than they need for immediate use. While the actual quantity of cotton being processed has been decreasing since the beginning of June—due to a general shift toward producing finer, more delicate fabrics—purchases of cotton have been increasing. In October, purchases reached the unprecedented amount of 217,000 bales. A slowdown has now occurred, and we believe we are correct in assuming that industry purchases during the last nine weeks of this year will not exceed 205,000 bales. In that case, they will hold 50,000 more bales in stock than usual at the end of the year. This would put the year’s total consumption at 1,650,000 bales. Our own impression is that this estimate is likely too high rather than too low, and that <term>spinners</term> <note>original: "spinners"; factory owners or workers who turn raw cotton into yarn or thread.</note> hold a larger stock than we assume; regardless, we cannot be far enough from the truth to change our conclusions.

| Year | Weekly consumption of cotton in Great Britain | Year | Weekly consumption of cotton in Great Britain |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1840 | 24,868 | 1845 | 30,120 |
| 1841 | 22,134 | 1846 | 30,000 |
| 1842 | 22,949 | 1847 | 21,270 |
| 1843 | 26,693 | 1848 | 28,950 |
| 1844 | 27,439 | 1849 | 31,730 |

Now, we want our readers to consider this table carefully and notice the extraordinary *fluctuations* in the amount of cotton processed each year, in connection with the facts we are about to state. The weekly average fell by nearly 3,000 bales from 1840 to 1841, then jumped up by nearly 4,000 bales from 1842 to 1843. In 1845 and 1846, it remained steady at a high level. Passing over the <note>original: "anomalous year of 1847"; 1847 was a year of severe economic crisis in Britain, known as the Panic of 1847, which disrupted trade and manufacturing.</note> unusual year of 1847 for obvious reasons, consumption had fallen again by 1848, when the quantity only exceeded the amount from *eight years earlier* by 4,000 bales. *Yet, throughout this entire period, the machinery used in cotton manufacturing was constantly, though not regularly, increasing.* Except for a short period in 1842 (and in 1847, which we have excluded from our calculation), we believe it is correct to say the mills were all working at full capacity. Indeed, <term>short time</term> <note>original: "short time"; a practice where factories reduce working hours or days to avoid overproduction or because of high material costs.</note> results in such a massive loss to the mill owner that it is never used except under the most extreme pressure. During the last year, we see that consumption increased by nearly 3,000 bales a week, even though the hours of labor have been reduced by law from eleven to ten <note>original: "per diem"; Latin for "per day."</note> per day.

All of these considerations point clearly to the conclusion *that our consumption of the raw material is not a fixed amount, but a changing one.* It is affected by causes other than the total amount of machinery in use or the hours it is operated. We can easily discover what this cause is and how much influence it has.

The weight of raw cotton used by a specific amount of machinery varies according to the nature of the item being produced. In England, we produce fabrics where the raw material makes up *two-thirds* of the value, and other fabrics where it does not even make up *one-fiftieth* of the value. We spin yarns where the raw materials cost *three-fourths* of the finished price, and others where it costs only *one-twentieth*. We have spindles that produce two pounds of yarn a week, and others that do not produce even two pounds in three months. But, without—

| | | |
|---|---|---|
| 840 spindles | working <term>20's twist</term> <note>original: "20's twist"; a measurement of yarn fineness. The number represents how many "hanks" (840 yards each) weigh one pound. Lower numbers are thicker and coarser.</note> | will consume 1,340 lbs. of cotton |

| 840 spindles | working 60's twist | will consume 224 lbs. of cotton |

Now, although machinery accustomed to producing No. 20 yarn cannot produce No. 60, it can, without significant change or difficulty, produce No. 30. Likewise, machinery adapted for No. 30 can change to No. 40, and so on. In fact, every mill has a range of *at least ten numbers*. By varying these, a mill can easily reduce or increase its consumption of cotton *by 25 to 50 percent.* 

The same may be said of weaving mills. In many mills, looms of the same construction may be seen working side by side; some of these produce 60 lbs. a week, while others produce only 25 lbs. We could mention at least one mill where the amount of raw cotton processed weekly varies from 30,000 lbs. down to 18,000 lbs. to meet the fluctuating demands of the market, depending on the fineness of the article produced. We also find the following corroborating statement in last Saturday's *Manchester Guardian*:

> “Some idea of what a change of yarn numbers can achieve may be gathered from the following instances; the names of the firms are known to us:

| | Reduction | Previous weekly consumption |
|---|---|---|
| No. 1 . . . . . . . | 10,000 lbs. | out of 40,000 lbs. |
| No. 2 . . . . . . . | 18,000 lbs. | — 60,000 lbs. |
| No. 3 . . . . . . . | 25,000 lbs. | — 115,000 lbs. |
| No. 4 . . . . . . . | 10,000 lbs. | — 30,000 lbs. |
| No. 5 . . . . . . . | 10,000 lbs. | — 30,000 lbs. |
| No. 6 . . . . . . . | 70 bales | — 120 bales |

We have been informed by another very large-scale spinner that the reduction in his establishment is more than 40,000 lbs. per week.”

It is not easy to determine the exact extent to which this change from coarser to finer yarn numbers is actually carried out at any given time. We know, however, that it occurs to a very great extent. This has happened, perhaps almost unprecedentedly, during the last six months. 

When we consider the immense proportion of the *weight* of cotton used in England—which is consumed by the makers of heavy cloths and coarse yarns—we think we may safely state a conclusion. A *brisk* demand for <term>printers</term> <note>original: "printers"; plain cotton cloth intended to be printed with a pattern.</note>, <term>shirtings</term> <note>original: "shirtings"; fabric used specifically for making shirts.</note>, and India yarns on one hand, combined with a dull demand for <term>domestics</term> <note>original: "domestics"; heavy, durable cotton fabrics intended for everyday household use.</note>, <term>long-cloths</term>, and German yarns on the other (or vice versa), will make a difference of at least 25 percent in the weight of raw cotton consumed if continued for any time.

Now, an increase in the price of cotton is felt much more strongly in coarse yarns and heavy cloths than in finer ones. Over the last twelve months, an increase of nearly 3<term>d.</term> <note>original: "d."; abbreviation for pence (from the Latin denarius).</note> per pound on the raw material of a stout <term>calico</term> <note>original: "calico"; a plain-woven cotton textile.</note>—which usually sells finished at 8d. per pound—is nearly a 40 percent increase on the manufactured article. On a printing cloth or a fine shirting that sells at 12d. per pound, it is only 25 percent. On the piece *after it has been printed*, it is far less than this—in fact, a mere trifle. 

To put it even more clearly: an increase of 3d. per pound on a heavy domestic calico will force the purchaser to pay 4d. per yard where he formerly paid only 3d. That same 3d. per pound increase will add 15d. to the cost of a 30-yard piece of printing cloth. When that cloth is printed and sold in shops for about 12<term>s.</term> 6d. <note>original: "s."; abbreviation for shillings.</note>, the price to the customer only rises from 5d. to 5½d. per yard. 

This 10 percent increase is not enough to significantly or quickly slow down consumption, but the other 40 percent increase is. It is clear, therefore, that an increase in the price of the raw material will reduce the demand for—and consequently the production of—heavy fabrics much sooner and more decisively than light ones. Accordingly, as the following table will show, the price range is more limited in the former than in the latter, and it never keeps pace with the price of the raw material:

<meta>This page continues the discussion on how cotton manufacturers adapt to high raw material costs by switching from heavy, coarse fabrics to finer ones to conserve capital and manage stock.</meta>

# THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.

In trade, the opposite is true for "heavy domestics" <note>original: "heavy domestics"; coarse, thick cotton fabrics used for household items like sheets or heavy clothing</note> when following market fluctuations. A very large amount of raw cotton is used in these heavy goods compared to the amount of machinery required to make them. There is a high demand for these items *at low prices*, but if prices rise significantly, this demand immediately drops. A large portion of these goods is exported as "T cloths" <note>original: "T cloths"; a type of plain, coarse cotton cloth manufactured specifically for export markets</note> and "long-cloths" <note>original: "long-cloths"; a fine but sturdy cotton cloth</note> to Portugal, the Mediterranean, and the Levant, as long as prices stay around 8 pence per pound. However, when the price approaches 9 pence, these exports almost completely stop. The manufacturers who usually supply those markets are then forced to switch their production to other types of fabric.

Another factor contributes to this shift. In unprofitable years—which always happen when the raw cotton supply is low and its price rises quickly (as it has this year)—every manufacturer naturally wants to minimize his losses. He wants to make his capital go as far and last as long as possible. The best way to do this is to set his machinery to produce the finest range of yarn it can handle. For example, he might process 20,000 lbs. of cotton per week instead of 30,000 lbs. 

Furthermore, when trade is slow and manufacturers cannot sell their goods, they are forced to build up stock. In these times, the incentive to produce the finest fabrics possible is even stronger. A manufacturer with 500 looms making light printing cloths can afford to hold a stock of 50,000 pieces (about four months of production). However, a manufacturer with 500 looms making heavy domestics would need much more capital to hold 25,000 pieces (also four months of production). In round numbers, the first manufacturer would have £12,000 tied up in stock, while the second would have £18,000.

Taking all these factors into account—observing that the shift from coarse to fine fabrics has happened often in the past, knowing how easily it can be done, and seeing the massive incentive created by the recent rise in cotton prices—we are certain that this change has been more widespread over the last six months than most people realize. We doubt whether the actual consumption of cotton is currently within 5,000 bales per week of what it seemed to be last May, or within 3,000 bales of what it actually was. 

We are also convinced that, given our current and future outlook for the supply and price of raw cotton (as explained earlier in this paper), our manufacturing industry must focus more on finer yarns and fabrics than it has in recent years. Consequently, our total consumption of cotton is likely to *decrease* rather than increase—despite the growth and improvement of machinery—until the supply from various other sources increases significantly. *To sum up: speculators who refuse to believe that consumption has dropped, and manufacturers who refuse to accept that the supply is inadequate, will both find themselves mistaken and in financial danger.* We especially want manufacturers to consider that whether the upcoming American crop is slightly better or worse does not change our argument. We have estimated it at 2,350,000 bales, while the highest estimate is 2,400,000 bales.

There are other reasons that support this conclusion. There are signs that we have over-estimated and outpaced the demand for manufactured goods in our existing markets, just as we have outpaced the supply of raw cotton from existing sources. It is likely that the world's need for cotton goods roughly keeps pace with the world's growth of raw cotton. Unfortunately, our machinery has increased faster than both. We can produce more calico <note>original: "calico"; a plain-woven cotton cloth</note> than is wanted, and we can use more cotton than is grown. To verify this, we can look at the data from the last five years. During that time, demand for our goods was hampered by a massive political and commercial upheaval <note>likely referring to the Revolutions of 1848 and the subsequent economic instability</note>. On the other hand, demand was boosted for a time by the high wages paid to the working classes, such as railway laborers. Meanwhile, the supply was limited by one of the worst cotton crop failures in many years.

It is important to observe that the experience of individual business owners will not disprove the conclusions of these tables. They show the difference between the cost of raw materials and the manufactured goods at the *standard prices of the day*. These prices vary greatly during the year. A manufacturer who bought his cotton at the cheapest time and made his sales contracts at the peak of the market might still make a profit, even though the general trade is suffering a loss. 

The only situation where these tables might lead to an incorrect conclusion is when the relative prices in November do not accurately represent the average prices for the entire year. In 1847, this was the case: the gap between the cost of cotton and the price of yarn or cloth was much *greater* in November than during most of the year, so the loss appeared much *smaller*. On average, that year resulted in a large loss on all items.

From these tables, it appears—as everyone in the trade well knows—that our cotton spinners and manufacturers have, with few exceptions, been operating at a loss since 1845. This has happened during a period when the price of raw materials fluctuated up and down by at least 40 percent. Is it likely that they would have found it impossible to obtain profitable prices—as they clearly have—if they had not produced more than our actual markets can absorb on average?

At the beginning of this year, there were great expectations for our domestic demand. It was argued, with good reason, that we have never had a year with both full employment and low food prices that was not also a year of very high domestic consumption of manufactured fabrics. This year, labor has been in very high demand, and food has not been so cheap and plentiful since 1836. Yet our expectations...
