# THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.

The conclusions drawn from these facts have not been fully addressed. Sellers of printed fabrics and medium-grade shirtings report that their domestic demand has, on the whole, been good. Conversely, sellers of "domestics" <note>original: "domestics"; plain, sturdy cotton fabrics used for everyday household items like bedding or coarse shirts</note> report a decidedly dull business, worse than that of last year. However, we believe all agree that the expectations they held at the beginning of the year have by no means been realized. 

We suspect the cause to be this: the loss of value in railway property, the effects of the Irish Famine <note>The Great Famine (1845–1852) caused mass starvation and emigration in Ireland, severely disrupting the British economy</note>, and the commercial crash of 1847 have impoverished all classes of the community to a much greater extent than our tradesmen allowed for in their calculations. We question whether the purchasing power of the British community is nearly equal to what it was in 1845. One fact alone may enable us to guess the degree to which its total spending power must have been reduced: in round numbers, the sum actually spent on railways is 210 million pounds; their actual value at today’s prices does not exceed 100 million pounds; and many of them pay little or no dividend.

Let us now summarize the conclusions which our tables have resolved:

1.  Our supply of cotton has significantly fallen off during the last few years and will not increase except under the pressure of much higher prices than have prevailed (until the last few months).
2.  Under such price ranges, our consumption will not maintain its current apparent rate (roughly 32,000 bales a week), regardless of any increases or improvements in machinery.
3.  Except under the incentive of low prices, our existing markets *cannot buy* as much as our machinery *can produce*.
4.  The practical conclusions pointed to by these facts are: *first*, a permanent tendency toward the production of higher-quality, finer fabrics; and *secondly*, a halt to the construction of new mills and machinery—our producing power—until the increased supply of raw material on one hand, and an increased consumption of manufactured goods on the other, shall once more restore the balance.

It is stated here that the consumption of the last five years is greater by 3,600 bales per week than in the previous five, but it is not shown where this cotton came from. The total quantity kept for consumption in the second period is 269,000 bales less than in the first. Yet, consumption is said to have been greater by 187,000 per year, or a total quantity of 935,000 bales. When added to the deficiency in the quantity kept, this would create a gap of 1,200,000 bales. The stock of American cotton on hand at the end of 1849 was 400,000 bales lower, and other types may have been reduced by 250,000; but even this leaves 550,000 bales unaccounted for. It is almost impossible to examine the figures given in this paper without concluding that the consumption levels are exaggerated.

Admitting, however, all that is claimed, I will now proceed to show how a large portion of this increase resulted from the existence of protectionist policies elsewhere. It has been shown <margin>* Page 394, earlier in this volume.</margin> that our import of cotton goods in the two years ending June 30, 1843—a period of *almost free trade*—was very small, the average being only $7,184,000. If we now add to this the increased imports of the year ending June 1844, we get an average of about $9,000,000. 

From June 1844 to June 1849, the average was about $16,000,000. During half of this period, the protectionist Tariff of 1842 <note>A protective tariff meant to help American industry by taxing imports</note> was in effect. For more than half of the remaining time, the Tariff of 1846 <note>A lower, "free trade" tariff that reduced duties on many goods</note> was almost entirely ineffective—and for the rest of that time, the duty has been thirty percent. Nevertheless, the amount *imported* <margin>† By referring to the tables in Chapters II and III, it will be seen that much of these imports in the last two years was obtained in exchange for certificates of debt <note>Essentially IOUs or bonds; the author is arguing that the US was buying goods on credit rather than paying with earned money</note>. Therefore, they are deducted from the import amounts given there. The purpose of those tables was to show the *power of consumption* resulting from the *power of production*, not that which resulted from the impoverishing system of buying goods on credit.</margin> has been almost double, and the excess is no less than three-quarters of a pound per person, making an average of about 35,000 bales per year.

It is obvious that the increase, trivial as it has been, among the *unprotected consumers*, has been obtained at the cost of the planter. This amounts to a rate of 9 shillings and 6 pence (equal to $2.28) per person. This sum is what remains to be used for the purchase of cotton, sugar, coffee, tea, silks, dyeing materials, timber, and all other articles of necessity or luxury required for domestic consumption—with the exception of grain, potatoes, live animals, and cured provisions.

If the reader compares this statement with those of previous years already mentioned,\* I believe there will be no difficulty in seeing that the "purchasing power" <note>original: "power of purchase"</note> of the people of Great Britain is rapidly declining. This fact is the cause of the distress currently existing among its people.

Some might argue, however, that the nation *does* consume much more than this amount. This is true, and I now intend to show how she is able to do so. Thus far, however, the accounts for various periods have been calculated in exactly the same way, allowing us to compare the present with the past.

It is clear that the prices of all the items I have listed would be considered low even here in America. Of the grain, nearly three-quarters are wheat or wheat flour, and the price is 4 shillings (or 88 cents) per bushel, delivered in England. The bacon, beef, pork, lard, and butter are priced at 6¼ cents per pound, also delivered in England. Flax is at seven cents per pound. Wool is at a shilling per pound, and cotton is estimated to be about 5¼ pence per pound. These are prices at which we would not want to deliver the same goods to New York or Philadelphia on their way to Liverpool. Nevertheless, Great Britain obtains all of these, along with immense quantities of other goods, and yet still leaves us largely in debt at the end of the year's business. Britain uses sugar valued at £5,000,000. Large quantities of cotton, silk, hemp, and hides are consumed domestically. Her consumption of tea is 40 million pounds. She consumes a million "loads" <note>a "load" was a standard measure for timber, roughly 50 cubic feet</note> of timber, and the price of Canadian red pine is £3 per load. How does she acquire the power to do all of this?

The cotton that comes from Bombay <note>modern-day Mumbai, India</note>, as stated above, frequently yields only a penny per pound to the shipper at that port. This price will not even cover the cost of transporting it from the farm to the shipping port, leaving nothing at all to cover the actual cost of production. Yet, the poor producer still pays heavy taxes to the Company <note>The East India Company, which exercised administrative and tax control over parts of India</note> for the use of that land. These taxes are then sent to England to pay for expenses, pensions, dividends, and other costs.

The sugar from Mauritius <note>an island nation in the Indian Ocean, then a British colony</note> sells for 22 shillings per hundredweight, or 2¾ pence per pound. This is a price that can yield the shipper very little, if anything, more than a penny per pound. The producer receives almost nothing. The financial records of several large firms that own land on that island show that for years, the estates received no profit whatsoever. The same situation applies to Canada and its lumber trade.

<meta>This page continues the economic critique of Great Britain's trade system, arguing that the nation maintains its high consumption by shifting the costs of production and trade onto foreign farmers and planters, leading to a decline in domestic purchasing power.</meta>

# THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.

The costs for all goods that pass into England are huge, and they cannot be anything else. Producers are few and consumers are many, and the latter must be supported by the former. Whenever four families must eat but only one grows food, the portion that goes to the consumers must be small; this is why the farmers and planters of the world are kept so poor.

With every drop in price, the system becomes more severe. A penny taken out of a pound of cotton selling for a shilling is a trifle, but a penny taken out of three pence <note>original: "3d."; the 'd' refers to the old British penny (denarius)</note> is a heavy burden. When cotton prices are high, it sells quickly and the overhead costs are lower. When the crop is large and sells slowly, the costs are many. This is true for sugar, tobacco, rice, and all other products of the earth. As the power to consume has diminished, prices have generally fallen, while the need for financial advances, storage, etc., has increased. This gives the middleman <note>original: "exchanger"</note> the power to take for himself not only a larger proportion but also a larger quantity than before. This is how Great Britain is able to consume so much while producing so little.

Reduce her power to tax the planters and farmers of the world, and it will quickly be seen that even her current level of consumption exists only because she can shift the burdens she should bear alone onto others. The *Economist*—a journal that cannot be accused of exaggerating the problems of the current system—expresses its belief that "the purchasing power" <note>original: "power of purchase"</note> of the British public is *not nearly equal to what it was in 1845.*\* This is undoubtedly true, and that the

---

\* This same journal, only two weeks earlier, assured its readers that "ever since there was a reduction of the import tariffs (the sliding scale) and a probability that the Corn Laws <note>Corn Laws: 19th-century trade laws designed to protect British cereal producers by taxing imports</note> would be abolished, farmers have steadily improved their cultivation and produced more." If production has increased, why has purchasing power decreased? If purchasing power has decreased, how can the people afford all this *supposed* increase in domestic products plus the massive amount of imports? The power to consume and the power to produce go hand in hand; if "purchasing power" has fallen, as it certainly has, it is because the power to produce goods *to trade with* has declined.

Much of the decrease in "purchasing power" is attributed to railroad speculation, but it is difficult to see how that could have caused it. Under that system, much property changed hands, but the actual spending was merely the cost of preparing the land and laying the tracks. There is no doubt that the labor saved by using the railroads has been at least equal to the amount spent on them. The money paid for land and the fees to parliamentary agents <note>lobbyists or lawyers handling the legal requirements for railroads in Parliament</note> were simply transfers from one person’s pocket to another’s and could not have weakened the nation's "purchasing power." The railroad speculation created the roads themselves, and since they exist, they tend to increase the capacity for production and consumption. We must therefore look elsewhere for the causes of England's current state. They are found in the *necessity* of competing with the cheapest and most exploited <note>original: "worthless"</note> labor in the world. The results of that necessity are shown in the following facts, which explain not only the current drop in "purchasing power" but also why it will continue to drop in the future.

In Scotland, it has risen in three years from £185,000 to £560,000. In Glasgow, before 1846, it was £30,000; in 1848-9, it was £200,000. The number of paupers <note>people living in extreme poverty receiving public aid</note> in 1845-6 was 7,454; in 1847-8, it was 51,852. Railroad revenue <note>original: "tolls"</note> per mile averaged £2,640 in 1845; in 1849, it was £1,780.—*Ibid.*

# THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.

It is quite certain that purchasing power must continue to decline as the power of production further decreases.

We see that, despite low prices for grain, imports are immense, averaging more than nine million of our bushels per month. Will this continue? In response, the domestic crop of this year has not failed, nor have there been any reasons why exports from the world's grain-producing countries should be larger than usual. We are assured that Russia can supply fifty million quarters <term>quarter: a British unit of volume for grain, equal to eight bushels</term> annually, and that much of it is currently wasted for want of a market. Russia now has a market, and as long as a bushel of wheat will earn the producer the price of a yard of cotton cloth, he will accept even that rather than waste it. We are told that he cannot afford to grow it at such a price, but what else can he do? Deprived of other employment for his time, he must grow food for himself and purchase clothing with the surplus—even if he has to starve himself to obtain the little that he wears. The error of English writers consists in assuming that there is such a thing as a "necessary price" <note>original: "necessary price"; the minimum price required to cover the costs of production</note>. The poor laborer in India, we are assured by this same writer, obtains for his cotton no more than the mere rent of his land, leaving nothing for his labor; yet he still cultivates cotton to exchange for the yard of cloth with which he covers his loins.

The people of England first inflicted upon themselves a necessity for competing with the "cheap" labor of India in the manufacture of cotton goods. That produced a necessity for competition with the "cheap" labor of Russia in the production of food, the consequences of which are described in the recent quarterly report of the Registrar-General: "*The population of England has suffered, died, and decreased during the quarter, to a degree of which there is no example in the present century.*" Emigration has increased so rapidly, and so far ahead of immigration, that "*England now has several thousand fewer inhabitants than were within her shores at midsummer.*"

The system tends to increase man’s necessities and to diminish his power. It is shown here how enormous the difference was in the prices of cotton in the two periods, and we may now look to see whether the price of cloth and iron changed along with it. From 1840 to 1844, the average price of a piece of gray cotton cloth was 6s. 7d. <note>6 shillings and 7 pence</note>; from 1845 to 1849, it was above 6s. Here is a reduction of ten percent to set against price changes of 40 percent in raw cotton. The average price of iron in 1845, 1846, and 1847 was 50 percent higher than that of the four previous years; thus, while cotton was lower than before, the thing which the cotton producer desires to use above all others—iron—was vastly higher. He was steadily giving more and receiving less, and it is no surprise that his power of production diminished and his condition steadily deteriorated.

Because of this, the power to pay for cotton cloth on the part of the people subjected to the system is steadily diminishing, and "the consumption cannot be maintained." Nothing, "we are assured, but the stimulus of low prices" will enable "the existing markets" to buy up the products of England’s machinery. To secure a supply at low prices, every English writer on the subject is looking for what is called "cheap labor." That of the Zulus <note>original: "Zooloos"</note> may be had at 10s. per month, and Natal <note>a British colony in South Africa</note> is advantageously situated for maintaining "competition with the United States" <note>original: "the States"</note>.

The "practical deduction pointed to by these facts," and that which most interests the planter, is that there must be "a check to the increase of mills and machinery" until "the increased supply of the raw material" shall bring down the price of cotton to the level of what consumers can afford, or until "purchasing power" shall rise to a level with existing prices. That the latter, among the unprotected communities of the world, has...

# THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.

It is obvious that purchasing power has steadily declined over many years, and there is no reason to suppose the future will be any different from the past. The only remaining way to "restore the balance" is to reduce the price of cotton to match a constantly diminishing "purchasing power."

There is no doubt that this power will continue to diminish unless the planters decide to help themselves. Men who previously grew sugar and coffee are now turning their attention to cotton, believing it will be more profitable. The people of Jamaica have been forced to abandon coffee, and their journals inform us that sugar can no longer be grown profitably. The *Economist* <note>A prominent British weekly magazine focused on international business and politics, founded in 1843.</note> explains why this is the case.

The same issue of the *Economist* that provided the previous long extract informs us that the sugar market is "drooping," as the "expectation of a large additional consumption has not been realized." The result is seen in the fact that sugar from the distant Isle of France <note>original: "Isle of France"; the island known today as Mauritius.</note> is quoted at 22 shillings and 5 pence per hundredweight <term>cwt: a hundredweight, a unit of weight equal to 112 pounds in the British system.</term>. This equals two and two-fifths pence per pound. After paying for freight and charges, this yields the shipper about the same as the cotton shipped from Bombay mentioned earlier—namely, one penny. This leaves the producer on his plantation with little more than what is necessary to pay his rent. Under such circumstances, the labor of the people of Mauritius becomes "cheaper," and may eventually become as "cheap" as that of the Zulus <note>original: "Zooloos"; referring to the ethnic group in Southern Africa, used here as a benchmark for the lowest-paid labor.</note>.

This is the case everywhere. The former cotton planter of Alabama is trying to grow sugar, and the sugar planter of Jamaica is determined to try cotton, under the impression that "a sufficient supply has not yet been raised to meet the demand." The real cause of the difficulty is that the cotton planter and his neighbors are unable to obtain even one-third as much sugar as they want to consume, and the sugar planter cannot obtain one-third as much cloth as he wants. This happens because the cost of both goods in terms of *labor* is greatly increased by the necessity of making their exchanges in the distant market of England. 

If both groups were determined to create a market on their own land for the products of that land, each would receive three times as much in return for the same amount of labor. However, if they continue to support the English monopoly system, they will receive even less than the little they get now. Among the world's planters, there is a perfect harmony of interests; the prosperity of all is promoted by adopting a system that raises the value of labor. This would enable a man in Ireland, who currently consumes only one pound of cotton, to become a man in America, consuming twelve or twenty pounds.

The goal of every effort to maintain this great "monopoly of machinery" is to prevent any increase in the value of labor and land throughout the world, so that commodities may be bought "cheap." Anyone who studies the "sliding-scale system" <term>sliding-scale system: a trade mechanism where taxes or consumption levels are adjusted based on price fluctuations to keep costs low for the buyer.</term> will see how much power is exercised for this purpose. This system reduces consumption whenever prices rise slightly, thereby counteracting any upward trend. 

Current consumption can only be maintained at today’s minimum prices. The reason for this is that "cheap" cotton and "cheap" sugar make the *labor-cost* of cloth and iron so high that the poor cultivators of those "cheap" goods cannot afford to buy either. Even though cloth is expensive to consumers and cotton has yielded little to its producers, we are told that manufacturers have been working at a loss for nearly all of the last five years. Profits for 1845 are listed at only 1½ pence per pound—a year that Messrs. Rathbone, in their circular accompanying the diagram on page 75, described as one of "enormous profits to manufacturers." The differences between the prices of cotton and yarn given here and those provided by the Rathbones are sometimes remarkable. Despite this constant series of losses, we are assured there has been a steady increase in machinery to do the work, while the overall increase in consumption is tiny. It is difficult to reconcile these statements.

It is less difficult to determine what the planter's policy should be. It is to break down the ***monopoly*** and bring the ***machinery of England*** to the ***cotton fields***. This will happen whenever the producers of food and cotton declare to the world that it is their ***fixed policy to increase the consumption of cotton by enabling themselves to supply it cheaply to consumers***. This work is to be accomplished by freeing themselves from the control of those who now live, move, and exist by standing between the producer and the consumer, impoverishing the producer so that he cannot continue to produce, and the consumer so that he cannot continue to buy.

It must strike the reader as strange that the clever writer of this article assumes that the system which destroys farming in India and Brazil has no such effect in this country. He assumes that we produce all we can, whereas we know that the great goal throughout the South is to limit production. Producers are constantly fleeing from exhausted lands to seek new ones to exhaust again, wasting more labor on the road than would add hundreds of thousands of bales to the crop.

If the planters had decided eight years ago that the loom should come to the cotton, this year’s crop would exceed three million bales. The price would be higher than it is now with a crop of only two million; for we would be consuming more than a million bales ourselves. The buyers for this cotton would be found among prosperous iron makers, who would be producing 1.2 or 1.5 million tons of iron to be used for building roads for prosperous farmers and equally prosperous miners and manufacturers. An increase in price produced this way increases consumption, and such is the tendency of ***protection***. An increase in price resulting from small crops tends to decrease consumption, and such is the tendency of the ***monopoly system***. It destroys both the power to produce and the power to consume.

### CHAPTER SEVENTEENTH.
### HOW PROTECTION AFFECTS THE CURRENCY.

If ***protection*** is "a ***war*** upon labor and capital," it must tend to produce those disturbances of the ***currency*** that greatly diminish the returns for both. If, on the contrary, it is a peaceful measure of resistance to a system that tends to oppress the world’s laborers and capitalists, then it must produce that stability of the currency so desired by everyone: the laborer and mechanic, the farmer and planter, the ship-owner and merchant.

The world’s real currency consists of labor and the things for which men are willing to trade labor: food, clothing, fuel, iron, and so on. What is usually called "currency" is merely the standard by which their respective values are measured. The laborer sells a week’s work for five dollars and receives in return five bushels of wheat, also valued at five dollars. The capitalist sells a house for twenty thousand dollars and orders the purchase of a quantity of stock shares which, measured by the same standard, are found to be worth that same number of dollars.

The price of wheat changes with the size of the crop. So does that of—

# THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.

Consider sugar. If the supply of wheat is large and that of sugar is small, a great deal of wheat will be given for a small amount of sugar.

The introduction of a third commodity, which is itself subject to variations in supply—as is the case with money—tends to produce additional variations in the quantity of one commodity that must be exchanged for another. For example, if the supply of money is large among one group of wheat producers and small among another, the sugar producer will sell in the first market and buy in the last. He will obtain much money from the first and give very little to the second.

If all arrangements for the production, purchase, or sale of goods or property were carried out instantly, this cause of disturbance would hardly exist. The prices of everything would be affected similarly, being high when money was plentiful and low when it was scarce. The amount of sugar given for wheat, or wheat for sugar, would depend on the size of the crops almost as much as if no intermediate commodity like money were used. Such, however, is not the case. A merchant buys coffee in January and contracts to pay its value in money in July. By that time, money may be so scarce that six pounds of coffee will buy no more than four pounds would have bought in January. A merchant starts building a ship in July when money is scarce and the price of labor is low, but he finishes it when money is plentiful and wages are high. It ends up costing him ten, fifteen, or twenty percent more than he had calculated. The small trader, on the other hand, who buys and sells from day to day, loses nothing. If he buys at a high price, he sells at a high price; if prices are low when he buys, he lowers them when he sells. The scale of his business is the measure of his profits.

The people who suffer most from such variations are those whose property or business requires them to make arrangements far in advance. They must take the risks associated with changes in the currency throughout the entire period between the start and the finish of a project. This includes all people whose labor results in products not meant for immediate consumption—owners of houses, farms, factories, furnaces, and railroads—everyone, in fact, involved in the improvement of land. In a time of financial pressure in one location, flour, cotton, cloth, and other items intended for daily use can be moved to other places where money is plentiful. Therefore, the changes in their prices are small compared to the changes experienced by those who own property that cannot be moved. This fixed property is forced to bear the full burden of the economic shift. In such cases, land becomes entirely unsaleable except at a massive price reduction, which the owners must accept if they are forced to sell. This is why so many people connected with land and its improvement are ruined by revulsions <note>original: "revulsions"; sudden, violent changes or reactions in the economy, similar to a market crash or panic.</note> that only slightly affect the business of a retail grocer.

The same is true for labor. A man who has a family and finds no demand for his labor cannot easily change his location. He and his family must suffer together. Food may have a *low money-price*, but if he can find no work, the *labour-price* <note>the amount of work or effort required to earn the money to buy goods.</note> is so high that he cannot afford to buy it. Land and labor, then, are especially interested in maintaining a uniform standard by which the products of both are measured. They are the primary victims of the changes that occur over time.

In this respect, time and distance are equivalent to each other. The man who builds a house assumes that the conditions existing at the start will continue until the house is finished. Similarly, the person who sends money to China to buy tea bases his calculations on the state of affairs that existed in that country three months earlier. If money in...

### THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.

In the meantime, as money has become more abundant, a merchant may pay more for his teas than he had calculated. If money becomes less abundant before the teas arrive, he will receive less for them, and thus he will suffer a loss instead of making a profit. The man who grows cotton when he might have grown sugar or wheat bases his calculations on the state of affairs he expects will exist in a foreign country; he is thus forced to add the risks of distance to the risks of time. 

If he exchanged his products with his neighbor, both would be subject to the same variations in the value of the currency. If money were less abundant, flour, sugar, pork, cloth, and iron would feel its effects exactly as cotton felt them. Although he might receive less money, he would have exactly the same quantity of the goods he intended to buy with that money. The proximity of the consumer and the producer, therefore, tends to reduce the difficulties resulting from changes in the currency, from which land and labor are always the primary sufferers.

The object of the <term>colonial system</term> <note>original: "colonial system"; the policy of a mother country controlling the trade of its colonies to its own advantage, often forcing raw materials to be sent to the home country for processing.</note> was to compel the farmers and planters of the world to make their exchanges in a distant market. This increases the *time* during which such risks must be endured, while also adding the risks that result from *distance*. When the <note>original: "Hindoo"; an archaic term for an Indian person or a resident of India.</note> Indian exchanged his cotton on the spot for cloth, the prices of cotton, cloth, and labor were governed by the same circumstances because the exchanges were made instantly. To make those exchanges now, two years' time is required. During that entire period, he is subject to the risk of financial changes like those that marked the years 1847 and 1848 <note>The Panic of 1847 was a major financial collapse in Great Britain caused by a collapse in wheat prices and a burst of the "Railway Mania" bubble.</note>. His livelihood is turned into mere gambling, and he does not even get to hold his own cards, though he is still forced to pay for the losses.

As anyone who studies the system will see, he and his fellow planters *do pay* all those losses. The cotton, wool, sugar, and food of the world are sent to England for exchange. Her people buy and sell instantly; the time required to pass between the purchase of raw wool and the sale of finished yarn does not exceed a single week. If the price of yarn falls, so does the price of cotton. If cotton rises, so does yarn. The entire loss from currency changes resulting from time and distance is thus thrown upon the planter. The entire gain from reducing these risks goes to the owner of the small and easily transported spindle—the cost of which is nothing compared to the cost of the great machine (the land) required to produce the wool.

A nation that seeks to compel all other nations to bring her their products—so they may be measured by her standards—ought to be able to show that her standard of measurement remains unchanged under every circumstance. The standards of weight and length are fixed and unchangeable; the standard of value should be as well. However, the reality is far different. The control of that great and important standard for measuring the world's values is placed in the hands of the Bank of England. Its directors have proven their utter incompetence for this important task by bringing the institution to the brink of bankruptcy four different times within the last thirty years. 

Their goal is to pay out large dividends to shareholders. To accomplish this, money is made "plentiful"—that is, the directors <term>overtrade</term> <note>original: "overtrade"; to engage in excessive commercial activity, specifically by over-extending credit or issuing too much paper currency beyond what is supported by actual capital.</note> significantly. This blocks up the capital of individuals who find themselves forced to accept from the bank "evidences of debt" (certificates of deposit) that do not earn interest. They would have preferred other investments that did earn interest and could have obtained them at reasonable prices if the bank had not begun to overtrade. With every increase of this debt, called deposits, the bank considers itself richer and overtrades even further. Eventually, this produces speculation: railroads are built, and ships and houses are constructed. Then, the day of settlement arrives—

The English businessman, who buys cotton and sells yarn or cloth, suffers little from these changes. At the first sign of a shift, he reduces his working hours or cuts his staff, and then, when the time comes, he closes his factory entirely. His workers are thus, in whole or in part, deprived of wages and rendered unable to purchase food or clothing. The consequence of this is a lower demand and reduced prices for both food and textiles. In this way, all the losses are thrown upon the farmers and planters of the world. They are ruined by their forced dependence on a country that wants to establish a monopoly on the machinery for producing iron and for converting wool into cloth—items these farmers could provide for themselves at a lower cost than they are forced to pay every single year.

***

It is common to blame the disasters of the period from 1836 to 1842 on disruptions in our currency caused by mistakes made here at home; but those who examine the situation more carefully will find that those disruptions were themselves effects resulting from other causes, as I now propose to show.

It is common to speak of capital as money; but money is only the standard by which commodities are measured, and a very small amount of money is enough to measure a large quantity of goods. The same dollar may be used a thousand times in a week, acting each time as the standard by which labor, flour, cotton, sugar, and other goods have been measured. The person who has sold a cargo of sugar has earned a credit with someone, which he can use to obtain a cargo of flour. The person who borrows from a bank has acquired a credit which he transfers to his neighbor, and that neighbor transfers it to a third person, who divides it among his workmen; with that credit, the workers obtain food, clothing, and shelter.

Whenever the daily demand for labor and its products is equal to the daily supply, the rate of interest—or the price of capital looking for investment—will remain stable, which is a great advantage to the owners of land and other fixed capital. However, whenever the daily demand is less than the daily supply for any reason, the accumulation of unemployed capital begins. Fewer houses are built, and as a result, there is less demand for labor. The price of labor falls, and the power to buy food and clothing is diminished. The demand for iron and cotton lessens, and people stop building furnaces and mills, which further diminishes the power to consume food and clothing. 

With each step in this process, there is a tendency for unproductive capital to pile up. One person holds it in the form of iron, another in the form of cloth, a third in the form of idle labor, and a fourth has it in the form of a debt owed to him by a bank that pays him no interest. Gradually, the iron and cloth are sold off to be consumed, and because their owners do not wish to reinvest the profits, they take further credit at the bank, which still pays no interest. In this manner, capital is blocked up, bank deposits accumulate, interest rates necessarily fall, and the prices of existing stocks and bonds rise.

With this rise in price comes a desire to create more investments similar to those that still pay interest, and there is a rush to grab those thought to have greater advantages than others. Speculation begins, and prices skyrocket. Having reached their peak, the downward slide begins. From that point on, the process is rapid, and fortunes disappear in a mo— <note>The text cuts off here, likely continuing "moment" on the next page.</note>

...ment, leaving not even "a wreck behind." <note>original: "a wreck behind"; a reference to Shakespeare’s *The Tempest*, meaning nothing is left.</note> The capitalist, after having been for a long time deprived of interest, now loses the capital itself.

By the laws of 1832 and 1833, railroad iron, French merchandise generally, linens, and other commodities were freed from import duties. Some types of woolen manufactures were reduced to a ten percent tax, and a general reduction was established. This began in 1833 and increased every two years thereafter, until a uniform rate of 20 percent was to be reached.

The passage of these laws diminished the demand for capital to be used in the production of iron. As these laws gradually took effect, there was a decline in the construction of mills. Instead of producing our own iron and cloth, we bought them on credit. Capital accumulated in banks, and the prices of stocks that paid dividends rose. Next, companies were established to build railroads, and States built roads and canals, for which the iron and cloth were purchased on credit. Because it was difficult to employ capital in the East, investors sought opportunities in the South and Southwest. There, the money was used to establish banks and roads, where it was eventually lost forever. 

The day of payment inevitably arrived. The imported iron and cloth had already been consumed, but the certificates of debt given in exchange for them were held by foreign creditors. The banks were heavily in debt to the people whose capital had accumulated in their hands. Being unable to pay, the banks had to stop operations. Thus began a period more disastrous to laborers and owners of <term>fixed capital</term> <note>assets like land, houses, and infrastructure</note> than any the country had ever seen.

An examination of the tables I have provided will show that, during this period, the productive power of the country stood still. Capital was in demand for distant speculation, but for little else. Houses, ships, factories, mills, furnaces, and all other investments that give value to land felt this effect equally. Thus, while the laborer suffered from falling wages, the landowner suffered from the decreasing value of his land. Had the roads and canals built between 1835 and 1839 been based upon American-made cloth and iron, they would have produced nothing but good. However, because they were made with borrowed cloth and borrowed iron, they were accompanied by a general decline in conditions throughout the community, resulting in the disgrace of bankruptcy and <term>repudiation</term> <note>the refusal of a government to pay its debts</note>.

For those who will take the trouble to look below the surface, it is easy to see that the state of things described here is exactly what is happening now. The process currently underway is the same one that brought ruin eight years ago. Companies are obtaining large quantities of English iron by offering securities <note>financial guarantees or bonds</note> that would not be accepted in this country. When the day of <term>defalcation</term> <note>failure to meet a financial obligation; default</note> comes, as it surely must, the cry of "American bankruptcy" will be as common throughout Europe as it was only five years ago. Scarcely a week passes without a notice like the following—*and yet the quantity of iron consumed is less than when it was produced at home and paid for with labor that is now being wasted:*

> “The agent who went to England to purchase iron for the Great-Western Railroad of Illinois has returned in the *Cambria*. He brings proposals to furnish the entire quantity required for the road from Cairo to Chicago, receiving in payment the six percent sterling bonds of the Company, payable in London.”

Capital is said to be abundant, and interest rates are low—at least for those who have unquestionable collateral. The reason for this is that the natural outlets for capital are closed.* Iron is overabundant, so no new furnaces are built. Coal is overabundant, so no new mines are opened. Cotton cloth is overabundant, so no new mills are built. Ships are overabundant, and the building of ships—

***

\* It would be nearly impossible to find a type of investment that creates a demand for labor in which capital could be profitably employed. This is why there is such a universal demand for bank charters <note>legal authorizations to start a bank, often used for speculation rather than production</note>.

He warns that the current trend of borrowing English iron for American railroads is repeating the same dangerous cycle.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Henry Charles Carey’s argument that economic instability is caused by a reliance on foreign trade and debt rather than domestic manufacturing. He argues that when domestic production fails, the value of labor and land inevitably drops.</meta>

# THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.

The number of <term>brigs and schooners</term> <note>original: "brigs, and schooners"; types of two-masted sailing vessels used for trade.</note> is decreasing. We are buying cloth and iron on credit when we should be making them ourselves. Meanwhile, the labor and capital that should be used to produce these goods are searching in vain for work. The people who suffer most, and will continue to suffer, are those tied to labor and land. 

The financial broker still takes his usual <term>shave</term> <note>original: "shave"; a slang term for a commission or a discount taken when cashing a promissory note or bill of exchange.</note> for the notes that pass through his hands, and the grocer still charges his usual cent-per-pound profit on sugar. However, the iron furnace is closed, and with it, the demand for food and labor disappears. The mine is abandoned, leaving the miner without the means to buy clothing. The railroad builder receives no <term>dividends</term> <note>original: "dividend"; a share of the profits paid to stockholders.</note>, and the desire to invest capital in building new roads has vanished. Consequently, the demand for labor, food, and clothing in that sector has also died away. 

Gradually, every interest in the nation must experience these same results. The return on labor is shrinking. The value of land, houses, ships, railroads, and every other type of property depends entirely on the productivity of labor—rising when labor is profitable and falling when it is not.

The closer the consumer and the producer can be brought to each other, the more perfectly production and consumption will balance. This proximity creates a steadier currency and increases the value of both land and labor. The goal of **protection** <note>In this context, Carey refers to "protective tariffs," or taxes on imported goods designed to encourage domestic manufacturing.</note> is to achieve all these objectives. It aims to bring the "loom and the anvil" (industry) to take their natural places alongside the "plow and the harrow" (agriculture), thereby creating a local market for the products of the land.

Of all the commodities used by humanity, none contribute as little to actual comfort or convenience as gold and silver. They are useless for clearing or draining land, building houses or mills, or constructing ships and railroads. They cannot be eaten, drunk, or—to any great extent—worn as clothing. Nevertheless, these are the two items whose arrival and departure are most carefully recorded.

Ten furnaces and rolling mills, capable of producing three million dollars' worth of iron in a year, may close down without a single newspaper mentioning it. Yet, no ship can arrive or depart with fifty thousand dollars in gold without the event being reported in half the newspapers in the country.

The <term>factitious</term> <note>original: "factitious"; artificial or manufactured rather than natural.</note> importance given to precious metals is a result of the **colonial system**. This system demands that all the world's commodities be brought to a single market to be judged by a single standard. Its effect at home has been to force every person to become a seller of almost everything they produce and a buyer of almost everything they consume.* 

"In our social system," says the accomplished traveler Mr. Laing,† "every man buys all he sells and sells all he produces. The very bread of our laborers," he continues, "is often bought at the manufacturer's shop." This system has turned many small landholders into hired laborers who earn only six to nine shillings a week.‡ They live in poor houses in poor villages, where—

---

* "The evil of our economic system is that too many of us live on wages. When masters suffer, the servant starves. When wages stop, the worker has nothing to fall back on. When he needs to eat, he must buy everything—and if his wages have stopped, what does he buy with? But the 'seed-time and harvest' of the <term>spade husbandman</term> <note>original: "spade husbandman"; a small-scale farmer who works his own land manually rather than as a hired hand.</note> never fail him. He may lose one crop, but something is always left. When pests eat his wheat, he can kill them, or plant cabbages, barley, or vetches instead. The cow will give her milk whether ports are open or <term>interest rates</term> <note>original: "discounts are raised"; referring to the central bank raising the cost of borrowing money.</note> are high. If you take labor out of the overcrowded market and put it on the land, wages rise. The great body of consumers then has more money to pay for goods, and manufacturers and tradesmen flourish because of cheap food and better wages. The farmer’s taxes are reduced, and the landlord gets a better rent for his land." —*The Mother Country, by Sidney Smith.*

† *Notes of a Traveler*, page 152, American edition.         ‡ See pages 113—117, *above*.

<summary>Carey argues that true economic prosperity comes from connecting domestic agriculture and industry ("the plow and the loom") rather than relying on the "colonial system" of international trade and gold markets. He warns that when a nation relies on wages and foreign goods, laborers and landowners are the first to suffer during economic shifts.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Henry Charles Carey’s argument for localizing trade. He argues that the closer producers and consumers are, the less they depend on expensive middlemen and the volatile fluctuations of the gold market.</meta>

# THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.

...they are forced to waste much of the time that would, under a different system, be used with immense advantage to themselves and others.

A man who exchanges food and labor directly with his neighbor for coal or iron has little need for money. He exchanges labor for labor. If the account does not balance perfectly, it is often settled by transferring the difference to the credit of another person. In this way, every community where people work together establishes a type of <term>clearing house</term> <note>original: "clearing house"; a central office where merchants or banks settle debts and exchange credits rather than using physical cash for every transaction.</note>, which is just as effective as the famous one in London.

A man who sends his cotton to Liverpool <note>Liverpool, England, was the primary global hub for the American cotton trade in the 19th century.</note> or Lowell <note>Lowell, Massachusetts, was a major center for American textile manufacturing.</note> trades entirely for money. He wants to know how much gold he can get for a <term>bale</term> <note>original: "bale"; a large bound bundle of cotton, typically weighing about 500 pounds.</note>, and how much iron he can buy for a pound of gold. He must use financial machinery that the local traders can do without.

Anything that increases the amount of machinery required to achieve a specific result also increases the friction and the power needed to make it work. That is the case here. The *necessity* of using gold introduces a new and powerful cause of disruption for the <term>planter</term> <note>original: "planter"; here referring to a large-scale farmer, typically in the American South, who grew cash crops like cotton.</note> and greatly increases his costs, thereby increasing friction and reducing his profits. Gold and silver coins are reduced in weight by <term>abrasion</term> <note>original: "abrasion"; the wearing away of the surface of metal coins as they pass from hand to hand, which reduces their actual value.</note>, and *the producer and the consumer pay for all this loss*. The <term>exchanger</term> <note>original: "exchanger"; a middleman, banker, or broker who facilitates trade but does not produce physical goods.</note> pays nothing. He lives at their expense.

Twenty-five years ago, we valued gold and silver highly, because we were—

***

* "One primary cause of the extraordinary productivity of land managed by small farmers is that most or all of the cultivators have a direct interest in the success of their work; they work for themselves, and therefore with a passion that cannot be expected from hired laborers. Every farmer could, however, make his servants almost as dedicated by changing how they are paid. If, instead of receiving a fixed wage, they were entitled to a certain portion of the crops, they would strive to make the crops as plentiful as possible. . . . Nothing more is needed to solve <term>over-population</term> than to make people comfortable, and to make that comfort depend on their own efforts."—*Thornton on Over-population*.

† These are the "protective societies" established in New England, in which workers supply themselves with the various goods they need. They wish to avoid using the services of the middleman as much as possible, as common sense would teach everyone to do. I have taken the following paragraph, which illustrates this movement, from a current newspaper:

> "Mr. Kaulback, the purchasing agent for several protective unions in New England, has paid $102,000 for goods for the quarter ending January 1, 1850. This is an increase of about $23,000 over the previous three months. This is an important branch of trade that has recently grown up among us, all the more so because it is a cash business and credit is never requested. There are now 109 union cash stores actively operating in New England, nearly all of which are stocked by the agent named above."—*Boston paper*.

One of the most remarkable cases of cooperative action is currently being reported in the newspapers. Captain George Kimball decided to build a ship in a remote district of Maine. Alone, without partners or capital, in a forest far from deep water, he began his noble project. He was soon joined by one man; in a few weeks, others followed. Women contributed food, and farmers sent in cattle which were traded for shipbuilding materials. The unusual nature of the project attracted workers from far away, and experienced shipbuilders and carpenters arrived to contribute their strength and skill. Everyone who helped—men, women, or children—received a proportionate share of ownership in the ship. The work began last April, and in November she was launched: a magnificent ship of more than six hundred tons, named the *California Packet*. She is now in Boston with her owners and builders on board, as she is now their home. We do not need to say that the men and women of this company are examples of our New England population of whom we can be proud.—*Boston Transcript*.

# THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.

...we were then forced to export it [the gold]. Under the <term>Tariff of 1828</term> <note>original: "Tariff of 1828"; a high protective tariff designed to protect American industry from foreign competition.</note>, we imported gold, and at that time, it was hardly a concern. Under the <term>Compromise Tariff</term> <note>original: "Compromise"; the Tariff of 1833, which gradually lowered duties, leading to the Panic of 1837.</note>, the demand for coin became so great that the country went bankrupt, and a desperate scramble for gold followed. Under the protective <term>Tariff of 1842</term>, we imported a large amount of gold, and the issue stopped worrying the public. Under the <term>Tariff of 1846</term> <note>original: "Tariff of 1846"; also known as the Walker Tariff, it significantly lowered rates toward a free-trade model.</note>, we have exported a great deal of gold and have fallen deeply into debt, setting the stage for another crisis. When that crisis arrives, gold will be sought after just as desperately as it was before 1842.

One sign of the wastefulness of our current system is the obsession with increasing the number of places where gold is weighed and stamped—called <term>mints</term>. A mint neither increases the amount of gold nor improves its quality, yet there is now a proposal to spend $600,000 or $800,000 to build more of them, even though we already have more than we need. The goal is supposedly to save on shipping costs and interest. However, if the government were to buy raw gold in New York at full price and then pay for its transportation itself, the cost of shipping and interest wouldn't even equal half of what we pay in salaries to mint officials. If that same capital were spent on building iron furnaces, it could build enough to *produce* iron worth more than half of all the gold and silver coined in the year 1848, which totaled $4,450,000. It is time for the nation's farmers and <term>planters</term> <note>original: "planters"; large-scale farmers, primarily in the South, who grew cash crops for export.</note> to look into these matters for themselves, because they are the ones who suffer when capital is wasted.

Clear proof that the people of Great Britain and Ireland are losing the ability to afford the comforts of life can be found in the following data. It shows the quantity of gold and silver <term>plate</term> <note>original: "plate"; household items like spoons, forks, and dishes made of solid precious metals.</note> officially stamped during these periods:

| Year | Population | Gold-plate ounces | Silver-plate ounces | Value of bullion per head |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1801–10 | 17,000,000 | 5,471 | 1,015,147 | 6.5 cents |
| 1810–29 | 21,000,000 | 6,926 | 1,209,616 | 6.75 cents |
| 1839–47 | 28,000,000 | 7,011 | 1,118,550 | 4.45 cents |

The last thirty years have seen a series of laws passed to force the public to use more gold and silver. Yet, as this system has expanded, the people's ability to buy from the men who mine those metals has declined by nearly a third. The market for the miner is shrinking, just like the market for the planter.

As a person's *needs* decrease, their *power* constantly increases. Having a local iron furnace or a mill reduces his need to travel to a distant market, while the prosperity it creates provides him with the roads to go there whenever he pleases. Ships bring immigrants to eat the local food and wear the local cotton; the money earned from their passage helps lower the cost of sending food and cotton to other countries. The same is true of gold. The closer we bring the consumer and the producer together, the less we *need* gold for trade, and the more *power* we have to actually acquire it. The <term>Tariff of 1846</term> does the opposite: it increases our *need* for gold while making it harder to get, because it lowers the value of both land and labor.

He also criticizes the wasteful expansion of government mints, suggesting the funds would be better spent on industrial infrastructure like iron furnaces.</summary>

# CHAPTER 18.

## HOW PROTECTION AFFECTS THE FRIENDS OF PEACE.

The more spades and plows used, the greater the return on labor. The more perfectly peace is maintained, the greater the number of people who can employ themselves with spades and plows; the increase in production will be more rapid, and the rewards for both the laborer and the capitalist will be larger.

The more swords and muskets used, the smaller the return on labor must be. The more wars are fought, the greater the number of people who must employ themselves with swords and muskets; the increase in production will be slower, and the rewards for the laborer and the capitalist will be smaller.

Protectionism is sometimes said to be a "war upon labor and capital." If that were true, it would naturally tend to promote actual war. We are urged to adopt measures to maintain the *English monopoly system* <note>Carey refers to the British economic policy of "Free Trade," which he argues was designed to keep other nations as mere suppliers of raw materials for British factories.</note>, and we are assured that by doing so, we will help establish peace. To prove that this would be the result, it would be necessary to show that the colonial system has historically helped achieve that great goal of peace.

However, if we examine the causes of most of the wars of the last 150 years, we find they have been driven by a desire to possess colonies whose people could be forced to become "customers," and thus taxed to support the country that ruled them. France held Canada and desired the territory west of the Mississippi; she held islands in the West Indies and wanted more. England held some and wanted more. France and England were both in India, and to settle the question of which nation should tax the entire region, that country was devastated by the marches of rival armies over many years. France had colonies to lose, which led to the war of 1793. France wanted colonies in the Mediterranean, which led to the breaking of the <term>Peace of Amiens</term> <note>original: "peace of Amiens"; a brief peace treaty (1802–1803) between France and Britain during the Napoleonic Wars.</note> and the series of wars that ended at Waterloo. Since then, we have seen a succession of wars in India to extend British power over Ceylon, Siam, Afghanistan, <term>Scinde</term> <note>Modern-day Sindh, Pakistan.</note>, and the <term>Punjaub</term> <note>Modern-day Punjab.</note>.

The primary goal of the war with China was to force her to open her ports to foreign trade, and it was considered a "righteous enterprise" to force the poor Chinese to open their eyes to the "blessings of free trade" <note>This refers to the First Opium War (1839–1842), where Britain forced China to allow the importation of opium.</note>. In South Africa, the war with the <term>Caffres</term> <note>original: "Caffres"; a historical term for the Xhosa people. The "Caffre Wars" or Xhosa Frontier Wars were a series of conflicts between the Xhosa Kingdom and European settlers/the British Empire.</note> has cost millions. France, not wanting to be outdone, seized Tahiti and deposed its queen; currently, she makes war on the poor <term>Sandwich Islanders</term> <note>The native people of Hawaii.</note> because they will not allow her to do with brandy what England did in China with opium. One part of the English nation sells gunpowder to the people of Africa to help them wage wars to take prisoners who are sold as slaves, while another part of the nation watches the coast to ensure those slaves are not transported to Cuba or Brazil. This hunger for colonies has caused the waste of hundreds of thousands of lives and hundreds of millions of dollars on the worthless territory of Algeria. It is the same everywhere: the desperate drive for trade stimulates nations to take actions that impoverish and destroy their fellow humans.

The ability to wage war depends on how human life is valued. Russia goes to war easily because men are considered cheap there. France maintains large armies at a low cost. The East India Company’s army consists of hundreds of thousands of men because men in India are cheap. Belgium supports only a small army because human life is more valuable there. England is burdened by the cost of her fleets and armies because wages are higher there than on the European continent; she is therefore forced to rely on voluntary enlistment. If the value of men could be raised, she would be forced to do away with her fleets and—

<sig>25</sig>

<summary>Carey argues that the global "free trade" system, or the British colonial model, is the primary driver of war as nations fight to secure exclusive markets. He contrasts this with protectionism, which he believes increases the value of human labor and promotes peace by reducing the need for foreign conquest.</summary>

armies, and the necessity for colonies would cease to exist. Throughout the world, armies have been large where men were held of small account, and throughout history, men have tended to become less valuable as armies became more numerous.

The cause of war is to be found in the diminished or diminishing productivity of labor, as our own experience shows. The increasing difficulty of obtaining the means of support from 1835 to 1842 produced a scattering of people that led to the war in Florida <note>The Second Seminole War (1835–1842), a costly conflict between the U.S. and the Seminole people.</note>, the occupation of Texas and Oregon, the diplomatic friction with Great Britain, the war with Mexico, and the occupation of California. This last event is now leading us into discussions with Great Britain about the rights of the Miskito King <note>original: "Mosquito king." The British claimed a protectorate over the Miskito Coast in modern-day Nicaragua, which conflicted with U.S. interests in a potential canal route.</note>, which, if not for the migration to California, would interest us little more than would the rights of the King of Bantam <note>An Indonesian sultanate; Carey uses this as an example of a remote and irrelevant foreign power.</note>. The colonial system is for us, as it is for all, the path to war, because it tends to diminish the value of labor and land.

When we look at the internal condition of those nations that, out of an anxiety for "ships, colonies, and commerce," have been constantly engaged in wars, we find a scene of universal discord. Louis Philippe <note>The King of the French from 1830 to 1848.</note> maintained fleets and armies, engaged at one time in the conquest of Algeria, and at others in the seizure of Tahiti and similar enterprises elsewhere. The unproductive class increased in numbers, and the burden to be borne by the productive class increased in weight until the explosion of 1848 <note>The Revolutions of 1848, a series of political upheavals throughout Europe.</note>, followed by the barricading of towns and a series of disturbances. These events created a need to increase even further the number of unproductive consumers—men carrying muskets—required to maintain internal peace. England maintains large fleets and armies for the protection of commerce and colonies, and her whole empire is a "scene of violent commotion." At home, we see her Chartists <note>A working-class movement for political reform in Britain that existed from 1838 to 1857.</note> attempting revolution; in Ireland, massive demonstrations and efforts at separation followed by appeals to arms; in Canada, efforts at revolution followed by the current determination to achieve a peaceful separation; in the West Indies, universal discord between employers and employees; in India, perpetual difficulties; and everywhere, a necessity for maintaining large armies to keep internal peace. In other words, these armies exist to prevent those who have property from being plundered by those who have none, and to enable those who are strong to tax those who are weak.

With the gradual decline in the productive power of the people of England, we see an increase in discord between employers and employees. Strikes are becoming more numerous and are accompanied by more serious results; the destruction of buildings and machinery is now added to the damage resulting from long suspensions of work. In Scotland, the population of entire districts is expelled to make way for sheep <note>Referring to the Highland Clearances, where tenants were evicted so landlords could use the land for large-scale sheep farming.</note>, while other districts show signs of violent unrest similar to those seen in the lands further south. In Ireland, we see a scene of almost universal war: the landowner in one place expelling his tenants and destroying their houses, while in thousands of other places, tenants are seen carrying off and hiding their crops to avoid paying rent.

If we look at home, we see similar events resulting from every attempt to tear down the barrier of protection and harmonize our system with the one that has produced the ruin of the British colonies. At no period of our history has there been such universal discord between employers and employees as during the last few years of the Compromise Act <note>The Compromise Tariff of 1833, which gradually reduced U.S. tariffs and was blamed by protectionists for subsequent economic instability.</note>. The productivity of labor was, as we have seen, gradually diminishing, and employers were unable to pay employees such wages as would allow them to afford the same comforts and conveniences they had enjoyed before. The year that has now closed has been marked by this same state of affairs.

# THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.

Throughout the coal region, as labor became less productive, tensions rose. At one time, we had strikes <note>original: "turn-outs"; collective withdrawals of labor</note> among coal operators, and at another among miners and laborers; the result has been that the year was one of almost total loss.

If we compare this with the period between 1844 and 1847, we see in the latter a steady increase in productivity, accompanied by a growing harmony between employers and employees—the natural result of improved living conditions.

The exhaustion resulting from maintaining the colonial system <note>Carey uses this term to describe the British economic policy of forcing colonies to export raw materials and import finished goods, which he argues impoverishes the producer.</note> thus produces a tendency toward social unrest and radicalism. This necessitates the maintenance of large armies, which leads to further exhaustion; all these harmful results are borne by labor and land. Consumption cannot exceed production. Therefore, whatever decreases the ratio of workers (those who produce) to the mouths that must be fed and backs that must be clothed diminishes the share of food and clothing that falls to each person. England now collects almost seventy million pounds in taxes, much of which is required simply to pay the officials employed to collect the remaining millions that go into the treasury. To these millions raised by the State, we must now add eight million for the support of the one-ninth of the English population who are paupers, and many more millions for the support of the paupers in Ireland. 

Here is a burden of over four hundred million dollars, the entire weight of which must be carried by the labor and land of England and the world—and ultimately by her land alone. People can flee, but the land cannot. The power to pay rent depends upon the power to make the land produce. Just as productivity increases with an increase in population and an improvement in the physical, *moral*, and intellectual condition of the laborer, it diminishes as population declines and conditions deteriorate. 

In the three years ending with 1845, the consumption of domestic and colonial spirits <note>distilled alcohol</note> amounted to 23,422,295 gallons.
In the three years ending with 1848, it was 25,326,861* gallons.

This shows a tendency toward drunkenness increasing as the power to obtain a suitable reward for labor decreases.

Social decay produces poverty, and poverty increases social decay; these impoverished alcoholics must be supported out of the products of the land. The surplus grain of Russia has reduced farming in Ireland and has, of course, reduced production there. England is now overrun with Irish laborers and paupers, and what has happened in Ireland must eventually follow in England. More grain will continue to be imported and more cotton goods will be exported; however, the products of the land—from which rent and taxes must be paid—will diminish. While the number of mouths to be fed will increase, the quantity of food available to feed them will continue to decrease. 

The Corn Laws <term>Protectionist tariffs on imported grain in Great Britain, repealed in 1846</term> constituted the barrier used by English landowners against the effects of the system by which England was devaluing labor and land throughout the world. Their abolition tends to bring these negative effects daily more and more upon the landowners themselves. The only remedy is to be found in the abolition of the colonial system and the dismantling of the fleets and armies that its existence requires. A reduction in "unproductive consumers" (such as soldiers and tax collectors) will be followed by an increase in productive workers. England’s exports will then again represent home-grown food, exchanged for sugar, tea, coffee, and cotton. With every step in that direction, the necessity for taxes will diminish, and the power to pay them will increase.

If we look at our own country, we see a tendency toward an increase in the necessity for taxation—

<summary>Carey argues that the British economic system causes social decay, evidenced by rising pauperism and alcohol consumption, and claims that only by ending the "colonial system" can land and labor become productive again.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Henry Charles Carey’s argument that government spending and the risk of war increase when the United States abandons protectionist policies in favor of the British "colonial system" of free trade.</meta>

# THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.

We see a decline in stability with every step toward subjection to the colonial system <note>original: "colonial system"; Carey’s term for the British economic policy of forcing other nations to export raw materials and import finished goods</note>, and a reduced tendency toward instability as we move in the opposite direction. The expenses of the government under the administration of James Monroe averaged thirteen million dollars. Those of the John Quincy Adams administration averaged a little over twelve million. During the existence of the Tariff of 1828, and in the early period of the Compromise Tariff, we find expenditures maintained at thirteen million. 

However, as the population began to scatter, we arrived at the Florida War <note>A series of conflicts (1817–1858) between the U.S. and the Seminole people; the Second Seminole War (1835–1842) was famously expensive</note>, with expenditures reaching thirty, thirty-seven, and thirty-three million dollars in three successive years. Afterward, spending fell gradually until it reached twenty million dollars in the period from 1843 to 1844. With the adoption of free-trade doctrines, we see an increasing tendency toward war, and expenditures rising to sixty million dollars. 

Looking at all these facts, it is difficult to reach any other conclusion than that protection tends to increase the demand for spades and plows—and thus the reward for labor—while diminishing the demand for swords and muskets, which leads to the destruction of both the laborer and the plow. Therefore, any friend of peace is directly interested in the destruction of the English monopoly on machinery.

If protection were truly a "war" upon labor and capital, we would expect to see it accompanied by diminished production and increased government spending. If, on the contrary, it is what its name implies—protection for both the laborer and the capitalist—then it should lead to increased production and diminished spending. 

We now have the facts before us. While the government from 1824 to 1833 was administered at a cost of about one dollar per person, the cost of administration rose during the free-trade period to more than two dollars. It fell again to one dollar during the period of protection and has risen to almost three dollars in the current free-trade period.* 

Protection looks homeward. Free trade, under existing circumstances, looks abroad; it requires fleets and armies with hosts of officers, large custom-houses and warehouses, branch mints in California and New York, and countless <term>ministers plenipotentiary and chargés</term> <note>high-ranking diplomatic representatives and their subordinates</note> abroad, along with a multitude of officers at home—all to be supported by the proceeds of labor and land. The one policy seeks a cheap and efficient government; the other seeks a "splendid" one, which is profitable to those who govern but fatal to those who are governed.

We have seen that under protection, the value of labor at home has increased, and with it, there has been an increase in the power to consume foreign goods that we do not produce ourselves. We have also seen that while protection tends to increase immigration from abroad, it also makes it easier to ship our bulky goods to Europe by enabling us to send them at very low freight rates. Thus, while protection raises the value of labor throughout the world by reducing the number of people desperately seeking employment, it also raises labor's value by enabling those who remain abroad to obtain sugar, cotton, coffee, and other Western products at a lower cost. 

The way to promote harmony among nations, and within nations, is to increase the value of the human being. This has been, and must continue to be, the result of protection. Once that object is accomplished, the need for custom-houses—whether for protection or for tax revenue—will cease.

***

The man who contributes to the support of war makes war, and if he does so voluntarily, he is accountable for the resulting damage and deterioration...

Estimating this land at the government price of $1.25 an acre, we reach a total of $17,230,000.

# THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.

...destruction of his fellow men. Of all the people in the world, none have contributed as much as we have to the maintenance of the fleets and armies by which Ireland has been ruined, and by which war has been carried throughout Europe and Asia. To the extent that we have done this voluntarily, we are just as responsible for the destruction of life and property in China, Sindh <note>original: "Scinde"; a province in modern-day Pakistan annexed by the British in 1843</note>, Afghanistan, and the Punjab <note>original: "Punjaub"; a region in South Asia annexed by the British in 1849 after the Sikh Wars</note> as the men who ordered these things to be done.

We have seen that although England produces little for export, she is still able to consume a great deal. The producer receives very little for his cotton, yet the laborer receives very little clothing for the time he spends converting that cotton into cloth. The sugar planter receives very little iron for his sugar, yet the miner has very little sugar for his labor. The tobacco grower has very little cloth for his product, but the spinner can consume very little tobacco. 

The reason for all this is found in the fact that a host of middlemen stands between the consumer and the producer. The greatest of these is the government, which collects taxes to be paid out for the support of fleets and armies. Every pound of cotton that travels on an English railway contributes its share to the £108,000 in taxes paid by the London and North-Western Railway alone, or the £68,000 paid by the Great Western, or some other of the immense sums paid by other railways. Every pound of tobacco pays 3 shillings <note>approximately 72 cents at the time</note> toward the maintenance of the fleets and armies of Great Britain. This is in addition to its share of the taxes on warehouses, bills of exchange, promissory notes, and the thousand other taxes paid by the various people who stand between the producer and the consumer. These men produce nothing themselves, and their taxes must be paid for them by the land and labor that *do* produce—whether that production is foreign or domestic.

England is now the great warmongering power of the world. It is through her monopoly on the machinery for producing iron and converting cotton into cloth that she is able to tax the world to maintain her fleets and armies for the prosecution of those wars. To destroy her power to make war would be to bring about peace. Protectionism tends to limit her power to tax the farmers and planters of the world, and thus limits her power to raise revenue for the payment of soldiers and sailors. At the same time, it tends to raise the value of individual human beings, making soldiers and sailors more costly to hire. In both ways, it tends to diminish the power to maintain fleets and armies and promotes the maintenance of peace. Every friend of peace is therefore bound to work for the destruction of this *monopoly system*.

The London *Times* recently published, with approval, a letter from the East Indies written by a British officer engaged in the Battle of Gujrat <note>original: "Goodjerat"; a decisive 1849 battle in the Second Anglo-Sikh War</note>. The following is an extract from it. It deserves the careful consideration of every man who has previously helped maintain this system:

> "The enemy were in the sands trying to escape, and our men were *knocking them over like dogs*. . . Some of our men screamed out, '*They are off!*' Fordyce’s troops went off at a gallop, our men giving them three cheers—such cheers—*it was a perfect scream of delight and eagerness!* And you may be sure I assisted and yelled until I was hoarse! . . . Every wounded Sikh was either shot or bayoneted (!!) . . . I rushed up with a few of the grenadiers and found four men reloading their pieces; three were bayoneted, *and I was hacking away at the head of the fourth* when Compton, of the grenadiers, shot him."
