## CHAPTER NINETEENTH.

### HOW PROTECTION AFFECTS THE EXCHANGER.

The middleman <note>original: "exchanger"</note> stands between the producer and the consumer. He produces nothing himself, although he consumes much, and in return for his consumption, he only provides services. He buys a bale of cloth and divides it among consumers—giving a piece to one and a yard to another—but he makes no change in the quantity or quality of the goods that pass through his hands. The bale of cloth would clothe just as many men, and the cargo of flour would feed just as many, without his services as with them. Nevertheless, the middleman takes a higher rank than the producer. The merchants of London, New York, and Boston have more influence over government actions and public opinion than twenty, fifty, or even one hundred times the number of men whose every hour is dedicated to increasing the quantity and improving the quality of things necessary for human use.

The reason this is the case is that the current system of trade tends to increase the need for producers to travel to distant markets, while simultaneously diminishing their power to do so. When the iron producer takes his place alongside the food producer, the farmer exchanges his potatoes, cabbages, veal, milk, and butter directly with the ironworker, obtaining his iron at a low cost of labor. This enables the farmer to improve his wagon and his roads and to go to market cheaply, thereby increasing his capabilities while diminishing his needs. The more distant the consumer and the producer are from each other, the more machinery of exchange <note>referring to the infrastructure of trade, such as shipping, middleman networks, and long-distance transport</note> is required, and the poorer its quality must be. Every such change in this direction tends to impoverish the farmer and the planter.

Since this is the case, one might suppose there is a conflict of interests here. It might seem that middlemen would suffer from the adoption of measures that bring consumers and producers closer together. However, the exact opposite is true. The quantity of goods to be exchanged depends on the size of the *surplus* produced, and that surplus increases with incredible speed as the power of production increases. A man who produces no more food than is absolutely necessary for his own consumption has nothing to exchange for cloth or iron. Once he is fed, he can exchange his entire surplus, whatever it may be. Therefore, the volume of exchange increases with wonderful rapidity when production increases, as was the case from 1843 to 1847.

The larger the return on labor applied to production, the less necessity there is to seek employment in the work of exchange, which leads to less competition in trade. Our cities are filled with young men from the country who would have remained at home with their parents and friends if a cotton or wool factory, a furnace, or a rolling mill had been there to provide them with employment. Because those industries were not there, they have been forced to join the already nearly infinite number of clerks, hoping—often in vain—to obtain stores or shops of their own. By bringing the consumer to the side of the producer, these young men would, in the future, remain at home to join the ranks of the producers. This would increase total production, enabling every middleman to conduct a larger volume of business and grow rich with the same commission rate that currently keeps him poor.

<summary>Carey argues that while middlemen (merchants) currently hold disproportionate power, they actually benefit from protectionist policies that promote local manufacturing, as increased production creates a larger surplus for trade and reduces job competition in cities.</summary>
<keywords>middlemen, exchangers, producers, consumers, protectionism, trade surplus, economic harmony, urban migration, machinery of exchange</keywords>

# THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.

It is claimed that four-fifths of all the people engaged in trade in our cities eventually fail. The cause is found in the fact that so many people are forced into trade because they are unable to find work in production <note>original: "production"; here referring to manufacturing and farming</note>. Once they enter the trading sector, they are exposed to the massive economic shifts caused by the English monopoly system. For example, the price of iron may be ten pounds at one moment and fall to five pounds soon after. A small-scale merchant who has stock on hand is ruined by such a drop. The prices of cottons and woollens change in the same way. At one moment, England wants to sell iron and cloth in exchange for certificates of debt <note>original: "certificates of debt"; government or corporate bonds and credit</note>, and money is said to be "plentiful." At the next moment, England demands to be paid in cash, and money becomes scarce. The small capitalist is ruined by these fluctuations. Consequently, our cities are filled with men who tried their hand at trade and went bankrupt.

In England, these disastrous effects are felt even more widely. The country is full of young men anxious to find work in any branch of trade, because there is no demand for their time or talents in production unless they already possess large amounts of capital. The result is a perpetual struggle to obtain even the basic means of survival among shopmen, clerks, and laborers, while constant market changes bring ruin to their employers at short intervals. Over the last three years, a large number of the major trading firms in the United Kingdom have disappeared. The public records of their financial failures provide conclusive proof of how ruinous this system is. In Liverpool, at one time, there were 7,000 houses and stores sitting empty. What had become of the people who once lived and worked in them?

The tendency of this entire system is to create a *necessity* for trade while simultaneously diminishing the *power* to maintain it. In that system, "Commerce is king," and like other kings, he is exhausting his own subjects. Having plundered and ruined India, the West Indies, Ireland, Portugal, and all other countries under his control, he is now doing the same at home. With every step, he reduces the ability to apply labor to production and increases the need to look to trade as the only way to employ time, talent, or capital—all while the returns for everyone continue to shrink. This is why so many people in the United Kingdom want to escape to other lands where Commerce is treated as an equal to agriculture and manufacturing, rather than as their king. In his proper place, Commerce is extremely useful, but as a master, he has always proven to be a worse tyrant than any recorded even in the history of Ancient Rome. 

The goal of the colonial system was to make Commerce the master, and its effects are now felt both at home and abroad. The goal of protection <note>original: "protection"; the economic policy of using tariffs to support domestic industry</note> is to end this tyranny and return Commerce to its proper role. Among all people, there are none whose interests would be better served by this than those currently engaged in commerce. This is because protection will increase the total amount of goods being exchanged without causing a matching increase in the number of middlemen <note>original: "exchangers"</note> competing for the work.

The curriers <note>original: "curriers"; workers who process and color tanned leather</note> and leather-dressers are in the same situation. ## CHAPTER TWENTIETH.

### HOW PROTECTION AFFECTS WOMAN.

With every increase in the value of labor and land, the condition of women is improved. With every improvement in her condition, she has more leisure to devote to the care of her children and to preparing them to worthily fill their place in society, which in turn gives more value to labor and land. If protection were truly "a war upon labor and capital," it would lead to a decrease in the value of labor and land and to the worsening of the condition of the weaker sex. Let us now examine how far that is actually the case.

Throughout a large portion of this country, women's time is treated as almost entirely worthless. They would gladly work if they could, but there is no employment available except for farm work, for which they are not physically suited. If we were to place a mill in every county of the United States, it would create a demand for this currently surplus labor. The women working in those mills would obtain more and better food and clothing; they would be able to afford education and books to improve their minds and prepare them for their future roles as mothers. 

For want of local employment, young men are forced to move to the cities or flee to the West. Consequently, thousands and tens of thousands of women remain at home unmarried. Meanwhile, thousands of others also head to the cities in search of work and end up finishing their careers as prostitutes. This happens because they are unable to compete with the "cheap" labor of the unhappy subjects described in the following article, which I have taken from a newspaper of the day:

> "The <term>distressed needle-women</term><note>original: "distressed needle-women"; seamstresses living in extreme poverty in Victorian London, often working in sweatshop conditions</note> of London have been the subject of a commission of inquiry established by the *Morning Chronicle*. Three gentlemen well known in literature have examined the state of this unfortunate class. Their finding is that there lives in London a group of about 33,000 women permanently at the point of starvation, working for wages of only a few pence a day.
>
> "The majority of these poor creatures, living as they do far outside the traditional social order, resort to prostitution as a means of supplementing their miserable income. Whenever the pressure of poverty threatens their very existence, they turn to the streets; thus, poverty runs into inevitable vice. Since the disclosures of the *Morning Chronicle*, many humanitarian people have sent considerable sums of money to that journal’s office to be distributed among the most needy; and Mr. Sidney Herbert has come forward to found a society to promote their emigration. There are about half a million more women than men in Great Britain, while there is a corresponding excess of males in the British Australian colonies. The society mentioned above aims to bring these marriageable parties together. It is hoped that once it is operating, the government will assist it with funds. It costs about £15 to transport one passenger to Australia. Now, if private charity raises £30,000, this will only relieve 2,000 sufferers—a mere fraction of the whole, whose absence would hardly be noticed in the city. It would require ten times that amount to export the misery to the necessary extent and also satisfy the needs of the colonists."

"Commerce is king," and these are his female subjects. Everyone who is forced to compete with them must fall to this same level. Such are the results even now as we approach a system that views the maintenance of the English monopoly as "freedom of trade." The compensation for female labor is miserably small even now, but it must fall much lower when we are eventually called upon to settle our accounts for the small amount of iron, wool, silk, and earthenware we receive in exchange for all our cotton, tobacco, rice, flour, pork, cheese, butter, and <term>certificates of debt</term><note>original: "evidences of debt"; bonds and IOUs used to pay for imports when exports did not cover the cost</note>.

unto them, “Be fruitful and multiply, and replenish the earth and subdue it.”

Such was the first command of God to man on earth, and, as he does or does not comply with it, he is found to be a moral or immoral being. If the association of man with his fellow man tends to the elevation of character and to the promotion of civilization, how much more is this the result of that intimate association resulting from obedience to the command, “Be fruitful and multiply.” The relation of husband and wife, and that of parent and child, are both essential to the development of all that is good, kind, gentle, and thoughtful. The desire to provide for the wife and the child prompts the husband to labor—both to acquire the means for present support and to practice economy as a means of preparation for the future. The desire to provide for the husband and the children prompts the wife to exertions that would otherwise have been deemed impossible, and to sacrifices that none but a wife or a mother could make.

The modern school of political economy <note>This refers to the "Malthusian" school of thought, named after Thomas Malthus, who argued that population growth would inevitably outpace food production unless restricted.</note> says, “Be not fruitful; do not multiply. Population tends to increase faster than food.” It prescribes disobedience to the earliest of God’s commands. Obedience to this command among those who are poor is denounced as improvidence <note>original: "improvidence"; a lack of foresight or failure to save for the future.</note>. For those who are so reckless as to marry “with no provision for the future, and no sure and ample support even for the present,” this school thinks it “important to pronounce distinctly that, on no principle of social right or justice, have they any claim to share the earnings or the savings of their more prudent, more energetic, more self-denying fellow-citizens.”* To have a wife for whom to labor, and with whom to enjoy the fruits of labor, is treated as a luxury; abstinence from marriage is placed high among the virtues. To have children, which develops all the kindly and provident feelings of the parents, is treated as a crime worthy of punishment. Charity is denounced because it tends to promote the growth of the population. To rent land at less than the full market price is seen as an error because it tends to increase the number of people to be fed. To clear the land of thousands whose ancestors have lived and died on the spot is called “improvement.” Small cottage allotments are viewed merely as places for breeding paupers.

The fact that any feelings of kindness toward those who are so unfortunate as to be poor still remain in England is due to the fact that those who teach this doctrine do not have enough faith in it to actually practice what they preach.

The direct tendency of the existing monopoly of machinery—which it is the object of *free trade* to maintain—is toward barbarism. It drives hundreds of thousands of Englishmen to abandon their mothers, wives, and sisters, and to become like barbarians in the wilderness. This would have happened long ago if not for the existence of this most unnatural system.

## CHAPTER TWENTY-FIRST.

### HOW PROTECTION AFFECTS MORALS.

The moral man is conscious of the duties he owes to his wife, his children, society, and himself. He frequents neither taverns nor gambling houses. His place is at home.

The more perfect the morality of a community, the more productive its labor will be, and the greater the power of its members to improve their moral and intellectual condition. If protection were truly "a war upon labor and capital," it would inevitably lead to the decline of morality and the reduction of the rewards for work.

The more equal the balance between the sexes in a community, the greater the opportunity for people to marry, which leads to higher morality. The monopoly system <note>original: "monopoly system"; the author’s term for the British system of free trade, which he argued created a global monopoly on manufacturing for England.</note> tends to drive men away and produce an inequality in the number of men and women. This diminishes the ability of people to marry, thereby creating a tendency toward immorality. The object of protection is to enable men to remain at home and thus bring about a balance between the sexes—an equality that cannot exist where there is a constant pressure for people to scatter and emigrate.

The more men are able to remain at home, the better they can fulfill their duties to their children. The monopoly system tends to force them to conduct their trade in distant markets and to separate themselves from their wives and children. The goal of protection is to bring the consumer to take his place by the side of the producer, enabling them to conduct their exchanges at home.

The more directly the consumer trades with the producer, the less desire and opportunity there will be to commit fraud. A farmer in Illinois has no reason to adulterate his corn, because corn is cheap there; but a miller in England mixes beans with the corn because corn is expensive there. A planter in Alabama would gain nothing by substituting flour for cotton because cotton is cheap there; but a manufacturer in England does so because cotton is expensive. The coffee planter delivers pure coffee, but the English shopkeeper substitutes chicory for coffee because the latter is expensive.

The incentive for fraud in these cases results from the distance between the producer and the consumer, a distance which protection aims to diminish. A shoemaker makes good shoes for his local customers, but he may make inferior ones for traders who deal with distant people. A gunsmith provides his neighbors with guns that are proven to be safe, but when he makes guns to be sold in Africa, he cares little if they burst at the first fire. The necessity for England to maintain its monopoly on machinery leads to frauds and forgeries of every description, intended to replace foreign products and deceive foreign producers.*

---

\* As an example of this, I take the following from a modern journal:
> "We are surprised to see ginghams <note>original: "ginghams"; a type of plain-woven cotton fabric, usually striped or checked.</note> in the market sent from England by the firm of A. & S. Henry & Co. of Manchester, which imitate American goods in their patterns, width, and style of finish. But a most obvious and unfair imitation is found in the label; while preserving the same general appearance in size, paper color, and ornaments, the word *Lancasterian* is substituted for *Lancaster*. There is no doubt that the whole thing is a deliberate and intentional counterfeit. These goods will undoubtedly be sold as American 'Lancaster ginghams,' even though they are inferior in the strength of the fabric and the quality of the dye—to the clear injury of the profits and reputation of the American manufacturer. —*Boston paper*."

<meta>This page continues the argument that protectionism—supporting domestic industry—improves social morality by reducing the distance between producers and consumers, thereby preventing fraud, dissipation, and the forced migration of labor characteristic of the "English system" of free trade.</meta>

-># THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.<-

Fraud results from the distance between the consumer and the producer. Protection aims to bring them closer together, thereby diminishing the power to commit such fraud.

The planter who exchanges his goods on the spot with the iron-master and the miller produces large crops and grows wealthy; for him, the gain resulting from successful fraud would be trifling compared to the loss of his reputation. However, the planter who is distant from both producer and consumer makes smaller crops, which seem significantly increased in amount by substituting stones for cotton or tobacco. The *inducement* to commit fraud here results from the distance between the consumer and the producer. This incentive is diminished as the loom and the anvil <note>original: "the loom and the anvil"; symbols for manufacturing and industry.</note> come nearer to the plow and the harrow <note>original: "the plough and the harrow"; symbols for agriculture.</note>.

A man who conducts his exchanges in distant markets spends much time on the road and in taverns, making him liable to be led into dissipation <note>original: "dissipation"; excessive drinking or wasteful, immoral living.</note>. The more he can conduct his exchanges at home, the less danger there is of such a result. The object of the monopoly system <note>The author’s term for the British system of global free trade, which he argues centralizes manufacturing in England.</note> is to compel him to conduct all his exchanges at a distance and to employ numerous wagon drivers, porters, sailors, and other persons for that purpose—most of whom have almost no home except the tavern.

The more uniform the standard of value, the less trade resembles gambling. The object of the monopoly system is to subject the world's produce to a highly variable standard, rendering agriculture, manufacturing, and trade into mere gambling. The goal of protection is to withdraw the world's products from that unstable standard, enabling every community to measure the products of its labor by its own standard, exchanging labor for labor.

The object of the English system is to promote centralization, and its necessary consequence is the forced dispersion of people in search of food.* London and Liverpool, Manchester and Birmingham, have grown with vast rapidity through the same system that has exhausted Ireland, India, and the West Indies. The same journals inform us of the construction of a new town opposite Liverpool and great additions to London, while simultaneously reporting the absolute necessity of promoting emigration from Ireland, Scotland, and even from England itself. As each successive province is exhausted, there arises a desire, and even a necessity, for adding more to the list. Since Bengal and Bombay have ceased to be productive, an attempt is made on Afghanistan, and the Punjab is conquered. The ruin of the West Indies is followed by an invasion of China for the purpose of compelling the Chinese to accept "perfect freedom of trade." The Scottish Highlands are depopulated, and Australia is colonized.

Mr. Jefferson considered great cities to be "great sores." He desired that the manufacturer should take his place by the side of the agriculturist—that the loom and the anvil should be in close proximity to the plow and the harrow. Mr. Jefferson looked and thought for himself. He had studied political economy before it became necessary for Mr. Malthus <note>Thomas Malthus (1766–1834), an economist known for his theory that population growth would outstrip food supply.</note> to invent a theory of population that would satisfactorily account for the scarcity of food under the British system.

***

Jefferson studied the matter, too, before Mr. Ricardo <note>David Ricardo (1772–1823), an influential English economist known for his theory on wages and profit, and his "theory of rent."</note> had invented a theory of rent. To maintain that theory, it was necessary to prove that the poor cultivator, beginning the work of settlement, always started upon the rich soils—the swamps and river-bottoms—and that as population grew, he had to resort to the poor soils of the hills, which yielded a constantly diminishing return on labor. Because of this, Jefferson thought for himself. Modern financiers have blindly adopted the English system, based on the theories of Malthus <note>Thomas Malthus (1766–1834), an English cleric and scholar who famously argued that population growth would eventually outpace food production.</note> and Ricardo. Today, the perfection of civilization is thought to be found in a system that most rapidly builds up great cities and most widely separates the manufacturer from the farmer. The more perfect the centralization, the greater—according to them—will be the tendency toward improvement.

Mr. Jefferson favored combined action, as he believed it was the best way to promote human improvement: physical, moral, intellectual, and political. That it does so seems obvious, as it is where people act in combination that they live best and are best educated—committing the fewest crimes and thinking most for themselves. It is there, too, where the strongest desire for protection exists.

A recent traveler <margin>* Sir Charles Lyell <note>A famous Scottish geologist (1797–1875) who traveled extensively in North America.</note></margin> in the United States says that “the ease with which every people conscientiously adapt their theoretical opinions to their local and individual interests is sufficiently demonstrated by the fact that the various States and regions, as they successively embark on manufacturing—whether of iron, cotton, or other articles—immediately become converts to protectionist views, against which they had previously argued.”

It is assumed here that the desire for protection results from a selfish wish to tax others. However, the people exclusively devoted to manufacturing of any kind are too few in number to affect elections; yet, wherever mills or furnaces are established, the majority of the people become advocates of the doctrine of protection. That majority mainly consists of agriculturists—farmers and planters. The reason for this is found in the fact that they experience the benefits resulting from creating a market on the land for the products of the land, and they desire for their neighbors to do the same. Ignorant selfishness would lead them to want to keep the advantage they had gained for themselves. Enlightened selfishness would lead them to teach others what they themselves have learned.

Ignorant selfishness is the characteristic of the primitive state <note>original: "the savage"; the author uses this term to describe a lack of social development or association.</note>. It disappears as people acquire the habit of associating with their neighbors. The stated object of the monopoly system <note>The author’s term for the British system of global trade, which he argues forces other nations to remain purely agricultural while England controls manufacturing.</note> is to create a necessity for scattering ourselves over vast areas, thus increasing the difficulty of social association—and that object is achieved. “The prospect of heaven itself,” says Cooper <note>James Fenimore Cooper (1789–1851), a popular American novelist known for his stories of the frontier.</note> in one of his novels, “would have no charm for an American of the backwoods if he thought there was any place further west.”

Such is the common impression. It is believed that people separate from each other because of something in their nature that makes them want to flee to wild lands—where they will probably perish of fever brought on by exposure, and certainly leave behind everything that makes life desirable. Such is not the character of humanity anywhere. People everywhere are inclined to stay at home when they can. If the farmers and planters of the Union can be brought to understand their true interests, they will remain at home; by doing so, their condition, and that of everyone around them, will be im...

"I wish," says the author of a recent agricultural speech, "that we could create a general passion for gardening and landscaping <note>original: horticulture</note>. Flowers are, in the language of a late cultivator, 'the playthings of childhood and the ornaments of the grave; they raise smiling looks to man and grateful ones to God.'"

We do need more beauty around our houses, and not only around our houses but within our minds. To obtain this, we must rid ourselves of a system that makes the producer a servant to the middleman <note>original: exchanger</note>. Such is the objective of protectionism.

It is very truly said that "there is no friendship in trade." As it is currently conducted, trade certainly does not tend to promote kindly feelings among the human race; nor can it do so while the system remains unchanged. The great object of traders appears to be the creation of discord. By doing so, England has obtained supreme control over India. Her journals are unceasingly engaged in sowing discord among the various parts of this Union, and the effort would be successful if it were not for the fact that there is no real conflict between their true interests.

It is time for the people of Great Britain to open their eyes to the fact that their progress is heading in the same direction as the communities of Athens, Rome, and every other nation that desired to support itself through the labor of others. It is time they woke up to the realization that the numerous and flashy gin-shops, the repeated instances of child-murder for the purpose of robbing burial societies, and the enormous increase in crime* and poverty <note>original: pauperism</note>, are merely the natural consequences of a system that tends to drive capital away from the land to be employed instead in spindles and—

...ships, and labor from the healthful and inspiring pursuits of the country, to seek employment in Liverpool and Manchester. In those cities, severe labor—in the effort to undersell the poor Indian <note>original: Hindoo</note> and drive him from his loom—is rewarded with just enough to keep the laborer from starving in the lanes and cellars with which those cities so much abound.

That "there is no friendship in trade" is most true, and yet trade is the deity worshiped in this school of thought. In it, "commerce is king," and yet to commerce we owe much of the existing demoralization of the world. The anxiety to sell cheaply induces the manufacturer to substitute cotton for silk, and flour for cotton, and leads to frauds and adulterations of every description. Bankruptcy and loss of honor follow in the train of its perpetual economic crashes <note>original: revulsions</note>. To obtain intelligence an hour beforehand of an approaching famine—and thus be enabled to buy corn at less than it is worth—or to hear in advance of the prospect of good harvests and sell it at more than it is worth, is seen as nothing but evidence of superior wisdom. To buy your coat in the cheapest market, regardless of the sufferings of the poor tailor, and to sell your grain in the dearest, though your neighbor may be starving, is the cardinal principle of this school.

A very slight examination will suffice to convince the reader that, as has been already shown, these frauds and deceptions increase in proportion to the distance between the consumer and the producer. Food that has traveled far is expensive, and thus more likely to be mixed with beans <note>a common filler in flour</note>. Cotton produced in remote lands is expensive, and it becomes profitable to mix it with flour. The shoemaker who supplies the auctions uses poor leather and employs poor workmen.* The object of protection <note>economic protectionism</note> is that of bringing the consumer of food to the side of its producer, so they may eat plenty of good and nourishing food; the consumer of cotton to the side of its producer so that he may not need to wear a mixture of wool and paste; and the shoemaker to the side of the farmer and planter, so that the latter may be supplied with custom-work <term>high-quality, made-to-order goods</term> and not slop-work <term>cheap, mass-produced, low-quality clothing</term>. By this, the farmer gains doubly: he gives less food and gets better clothing in return. By doing so, his own physical condition and the moral condition of the shoemaker are both improved.

The whole tendency of the system is toward the production of a gambling spirit. In England, it makes railroad kings, ending in railroad bankrupts like George Hudson <note>The original text mistakenly says "Henry Hudson," but refers to George Hudson (1800–1871), the "Railway King" whose empire collapsed in scandal</note>. If we could trace the effect of the great speculation of which this man was the father, we should find thousands and tens of thousands of husbands and wives, parents and children, utterly beggared to build up the fortunes of the few, thus increasing the inequality of social condition which lies at the root of all evil. If we examine it here, we see it sending tens of thousands to California, eager for gold, only to lose both health and life.† It is sending thousands of boys and girls to our cities—the former

With every step of our progress in that direction, social inequality tends to increase. The skillful speculator realizes a fortune by the same operation that ruins hundreds around him, and he adds to his fortune by buying their property under the sheriff's hammer <note>a forced auction of foreclosed property</note>. The wealthy manufacturer is unmoved by economic crashes <note>original: revulsions</note> in the British market which sweep away his competitors; when the storm blows over, he is able to double, triple, or quadruple his already excessive fortune. 

The consequence is that great manufacturing towns spring up in one part of the Union, while almost every effort to *establish manufacturing locally* <note>original: localize manufactures</note> (thus bringing the loom and the anvil truly to the side of the plow and the harrow) is followed by ruin. The system tends to make the rich richer and the poor poorer. The coal miner of the present year works for half wages, but the coal speculator obtains double profits. It is always thus—the producer is sacrificed to the middleman <note>original: exchanger</note>. With the growth of this middleman class, great cities rise up, filled with shops where men can cheaply become intoxicated. New York has 4,567 places where liquor is sold, and the *Five-Points* <note>a notorious 19th-century slum in Lower Manhattan, known for poverty and crime</note> are populated with the men who caused the Astor Place riots <note>a deadly 1849 riot at an opera house that reflected deep-seated class tensions in New York City</note>. Single merchants employ 160 clerks, while thousands of those who are forced into our cities to seek a living by trade are ruined. Opera singers receive large salaries paid by the contributions of men whose shirts are made by women whose wages scarcely enable them to survive.

The whole system of trade, as it is currently conducted—and as it must continue to be conducted if the colonial system <note>Carey's term for the British economic model of global trade</note> is permitted to exist much longer—is one of mere gambling. Of all qualities, that which most distinguishes the gambler is ignorant selfishness. He ruins his friends and wastes his winnings on a racehorse or on a prostitute. As a necessary consequence of this system, money becomes more and more of a factor when entering into the important commitment of marriage <note>original: matrimony</note>, and marriage settlements <note>legal contracts regarding the distribution of property and wealth in a marriage</note> are beginning to appear among us. The newspapers of the day inform us of the recent signing of one for $200,000.

If we look westward, the situation is the same. Centralization produces depopulation, which is followed by poverty and crime. London grows by using a system that ruins India and fills it with bands of plunderers. The West and Southwest are filled with gamblers, and land-pirates <note>dishonest land speculators</note> abound. The late war has brought into existence a new species of fraud—the counterfeiting of land-warrants <note>documents granting a soldier or veteran the right to a specific plot of public land</note>—and this is but one of the many evils resulting from that measure.

If we look back just a few years, we can see that the period between 1835 and 1843 was remarkable for the existence of crime; that was the same period in which the tendency toward dispersion <note>the scattering of the population away from established social centers</note> was most prevalent. If we now look at the period between 1843 and 1847, we can see that there was a gradual tendency toward the restoration of order, quiet, and morality throughout the Union. In the last year, however, we see the reverse. It was marked by strikes <note>original: turnouts</note>, insubordination, and various kinds of violence in both the country and the city. Such is the direct consequence of a decrease in the productivity of labor. The employer must pay less, and the employee is unwilling to receive less than what he has been accustomed to.

The tendency of the colonial system is to increase the number of wagons and wagon-drivers, ships and sailors, merchants and traders—the men who necessarily spend much of their time in hotels and taverns, living by exchanging the products of others. The tendency of protection is to increase the number of producers—the class of people who live at home, surrounded by wives, children, and friends. The former builds up the city at the expense of the country; the latter causes both to grow together.

Cities are rivals for trade, and when a farmer desires a new road to market, he is opposed because it might enable him to go more cheaply to Charleston than Savannah, or to New York more readily than to Philadelphia. London is jealous of Liverpool, and Liverpool of London. Discord is everywhere, and the smaller the amount of production, the greater that discord must necessarily be. Protection seeks to increase production and thus establish harmony.

It is asserted that protection tends to increase smuggling and therefore to damage public morals. To settle this question, one would only need to determine what kind of men transact business at our custom-houses. From 1830 to 1834, the majority of business was done by men who had homes occupied by wives and families, for whose sake their reputations were dear. But from 1835 to 1842, it passed almost entirely into the hands of men who lived in hotels and boarding-houses, and who had neither wives nor families to maintain. From 1843 to 1847, it went back to the former class. It has now returned almost entirely into the hands of agents—men whose business is trade, and who will swear to a false invoice <note>falsifying the value of imported goods to avoid paying higher tariffs</note> for a commission. The honest man, who desires to perform his duties to his wife and children, to society, to his country, and to his Creator, cannot import foreign merchandise under this system. The current system acts as a reward for immorality and fraud.

The object of protection is the establishment of perfect free trade through the "annexation" of men and of nations <note>Carey argues that bringing immigrants to America expands the internal "free trade" zone</note>. Every person brought here increases the domain of free trade and diminishes the need for custom-houses. Every person brought here consumes four, six, ten, or twelve pounds of cotton for every one pound they could have consumed at home; and every one becomes a customer to the farmer for bushels of crops instead of tiny amounts <note>original: gills; a unit of measurement equal to a quarter of a pint</note>. ## CHAPTER TWENTY-SECOND.

### HOW PROTECTION AFFECTS INTELLECTUAL CONDITION.

The higher the degree of intellect applied to the work of production, the larger will be the return for labor, and the more rapid will be the accumulation of capital. If protection be "a war upon labor and capital," it must tend to prevent the growth of intellect.

The more men are enabled to combine their efforts, and the greater the tendency toward association <note>the act of people living in close proximity and cooperating within a community</note>, the larger is the return for labor, and the more easily they can obtain books and newspapers for themselves, and schools for their children. The object of the monopoly system <note>original: monopoly system; referring here to British free trade policies which Carey argued forced other nations to remain solely agricultural while England monopolized manufacturing</note> is to compel men to scatter themselves over large areas and into distant colonies, and thus to diminish the ability to obtain books, newspapers, and schools. The object of protection is to correct this error and to enable men to combine their efforts for mental as well as physical improvement.

The greater the tendency toward association, the greater is the facility for the dissemination of new ideas regarding modes of thought or action, and for obtaining help in carrying them into practical effect. The object of *the English monopoly system* is to separate men from each other and deprive them of this advantage. The object of protection is to enable them to come together; as such, it would seem to be the real friend to both the laborer and the capitalist.

If we look throughout the world, we shall see intellect increasing as men live more and more in communion with each other, and diminishing as they are compelled to separate. The man who is distant from a market spends much of his time in taverns, where he obtains little that tends toward the improvement of mind or morals. The man who has a market at his door may obtain books and newspapers, and he is surrounded by skillful farmers from whom he obtains information. Not being compelled to spend his time on the road, he is enabled to give both time and mind to the improvement of his land, to which he returns the refuse in the form of manure; thus, he himself grows rich.

Of all the pursuits of man, agriculture—the work of production—is the one that most tends toward the expansion of intellect. It is the great pursuit of man. There is none "in which so many of the laws of nature must be consulted and understood as in the cultivation of the earth. Every change of the season, every change even of the winds, every fall of rain, must affect some of the manifold operations of the farmer. In the improvement of our various domestic animals, some of the most complex <note>original: abstruse</note> principles of physiology must be consulted. Is it to be supposed that men thus called upon to study or to observe the laws of nature, and labor in conjunction with its powers, require less of the light of the highest science than the merchant or the manufacturer?"* It is not. It is the science that requires the greatest knowledge, and *the one that pays best for it:* and yet England has driven men, wealth, and mind into the less profitable pursuits of fashioning and exchanging the products of other lands. She has expended thousands of millions on fleets and armies to enable her to conduct poor trade with foreign nations, when her own soil offered her the richer trade that tends to produce—

...that increase of wealth and concentration of population which have in all times and in all ages given the self-protective power that requires neither fleets, nor armies, nor tax-collectors. In her efforts to force this trade, Britain has driven the people of the United States to spread themselves over vast tracts of inferior land when they might more advantageously have concentrated themselves on rich ones. In doing so, she has delayed the progress of civilization both abroad and at home. She has made it necessary for the people of grain-growing countries to rejoice in the failures of her harvests, as these failures provide them an outlet for surplus food they could not consume themselves—food that was sometimes abandoned in the field because it was not worth the cost of harvesting. Instead, they should have been able to rejoice in the knowledge that others were likely to be fed as abundantly as themselves. Her internal system was unsound, and her wealth gave her the power to make that instability a cause of disturbance to the rest of the world; hence, she has appeared to be regarded everywhere as a sort of common enemy.

To this unsound system, we owe the very flawed ideas that exist regarding the **division of labor** <note>the assignment of different parts of a manufacturing process or task to different people in order to improve efficiency</note>. Men are crowded into large towns and cities to labor in great shops, where the only skill ever acquired is the sharpening of a needle, and that skill is acquired at the cost of their health and life. The necessary consequence is the general decline in physical, moral, and mental condition that is observable in all classes of English workmen.

Of all machines, the most costly to produce is Man; and yet the lifespan of this expensive and beautiful machine is reduced to an average of twenty-five or thirty years, under the vain idea that by doing so, pins and needles may be obtained at a lower cost of labor. This is the same principle that is said to govern the plantation owners of Cuba when they stock their estates exclusively with males, believing it cheaper to buy slaves than to raise them. As a necessary consequence, the duration of life there is short, and it is the same in the crowded factories of the great "**workshop of the world**" <note>a common 19th-century nickname for Britain during the Industrial Revolution</note>. This idea is useless. Pins and needles would be obtained at a far lower cost of labor if the workshops of Sheffield and Birmingham were scattered throughout the kingdom. This would allow the producers of pins to take their places alongside the producers of food, enabling everyone to enjoy the pure air and water of the countryside, instead of being compelled—after breathing the foul atmosphere of the workshop during the day—to sleep at night in the filthy basements of undrained streets. If the iron ore of Ireland were converted into axes and railroad tracks by the aid of Irish coal and Irish labor, the basements of Manchester and Birmingham would not be filled with starving Irishmen fleeing by the hundreds of thousands from disease and famine, forcing English laborers to flee to the United States, Canada, or Australia.

The English school of **political economy** <note>the original term for the study of production and trade and their relations with law, custom, and government</note> treats man as a mere machine, placed on the earth for the sole purpose of producing food, cloth, iron, pins, or needles. It takes no account of him as a being capable of intellectual and moral improvement. It looks for physical power in connection with ignorance and immorality, and the result is disappointment.* The workman of—

->THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.<-

The worker in this country is infinitely superior to the workman of Manchester, and the reason is that he is not treated as a mere machine. The object of what is called "free trade" is to degrade the one to the level of the other. The purpose of protection <note>economic policy of restricting imports from other countries through methods such as tariffs on imported goods</note> is to enable the poor artisan of Manchester or Leeds, Birmingham or Sheffield, to move to a country where he will not be treated this way, and where he may have access to books and newspapers, and his children may be educated.

The colonial system requires spending on warships, soldiers, and sailors that is greater than what would be needed to give every child in the kingdom an education of the highest order. Those ships and men are supported by the taxes paid by poor mechanics and agricultural laborers, whose children grow up without even the knowledge that there is a God. The goal of protection is to eliminate the necessity for such ships and men, and to raise the value of labor to a point that will enable the people of England to provide schools for themselves.

In the colonies, the perpetual exhaustion of the land and its owners has prevented, and continues to prevent, any idea of intellectual improvement. No Englishmen went to the West Indies to stay. The plantations were managed by agents, and the poor Black people under their management died so quickly that it was necessary to import more people every year just to keep the population numbers steady. In India—where education was an interest of the government from the earliest period, and where every well-regulated village had its public school and schoolmaster—the system has almost disappeared. This was a system where information was taught so well and so cheaply that it inspired the **Lancaster system** <note>a method of schooling where more advanced students taught those below them, allowing for many students to be educated by one teacher</note>. In the *thana* <note>original: "thana"; a sub-district or administrative unit in India</note> of Nattore, which contains 184,509 inhabitants, there were only 27 schools with 262 students a few years ago. The teachers were simple-minded and uneducated, with salaries of only $2.50 per month, and the students had no books. Only 6,000 people could read and write. Such was the state of education in one of the best parts of Bengal. In the Bombay presidency, with a population of six and a half million, there were only 25 government schools with 1,315 students, and 1,680 village schools with 33,838 students. In the Madras presidency, out of 13 million people, there were 355,000 male and 8,000 female students, and the instruction was of the worst quality.

In Upper Canada, in 1848, the number of children (both boys and girls) under fourteen years of age was 326,050, but only 80,461 attended school.* While this is better than in other colonies, the difference is not very great when we look closer. A person's intellect is sharpened by interaction with others, but there can be little interaction where the **loom is widely distant from the plow** <note>a metaphor for the physical distance between manufacturing (the loom) and farming (the plow)</note>, and people live far apart, all engaged only in agriculture. How slowly concentration has grown in that province can be seen from the following facts. In that great district of the country, much of which has been settled for so long, there is consequently little or no employment for the mind. The result is that all who desire to engage in pursuits other than agriculture flee to the South <note>meaning the United States</note>. It is said that there are now no fewer than 200,000 Canadians within the Union, and the tendency toward emigration increases every day.* If we look at Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, the situation is the same. There is no demand for intellect there, and any man possessing it flees southward. 

Forty years ago, it was asked, "Who reads an American book?" <note>A famous taunt by British critic Sydney Smith in 1820, questioning American cultural relevance.</note> That question has long since been answered; however, it may now be repeated in reference to all the British provinces. Who reads a Canadian, a Nova Scotian, or a New Brunswick book? Upper Canada <note>The region now known as Ontario.</note> has two paper mills capable of producing about ten reams of paper per day. This is perhaps only a tenth of what is required just to supply the newspapers of Cincinnati. 

Forty years ago, the question might have been asked, "Who uses an American machine?" And yet today, the machine shops of Austria and Russia are directed by our countrymen, and the latest improvements in machinery for converting wool into cloth are American inventions. The British provinces have had the advantage of perfect free trade with England. The consequence is that they are almost entirely lacking in paper mills and printing offices, and machine shops are unknown. Meanwhile, the Union has been a "prey" to the *protective system*—that "war upon labor and capital"—the consequence of which is that paper mills and printing offices abound to an extent unknown elsewhere in the world. In fact, they are almost equal in number and power to those of the rest of the whole world combined.† Machine shops exist almost everywhere in the Union. 

These differences are not due to any difference in the abundance or quality of land, for the land of Upper Canada is still largely unoccupied and is inferior in quality to none on the continent. They are not due to differences in other natural advantages, for New Brunswick has every advantage possessed by Maine and New Hampshire, and Nova Scotia has coal and iron ore situated more advantageously than any in the Union. They are not due to differences in taxation, for Great Britain has paid almost all the expenses of their government. 

To what, then, can these differences be attributed, but to the fact that those provinces have been subject to the *monopoly system*? <note>The British colonial system that restricted the colonies' ability to manufacture their own goods.</note> They have been compelled to waste their own labor while giving their *products* in exchange for the *services* of English men, women, and children employed in doing for them what they could have done better for themselves. In doing so, they lose four-fifths of their products in the costs of transit between the producer and the consumer. Place the colony within the Union—give it protection—and in a dozen years its paper mills and printing offices will become numerous, and many people will then read Canadian books.

In England, a large portion of the people can neither read nor write, and there is scarcely any effort to provide them with an education. The colonial system seeks low wages, which is necessarily followed by an inability to devote time to intellectual improvement. Protection, however, seeks the high wages that enable the laborer to improve his mind and educate his children. The English child, when transferred to this country, becomes an educated and responsible being. If he remains at home, he remains in brutish ignorance. To increase the—

->THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.<-

For labor to be productive, education is necessary. Protectionism tends to spread education and improve the condition of the laborer.

At no period in our history has the demand for books and pictures, or the payment of authors and artists, been lower than in the years 1842–43 <note>During this time, the U.S. was recovering from the Panic of 1837 and transitioning between tariff policies.</note>. At no time did they grow as rapidly as they did from 1844 to 1847. Now, they are trending downward again, despite a demand that is currently sustained only because we are still able to obtain goods in exchange for certificates of debt <note>original: "certificates of debt"; Carey refers to the practice of importing foreign goods by issuing bonds or taking on international debt rather than paying with domestic production.</note>. When that ability disappears, we will see a return to the hardships of the free trade period.

If we want to raise the intellectual standards of people throughout the world, our goal can only be achieved by raising the value of a human being as a productive "machine" <note>original: "man, as a machine"; a 19th-century economic term for "human capital" or the productive power of an individual.</note> throughout the world. Every person brought to this country is improved, and every person who arrives helps to reduce the supposed "surplus" of people elsewhere. People immigrate when the reward for labor is high, as they did between 1844 and 1848. They return home disappointed when the reward for labor is low, as is the case now. Protectionism tends to increase the reward for labor and improve the intellectual condition of mankind.

### CHAPTER TWENTY-THIRD.

->HOW PROTECTION AFFECTS THE POLITICAL CONDITION OF MAN.<-

The larger the return on labor, the greater the power to accumulate capital. The larger the amount of capital looking for employees compared to the number of laborers available, the higher wages will be. This gives the laborer a greater power to save for himself and more perfect control over how he uses his labor and its earnings, whether for private or public purposes.

A free person chooses their employer, sells their labor, and spends the proceeds however they like. A slave does none of these things. His master takes the product of his labor and returns only whatever portion he chooses.

Throughout the world and in all ages, freedom has advanced whenever the ratio of wealth to population has increased. When the people of England were poor, they were enslaved; but as their wealth grew, they became more free. The same has happened in Belgium and France. It is happening now in Russia and Germany, and it must happen everywhere. India is poor, and the many are slaves to the few. The same is true in Ireland, where freedom is unknown. The poor Irishman, limited to agricultural labor, desperately wants a small piece of land. He gives the vast majority of his year's labor just for permission to starve on whatever is left, happy to be allowed to stay as long as he pays this enormous rent. He is the slave of the landowner, but without even a slave’s right to demand support in case of sickness. If he escapes famine and survives to an age where he can no longer work, he has no claim to support. 

England uses fleets—paid for by taxes imposed on starving Irishmen—to prevent the people of Brazil from *buying* black men, women, and children on the coast of Africa. Yet, at the same time, she is ready to *give away* white men, women, and children to anyone who will take them from her shores. She will even pay for part of the cost of their transportation. She does this without requiring the transporter to provide even the slightest evidence that they arrived at their destination in "good order and well-conditioned." When Ireland becomes rich, labor will become valuable, and people will become free. When Italy was filled with prosperous communities, labor was productive and in high demand; back then, the men who had labor to sell fixed the price for it. With growing poverty, labor...

<meta>This page continues Henry Charles Carey’s argument for economic protectionism by linking it to the growth of wealth and the transition from slavery to freedom. He compares the American system of domestic production to the British "colonial system" of distant trade.</meta>

Labor ceased to be in demand, and the buyer dictated the price. The laborer then became a slave. In the history of Tuscany, we see men becoming enslaved as poverty replaced wealth. Conversely, we can see them becoming increasingly free as wealth grew during times of peace. This has also happened in Egypt, Sicily, and Spain. Everywhere, poverty—or a lack of the tools that make labor productive—has always been the companion of slavery. Everywhere wealth—an abundance of tools like ploughs, harrows, horses, cows, oxen, cultivated lands, houses, and mills—has always been the companion and the cause of freedom.

If protectionism were a "war upon labor and capital," it would prevent the growth of wealth and degrade the political status of humans.

A farmer who trades his food for iron through a long chain of middlemen—horses, wagons, canal boats, merchants, ships, and sailors—gives away a lot of food for very little iron. The iron producer, who trades his products for food through that same complex machinery, gives away a lot of iron for very little food. The majority of the value is consumed by the middlemen, who grow rich while the actual producers stay poor. This prevents the growth of wealth and maintains political inequality.

A farmer who trades directly with an iron producer exchanges labor for labor. Both grow rich because the class of people who want to stand between them has no opportunity to enrich themselves at their expense. This promotes equality of condition.

The goal of protectionism is to bring the consumer of food (the manufacturer) to live alongside the producer of food (the farmer). This promotes wealth and improves political conditions. This effect is obvious: during periods of protection, huge numbers of immigrants come to our shores. Immigration stops or shrinks whenever we move toward the system usually called "free trade."

The colonial system <note>The "colonial system" refers to the British economic policy of the time, which discouraged manufacturing in colonies or foreign nations to keep them dependent on British goods.</note> relies on cheap labor. Protectionism seeks to increase wages. The former fills factories with young children and drives men to emigrate to Canada and Australia; the latter unites families and sends the children to school.

The Irishman in his own country is a slave. He begs for permission to stay and pay high rent for a tiny plot of land, but his request is refused. If he moves here, he becomes a free man who chooses his employer and sets the price of his own labor. The Scottish Highlander is a slave who would gladly stay home, but he is evicted to make room for sheep <note>Carey refers to the Highland Clearances, where tenants were forcibly removed from their land to make way for large-scale sheep farming.</note>. One-ninth of England’s population are slaves to local charity officials <note>original: "parish beadle"; an official who administered poor relief under the English Poor Laws.</note>, eating the bread of forced welfare. Most of the rest are slaves to an economic policy that causes constant instability—extreme overwork for low wages one moment, and no work at all the next. If they move here, they become free men who select their employers and set their own hours and pay. 

The person in India <note>original: "The Hindoo"; Carey uses this as a general term for the people of India under British rule.</note> is a slave. His landlord’s officials dictate how much land he must farm and how much rent he must pay. Even if he pays the high taxes fixed on a field, he is not allowed to choose which fields to farm. His tasks are assigned to him, and he is forced to work whatever land the revenue officers give him. Whether he farms them or not, he is burdened with the rent for all of them. If he flees this oppression to find work elsewhere, he is hunted down and oppressed at will, or deprived of any advantage he hoped to find by moving. If he works for wages, he is paid in money when grain is expensive and in grain when it is cheap. He, therefore—

Protectionism aims to improve the political condition of the human race. To achieve this, the value of human beings must be raised. Men everywhere should be in a position to sell their labor to the highest bidder—that is, to the person who will provide the most food, clothing, shelter, and other comforts of life in return. To enable the Indian <note>original: Hindoo</note> laborer to sell his labor and set its price, the price of his main product—cotton—must be raised. This is achieved by increasing consumption and by reducing the waste of labor that occurs during transport between the producer and the consumer. 

If we fill this country with iron furnaces and textile mills, railroads will be built in every direction. The consumption of cotton will quickly rise to twenty pounds per person. Meanwhile, millions of European laborers, mechanics, farmers, and investors <note>original: capitalists</note> will cross the Atlantic. Every million of these immigrants will become customers for one-fourth of the amount of cotton consumed by the entire population of Great Britain and Ireland in 1847. There is a perfect harmony of interests among cotton growers worldwide; any conflict only arises from the power of middlemen <note>original: exchangers</note> to create the appearance of discord.

It is argued, however, that protectionism tends to enrich a small group of wealthy owners at the expense of the consumer, thereby creating social inequality. It is true that *inadequate* protection has this effect. As long as we are *forced* to look to England for a market for our extra products, English markets will set the prices for the entire world. Furthermore, as long as we are *forced* to seek even a small supply of cloth or iron from there, English prices will dictate the price of everything. Domestic producers of cloth and iron will then profit from the difference in shipping costs <note>original: freight</note> for both imports and exports. 

However, along with this profit, the producer risks total ruin—a common occurrence for those with little capital. Those who are already wealthy can simply shut down their furnaces or mills until prices rise again. They then take over the entire market because their poorer competitors have been bankrupted. This is the history of many of the large fortunes made in the American cloth and iron industries. It is also the typical history of almost every attempt to establish manufacturing in the South and the West, outside of New England.

Inadequate and inconsistent protection provides little benefit to the farmer or the plantation owner <note>original: planter</note>. The resulting uncertainty tends to make the rich richer and the poor poorer, creating social and political inequality.

On the other hand, adequate and reliable protection leads to equality. First, it ends the need to depend on foreign markets to sell our products or supply our needs. From that point on, prices will be set at home and remain steady. This allows the smaller investor to compete with the larger one, which greatly benefits consumers—including farmers, plantation owners, and laborers. Second, the benefits of protection are felt primarily by the majority of people, whose only source of income is the price of their labor.

If we look at the labor employed in factories across the entire country, we find that almost all of it would be wasted if it were not used in this way. If we look at the labor used to harvest timber and quarry stone for building factories and furnaces, we find that a large portion of it would otherwise be wasted. When we examine the farmer's work, we find that being located near a factory, or...

A blast furnace <note>original: "furnace"; here referring to iron production</note> enables the owner to save much of the labor of transportation and to sell many things that would otherwise go to waste. So far, the advantage would seem to be entirely on the side of the employee, rather than the employer.

Let us now suppose that all protection <note>Economic policies, like tariffs, designed to protect domestic industries from foreign competition</note> were abolished and that perfect free trade were established. The result would inevitably be to close every factory, furnace, rolling mill, and coal mine in the country. Let us see what the result would be. The owners of such property would lose a few million dollars in rents or profits. However, the supply of fuel would decrease by three million tons, iron would decrease by eight hundred thousand tons, and cotton cloth would decrease by almost a thousand million yards. 

The demand for the labor now used to produce those goods would end. The spare labor of men, women, and children—along with the use of wagons, horses, and the various things now used in and around factories and furnaces—would then be wasted. Coal, iron, and cloth would double in price, and the value of labor would diminish at a similar rate. The power to import iron, coal, or cloth would not increase by a single ton or yard, and the people would be forced to go without the basic necessities of life that are currently easy to get. The capitalists whose money was tied up in factories or furnaces would suffer some loss. However, the group of people who hold liquid capital <note>original: "disengaged capital"; cash or assets easily converted to cash</note> and those who receive *State* dividends <note>Government interest payments</note> would be able to command a much larger quantity of labor for the same price than they could before.

The goal of protection is to secure a demand for labor, and its tendency is to produce equality of condition. Jealousy toward "overgrown capitalists" has caused many changes in policy. However, as far as those changes have led to the abolition of protection, they have always tended to produce inequality. The wealthy capitalist suffers some loss, but he is not ruined. When a change occurs, he is ready to take advantage of it and immediately regains all that was lost, with a vast increase. Meanwhile, the small capitalist is swept away, and his mill is left in ruins. By the time he can prepare himself to restart his business, the opportunity has passed; he is swept away again, perhaps for the last time.

For months past, interest rates on certain types of securities have been very low. The wealthy man could borrow at four percent. The poor man, requiring a small loan on second-rate security, could scarcely obtain it at any price. The man who has coal or iron to sell must have the help of middlemen to co-sign the credit notes <note>original: "paper"; financial documents or promissory notes</note> received from his customers, and their commissions eat up his profits. The wages of the miner have been greatly reduced, while the profits of the speculator have increased. 

The reason for all of this is that, throughout the nation, there is no confidence in the future. It is clear that we are consuming more than we produce; that our exports do not pay for our imports; that we are running into debt; and that furnaces and mills are being closed. Everyone knows how such a system must end. Re-enact the Tariff of 1842 <note>A protective tariff passed by the Whig party that significantly raised rates to help the struggling U.S. economy</note>, and the business of the middleman would end, because confidence in the future would be felt from one end of the land to the other. Should we not find in this some evidence of the soundness of the principle upon which that tariff was based? The system that provides confidence must be right; the one that destroys it must be wrong.

Confidence in the future—Hope—gives power to individuals and communities. It is what enables the poor man to become rich, and the character of all legislative action should be judged by whether it helps or hinders this effect. A review of the measures pushed upon the nation by the advocates of the system miscalled "free trade" shows that, almost without exception, they have tended toward the destruction of confidence, and there-

The direct effect of the insecurity that has existed has been to centralize the business of manufacturing in one part of the United States <note>original: "the Union"</note> and in the hands of a relatively small number of people—those who could afford to take large risks in the hope of making large profits. If the Tariff of 1828 <note>A high protective tariff designed to protect northern industry; Carey argues its stability would have benefited everyone</note> had been made the permanent law of the land, the Middle and Southern States would now be filled with factories and furnaces. While the North and East would not have been any less wealthy, they would actually be far richer, and the current inequality of wealth would not exist today.

The power of the North, compared to that of the South, is due to the South's jealousy of the North. This jealousy has prevented the establishment of a firm economic system intended to destroy the English monopoly and eventually establish true free trade.

The goal of the colonial system was to tax the world to support a great mercantile, manufacturing, and land-owning aristocracy. The way they achieved this was by securing a monopoly on machinery <note>The British policy of preventing other nations from acquiring industrial technology</note>. The goal of protection is to break down that monopoly, and with it, the aristocracy that collects massive taxes from the people of Great Britain and the world. These taxes are used to pay for navies and armies led by "younger sons" <note>In the British system of primogeniture, the eldest son inherited the estate, while younger sons often sought careers as officers in the military</note>, which are maintained to preserve the existing inequality in Great Britain, Ireland, and India. Therefore, everyone who wishes to see the political condition of the world’s people improve should support the system that works to break down monopolies and establish true freedom of trade.

## CHAPTER TWENTY-FOUR.

### HOW PROTECTION AFFECTS CREDIT—INDIVIDUAL AND NATIONAL.

The existence of credit is evidence of confidence: the belief that a person who borrows property intends to return it. The more universal this confidence becomes, the more easily a capitalist can invest his funds, and the larger his return will be. Furthermore, the more universal it is, the more easily a laborer can obtain the tools and resources necessary for work, making that labor more productive. If protection were truly "a war upon labor and capital," it would have to result in destroying the confidence people have in one another.

The goal of protection is to bring the consumer to the side of the producer so they can exchange labor for labor directly, thereby reducing the need for credit. Its effect is to reduce the "machinery of exchange" <note>The costs and middlemen associated with long-distance trade, such as shipping and insurance</note> and thus increase the productivity of labor, which in turn increases the ability to obtain credit.

The goal of the monopoly system is to separate the consumer from the producer and *force* both to trust people far away, thus increasing the necessity for credit. Its effect is to increase the machinery of exchange and decrease the productivity of labor, thereby decreasing the *power* to obtain credit.

We know this is the effect in the colonies of Great Britain. In India, which was once so wealthy, the standard interest rate is twelve percent; however, a poor farmer must borrow seed at a rate of one hundred percent interest. Credit does not exist there, and yet almost all the trade of that country is conducted across distances of many thousands of miles by men in whom the consumer and producer are *compelled* to place their trust.

In the West Indies, credit has almost entirely disappeared. In Canada,

# THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.

Even the British government cannot secure loans without a guarantee from Parliament. This same lack of trust exists throughout all the colonies.

In Britain <note>original: "At home"</note>, capital is cheap because of a general lack of confidence. The capitalist accepts a two percent return, yet the laborer cannot borrow even at thirty percent interest. The capitalist who owns the machinery is able to dictate the terms for the people who work. Sometimes he employs many workers; at other times, he employs few. Sometimes he runs the machines for long hours, and at other times, for short periods. At all times, his workers receive only a small portion of the products of their labor; however, there are many times when they receive *a very small proportion*, and other times when they are unable to obtain the use of machinery at any price.

Internationally, the credit of English merchants is falling daily. Recently, in the great city of Liverpool, there were barely half a dozen business houses that could be trusted with a cargo of cotton. Such are the effects of a system where "Commerce is king," and both the consumer and the producer are left at the mercy of the middleman <note>original: "exchanger"</note>.

In the United States <note>original: "this country"</note>, economic confidence never grew more rapidly than during the period between 1830 and 1834. Conversely, it never declined as fast as it did between 1835 and 1842. With the implementation of the Tariff of 1842 <note>A protective tariff that increased duties on imports to encourage domestic industry</note>, confidence was restored, but with the Tariff of 1846 <note>The Walker Tariff, which moved toward free trade by reducing rates</note>, it is declining again. There is no demand for capital, so it is cheap. There is little demand for labor, so it too is cheap.

Probably never since the settlement of this country did the poor man find it so difficult to obtain the aid of capital as in 1842, a period of free trade. He never found it easier than between 1844 and 1847. Now, a period of distrust has arrived again. Money is said to be abundant, but the required security must be beyond doubt. As a result, the poor man pays two percent interest a month for the use of capital that the rich man cannot invest to earn more than four percent per year. There is currently no confidence in the market.

> "Despite money being cheap and abundant," says the *New York Herald*, "no one seems disposed to engage in any kind of speculation. Capitalists prefer lending money at four percent interest on good security rather than purchasing stocks at current prices. They say that when they lend money on first-rate security at a low interest rate, they are certain of getting their principal and a small amount of interest back whenever they need it."

Re-establishing the Tariff of 1842 would restore confidence and create a demand for labor, causing wages to rise. It would also create a demand for capital, causing its price to rise as well. Thus, it appears that protectionism is where the harmony of interest between the laborer and the capitalist is truly found.

### NATIONAL CREDIT.

From 1830 to 1835, the national credit grew because we paid for what we imported. From 1835 to 1840, credit declined because we went heavily into debt for imported cloth and iron that our exports could not cover. In 1842, national credit vanished because we were unable to pay even the interest on our debts. From 1843 to 1848, national credit grew because we paid our interest and began to reduce the national debt. In the last two years, we have gone largely into debt again and must now either reduce our imports or borrow even more.

How long we can continue to do this does not depend on us alone. Any event that changes the interest rates in Europe would cause our certificates of debt <note>government bonds or IOUs held by foreign investors</note> to be sent back to us for immediate payment. What would be the state of the national credit then? A nation that is deeply in debt is always in danger of losing its credit.
