# THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.

### CHAPTER TWENTY-FIFTH.

### HOW PROTECTION AFFECTS REVENUE AND EXPENDITURE.

The more people live and work in close contact with one another, the greater is their *power* to protect themselves. Conversely, the more widely they are separated from each other, the greater is their *necessity* to seek protection from others.

The more they live in connection with one another, the larger the product of their labor will be, and the greater will be their ability to contribute toward maintaining peace and order. The less they live in connection with each other, the less productive their labor becomes, and the less they can contribute to that goal.

With every increase in the productivity of labor, the power of self-government increases, along with an increased ability to pay for the expenses necessary to maintain a government. With every decrease in productivity, the power of self-government declines, along with a diminished ability to contribute to the public revenue needed to pay others for performing the duties of government.

If protection is, as some claim, a "war upon labor and capital," it must increase the need for government oversight and diminish the people's power to pay for its maintenance.

The goal of protection, however, is to enable people to live in connection with one another, bringing the consumer to the side of the producer so that each protects and is protected by the other. This would seem to diminish the *necessity* of seeking protection from outside sources. Another goal of protection is to enable people to trade with one another, exchanging labor for labor without paying so many middlemen to stand between them. This would seem designed to increase their power to pay for protection, should it be needed.

The goal of the monopoly system—now known by the name "free trade" <note>Carey argues that the British "free trade" system was actually a monopoly designed to keep other nations dependent on British manufacturing and shipping.</note>—is to separate the consumer from the producer and diminish their power to protect each other. Under this system, their exchanges must always be made in distant markets. Consequently, many wagons, ships, and men must stand between them, requiring fleets and armies for their protection. This would seem to increase the *necessity* for government protection, while the diminished power of collective action would tend to decrease the people's *power* to pay for it.

What are the facts? This question can be answered by comparing the government expenditures under the different systems:

| Protection | Per year | Free trade | Per year |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1829 to 1834 | $16,800,000 | 1834 to 1841 | $31,700,000 |
| 1843 to 1845 | $20,700,000 | 1846 to 1849 | $44,500,000 |

The necessity of contributing toward the support of government seems to have increased as we moved toward free trade and to have diminished as we approached protection.

The revenue from customs <note>Customs: Duties or taxes imposed by a government on imported goods.</note> during these several periods was as follows:

| | Per person | | Per person |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1830 to 1834 | $1.75 | 1835 to 1841 | $0.84½ |
| 1843 to 1847 | $1.36 | 1848–1849 | $1.00 |

I have excluded the year 1847–1848 because it was entirely exceptional. We had imported a large amount of duty-free <term>specie</term> <note>original: "specie" — gold or silver coin.</note> in the preceding year and exported it again in 1847–1848 to exchange for duty-paying goods...

The revenue from profitable imports, along with the total amount of duty received on goods obtained in exchange, should be added to the revenue of 1846–47.

The power to *contribute* toward the national revenue certainly decreased during the years of free trade, precisely as the *necessity for contributions* increased. The amount actually paid was higher than what is recorded here because, between 1834 and 1841, the government collected a large amount of duties on goods received in exchange for certificates of debt <note>These were essentially government IOUs used to fund imports on credit</note>. However, that was merely a payment in *advance of production*. The consequence of receiving such payments was that the government was nearly bankrupt in 1842. It was compelled to borrow almost thirty million dollars just to ensure its own continued existence.

We are now doing the same thing. The amount of debt incurred in the last year was no less than twenty-two million dollars. Upon this debt, the government obtained duties—as it did before—in *advance of production* to the extent of almost seven million dollars. If our ability to buy on credit were to cease today, the amount collected would fall to twenty-two million. If the debt contracted last year had to be paid now, that revenue would fall to fifteen million, and a large addition would have to be made to the public debt, just as happened in 1841–42. I cannot predict how much time will pass before we reach that state of things. however, if we add another twenty million to our foreign debt this year and close as many iron furnaces as we did last year, that day cannot be far off.

The power to contribute toward the maintenance of government depends upon the power of production. Every circumstance that tends to diminish production tends equally to diminish revenue. At present, the power of production is rapidly diminishing and must continue to do so.

This is also the case in England. Year after year, the payment of taxes is becoming more and more burdensome. This is true even though a large portion of those taxes is pushed onto the world's farmers and planters through a system where they are compelled to give more food, cotton, tobacco, and sugar for less and less cloth and iron. Yet, despite this, expenditures have been increasing every year. Poverty produced rebellion in Ireland and Chartism <note>original: "chartism" — a working-class movement for political reform in Britain that existed from 1838 to 1857</note> in England, which increased the need for soldiers and sailors. The exhaustion of the older provinces of India led to a desire to conquer Afghanistan, Sindh <note>original: "Scinde"</note>, and the Punjab <note>original: "Punjaub"</note>. Additionally, the failure of the labor market for cotton drove the Hindus <note>original: "Hindoo"</note> to the opium trade, which led to a war in China <note>The First Opium War (1839–1842)</note>. All of this created a demand for larger fleets and armies. The poverty of Canada led to rebellion and the building of more forts and ships. The anxiety to secure foreign markets has led to immense expenses for steamships and mail steamers. Thus, the more the system fails, the greater the expenditure required to maintain it, and the less the people of England—and the farmers and planters of the world—are able to contribute to it.

Let us now look to the other source of our national revenue: the **PUBLIC lands**.

The higher the value of labor, the more people will be attracted to this country to sell their labor. The more people who come here, the more land will be required. Furthermore, the larger and more valuable the inbound freights are, the lower the cost of outbound freight will be. This increases the number of commodities that can be exported to pay for the things we choose to import.

If we were now importing a million men annually, the sales of land would soon reach ten million acres per year. We could reach that point within five years of perfect and fixed protection. Only a few more years would be required to double both the number of immigrants and the sales of public lands. This is a vast source of public revenue.

Perfect protection would, by degrees, diminish the import of cotton goods and iron...

...and other goods that pay duties, but we would consume triple or quadruple the amount of coffee, tea, and raw materials that our own soil or climate is not suited to produce. In doing so, we would raise the value of agricultural labor throughout the entire world.

It is often asked, "If we converted all our cotton into cloth ourselves, what would Europe produce to pay us for it?" In answer, it may be said that the goal of protection is to enable the consumer of food to take his place by the side of the producer of food, rather than separating them. It is in our interest that the people of England should supply themselves with clothing made by workers who eat English food. The same should be true for the people of Germany, Russia, Spain, and Italy. With every step of their progress, they would need more cotton. To pay for it, they would use their labor to produce thousands of items of taste and luxury, which we would then consume in immense quantities. This would lead to an improvement in taste, a refinement of feeling, an elevation of character, and an increase in individual and national strength that we cannot currently even imagine.

The duties on such luxury commodities would be moderate. As the imports of the bulkier items that currently pay duties decreased, the customs revenue would gradually decline. Eventually, the *necessity* for customhouses would pass away, because the *power* to maintain the government through land revenue <note>Carey refers to revenue derived from the increased value and productivity of the land as industry moves closer to the farm.</note> would have grown to take its place. In this way, we might realize the wonderful idea of a government for a massive nation maintained without the necessity of employing a single man to collect taxes.

It would appear, then, that there is a perfect harmony of interests between the treasury and the people; the farmer, planter, manufacturer, and merchant; the large and small trader and the shipowner; the slave and his master; the landowners and laborers of the Union and the world; and even the free trader and the advocate of protection. The way to the <unclear>establishment</unclear> of universal peace and universal free trade is to be found in adopting measures that destroy the *monopoly of machinery* <note>The concentration of manufacturing power in England, which Carey argued forced other nations to remain purely agricultural and dependent.</note> and place the loom and the anvil <note>Symbols of manufacturing and industry.</note> in the vicinity of the plow and the harrow <note>Symbols of agriculture.</note>.

## CHAPTER TWENTY-SIX.

### HOW PROTECTION AFFECTS THE GOVERNMENT.

A man whose labor is productive and whose habits are economical enjoys the world's confidence. However, a man whose labor is unproductive and whose habits are wasteful is looked upon with distrust. With the first man, each day is marked by an increase in strength; with the other, it is marked by an increase in weakness.

The same is true for communities. The peaceful and industrious grow rich and strong. The warlike and wasteful become poor and weak.

If protection were truly "a war upon the labor and capital of the world," it would lead to a decrease in wealth and strength, and the *monopoly system of England* would lead to an increase in both.

At no earlier period had the wealth and strength of this country grown as rapidly as it did from 1830 to 1835. The nation was at peace and everyone was employed. At no period has decline been so obvious, or the descent more complete, than in the period that followed. The nation was at war, and production declined until it almost ceased in many departments of industry. The name of America became almost a proverb for weakness and lack of faith. In the four succeeding years, the recovery was so great as to be almost marvelous, and it was then that the power of the nation first began to be admitted. That period has been followed by one of war and waste,

During the existence of the Tariff of 1842 <note>The Tariff of 1842 was a protectionist measure that raised duties on imports to help domestic industry and pull the US out of an economic depression.</note>, the government paid its own way and was therefore strong. It is now carried on by credit and is therefore becoming weak. To the extent of the foreign debt created, the country has eaten, drunk, and used goods for which it has yet to pay, and the government has taken its thirty percent cut; but a demand for payment would immediately reduce imports as much below exports as they now exceed them. Consequently, the government would find its revenue decreased by the full amount of the current excess.

The contrast presented by reviewing the history of Great Britain and this country is most instructive. Sixty years ago, Britain was rich and populous, while the United States was poor and its population was small and widely scattered. In wealth, the Union already exceeds her competitor, and in population it will do so at the close of the next decade.

The reason for this is found in the fact that the policy of one has tended toward the separation of the consumer from the producer, while the policy of the other has, to some extent, tended toward bringing them together. The English system is based upon “ships, colonies, and commerce,” and in carrying it out, her colonies have been exhausted one after another. Ireland now lies prostrate and helpless—a burden on her hands—an encumbrance rather than an advantage. Poverty and distress are coming gradually closer and closer to the British home, while she is burdened with an enormous debt that she cannot pay. The interest on this debt is still paid only through a series of repudiations <note>original: "repudiations"; here meaning the refusal to pay the full agreed interest or changing the terms of the debt to the disadvantage of the lender.</note> quite as discreditable as those she usually accuses Mississippi and Florida of committing.*

The American system <note>The "American System" was an economic plan that advocated for high tariffs to protect domestic industry, a national bank, and federal subsidies for "internal improvements" like roads and canals.</note> is based on agriculture and the work of production. Its object has been to create a prosperous agriculture by bringing the consumer to sit beside the producer, thereby establishing that great commerce which is conducted without the need for ships or wagons. With the help of that system, the original thirteen States have planted numerous colonies <note>By "colonies," Carey refers to the newly settled Western states and territories.</note>, all of which have grown and thrived, giving and receiving strength. In contrast, the colonies of England, long the subjects of immense taxation, are now everywhere a cause of weakness. All desire to abandon her, while all would desire to unite with us, if they were at liberty to exercise their—

The *free trade* of England consists in maintaining a *monopoly*, and therefore it is repelling <note>original: "repulsive"; in this context, it means "driving away" rather than "disgusting."</note>. The protective system of this country seeks to break down monopolies and establish *perfect free trade*, and therefore it is attractive.

One system looks for "cheap" labor and therefore drives away both individuals and communities. The other looks toward raising the value of labor and therefore attracts both individuals and communities.

Protection tends to maintain peace and increase wealth and power. The colonial system tends to produce causes for war and the reduction and eventual destruction of both wealth and power.

Therefore, there is perfect harmony between the views of those who wish to see their government strong enough to defend them in the enjoyment of all their rights in relation to other world communities, and those who wish to see the government administered peacefully and economically.

### CHAPTER TWENTY-SEVENTH.

->HOW PROTECTION AFFECTS THE NATION.<-

The man whose labor is productive exercises the power of self-government, which increases with every increase in the productiveness of his labor. With every decrease in his power of production, he loses more and more of the power of self-government and eventually becomes a slave.*

The same is true for nations. With every increase in the productiveness of their labor, they are better able to determine their own course of action for themselves, uninfluenced by the actions of surrounding nations. With every decrease in production, they are more and more compelled to shape their course of action by that of others, losing the power of self-government.

With a diminished *necessity* for forced combination with their neighbors, there is an increased *power* for voluntary combination (annexation <note>In Carey's view, "annexation" refers to the peaceful, voluntary joining of states or territories into a larger union, as opposed to forced colonial rule.</note>), which tends to further increase the rewards for labor. With an increased *necessity* for combination, there is a diminished *power* for voluntary combination, along with a diminished return for labor.

If protection were "a war upon labor and capital," it would have to diminish the power of voluntary union and increase the necessity of uniting our efforts with those of distant nations. If the English monopoly system tended to increase the value of labor and capital, it would have to increase the power of voluntary union and diminish the necessity for involuntary union.

Of all the nations in the world, there is currently not one that exercises the power of self-government to a lesser degree than Great Britain. For the last thirty years, her policy has been dictated by others. The repeal of the laws prohibiting the export of machinery was a matter of necessity, and so have been, in succession, all the laws regarding duties on imports. The duty on cotton was abolished because other nations had obtained machinery. Slave-grown cotton was admitted duty-free, while slave-grown sugar was subjected to heavy duties, because a supply of cotton was—

The poor and the weak are enslaved by those who are stronger and wealthier."—*Spectator, March, 1840.*

This was a matter of necessity. The restrictions on slave-grown sugar were abandoned because the abandonment was necessary. The navigation laws <note>These were acts of Parliament that restricted the use of foreign ships for trade between Britain and its colonies.</note> have, step by step, been abandoned as a matter of necessity. The corn laws <note>Tariffs and other trade restrictions on imported food and grain ("corn") enforced in Great Britain between 1815 and 1846.</note> were repealed because it was deemed necessary to persuade the farmers into becoming large purchasers of cloth and iron. 

With each step in this progress, poverty and crime increase. Consequently, the need for places to exile criminals increases, and with each step, there is increased difficulty in finding places willing to receive them. Having exhausted *Van Diemen’s Land* <note>original: "Van Diemen’s Land"; the historical name used by Europeans for the island of Tasmania.</note> and Norfolk Island, the Cape of Good Hope was recently selected for this purpose, but the colonists there have set an example of successful resistance that will be followed elsewhere. Canada is now to be set free, and Ireland is to be retained—neither of them by choice, but both as matters of necessity. The nation has lost the power of self-government. Its policy is being dictated to it by the other nations of the world. The tendency toward voluntary union has ceased to exist, and each day brings new evidence that the dissolution of the British Empire is at hand.

If such is the case with the owners of the loom and the anvil <note>The "loom and anvil" represent the manufacturing and industrial sectors.</note>, how is it with their subjects who hold the plough and follow the harrow <note>The "plough and harrow" represent the agricultural sector.</note>? Ireland has no power of self-government. She is a mere machine in the hands of those who perform the duties of government. Poor-laws are forced upon her to such an extent that they almost amount to a seizure <note>original: "confiscation"</note> of property. Then, other laws are passed to authorize commissioners to take possession of and sell a large portion of the property of the kingdom, which is already burdened by these debts.

The West Indies were gradually exhausted under this system. Their people were robbed of their property by laws passed by men who paid no portion of the enormous loss they inflicted upon their fellow subjects. The people of Canada have had new systems forced upon them with the goal of maintaining peace, but there is no peace. All desire to obtain the right of self-government; the first step in achieving this will be resistance to the monopoly system.

Of all the colonies of England, the only one that has prospered is this Union <note>Referring to the United States.</note>. It has done so because it has, to a certain degree, exercised the power of self-government. This is shown by a determination to bring the loom and the anvil to take their natural places by the side of the plough and the harrow. Because of this, every colony of Great Britain, including Ireland, desires to be annexed to us and separated from her. The tendency toward voluntary union exists here to a degree exceeding anything the world has yet seen. Nevertheless, we are still little more than a colony ourselves. Our people have no control over their own actions. They are almost as dependent upon the will of those who now try—though in vain—to guide the movements of England as the people of Canada are.

If the people of that country determine to make railroads, the price of iron rises. In response, we build furnaces and open coal mines, and we bring in people to make iron and mine coal. If they stop making roads, we shut up our furnaces—

<header>THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.</header>

...and mines, and then the iron and coal producers have to try to grow their own food. If they charge a high price for cloth, we build our own mills. If jobs become scarce for them and their people stop buying cloth, we close our mills, and our workers are forced into idleness. If the Bank of England makes credit easy <note>original: "make money cheap"</note>, we buy iron and cloth on credit; if it makes credit tight, we are suddenly asked for payment, and then we go bankrupt. If there are no opportunities to invest capital at home, the price of our houses and lands rises; if capital becomes scarce, the value of our houses and lands falls. If we build mills and furnaces, our people stay at home; if we close them, they scatter abroad. If money is easy to borrow in England, our government collects a large revenue from taxes on the goods bought on credit; if it is hard to borrow, the revenue drops, and our government has to beg for loans in Europe. 

The value and movement of everything in this country is determined by the actions of the Bank of England. Of all the world's large institutions, the Bank of England is managed with the least competence; it is the institution that possesses the smallest degree of self-control. Four times in thirty years it has been on the brink of bankruptcy. Yet, the United States <note>original: "this Union"</note> remains hitched to the wagon of the Bank and the British government—which is currently struggling in a sea of troubles—through the system now known as "free trade."

For giving up our power of self-government, we should receive something significant in return. Yet, for everything we send to Europe, all we receive back is fifty cents' worth of iron, half a pound of wool, half a pound of flax, an ounce or two of silk, a cup and saucer, and the processing <note>original: "weaving and twisting"</note> of a pound and a half of cotton for every person in the country. All of this could be produced or performed here by fewer people than the number of immigrants who have arrived in a single year when we provided a market for their labor. Half a million people could produce three times <note>original: "treble"</note> the flax, wool, silk, iron, and china—and process three times the quantity of fabric—that we currently receive from Europe in exchange for all the land and labor we use to produce the cotton, tobacco, rice, grain, butter, cheese, pork, and other goods we send there. Those half a million people would consume almost as much cotton as the entire population of Ireland, while also buying fifty million dollars' worth of food, timber, and other agricultural products from our farmers. We thus surrender our power of self-government without receiving anything equal in value; in fact, we give away our property for nothing, which is why the farmers and planters of the Union remain poor when they could be rich.

They would grow rich because the people moving here to work would require a vast amount of shipping. Cotton, rice, and tobacco would be shipped cheaply abroad, while high demand at home would keep prices stable. Both farmers and planters would then be able to afford more coffee, tea, silks, books, artwork, gold, silver, and other necessities or luxuries not made at home. The producers of those commodities would, in turn, buy more of our cloth and iron. We would then produce cloth and iron so cheaply that we could export them, leading to wealth, prosperity, happiness, and independence.

---

The American Revolution was driven by the realization that the colonies needed protection against the British monopoly system. Resistance to this oppression led, on various occasions, to resolutions to stop importing British goods <note>original: "non-importation resolutions"</note>, and the people were encouraged everywhere to try to make their own clothes. The need for protectionist policies was recognized by the early sessions of Congress, and its importance was urged upon them by every presidential administration.

Fifty years ago, political power changed hands; but with the inauguration of Mr. <note>Carey likely refers to Thomas Jefferson, elected in 1800.</note>

<meta>This page continues Henry Charles Carey’s argument that American economic prosperity depends on "protection"—using tariffs to encourage domestic manufacturing. He argues that the early American presidents, despite being from the South, understood that a strong "home market" for farmers required having factories nearby.</meta>

<page-num>226</page-num>
<header>THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.</header>

With Thomas Jefferson, there was no change of policy. He believed that "the manufacturer should take his place alongside the farmer <note>original: "agriculturist"</note>." From that time, for a period of thirty-six years, every president <note>original: "chief magistrate"</note> elected by the people came from the Southern planting states. All were elected by the same party that elected Mr. Jefferson, and every one of them advocated a system that brought the factory <note>original: "loom"</note> close to the farm <note>original: "plough"</note>, thereby creating a local market for the products of the land. The last of these presidents, Andrew Jackson, expressed his views on this subject forcefully in a letter that has been frequently published, an extract of which follows:

> "I must ask, what is the real situation of the farmer? Where does the American farmer find a market for his surplus crops? Except for cotton, he has neither a foreign nor a domestic market. When there is no market at home or abroad, does this not clearly prove that too much labor is spent on agriculture, and that the *opportunities for work <note>original: "channels for labour"</note> should be multiplied*? Common sense immediately points out the remedy: draw this excess labor away from farming and employ it in machinery and manufacturing. This creates a home market for your grain and flour <note>original: "breadstuffs"</note> and distributes labor in the most profitable way, resulting in benefits to the entire country. Take 600,000 men, women, and children away from agriculture in the United States, and you will instantly create a domestic market for more grain than all of Europe currently provides us. In short, sir, we have been subject to the policy of British merchants for too long. It is time we became a little more 'Americanized.' Instead of feeding the paupers and laborers of England [as we do by purchasing her manufactured goods], let us feed our own. Otherwise, by continuing our current [free trade] policy, we shall soon all be reduced to poverty ourselves." — *President Jackson.*

At the close of that period, there was a change of policy. Martin Van Buren, though elected by the same party as his predecessor, adopted a policy that tends to separate the consumer from the producer. This led to the exhaustion of the land, the impoverishment of its owners, and the protection of the monopoly system by which England had gained control over global trade. The effects were disastrous, as can be seen by anyone studying the charts in the third chapter; the result was a political revolution. For the first time in forty years, a president <note>William Henry Harrison, elected in 1840</note> was elected by the people who did not belong to the party generally known as the Democrats. The Democratic party had changed its principles, and the people would not follow. 

The result of this shift was a return to the policy of protection nearly two years later <note>The Tariff of 1842</note>, which restored prosperity. With that prosperity, the party that had long controlled the country's direction was restored to power. However, unwilling to admit that the political shift of 1840 resulted from a policy error, they blamed various minor causes and proceeded to enact the Tariff of 1846. This led to another political revolution, which again restored the party of protection to power. 

Like the previous shift, this latest revolution is now blamed on minor causes. However, those who study the charts I mentioned earlier can hardly fail to see the truth: the party calling itself "Democratic" had adopted a policy that decreased the value of labor, devalued the laborer, weakened democracy at home, and supported the aristocracy abroad. I believe it is clear that no party opposed to protection can hold power in this country again. If this is the case, the interests of both parties—even if motivated by purely selfish reasons—should lead them to advocate for the same policy. The party in power should want it settled to avoid being ousted, and the party out of power should want it settled to end the constant political turmoil.

<summary>Carey argues that early U.S. presidents, including Jackson and Jefferson, supported protectionism to create a "home market" for farmers. He claims that modern "Democratic" shifts toward free trade caused economic distress and led to the political upheavals of 1840 and 1848.</summary>

## CONCLUSION.

Much is said of "the mission" of the people of these United States, but most of it is said by people who seem to limit themselves to considering the *powers* of the nation while rarely thinking of its *duties*. By such men, the grandeur of our national position is thought to be greatly increased by having spent sixty or eighty million dollars on a war with a weak neighbor <note>This refers to the Mexican-American War (1846–1848).</note>. They celebrate having acquired the power to purchase, at a high price, a vast body of wilderness that would have naturally been brought into the Union in due time without costing a single dollar or a single life. These same men see the fitting out of expeditions to spark civil war among our neighbors in Cuba <note>Carey is referring to "filibustering" expeditions, which were private military attempts to seize land in Central America or the Caribbean.</note> as further evidence of our greatness. Others would have us involve ourselves with all the revolutionaries of Europe, while a fourth and final group sighs at the thought that our fleets and armies are too small for the magnificence of our position.

By some, it is supposed that our "mission" is to monopolize the commerce of the world. They anxiously look forward to the time when we shall have "diplomatic relations" with "vast regions of the East"—Persia, Korea, Vietnam <note>original: "Cochin-China"</note>, Burma, and Japan—with whom "nothing but the steamship can successfully introduce our commerce." By "persevering and successful efforts," they believe we may secure the "commerce of Japan." Once that is done:

> "New York," it is thought, "would become the depot, storehouse, and distribution center <note>original: "entrepot"</note> of the world, the center of business and exchanges, the clearinghouse of international trade and business. It would be the place where assorted cargoes of our own products and manufactures, as well as those of all foreign countries, would be sold and reshipped. It would be the point to which gold and silver coin <note>original: "specie and bullion"</note> would flow, as the great creditor city of the world for the adjustment of balances. As the agent <note>original: "factor"</note> of all nations, New York would be the point from which this money would flow into the interior of our country through all the great channels of international trade and intercourse. With these great events accomplished, and with abundant facilities for the warehousing of foreign and domestic goods at New York, it must eventually surpass any European commercial center <note>original: "emporium"</note> in wealth, commerce, and population. As a necessary consequence, all our other cities and every portion of the Union and all our great interests would derive corresponding advantages."—*Treasury Report, December, 1848.*

The cost of a diplomatic mission to Japan would build half a dozen ironworks <note>original: "furnaces"</note> that would add more to the wealth of the nation in five years than the commerce of that country would do in half a century. The amount we have spent on the mission to Austria in search of a market for tobacco would bring enough German immigrants here to consume almost as much of our tobacco as is now consumed in the entire Austrian Empire. Furthermore, those tobacco consumers would do more for the growth of New York than either Japan or Austria.

The English doctrine of "ships, colonies, and commerce" is thus being reproduced on this side of the Atlantic. Its adoption by our nation would be followed by effects similar to those already seen in England. There, for a time, it gave the government the power to tax the world to maintain fleets and armies, just as had been done by Athens and Rome in the past. Today, it is producing the same results that have always followed that system: poverty, depopulation, exhaustion, and weakness.

Even a little study of our history is enough to satisfy any inquirer that the power of the Union and its magnificent position among the nations of the earth are due to the fact that we have largely avoided measures that require maintaining fleets and armies. The consequence has been that taxes have been light, capital has accumulated rapidly, and labor—

<meta>This page continues Henry Charles Carey’s concluding arguments in "The Harmony of Interests." Having critiqued expansionist foreign policy on the previous page, Carey now contrasts two competing economic ideologies: the "English system" of global trade and his proposed "American system" of domestic protectionism.</meta>

<page-num>228</page-num>

<header>THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.</header>

When production has been high, the laborer has received wages that have enabled him to feed, clothe, and educate his children, and the nation has thus performed its true "mission" in elevating the condition of man. If we wish to find exceptions to this, we must look to those periods in which the policies of Washington, Jefferson, Madison, Monroe, and Jackson were abandoned. Whenever the government adopted measures that maintained the British monopoly on manufacturing, we find heavier taxes, capital accumulating more slowly, labor becoming less productive, and wages so depressed that the laborer finds it difficult to feed or clothe his children, and even more difficult to educate them.

Two systems are currently before the world. One looks to increase the number of people and the amount of capital engaged in trade and transportation; this diminishes the number of people producing the actual goods to be traded, which *necessarily* reduces the return for everyone's labor. The other system looks to increase the number of people engaged in production and to diminish those engaged in trade and transportation. This leads to increased returns for all, giving the laborer good wages and the owner of capital good profits. 

One system looks to increase the quantity of raw materials we export while discouraging the arrival of new immigrants. This impoverishes both the farmer and the planter by forcing them to pay the high cost of freight. The other system looks to increase the immigration of people and diminish the export of raw materials, thereby enriching both the planter and the farmer by relieving them of those shipping costs. 

One system looks to trade the *products* of millions of acres of land and the labor of millions of men for the *services* of a few hundred thousand men in distant lands. The other looks to bring those distant men here, so they can consume the products of the land while living on that land, exchanging one day's labor for another day's labor. 

One system looks to compel the farmers and planters of the United States <note>original: "the Union"</note> to continue paying for the support of the fleets, armies, paupers, nobles, and monarchs of Europe. The other system looks to enable us to apply those same resources to the moral and intellectual improvement of the "sovereigns of America" <note>By "sovereigns," Carey refers to the American citizens themselves, who hold the ultimate power in a republic.</note>. 

One system looks to continue that *false* <note>original: "bastard"</note> freedom of trade which denies the principle of protection yet doles it out as "revenue duties" <note>Taxes on imports intended only to raise money for the government rather than to protect domestic industry.</note>. The other looks to extend the area of *legitimate* free trade by establishing perfect protection, followed by the addition of new individuals and communities to our nation, and ultimately the total abolition of custom-houses. 

One system looks to export men to occupy desert lands, the control of which is gained through diplomacy or war. The other looks to increase the value of our vast existing vacant lands by importing millions of men to live upon them. 

One system looks toward the *centralization* of wealth and power in a great commercial city that would rival the great cities of modern times—cities that have been, and are being, supported by taxes that have exhausted every nation subjected to them. The other looks toward *concentration*, by which a market is created directly on the land for the products of that land, enriching the farmer and the planter. 

One system looks to increase the necessity for commerce; the other to increase the power to maintain it. One looks to underworking the laborer in India <note>original: "the Hindoo"</note> and sinking the rest of the world to his level of poverty; the other looks to raising the standard of man throughout the world to our level. One looks to poverty, ignorance, depopulation, and barbarism; the other to increasing wealth, comfort, intelligence, cooperation, and civilization. One looks toward universal war; the other toward universal peace. One is the English system; the other is the system we—

Carey argues that by participating in the British-led global trade system, Americans are indirectly funding such suppressions.</note>. The farmers and planters of the United States are the chief contributors to this loan.

<meta>This page concludes Henry Charles Carey’s "The Harmony of Interests." Carey finalizes his argument by contrasting the "American system" of domestic development with the "English system" of global trade, framing the American approach as a moral and divine mission to elevate humanity through peace and economic cooperation.</meta>

<page-num>229</page-num>

<header>THE HARMONY OF INTERESTS.</header>

...we may be proud to call the American system, for it is the only one ever designed with a tendency to **elevate** while **equalizing** the condition of people throughout the world.

This is the true **mission** of the people of these United States. To them has been granted a privilege never before granted to mankind: the exercise of the right of perfect self-government. But, as rights and duties are inseparable, with the grant of the former came the obligation to perform the latter. Fortunately, their performance is pleasant and profitable, and involves no sacrifice. To raise the value of labor throughout the world, we need only to raise the value of our own. To raise the value of land throughout the world, it is only necessary that we adopt measures that shall raise the value of our own. To spread intelligence and to promote the cause of morality throughout the world, we are required only to pursue the course that shall spread education throughout our own land; this shall enable every man more readily to acquire property, and with it, a respect for the rights of property. To improve the political condition of people throughout the world, it is necessary that we ourselves should remain at peace, avoid taxation for the maintenance of fleets and armies, and become rich and prosperous. To raise the condition of women throughout the world, it is required of us only that we pursue that course which enables men to remain at home and marry, so that they may surround themselves with happy children and grandchildren. To substitute true Christianity for the detestable system known as the Malthusian <note>original: "Malthusian" — referring to the theory of Thomas Malthus, who argued that population growth would inevitably outpace food production, leading to poverty and starvation. Carey argues the opposite.</note>, it is necessary that we prove to the world that it is population that makes the food come from the rich soils, and that food tends to increase more rapidly than population, thus justifying the policy of God toward man. 

By doing these things, the addition to our population through immigration will quickly rise to millions. With each and every year, the desire for that perfect freedom of trade which results from being incorporated within the Union will be seen to spread and increase in its intensity. This will lead gradually to the establishment of an empire the most extensive and magnificent the world has yet seen—one based upon the principles of maintaining peace itself, and strong enough to insist upon the maintenance of peace by others. Yet, this empire will be carried on without the aid of fleets, or armies, or taxes, as the sales of public lands alone will be enough to pay the expenses of government.

To establish such an empire—to prove that among the people of the world, whether they are farmers, manufacturers, or merchants, there is a perfect harmony of interests, and that the happiness of individuals, as well as the grandeur of nations, is to be promoted by perfect obedience to that greatest of all commands, "Do unto others as you would have others do unto you"—is the object and will be the result of that mission. Whether that result shall be quickly attained, or whether it shall be postponed to a distant period, will depend greatly upon the men who are charged with the duties of government. If their movements are governed by that enlightened self-interest which induces a person to seek his own happiness by promoting the happiness of his fellow man, it will come soon. If, on the contrary, they are governed by that ignorant selfishness which leads to the belief that individual, party, or national interests are to be promoted by measures tending to the deterioration of the condition of others, it will be late.

->THE END.<-
